references.title: Customer churn prediction in telecom using machine learning in big data platform
references.harvard_reference: Ahmad, A.K., Jafar, A. and Aljoumaa, K. (2019) 'Customer churn prediction in telecom using machine learning in big data platform', Journal of Big Data, 6(1), article number 28. doi:10.1186/s40537-019-0191-6.
references.abstract_summary: The authors build a churn-prediction model for the Syrian mobile operator SyriaTel on a Hadoop/Spark big-data platform. Nine months of raw data (about 10 million customers, more than 70 TB, roughly 10,000 raw columns; churners about 5% of records) from five sources - customer/CRM data (subscription type, birthday, gender, location), towers and complaints databases, network logs, call detail records (charging information for calls, SMS, MMS and internet) and IMEI device data - are aggregated per customer into 'statistical' features (usage, complaints, device, competitor-contact percentages, coverage, etc.). A customer social graph is then built from four months of CDRs and Social Network Analysis (SNA) features (PageRank, Sender Rank, degree centrality, neighbour connectivity) are added. Four tree-based learners are compared using AUC: Decision Tree, Random Forest, GBM and XGBoost. With statistical features only the best AUC is 84%; adding SNA features raises XGBoost to 93.3% (GBM 90.89%, RF 87.76%, DT 83%). On a later, untouched 'NotOffered' population of 7.5 million prepaid customers XGBoost scores 89% AUC. The paper's stated contributions are the feature-engineering/selection pipeline on a big-data platform and the use of SNA features.

claims_supported.claim: Using rich behavioural data (call detail records, usage, complaints, network data) from SyriaTel, XGBoost reached an AUC of about 93 %, showing that richer behavioural features can lift performance well above what demographic and billing attributes alone achieve.
claims_supported.where: PARTLY supported, but the causal contrast in the second half is not made by the paper, so the claim as worded is not supported. (a) Supported: 'Data set' section lists customer/CRM data, towers and complaints database, network logs, CDRs and IMEI data; 'Data volume' subsection says data related to calls, SMS, MMS and internet 'with all related information like complaints, network data, IMEI, charging' were used; Abstract, Table 2 and Conclusion report XGBoost AUC 93.3% (93.301%). (b) NOT supported: the paper never trains or reports a model built only on demographic and/or billing attributes, so it cannot show that behavioural features beat such a baseline. Its only ablation (Table 2, 'Comparing AUC results before and after adding SNA to statistical features') is statistical features alone (XGBoost 84%, GBM 82%, RF 79.1%, DT 76%) versus statistical + SNA features (93.3%, 90.89%, 87.76%, 83%); the 84->93.3 gain is attributed specifically to Social Network Analysis features, not to behavioural versus demographic/billing data. Moreover the feature set already includes demographic fields (birthday, gender, location) and charging/billing data, so the comparison the claim implies is not one the study makes. Suggested rewording the source does support: 'Using nine months of CDR, usage, complaint, network-log and device data from SyriaTel, Ahmad et al. (2019) obtained an AUC of 93.3% with XGBoost; adding social-network-analysis features derived from the call graph raised AUC from 84% to 93.3%, illustrating how richer engineered features can substantially improve churn prediction.' Any contrast with demographic/billing-only datasets (e.g. the Kaggle Telco data) must be presented as the report author's own inference, not as a finding of this paper.

claims_supported.claim: [Verifier-proposed replacement] Using nine months of CDR, usage, complaint, network-log and device data from SyriaTel, XGBoost reached an AUC of 93.3%, and adding social-network-analysis features lifted AUC from 84% to 93.3%, showing that richer engineered features can substantially improve churn prediction.
claims_supported.where: Abstract ('the AUC value obtained is 93.3%'; 'The use of SNA enhanced the performance of the model from 84 to 93.3% against AUC standard'); 'Data set' section (five data sources incl. CDRs, complaints, network logs, IMEI); 'Data volume' subsection (nine months of transactions); Table 2 (statistical features 84% vs statistical + SNA 93.3% for XGBoost); Conclusion (XGBoost best, AUC 93.301%).

references.verification_notes: DOI 10.1186/s40537-019-0191-6 confirmed via CrossRef (journal-article, Journal of Big Data, vol 6, issue 1, article 28, 2019, Springer Science and Business Media LLC). Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 84186099, DBLP journals/jbd/AhmadJA19) and OpenAlex (published 2019-03-20, gold open access, 424 citations at time of check) agree on authors, title, venue and year. Verbatim abstract obtained from the arXiv export API for the preprint arXiv:1904.00690 (submitted 1 April 2019, journal-ref 'Journal of Big Data 2019 6:28'); NOTE the preprint title is longer ('...using machine learning and social network analysis in big data platform') - the published, CrossRef-registered title (used in the reference above) omits 'and social network analysis'. Springer landing page and PDF could not be fetched directly (cookie-authorisation redirect), so full-text checks were made on the arXiv PDF, which is the publisher's typeset version (24 pages, running header 'Ahmad et al. J Big Data (2019) 6:28'). Key full-text facts: ~10 million customers over nine months, >70 TB raw data, ~10,000 raw columns, churn class ~5%; prepaid customers; SNA graph built from last four months of CDRs; XGBoost 93.3% AUC (Table 2/3), GBM 90.89%, RF 87.76%, DT 83%; statistical-features-only best 84%; holdout on new 'NotOffered' data XGBoost 89% (Table 4). The lead's citation details ('Journal of Big Data 6, 28') were accurate. No page range exists; the article number is 28.
references.caveats: 1) The study does not contain a demographic/billing-only baseline; do not cite it as evidence that behavioural features beat demographic/billing attributes - cite it for the 93.3% AUC and for the 84->93.3% gain from SNA features. 2) The dataset is proprietary SyriaTel prepaid data, so results are not directly comparable to the public Kaggle/IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (different customers, features, class balance ~5% vs ~27%, and no billing-contract variables of the same kind). 3) AUC values come from a single train/test split with no confidence intervals; performance on a later, untouched period fell to 89%. 4) Cite the published title, not the longer arXiv preprint title.

references.title: Dynamic behavior based churn prediction in mobile telecom
references.harvard_reference: Alboukaey, N., Joukhadar, A. and Ghneim, N. (2020) 'Dynamic behavior based churn prediction in mobile telecom', Expert Systems with Applications, 162, 113779. doi:10.1016/j.eswa.2020.113779.
references.abstract_summary: Argues that monthly, static behavioural features miss day-to-day changes before churn and flag early-month leavers too late. It models each customer's daily behaviour as a multivariate time series and compares four daily models: RFM-based and statistics-based models on extracted features, and LSTM and CNN models that learn features. On 150 days of data from an MTN mobile operator, daily models beat monthly ones, predicting churners earlier and more accurately. LSTM beats CNN, but LSTM and CNN only equal the RFM-based model; all three beat the statistics-based model.

claims_supported.claim: Sequence (LSTM, CNN) churn models need daily usage series and, even then, only matched an RFM-feature model.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (publisher abstract via the Semantic Scholar API): daily behaviour modelled as multivariate time series; daily models beat monthly ones; LSTM and CNN performed equal to the RFM-based model. Full text not read.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.eswa.2020.113779): Expert Systems with Applications vol. 162, article 113779, issued December 2020, authors Nadia Alboukaey, Ammar Joukhadar, Nada Ghneim. Abstract read via the Semantic Scholar API (publisher abstract); OpenAlex confirms title, venue and DOI. Full text not accessed (paywalled). Supports: sequence/deep churn models need daily usage series and, even then, matched but did not beat an RFM-feature model. Checked again by an independent critic on 31 October 2026: The critique is right: Ahmad et al. tested only tree learners on aggregated features. The new source exists and supports the cell. Crossref (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.eswa.2020.113779) gives Expert Systems with Applications 162, article 113779, December 2020, by Nadia Alboukaey, Ammar Joukhadar and Nada Ghneim. The abstract, read through the Semantic Scholar API (https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1016/j.eswa.2020.113779), models daily behaviour as multivariate time series. Daily models beat monthly ones. The LSTM and CNN models performed equal to the RFM-based model, and all three beat the statistics-based model. The proposed Harvard entry and JSON fields match Crossref; the full text was not read. Word delta +6 raw, 0 counted (table row). references.title: Retention Futility: Targeting High-Risk Customers Might Be Ineffective
references.harvard_reference: Ascarza, E. (2018) 'Retention futility: targeting high-risk customers might be ineffective', Journal of Marketing Research, 55(1), pp. 80-98. doi:10.1509/jmr.16.0163.
references.abstract_summary: Ascarza challenges the standard practice of aiming proactive retention efforts at the customers a churn model flags as highest risk. Using two randomised field experiments (a Middle East wireless provider, Study 1, and a North American special-interest membership organisation, Study 2) combined with machine-learning (uplift random forest) estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects, she shows that the customers at highest predicted risk of churning are not necessarily the most responsive to a retention intervention: the overlap between the top-risk and top-sensitivity groups is roughly 50%, i.e. no different from independence, and in some risk deciles the intervention actually increased churn. Counterfactual evaluation on the experimental data shows that targeting on estimated sensitivity to the intervention ('lift') rather than on risk would cut churn by an additional 4.1 and 8.7 percentage points respectively; in Study 2, targeting the 40% highest-risk customers would have raised churn by 4.4 points while targeting the 40% highest-lift customers would have lowered it by 4.3 points. She recommends firms run pilot experiments, model heterogeneity in response, and target on sensitivity regardless of churn risk.

claims_supported.claim: Customers with the highest predicted churn risk are not necessarily those most responsive to retention interventions, so predicting who will churn is not the same as predicting who can be saved.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 80): 'customers identified as having the highest risk of churning are not necessarily the best targets for proactive churn programs'. Introduction (p. 81): 'customers' risk of churning does not necessarily relate to their sensitivity to the retention incentive'; the overlap between highest-sensitivity and highest-risk groups is 'approximately 50%; thus, the relationship between these two variables does not differ from independence' (p. 82). Conclusion (p. 96): 'customers' risk of churning is not necessarily related to their sensitivity to the retention campaign'. The RISK vs LIFT distinction throughout the paper is exactly the distinction between predicting who will churn and predicting who can be saved.

claims_supported.claim: Field experiments showed that targeting by predicted churn risk can be less effective than targeting by predicted sensitivity to the intervention (uplift).
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 80): sensitivity-based targeting 'is empirically demonstrated to be significantly more effective than the standard practice of targeting customers with the highest risk of churning'. Results (pp. 89-91, Figures 3-4): 'the LIFT-based approach is substantially more effective than the "at risk" approach'; e.g. Study 1, targeting top 40% by RISK reduces churn 1.9 points vs 6.0 points by LIFT; Study 2, top-40% RISK targeting would have increased churn by 4.4 points vs a 4.3-point reduction by LIFT. Summary of Results (p. 94) and Conclusion (p. 96): additional 4.1 and 8.7 percentage-point reductions relative to risk-based targeting. The paper explicitly builds on 'the uplift modeling literature' (p. 81) and uses uplift random forests (footnote 7, p. 84). Caveat on wording: the two field experiments randomised the retention intervention; the head-to-head comparison of the two targeting rules was a counterfactual/simulation evaluation using that experimental data (Methodology, p. 84: 'I leverage the experimental setup of the field studies to simulate what the impact of these retention campaigns would be had the focal firms implemented each of the two approaches'), not a live A/B test of one targeting policy against the other. Phrase as 'using data from two randomised field experiments, Ascarza (2018) showed...' to be precise.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (query.bibliographic) returned the journal article: DOI 10.1509/jmr.16.0163, Journal of Marketing Research, vol. 55, issue 1, pp. 80-98, published-print February 2018, publisher SAGE, single author Eva Ascarza; it also listed the SSRN working-paper version (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.2759170, 2016). Semantic Scholar API returned matching title/author/year but the abstract was elided by the publisher; a second Semantic Scholar call confirmed publicationDate 2018-02-01, journal volume 55 pp. 80-98, and open-access PDF via SSRN. OpenAlex returned the full abstract (inverted index) and biblio 55(1) 80-98 but lists publication_year 2017 with publication_date 2017-08-24 (online-first date); the printed issue is Vol. LV, February 2018, so 2018 is used for the reference. The doi.org redirect to journals.sagepub.com and the SSRN page both returned HTTP 403, so the publisher landing page could not be read directly. The full text was verified from the author-hosted PDF (https://www.evaascarza.com/papers/ascarza_18.pdf), whose first page carries the abstract verbatim (matching OpenAlex), the running head 'Vol. LV (February 2018), 80-98' and 'DOI: 10.1509/jmr.16.0163'. The AMA site confirms the article won the 2018 Paul E. Green Award and was in the February 2018 JMR issue; the author's site lists it as JMR 55(1), 80-98. All bibliographic fields are therefore verified from at least two independent sources.
references.caveats: The empirical settings are a Middle East wireless provider and a North American membership organisation, not the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset. The Kaggle dataset contains no randomised retention intervention or treatment indicator, so uplift/sensitivity modelling as in Ascarza (2018) cannot be replicated on it; the paper should be cited to frame the limits of pure churn prediction (risk is not the same as saveability) and to motivate future work with experimental data, not as a method implemented in the report. The comparison of targeting policies is a counterfactual evaluation using randomised experimental data rather than a direct field test of one targeting rule against another.

references.title: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities
references.venue: MIT Press (Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series)
references.harvard_reference: Barocas, S., Hardt, M. and Narayanan, A. (2023) Fairness and machine learning: limitations and opportunities. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. Available at: https://fairmlbook.org/ (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: An interdisciplinary textbook on fairness in algorithmic decision-making, published by MIT Press in 2023 and also released open access at fairmlbook.org. The nine chapters are: Introduction; When is automated decision making legitimate?; Classification; Relative notions of fairness; Causality; Understanding United States anti-discrimination law; Testing discrimination in practice; A broader view of discrimination; and Datasets. The Classification chapter formalises three statistical non-discrimination criteria for a score R, sensitive attribute A and target Y: independence (A independent of R; for binary classifiers also called demographic parity, statistical parity, group fairness, disparate impact), separation (R independent of A given Y; error-rate parity / equalized odds; equality of opportunity when restricted to false negatives) and sufficiency (Y independent of A given R; shown to be essentially equivalent to calibration by group). It then proves pairwise incompatibility propositions: independence and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent; independence and separation cannot both hold when Y is binary and both A and R are dependent on Y; separation and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent and the classifier has a nonzero false positive rate (or all events have positive probability). A section headed 'No fairness through unawareness' explains that dropping the sensitive attribute fails because sensitive attributes are generally redundant given the other features, so a learner finds a redundant encoding (proxy) of the attribute, illustrated with retinal photographs predicting gender, genomic ancestry markers, and web-visit features predicting gender.

claims_supported.claim: Fairness criteria such as independence (demographic parity), separation (equalised odds) and sufficiency (calibration) are formally defined and generally mutually exclusive; 'fairness through unawareness' fails because of redundant encodings (proxies).
claims_supported.where: Chapter 3 'Classification' (https://fairmlbook.org/classification.html). Definitions: sections 'Independence' (A independent of R; 'demographic parity' named as the binary-classifier case), 'Separation' (R independent of A given Y; 'equalized odds' named), 'Sufficiency' (Y independent of A given R; 'calibration by group implies sufficiency' and the two are described as essentially equivalent). Incompatibility: section 'Relationships between criteria', which states propositions that independence and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent; independence and separation cannot both hold when Y is binary and A and R are each dependent on Y; and separation and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent and the classifier has a nonzero false positive rate. Unawareness: section 'No fairness through unawareness', which states that sensitive attributes are generally redundant given the other features, so a classifier trained without the attribute finds a redundant encoding in terms of the other features (examples: retinal photographs, genomic ancestry markers, website-visit features). Caveat for the report: the book's result is pairwise incompatibility under non-degenerate conditions (A and Y dependent, non-trivial classifier), not a single three-way impossibility theorem; the wording 'generally mutually exclusive' is accurate provided the report signals those conditions.

references.verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-27. Existence and core metadata confirmed from three independent sources: (1) the authors' own site fairmlbook.org, whose recommended BibTeX gives title 'Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities', authors Solon Barocas, Moritz Hardt and Arvind Narayanan, publisher MIT Press, year 2023; (2) the Open Library edition record OL48231196M (search.json and isbn endpoints): same title/subtitle/authors, publisher MIT Press, publish_date 2023, ISBN-13 9780262048613, ISBN-10 0262048612, pagination 320; (3) a published review of the book in The Reasoner 20(1), 2026, doi:10.54103/1757-0522/29851, citing it as MIT Press, 2023. A web search additionally surfaced the Amazon listing (ISBN 9780262048613, 'Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series') and pages stating the hardcover appeared in December 2023; series and month are therefore from retail/secondary listings rather than the publisher's page. DOI: a Crossref search filtered on isbn:9780262048613 returned zero results, and the Crossref bibliographic search returned only a review of the book, so no DOI is registered for the book itself; the doi field is left empty deliberately. The MIT Press product page (mitpress.mit.edu/9780262048613) and direct.mit.edu returned HTTP 403, WorldCat and Library of Congress were bot-blocked, and Google Books and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429, so the publisher's own page could not be read; place of publication 'Cambridge, MA' in the Harvard reference is the MIT Press's standard imprint location and was not read from a fetched catalogue record. Volume/issue/page range are not applicable to a monograph and are left empty (Open Library gives a total extent of 320 pages). The claim was checked against the full text of the Classification chapter on fairmlbook.org, not just an abstract.
references.caveats: The book is a monograph with no registered DOI; cite the ISBN or the open-access URL instead. The open-access web edition (fairmlbook.org) and the MIT Press print edition have the same chapter structure, but page numbers for direct quotations should be taken from the print/PDF edition if the report needs them. Series name and December 2023 hardcover date come from retail listings, not the publisher page, so treat them as unconfirmed. When citing the mutual-exclusivity result, note it is pairwise and conditional (A and Y dependent; non-trivial classifier), not an unconditional three-way impossibility.

references.title: Bagging predictors
references.harvard_reference: Breiman, L. (1996) 'Bagging predictors', Machine Learning, 24(2), pp. 123–140. doi:10.1007/BF00058655.
references.abstract_summary: Introduces bagging: a predictor is refitted on bootstrap replicates of the learning set and the versions are combined by averaging (regression) or voting (classification). Experiments with classification and regression trees and with subset selection in linear regression show large accuracy gains, and the abstract names the instability of the base method as the key condition for bagging to help. The body (read in the 1994 Technical Report 421 version) classes classification and regression trees, neural nets and subset selection as unstable and nearest-neighbour methods as stable, and advises against bagging stable classifiers.

claims_supported.claim: Classification and regression trees are unstable predictors: small changes in the learning set change them a lot.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Springer): instability of the prediction method is the vital element for bagging; Section 1 of the author's Technical Report 421 version names classification and regression trees as unstable.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00058655): journal-article, Machine Learning 24(2), pp. 123-140, issued August 1996, sole author Leo Breiman. Springer landing page (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00058655) confirms title, author, volume, pages, date and the abstract's instability sentence. Body text checked in the author-hosted TR 421 (stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/bagging.pdf); the published PDF sits behind a cookie wall and was not read. Supports: decision trees are unstable predictors. Checked again by an independent critic on 31 October 2026: Breiman (1996) is verified. Crossref gives Machine Learning 24(2), pp. 123-140, August 1996, sole author. The Springer abstract (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00058655) says the vital element is the prediction method's instability. Section 1 of TR 421 (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/bagging.pdf) names classification and regression trees, neural nets and subset selection as unstable and k-NN as stable. The Breiman (2001) preprint (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf) uses 'stable' only for OOB estimates and error magnitudes, so it does not support the cell. The Harvard entry is correct. Place it before Breiman (2001); no a/b suffix is needed. Word delta 0.

references.title: Random Forests
references.harvard_reference: Breiman, L. (2001) 'Random forests', Machine Learning, 45(1), pp. 5-32. doi:10.1023/A:1010933404324.
references.abstract_summary: Breiman defines a random forest as an ensemble of tree classifiers in which each tree is grown from an independently sampled random vector with the same distribution (for example a bootstrap sample of the training set plus a random choice of candidate features at each node), and the trees vote for the most popular class. Using the Strong Law of Large Numbers he proves that the forest's generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as trees are added, so adding trees does not cause over-fitting, and he bounds that error in terms of two quantities: the strength of the individual trees and the mean correlation between them (PE* <= rho_bar (1 - s^2)/s^2). The recommended procedures, Forest-RI (choose F input variables at random at each node and split on the best of them) and Forest-RC (random linear combinations of inputs), grow unpruned CART trees on bootstrap samples. On 13 UCI, three larger and four synthetic data sets these forests match or beat Adaboost, are more robust to label noise (a 5% noise experiment), are much faster, and are described as simple and easily parallelised. Out-of-bag estimates give internal estimates of error, strength, correlation and variable importance. Results are reported as insensitive to F, with one or two features per node usually near optimal. The strength/correlation framework and empirical study are extended to regression, where the forest error is the average tree error scaled by the weighted correlation between tree residuals.

claims_supported.claim: Random forests combine bagging with random feature selection at each split, reducing variance and giving robust accuracy with few tuning parameters.
claims_supported.where: The mechanism, robustness and low-tuning parts are made explicitly; 'reducing variance' is a paraphrase of Breiman's strength/correlation argument rather than his wording. (a) Bagging plus per-node random feature selection: Section 3.1, 'In my experiments with random forests, bagging is used in tandem with random feature selection. Each new training set is drawn, with replacement, from the original training set. Then a tree is grown on the new training set using random feature selection. The trees grown are not pruned.' Section 4, 'The simplest random forest with random features is formed by selecting at random, at each node, a small group of input variables to split on ... Denote this procedure by Forest-RI.' Section 12 (regression), 'we use random feature selection on top of bagging'. (b) Variance: the paper never uses bias-variance vocabulary for its own method; its theory bounds the generalisation error by var(mr)/s^2 (eq. 4), expresses that variance through the mean correlation between trees (Theorem 2.3, PE* <= rho_bar (1 - s^2)/s^2), and in regression shows PE*(forest) <= rho_bar PE*(tree) (Theorem 11.2, 'The random forest decreases the average error of the trees employed by the factor rho_bar. The randomization employed needs to aim at low correlation'). Section 13 adds that forests' accuracy 'indicates that they act to reduce bias. The mechanism for this is not obvious.' So the source supports 'lower correlation between trees lowers the error bound'; if the report wants the explicit 'de-correlating trees reduces the variance of bagging' framing it should also cite Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (2009, ch. 15). (c) Robust accuracy: abstract, 'error rates that compare favorably to Adaboost ... but are more robust with respect to noise'; Section 3 list, 'i) Its accuracy is as good as Adaboost and sometimes better. ii) It's relatively robust to outliers and noise.'; Section 8 and Table 4, 5% label-noise experiment where Adaboost's error rises far more than Forest-RI/RC. (d) Few tuning parameters: not stated in those words, but Section 1.2 says results 'turn out to be insensitive to the number of features selected to split each node. Usually, selecting one or two features gives near optimum results'; Section 4, 'the procedure is not overly sensitive to the value of F'; trees are grown to maximum size without pruning; Theorem 1.2 shows forests 'do not overfit as more trees are added'; Section 3 list, 'v) It's simple and easily parallelized.' Safer wording: 'relatively insensitive to their main tuning parameter, the number of features tried at each split'.

claims_supported.claim: Component: random forests combine bagging (bootstrap resampling of the training set) with a random selection of candidate features at each node/split.
claims_supported.where: Section 3.1 ('bagging is used in tandem with random feature selection. Each new training set is drawn, with replacement ... Then a tree is grown on the new training set using random feature selection'); Section 4, definition of Forest-RI ('selecting at random, at each node, a small group of input variables to split on'); Section 12 ('random feature selection on top of bagging'). Section 1.1 credits bagging (Breiman 1996), Ho's random subspace method and Amit and Geman's per-node random feature search as precursors.

claims_supported.claim: Component: the combination reduces variance.
claims_supported.where: Supported only in Breiman's own strength/correlation terms, not in bias-variance language. Eq. (4) PE* <= var(mr)/s^2; eqs (5)-(7) and Theorem 2.3 express var(mr) via the mean correlation rho_bar, giving PE* <= rho_bar (1 - s^2)/s^2; Section 6 concludes 'better (lower generalization error) random forests have lower correlation between classifiers and higher strength. The randomness used in tree construction has to aim for low correlation rho_bar while maintaining reasonable strength'; Theorem 11.2 (regression) PE*(forest) <= rho_bar PE*(tree). Caveat: Section 13 states that forests' accuracy 'indicates that they act to reduce bias' and that the mechanism 'is not obvious', so Breiman does not attribute the gain solely to variance reduction. Cite Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (2009) for the explicit variance-reduction-by-decorrelation statement.

claims_supported.claim: Component: random forests give robust accuracy (competitive with boosting and robust to noise/outliers).
claims_supported.where: Abstract; Section 3 desirable-characteristics list items (i) and (ii); Section 8 'The Effects of Output Noise' with Table 4 (5% label noise: Adaboost error increases are far larger than for Forest-RI/RC on the nine data sets); Section 13, 'For a while, the conventional thinking was that forests could not compete with arcing type algorithms in terms of accuracy. Our results dispel this belief.'

claims_supported.claim: Component: random forests need few tuning parameters.
claims_supported.where: Paraphrase, not a verbatim statement. The only design choice the paper varies is F, the number of random inputs (or linear combinations) per node, and it reports low sensitivity to it: Section 1.2 ('insensitive to the number of features selected to split each node'), Section 4 ('not overly sensitive to the value of F. The average absolute difference between the error rate using F=1 and the higher value of F is less than 1%'), Section 6 ('the lack of sensitivity in the generalization error to the group size F'). Trees are unpruned (no pruning parameter) and Theorem 1.2 means the number of trees need not be tuned against over-fitting. Section 3 list item (v): 'It's simple and easily parallelized.' Note Section 4 also shows exceptions: with many categorical inputs 'F must be increased to about two-three times int(log2 M+1)', and larger data sets benefited from larger F (Section 4, F=100 runs).

OpenAlex confirmed sole authorship (Leo Breiman, University of California, Berkeley), source Machine Learning, volume 45, issue 1, pages 5-32, year 2001, type article, cited_by_count about 133,000; OpenAlex has no abstract for this record. The Springer landing page (reached after the idp.springer.com cookie redirect) confirmed title, author, Machine Learning volume 45 pages 5-32, publication date October 2001, keywords classification, regression, ensemble; it did not display the issue number, which is taken from Crossref and OpenAlex. The claim check used the full text of the author-hosted preprint at https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf (33 pages, text extracted with pypdf); its abstract matches the published abstract verbatim. Quotations are located by the preprint's section numbers (1 Random forests; 2 Characterizing the accuracy; 3 Using random features / 3.1 out-of-bag estimates; 4 Forest-RI; 5 Forest-RC; 6 Empirical results on strength and correlation; 8 Effects of output noise; 11 Random forests for regression; 12 Empirical results in regression; 13 Remarks and conclusions) because journal page numbers could not be checked against the paywalled version. All bibliographic fields are verified from at least two independent sources.
references.caveats: Breiman explains random-forest accuracy through tree strength and between-tree correlation, not through the bias-variance decomposition; the report should either phrase the mechanism in those terms or add Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (2009) for the 'variance reduction by de-correlation' framing. Breiman's classification experiments used F=1 and F=int(log2 M + 1) features per node (and larger F for data with many categorical inputs), which differs from the sqrt(M) default in scikit-learn, so do not attribute the sqrt(M) rule to this paper. The experiments use UCI and synthetic data sets, not churn data; the paper does not address class imbalance, probability calibration or cost-sensitive thresholds, which matter for the Telco churn task. Breiman also reports that random features work better in classification than in regression (Section 13). The variable-importance measure described in Section 10 is the out-of-bag permutation importance, which is the appropriate citation if the report uses permutation importance rather than impurity-based importance.

references.title: Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability
references.harvard_reference: Brier, G.W. (1950) 'Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability', Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), pp. 1-3. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1950)078<0001:VOFEIT>2.0.CO;2.
references.abstract_summary: The paper has no abstract: Crossref, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex all return none, which is normal for a 1950 article. This summary comes from how secondary sources describe the paper, not from reading it. Brier (U.S. Weather Bureau) proposes a verification score, P, for weather forecasts given as probabilities. On each of n occasions the event falls into exactly one of r mutually exclusive and exhaustive classes, and the forecaster gives a probability f_ij for each class. The score is P = (1/n) sum_i sum_j (f_ij - E_ij)^2, where E_ij is 1 if the event occurred in class j and 0 otherwise. In other words, it is the squared difference between forecast probabilities and the 0/1 observed outcomes, summed over classes and averaged over forecasts. P is 0 for perfect forecasts and 2 for the worst possible forecasts. This score later became known as the Brier score.

claims_supported.claim: The Brier score measures the mean squared difference between forecast probabilities and observed outcomes.
claims_supported.where: p. 1: the definition of the verification score P = (1/n) sum sum (f_ij - E_ij)^2, with E_ij = 1 or 0 depending on whether the event occurred in class j. This was checked through secondary descriptions of the original definition (Wikipedia 'Brier score', section on Brier's original definition; UVA Library 'A Brief on Brier Scores'). The AMS full text could not be opened directly. Caveat: the original score adds up the squared errors across all r outcome classes before averaging over the n forecasts, so it runs from 0 to 2. The modern binary Brier score is half of this (range 0 to 1). Brier also does not call it the 'Brier score'; he calls it the verification score P. The claim is accurate as a general description, but if the report states the binary formula or the 0 to 1 range, it should say that this is the common modern binary form, not Brier's original multi-category formula.

references.verification_notes: Metadata confirmed through the Crossref API: author Glenn W. Brier; title 'VERIFICATION OF FORECASTS EXPRESSED IN TERMS OF PROBABILITY' (all capitals in Crossref, changed to sentence case for Harvard); Monthly Weather Review, vol. 78, issue 1, pp. 1-3; published in print January 1950; publisher American Meteorological Society; type journal-article. The DOI resolves. Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 122906757) and OpenAlex (U.S. Weather Bureau affiliation, about 5,500 citations, closed access) agree. None of these sources has an abstract. The AMS landing page and PDF returned HTTP 403 or a bot challenge, which was not bypassed, so I did not read the full text myself. The content of the score definition was confirmed from consistent secondary descriptions of Brier's original formula: Wikipedia 'Brier score' and UVA Library 'A Brief on Brier Scores', both of which give the multi-category form ranging from 0 to 2. Monthly Weather Review is a long-established AMS journal and not a predatory venue. This is the correct primary source for the Brier score. Not an F1000Research item, so no peer-review status note is needed.
references.caveats: The full text was not accessed directly (the AMS site blocked automated access), so the claim check relies on the well-documented original formula as reported by secondary sources. Brier's original score sums over all outcome classes, so it ranges from 0 to 2, and for a binary event it equals twice the modern binary Brier score (mean squared error of the predicted probability of the positive class, range 0 to 1). If the report gives the binary formula or the 0 to 1 range, cite it as the modern or binary form of Brier's (1950) score, and optionally add a textbook or software source for that form (for example scikit-learn's brier_score_loss documentation). Brier does not use the name 'Brier score' in the paper.

references.title: On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation
references.harvard_reference: Cawley, G.C. and Talbot, N.L.C. (2010) 'On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11(70), pp. 2079-2107. Available at: https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: The paper examines model selection (hyperparameter tuning) driven by numerical optimisation of a criterion such as k-fold cross-validation. Decomposing the criterion's error into bias and variance, the authors argue that low variance matters at least as much as unbiasedness, because a non-negligible variance lets the hyperparameters over-fit the selection criterion just as parameters can over-fit the training data. Empirically, this over-fitting in model selection degrades generalisation by amounts comparable to the differences between competing learning algorithms. A second contribution shows that several common performance-evaluation protocols are susceptible to a selection bias arising from this over-fitting and are therefore unreliable, and the paper describes protocols that avoid the bias (treating model selection as an integral part of model fitting, performed independently inside each resampling fold). Although the study focuses on cross-validation, the authors state the conclusions apply to any model-selection practice that optimises a criterion over a finite sample, including Bayesian evidence and performance bounds.

claims_supported.claim: Selecting hyperparameters and estimating performance on the same cross-validation folds produces optimistically biased estimates; nested cross-validation avoids this selection bias.
claims_supported.where: Section 1 (p. 2080): the paper names 'the undesirable optimistic bias that can arise due to over-fitting in model selection' and states that unbiased performance evaluation is likely to require protocols 'such a nested cross-validation or double cross (Stone, 1974)'. Section 5 introduction (p. 2094): avoiding the bias requires treating training and model selection together as integral parts of model fitting, never performed separately during evaluation. Section 5.1 (p. 2095): the unbiased 'internal' protocol performs model selection independently within each fold of the resampling procedure, i.e. nested CV. Section 5.3 (pp. 2102-2103) and Table 8: when hyperparameters are tuned on the whole design set and the same data are then re-partitioned for cross-validated testing ('external' protocol), the test data are no longer statistically pure and 'we should therefore expect to observe an optimistic bias'; Table 8 shows the external protocol exhibits 'a consistently optimistic bias' relative to the internal (nested) protocol on all thirteen benchmarks, statistically significant on eleven, and the authors conclude it 'should not be used in practice'. Section 6 Conclusions (p. 2103): model selection 'should be conducted independently in each trial in order to prevent selection bias'.

references.verification_notes: Crossref: no record for this paper (JMLR does not register Crossref DOIs; the query returned only unrelated Cawley book chapters). Verified directly at the publisher, https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html: title, authors Gavin C. Cawley and Nicola L. C. Talbot, JMLR 11(70), 2010, pp. 2079-2107, abstract, and PDF https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume11/cawley10a/cawley10a.pdf. OpenAlex W2154776925 corroborates all bibliographic fields (1,989 citations) and lists DOI 10.5555/1756006.1859921, but https://doi.org/10.5555/1756006.1859921 returned HTTP 404 and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1756006.1859921 returned HTTP 403, so that DOI could not be confirmed to resolve and the doi field is left empty; the reference therefore uses the JMLR URL. Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 (rate limited) on every attempt, so the abstract was taken from the JMLR page and OpenAlex (permitted fallback). Claim 1 was verified against the full text of the JMLR PDF (29 pages; sections 1, 5, 5.1, 5.3, 6 and Table 8), not only the abstract.
references.caveats: The abstract itself does not use the phrase 'nested cross-validation' or 'optimistic bias'; those appear in the body. The paper's own terminology for the recommended protocol is the 'internal' cross-validation protocol (model selection repeated inside each fold), which it equates with nested cross-validation / 'double cross' in the introduction. The biased 'external' protocol studied in Section 5.3 tunes hyperparameters once on the entire data set before the same data are cross-validated, which is the leakage the claim describes; the paper does not literally use the wording 'same cross-validation folds', so the report should paraphrase rather than quote. The issue number 70 is JMLR's retrospective paper number shown on the article page; many citation styles cite JMLR papers by volume only (11), which is also acceptable.

references.title: SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
references.harvard_reference: Chawla, N.V., Bowyer, K.W., Hall, L.O. and Kegelmeyer, W.P. (2002) 'SMOTE: synthetic minority over-sampling technique', Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 16, pp. 321-357. doi:10.1613/jair.953.
references.abstract_summary: The paper addresses building classifiers from imbalanced datasets, where the minority ('abnormal' or 'interesting') class is rare and its misclassification is costlier. Rather than over-sampling the minority class by replication, SMOTE creates synthetic minority examples in feature space: for each minority sample it selects among its k (=5) minority-class nearest neighbours and generates new points at a random position along the line segment joining the sample and the neighbour. Experiments with C4.5, Ripper and Naive Bayes on nine datasets, evaluated with AUC and the ROC convex hull, show that SMOTE combined with majority under-sampling generally achieves better performance in ROC space than under-sampling alone, and than varying Ripper's loss ratio or Naive Bayes class priors. The authors explain the gain by SMOTE forcing the learner to build larger, more general minority-class decision regions instead of the small, overfitted regions produced by replication.

claims_supported.claim: SMOTE generates synthetic minority examples by interpolating between neighbouring minority samples, which can improve minority-class recall and ROC space performance relative to plain undersampling.
claims_supported.where: Mechanism: Section 4.2 'SMOTE' (p. 328) states the minority class is over-sampled by introducing synthetic examples along the line segments joining a sample and any/all of its k minority-class nearest neighbours (difference vector times a random number in [0,1] added to the sample); the pseudo-code Algorithm SMOTE (p. 329, lines 13-22) computes k nearest neighbours among minority samples only and sets Synthetic = Sample[i] + gap*dif. ROC-space improvement vs plain under-sampling: abstract (p. 321) and Section 7 'Summary' (p. 352): 'The combination of SMOTE and under-sampling performs better than plain under-sampling', with domination in ROC space and more points on the ROC convex hull (Section 5 results, Figures 6-25). Minority-class recall: the paper's ROC axes are %TP (true-positive rate, i.e. recall/sensitivity) vs %FP, Section 7 opens by saying SMOTE 'can improve the accuracy of classifiers for a minority class', and Figure 5 (p. 330) reports '% Minority correct' for SMOTE vs replication. Note the paper uses the terms TP rate / sensitivity / minority-class accuracy rather than 'recall' for its own results (recall is defined on p. 326 in the IR context), and the comparison is SMOTE+under-sampling vs under-sampling alone, not SMOTE alone vs under-sampling.

references.verification_notes: Verified via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1613/jair.953: authors N.V. Chawla, K.W. Bowyer, L.O. Hall, W.P. Kegelmeyer; container-title Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research; volume 16; pages 321-357; issued 2002-06-01; publisher AI Access Foundation; ISSN 1076-9757), Semantic Scholar (abstract, arXiv 1106.1813, CorpusId 1554582), OpenAlex (same metadata, full author names Nitesh V. Chawla, Kevin W. Bowyer, Lawrence Hall, W. Philip Kegelmeyer), the JAIR publisher page (jair.org article 10302, published 1 June 2002, Vol. 16) and the arXiv abstract page (journal reference JAIR 16, pp. 321-357, 2002). JAIR volumes carry no issue number, so the issue field is left empty by design. The claim was checked against the full text (arXiv PDF 1106.1813, identical to the JAIR article), specifically Section 4.2, the SMOTE pseudo-code, Section 5 results and Section 7 Summary. The lead's title capitalisation and journal name were correct; page range and DOI were added.
references.caveats: The paper's headline comparison is SMOTE combined with majority under-sampling versus under-sampling alone (and versus Ripper loss ratio / Naive Bayes priors), not SMOTE in isolation. Improvement is not universal: Under-Ripper beats SMOTE-Ripper on the Oil dataset, Naive Bayes beats SMOTE-C4.5 on Pima, SMOTE and under-sampling ROC curves overlap on Can, and SMOTE-NC on Adult performs worse than plain under-sampling on AUC (Section 6.1), which the authors attribute to high-variance minority features causing synthetic points to overlap the majority class. Classifiers used are C4.5, Ripper and Naive Bayes (2002-era); the paper does not evaluate gradient boosting or logistic regression, nor telecom churn data, so any transfer to the Telco churn dataset must be argued separately. The word 'recall' should be paraphrased as true-positive rate / minority-class accuracy if quoting the paper's own results.

references.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
references.venue: KDD '16: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
references.harvard_reference: Chen, T. and Guestrin, C. (2016) 'XGBoost: a scalable tree boosting system', KDD '16: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining. San Francisco, CA, 13-17 August. New York: ACM, pp. 785-794. doi:10.1145/2939672.2939785.
references.abstract_summary: Chen and Guestrin describe XGBoost, an end-to-end scalable tree boosting system used widely by data scientists to win machine learning challenges. Contributions stated in the abstract are a novel sparsity-aware algorithm for sparse data, a weighted quantile sketch for approximate tree learning, and system-level insights on cache access patterns, data compression and sharding. Combined, these allow XGBoost to scale beyond billions of examples using far fewer resources than existing systems. The body of the paper (Section 2) formulates a regularised learning objective (Omega(f) = gamma*T + 0.5*lambda*||w||^2, penalising leaf count and leaf weights) and optimises it with a second-order Taylor approximation using first- and second-order gradient statistics; Section 3.4 introduces sparsity-aware split finding that learns a default direction for missing values.

claims_supported.claim: XGBoost is a regularised, scalable gradient-boosting system with sparsity-aware split finding and second-order optimisation.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (scalable end-to-end tree boosting system; novel sparsity-aware algorithm; scales beyond billions of examples). Section 2.1 'Regularized Learning Objective' (regularisation term Omega(f) = gamma*T + 1/2 lambda ||w||^2, 'helps to smooth the final learnt weights to avoid over-fitting'). Section 2.2 'Gradient Tree Boosting' (second-order Taylor approximation of the loss using g_i and h_i; 'Second-order approximation can be used to quickly optimize the objective in the general setting'). Section 3.4 'Sparsity-aware Split Finding' (default direction for missing values learnt from data). Sections 4 and 6.5-6.6 (cache-aware access, out-of-core and distributed scaling).

Full text checked via the arXiv PDF (arXiv:1603.02754) and ar5iv HTML rendering; Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 3.4 confirm the regularised objective, second-order approximation and sparsity-aware split finding respectively. references.title: A comparative analysis of data preparation algorithms for customer churn prediction: A case study in the telecommunication industry
references.harvard_reference: Coussement, K., Lessmann, S. and Verstraeten, G. (2017) 'A comparative analysis of data preparation algorithms for customer churn prediction: a case study in the telecommunication industry', Decision Support Systems, 95, pp. 27-36. doi:10.1016/j.dss.2016.11.007.
references.abstract_summary: The paper treats data preparation as the step that converts categorical and continuous predictors into a form suitable for modelling, and asks how much the choice of preparation method matters for churn prediction. Using real cross-sectional customer data from a large European telecommunications provider, the authors tune a logistic regression (logit) model by comparing alternative data-preparation methods (citing papers name discretisation/binning and weight-of-evidence coding among them) and then benchmark this optimised logit against eight state-of-the-art data-mining techniques (including decision trees, neural networks, SVMs, naive Bayes and bagged/boosted trees) that use standard, unprepared inputs. Effective data preparation raised AUC by up to 14.5% and top-decile lift by up to 34%, and the well-prepared logit model was competitive with the more advanced single and ensemble classifiers. The authors conclude that practitioners' data-preparation choices genuinely affect churn-prediction performance.

claims_supported.claim: Data preparation choices (encoding, binning, transformation) significantly affect churn-model performance, and well-prepared logistic regression can rival more complex learners.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (and TL;DR/abstract summaries on Semantic Scholar and the UWA research repository): the study examines data-preparation alternatives for categorical and continuous variables to enhance a logit model; reports AUC improvements up to 14.5% and top-decile-lift improvements up to 34% from data preparation alone; and finds the optimised logit competitive with eight advanced single and ensemble data-mining techniques, concluding that the chosen data-preparation technique affects churn-prediction performance. Citing papers (Semantic Scholar citation contexts) confirm discretisation/binning and weight-of-evidence coding were among the techniques compared, and that the paper shows proper preprocessing makes logistic regression competitive with random forests, SVMs and other complex learners. Caveat: 'significantly' is supported in the sense of substantial effect sizes; the abstract does not state a statistical-significance test, so avoid implying one. The parenthetical 'encoding, binning, transformation' is a fair gloss of the categorical/continuous preparation methods, but the exact list of techniques should be checked against the full text before naming specific methods in the report.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.dss.2016.11.007; journal-article; Decision Support Systems vol. 95, pp. 27-36; published March 2017; ISSN 0167-9236), OpenAlex (same authors/volume/pages; records 2016 as online-first year) and Semantic Scholar (publicationDate 2017-03-01; DBLP journals/dss/CoussementLV17; 209 citations). references.title: Regression Models and Life-Tables
references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological)
references.harvard_reference: Cox, D.R. (1972) 'Regression models and life-tables', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 34(2), pp. 187-202. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1972.tb00899.x.
references.abstract_summary: Cox considers how to analyse censored failure times when each individual has one or more explanatory variables. In his model the hazard function (age-specific failure rate) is a function of the explanatory variables and unknown regression coefficients, multiplied by an arbitrary and unknown function of time: lambda(t; z) = exp(z beta) lambda_0(t) (eq. 9, Section 3), where lambda_0(t) is the hazard under the standard conditions z = 0. The paper leaves lambda_0(t) arbitrary, treating it as a nuisance function, and focuses on the regression parameters. To estimate them it conditions on the set of observed failure times and on the individuals still at risk at each one. This gives a conditional likelihood, later called the partial likelihood, that does not involve lambda_0(t) (Section 5, eqs 12-13), along with score and information expressions and a score test of beta = 0. The paper also extends the Kaplan-Meier product-limit approach and two-sample life-table comparisons, allows time-dependent covariates, and outlines some generalisations. It was read before the Royal Statistical Society on 8 March 1972 and printed with a published discussion.

claims_supported.claim: The proportional-hazards model relates covariates to the hazard of an event multiplicatively without specifying the baseline hazard, and handles censored observations.
claims_supported.where: All three parts are stated explicitly. (a) Multiplicative covariate effect on the hazard. Summary (p. 187): the hazard is 'taken to be a function of the explanatory variables and unknown regression coefficients multiplied by an arbitrary and unknown function of time'. Section 3 'Regression Models' (p. 189), eq. (9): lambda(t; z) = exp(z beta) lambda_0(t). Example 1 on the same page shows the two-sample hazards as lambda_0(t) and psi lambda_0(t) with psi = e^beta, and Example 2 names this 'a simple model of proportional hazards'. (b) Baseline hazard left unspecified. Section 3 (p. 189): lambda_0(t) 'is an unknown function' giving the hazard under z = 0. Section 4 'Analysis of Regression Models' (p. 190) says the paper will 'concentrate on exploring the consequence of allowing lambda_0(t) to be arbitrary', with lambda_0(t) treated as a nuisance function. Section 5 'A Conditional Likelihood' (pp. 190-191, eqs 12-13) builds a likelihood for beta that does not involve lambda_0(t), 'a method of analysis holding for all lambda_0(t)'. (c) Censoring. The Summary opens with 'The analysis of censored failure times is considered'. Section 1 (p. 187) defines censoring: for censored individuals 'we know only that the time to failure is greater than the censoring time'. Section 2 (p. 188) defines the risk set R(t), which includes individuals whose failure or censoring time is at least t, and this risk set enters the conditional likelihood in eqs (12)-(13). One point of wording: the phrase 'proportional-hazards model' is the later standard name. Cox himself calls it a regression model for the hazard and uses 'proportional hazards' only in passing (p. 189). This does not undermine the claim.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1972.tb00899.x, raw JSON) gives: type journal-article; title 'Regression Models and Life-Tables'; sole author D. R. Cox (Imperial College, London); container-title 'Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology' (the journal's current name under OUP, the DOI's current publisher of record); volume 34; issue 2; page 187-202; published-print 1972; published-online 2018-12-05 (the date the back issue was digitised, not the publication date). Crossref also holds the full Summary, which matches the printed Summary on p. 187 word for word. OpenAlex independently confirmed the title, year 1972, volume 34, issue 2, pages 187-202 and type article, with about 39,900 citations. Semantic Scholar's DOI lookup returned HTTP 404, so it was not used. On the journal title: the JSTOR cover sheet of the scanned article (web.stanford.edu/~lutian/coursepdf/cox1972paper.pdf, text layer read with pypdf) prints 'Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Methodological), Vol. 34, No. 2. (1972), pp. 187-220', and Wiley Online Library lists it as 'Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological)'. The reference uses that name because it was the journal's title in 1972. JSTOR's range 187-220 includes the published discussion. The paper itself runs to p. 202, matching Crossref, so 187-202 is used. The scanned pages 187-191 were rendered as images and read directly to check the claim: the Summary, Section 1 (censoring definition), Section 2 (risk set), Section 3 (eq. 9 and the 'proportional hazards' wording), Section 4 (arbitrary lambda_0) and Section 5 (conditional likelihood, eqs 12-18). Pages after 191 were not read. The paper is peer-reviewed: it is a discussion paper read before the Royal Statistical Society and printed in JRSS Series B, not a predatory venue. The Harvard reference follows the doi: format used by the other files in this folder.
references.caveats: 1) The 1972 paper calls the estimating function a 'conditional likelihood'. The term 'partial likelihood' and its formal justification come from Cox (1975, Biometrika 62(2), pp. 269-276). If the report uses the phrase 'partial likelihood', cite Cox (1975) as well, or keep to 'conditional likelihood' when citing only this paper. 2) Cox allows the covariates z to depend on time (p. 189), so the model is not limited to strictly proportional hazards. The proportional-hazards assumption holds only when the covariates are fixed over time, and the report should say it tested that assumption, for example with Schoenfeld residuals, which are not in this paper. 3) Cox's handling of censoring assumes that a censored individual's only information is that failure had not happened by the censoring time (p. 188). This is commonly read as non-informative censoring, although on p. 191 Cox does not require censoring times to be independent of z. In the Telco data, customers who have not churned are censored at their current tenure, which is administrative right-censoring. 4) The paper's examples are medical and reliability data, not customer churn. Applying the model to churn is the report's own step, and published churn-survival studies should be cited for it. 5) Tied failure times are handled separately in the paper (discrete-time conditioning, mentioned on pp. 190-191). The Telco 'tenure' field is recorded in whole months and has many ties, so the report should name the tie-handling method its software uses (Breslow or Efron). Those methods are not described in the pages checked here.

references.title: lifelines: survival analysis in Python
references.harvard_reference: Davidson-Pilon, C. (2019) 'lifelines: survival analysis in Python', Journal of Open Source Software, 4(40), 1317. doi:10.21105/joss.01317.
references.abstract_summary: A three-page JOSS software paper (no formal abstract; the 'Summary' section serves that role) introducing lifelines, a pure-Python survival-analysis library intended to spare data scientists from switching between R (survival, flexsurv) and Python when a fitted survival model must be deployed in a Python system. The paper describes three internal innovations: (1) implementing the Efron-tie partial likelihood, gradient and Hessian of the Cox proportional-hazards model with NumPy einsum for roughly a 4x speed-up; (2) a meta-algorithm, trained by linear regression on synthetic datasets, that picks at runtime the faster of two Cox partial-likelihood algorithms depending on the number of tied event times; and (3) user-defined parametric cumulative-hazard models, whose log-likelihood (with right-censoring and left-truncation) is maximised via automatic differentiation (Autograd) and SciPy's minimize, returning MLEs, standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals. It acknowledges Terry Therneau and the R survival package authors.

claims_supported.claim: lifelines implements Kaplan-Meier estimation, the log-rank test and Cox proportional-hazards regression in Python.
claims_supported.where: PARTIAL ONLY. The Cox proportional-hazards part is explicitly supported: the Summary (p. 1-2) describes 'the lifelines' implementation of Cox proportional hazard model' with Efron's tie-handling, its partial likelihood/Hessian computed via NumPy einsum, and a runtime meta-algorithm choosing between two Cox algorithms. However, the paper never mentions Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen or the log-rank test anywhere (0 occurrences of 'Kaplan', 'Meier', 'log-rank'/'logrank' in the version-of-record PDF and in the paper.md source). It only says generically that lifelines lets users 'perform common survival analysis tasks in Python'. Kaplan-Meier (KaplanMeierFitter) and the log-rank test (lifelines.statistics.logrank_test) are confirmed in the lifelines documentation (lifelines.readthedocs.io), not in this paper. Suggested fix: either (a) cite Davidson-Pilon (2019) for lifelines as the library and for its Cox PH implementation, and cite the lifelines documentation for Kaplan-Meier and the log-rank test, or (b) soften the sentence to 'lifelines, a pure-Python survival-analysis library (Davidson-Pilon, 2019), was used for Kaplan-Meier estimation, the log-rank test and Cox proportional-hazards regression' (i.e. cite the paper as the software citation, not as evidence that it lists those estimators).

references.verification_notes: Verified via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.21105/joss.01317): title, single author Cameron Davidson-Pilon, container Journal of Open Source Software (The Open Journal), vol. 4, issue 40, page 1317, issued 2019-08-04, ISSN 2475-9066, CC BY 4.0. Corroborated by Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 201207884, DBLP journals/jossw/Davidson-Pilon19), OpenAlex (author affiliation 'Independent researcher', Diamond OA, ~1,040 citations) and the JOSS landing page (published 4 Aug 2019; software repository github.com/camdavidsonpilon/lifelines; archive doi:10.5281/zenodo.805993; editor @trallard; reviewers @becarioprecario, @sunhwan). The version-of-record PDF (theoj.org, 3 pages, 'Submitted: 06 March 2019, Published: 04 August 2019') was downloaded and its full text extracted and searched; the current paper/paper.md in the GitHub repository matches it. The lifelines documentation page (lifelines.readthedocs.io) should be cited separately if the report needs a source that names Kaplan-Meier and the log-rank test; that documentation is undated/rolling, so cite it with an access date.
