references.title: A new hybrid classification algorithm for customer churn prediction based on logistic regression and decision trees
references.harvard_reference: De Caigny, A., Coussement, K. and De Bock, K.W. (2018) 'A new hybrid classification algorithm for customer churn prediction based on logistic regression and decision trees', European Journal of Operational Research, 269(2), pp. 760-772. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2018.02.009.
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes the logit leaf model (LLM), a two-stage hybrid classifier for customer churn prediction: a decision tree first segments customers into homogeneous leaves, then a separate logistic regression is fitted in each leaf. The motivation is that decision trees and logistic regression are both popular in churn prediction because they combine good predictive performance with good comprehensibility, but trees struggle with linear relations while logistic regression misses interaction effects. LLM is benchmarked on fourteen churn datasets from different industries against decision trees, logistic regression, random forests and logistic model trees, using AUC and top-decile lift. LLM scores significantly better than its building blocks (LR and DT) and performs at least as well as the ensemble/advanced methods random forests and logistic model trees. Comprehensibility is demonstrated through a case study with a proposed LLM visualization.

claims_supported.claim: Logistic regression and decision trees are widely used in churn prediction because of their comprehensibility; a hybrid (logit leaf model) can combine accuracy with interpretability.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (first sentence: 'Decision trees and logistic regression are two very popular algorithms in customer churn prediction with strong predictive performance and good comprehensibility'); Introduction, para 3 ('very popular techniques ... because they combine good predictive performance with good comprehensibility (Verbeke et al., 2012)'); Highlights ('designed to perform well in terms of both accuracy and interpretability'); Conclusions ('the LLM is proposed as a viable choice that scores high on both requirements').

claims_supported.claim: In their benchmark on 14 datasets, the logit leaf model was competitive with random forests.
claims_supported.where: Introduction, para 4 ('Fourteen customer churn datasets from different industries are used on which the LLM is benchmarked against ... DT, LR, random forests (RF) and logistic model trees (LMT)'); Section 4 'Data and experimental design' ('Experiments are conducted on fourteen churn datasets originating from different sources. Table 3 provides an overview'); Abstract ('performs at least as well as more advanced ensemble methods random forests and logistic model trees' on AUC and top decile lift). 'Competitive' is a fair paraphrase of 'at least as well as'.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified against the CrossRef record for DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2018.02.009 (title, three authors, container-title European Journal of Operational Research, volume 269, issue 2, pages 760-772, published-print 2018-09, publisher Elsevier BV, ISSN 0377-2217). Cross-checked with OpenAlex (same biblio; publication_date 2018-02-12 = available online) and Semantic Scholar (abstract, DBLP key journals/eor/CaignyCB18, ~482-528 citations). The ScienceDirect landing page (issue dated 1 September 2018, section 'Innovative Applications of O.R.') was read via the built-in browser and provides the Highlights, Abstract, full Introduction and section snippets; the 'fourteen datasets' statement was confirmed there directly, and also independently in a citing paper (Sustainability 2023, doi:10.3390/su15054543, which lists LLM as evaluated on '14 different churn datasets'). The lead reference given was accurate apart from omitting page numbers and the DOI. Full text is paywalled (Unpaywall: no OA copy), so the results tables were not inspected; the random-forest comparison is taken from the abstract and the conclusions snippet.
references.caveats: The paper uses the term 'comprehensibility' (and 'interpretability' in the Highlights); either wording is acceptable. 'Competitive with random forests' should be phrased as 'performed at least as well as random forests and logistic model trees' to match the authors' wording; the paper does not claim LLM beats random forests. It is not verified from the accessible text which fourteen datasets were used (Table 3 is behind the paywall), so the report should not state that the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset was among them. The case study uses 'a public dataset' whose identity is not visible in the accessible text.

references.title: Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach
references.harvard_reference: DeLong, E.R., DeLong, D.M. and Clarke-Pearson, D.L. (1988) 'Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach', Biometrics, 44(3), pp. 837-845. doi:10.2307/2531595.
references.abstract_summary: The paper addresses how to compare diagnostic tests that produce a continuous or graded score, where each test is summarised by its ROC curve and the area beneath it. Its central point is that when two or more empirical ROC curves are built from tests applied to the same individuals, the resulting AUC estimates are correlated and any test of their difference must account for that correlation. The authors propose a nonparametric method that treats the AUC as a generalised U-statistic and derives an estimated covariance matrix for a set of correlated AUCs, from which differences can be tested.

claims_supported.claim: The DeLong test provides a nonparametric comparison of correlated ROC AUCs computed on the same cases.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (PubMed PMID 3203132): the paper states that when two or more empirical ROC curves are constructed from tests performed on the same individuals, analysis of differences must account for the correlated nature of the data, and that it presents a nonparametric approach to analysing areas under correlated ROC curves using generalised U-statistics theory to produce an estimated covariance matrix. This is exactly the nonparametric, same-cases, correlated-AUC comparison described in the claim.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (query.bibliographic) returned the work as its top hit with DOI 10.2307/2531595, container-title Biometrics, volume 44, issue 3, year 1988, authors Elizabeth R. DeLong, David M. DeLong and Daniel L. Clarke-Pearson; the Crossref record (deposited by JSTOR) lists only the first page (837), as does OpenAlex. The full page range 837-845 and publication month (September 1988) were taken from the PubMed record (PMID 3203132) retrieved via the NCBI E-utilities XML endpoint (MedlinePgn '837-45'). Semantic Scholar has the paper (CorpusId 21877334, MAG 2328176404) but its abstract field was elided by the publisher, so the abstract was obtained verbatim from PubMed; OpenAlex's inverted-index reconstruction matches it in substance. The JSTOR landing page and the PubMed HTML page could not be fetched (JavaScript/CAPTCHA gates), but this did not affect verification. The lead citation was accurate in every field; only the page range was missing and has now been supplied. All metadata fields are verified from Crossref and/or PubMed; none were inferred.
references.caveats: The page range comes from PubMed rather than Crossref, whose JSTOR-deposited record carries only the first page. The Crossref/JSTOR DOI (10.2307/2531595) is the DOI of record and resolves via doi.org to JSTOR.

references.title: Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models
references.harvard_reference: Devriendt, F., Berrevoets, J. and Verbeke, W. (2021) 'Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models', Information Sciences, 548, pp. 497-515. doi:10.1016/j.ins.2019.12.075.
references.abstract_summary: The authors argue that uplift modelling (estimating the change in a customer's churn probability caused by a retention action) is a better basis for retention targeting than conventional churn prediction, but note the literature lacked a direct, like-for-like comparison. They introduce the maximum profit uplift (MPU) measure, extending the maximum profit (MP) measure used for churn-prediction models, together with a 'liftup' curve and measure as uplift counterparts of lift. Using data from a European financial institution's retention campaign (c. 200,903 customers; treatment group churn 13.25% vs control 25.52%), they build logistic-regression and random-forest churn-prediction (CCP) and churn-uplift (CCU) models. Evaluated with MPU, uplift models outperform prediction models: CCP models tend to rank 'lost causes' and 'sure things' highly, whereas CCU models pick out 'persuadables', producing a larger churn reduction and higher campaign profit. The authors conclude uplift modelling is the superior paradigm for data-driven retention, while calling for validation in other application domains.

claims_supported.claim: Uplift models that estimate the incremental effect of a retention action outperform conventional churn-prediction models for retention targeting.
claims_supported.where: Directly stated. Highlights: 'Customer churn uplift models are found to outperform customer churn prediction models.' Abstract, final sentence: uplift models outperform predictive models and improve the profitability of retention campaigns. Section 2.2.1, Eq. (1) defines uplift as P(churn | not treated) minus P(churn | treated), i.e. the incremental effect of the retention action. Section 4.3.1 (Profit curves): evaluated with the MPU measure, 'CCU models outperform CCP models'. Section 4.3.2 (Churn rates): CCP models select many lost causes whereas CCU models target persuadables, giving a larger churn reduction and higher returns, for both logistic regression and random forests. Section 5 (Conclusions): 'customer churn uplift models outperform customer churn prediction models' and 'uplift modeling is a superior paradigm to predictive modeling in the context of supporting customer retention efforts'. Caveats to state in the report: the evidence is one case study at a single European financial institution (not telecom) over a three-month window; under the conventional MP measure the churn-prediction models look better and the uplift advantage appears when the authors' MPU measure is used (Section 4.3.1); the authors themselves say further evidence across more application types is needed (Section 5).

claims_supported.claim: Uplift modelling requires data from randomised retention campaigns (treatment and control groups).
claims_supported.where: Supported in substance for the treatment-and-control requirement; one wording caveat. Section 1.2: uplift modelling 'requires the availability of data that captures the behavior of the modeled system under varying conditions and decision-making scenarios', such data 'may need to be actively collected by setting up experiments', and 'setting up control groups and collecting unbiased data' is what makes uplift modelling possible. Section 2.2.1: 'We assume that a sample of customers is divided into two groups defined as the treatment and control groups' (exposed vs not exposed to the campaign), with the treatment indicator T entering the uplift definition in Eq. (1). Section 4.1.2 (Methodology): the uplift (CCU) model is trained on data sampled from both the treatment and control groups, whereas the prediction (CCP) model uses only the control group. Section 4.3.1: 'it is only possible to calculate the MPU measure if both control and treatment groups are present, which is not the case in traditional customer churn prediction setups.' CAVEAT: the paper never uses the word 'randomised' for how customers are assigned to treatment vs control; it speaks of 'experiments', 'control groups' and 'unbiased data', and describes the case-study data only as a targeted group and a non-targeted group (the only 'random' assignment mentioned is the random stratified train/test split). To cite this source precisely, phrase the claim as 'uplift modelling requires experimental campaign data containing both a treated group and an untreated control group (Devriendt et al., 2021)'. If the report wants to state explicitly that assignment must be randomised, pair it with a second source that says so (to be verified separately).

references.verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-27. Crossref (query.bibliographic and direct DOI record) returns DOI 10.1016/j.ins.2019.12.075, title as given, authors Floris Devriendt (ORCID 0000-0003-3479-3398), Jeroen Berrevoets, Wouter Verbeke; container-title Information Sciences; volume 548; page 497-515; published-print 2021-02; Crossref 'issued' 2019-12-31 (online-first date); publisher Elsevier BV; ISSN 0020-0255; licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (open access). Crossref lists issue 'C', which is Elsevier's placeholder for a volume without a numbered issue, so the issue field is deliberately left empty and omitted from the Harvard reference. Semantic Scholar (paperId 5a44e4e985877f182075d3351878a5795dd6f946, DBLP journals/isci/DevriendtBV21) and OpenAlex agree on title, authors (all Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Solvay Business School, Data Analytics Laboratory), venue, volume 548 and pages 497-515; OpenAlex records publication_date 2019-12-31 (online-first) and publication_year 2019, whereas the volume/issue date is February 2021; year 2021 is used per Cite Them Right (year of the version of record). Manuscript history from the article front matter: received 22 March 2018, revised 8 November 2019, accepted 27 December 2019, available online 31 December 2019. Abstract taken verbatim from Semantic Scholar and cross-checked against the full text. Claims were checked against the full text: the DOI resolves to linkinghub.elsevier.com PII S0020025519312022; ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the full text was read from the KU Leuven Lirias open repository copy (Journal Pre-proof / accepted manuscript, CC BY-NC-ND), extracted with pdftotext. Section numbering matches the published structure (1 Introduction; 2 Customer churn prediction and uplift modeling; 3 Maximum profit measures; 4 Experiments; 5 Conclusions), but page numbers in that copy are the pre-proof's, not the version of record's, so no in-text page pinpoints are given. Citation counts at verification: Crossref 76, Semantic Scholar 87, OpenAlex 90. Lead supplied was accurate; volume, pages and DOI added.
references.caveats: Single case study at one European financial institution (contract-termination churn), not telecommunications; c. 200,903 customers, 162 variables, three-month outcome window. Only two learners (logistic regression, random forests) were compared. The uplift advantage is demonstrated under the authors' own MPU measure; under the conventional MP measure the churn-prediction models appear better. The paper does not use the word 'randomised' for treatment assignment. Not applicable to the Kaggle Telco dataset directly, because that dataset contains no treatment/control indicator, so the paper is best cited for the conceptual argument (why churn-probability ranking is not the same as retention targeting) and as a limitation/future-work source.

references.title: Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms
references.harvard_reference: Dietterich, T.G. (1998) 'Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms', Neural Computation, 10(7), pp. 1895-1923. doi:10.1162/089976698300017197.
references.abstract_summary: The paper reviews five approximate statistical tests for deciding whether one learning algorithm outperforms another on a given task and compares them experimentally on their Type I error (falsely detecting a difference when none exists) and their power. Two widely used tests, a difference-of-two-proportions test and a paired-differences t test over several random train/test splits (the 'resampled t test'), are found to have high Type I error in some situations and the author says they should never be used. A paired t test over 10-fold cross-validation has somewhat elevated Type I error. McNemar's test has low Type I error, and a newly proposed 5x2cv paired t test (five repetitions of two-fold cross-validation) also has acceptable Type I error. On power, the cross-validated t test is the strongest, and 5x2cv is slightly more powerful than McNemar's test. The recommended test depends on computational cost: when an algorithm can be run only once, McNemar's test is the only one with acceptable Type I error; when it can be run ten times, 5x2cv is recommended because it is slightly more powerful and directly measures variation due to the choice of training set.

claims_supported.claim: McNemar's test on paired predictions from a single test set has acceptable Type I error for comparing two classifiers, whereas the resampled t-test has elevated Type I error.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (verbatim text obtained from PubMed PMID 9744903 and reproduced identically by OpenAlex). The abstract states that the paired-differences t test based on taking several random train/test splits (which the paper's tables label 'Resampled t') has a high probability of Type I error in certain situations and should never be used, that McNemar's test 'is shown to have low type I error', and that for algorithms that can be executed only once (i.e. a single training run evaluated on a single test set) McNemar's test is the only test with acceptable Type I error. The claim's wording 'elevated' is if anything milder than the paper's own conclusion ('high probability of type I error ... should never be used'). The single-test-set framing matches the paper's 'executed only once' recommendation; McNemar's test in the paper is computed from the two classifiers' paired correct/incorrect outcomes on the same held-out test set.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified via CrossRef (DOI 10.1162/089976698300017197; MIT Press; ISSN 0899-7667 / 1530-888X), Semantic Scholar (DBLP journals/neco/Dietterich98; PMID 9744903), OpenAlex (volume 10, issue 7, pp. 1895-1923; ~3,800 citations) and PubMed E-utilities (Neural Comput. 1998 Sep 15;10(7):1895-1923). Semantic Scholar returned a null abstract (publisher restriction), so the verbatim abstract was taken from PubMed and cross-checked word for word against OpenAlex's inverted index. The MIT Press landing page and article PDF return HTTP 403 to automated fetches. An open copy of the PDF (sci2s.ugr.es) was downloaded but its fonts use non-Unicode encodings, so body text could not be extracted; only figure/table labels came through, which do confirm the five tests are named 'McNemar', 'Prop Test', 'Resampled t', 'Xval t' and '5x2cv t' in the paper. Claim assessment therefore rests on the verbatim abstract, which states the relevant findings explicitly. Author affiliation on the PubMed record: Oregon State University, Department of Computer Science. Lead reference was accurate apart from missing page numbers and DOI, now added.
references.caveats: The paper's Type I error results are empirical (simulation-style experiments on a limited set of tasks and learning algorithms in 1998), not analytical guarantees; the author frames all five tests as approximate. The paper also finds McNemar's test is slightly less powerful than the 5x2cv test and, for algorithms that can be run ten times, recommends 5x2cv rather than McNemar. When citing this for a single-holdout-split model comparison (e.g. one Telco Customer Churn test set), it is accurate to say McNemar's test is the appropriate choice among those studied, but the report should not imply McNemar's test is the most powerful option overall. The paper concerns classification error rates on a fixed test set; it says nothing about churn prediction specifically.

references.title: The foundations of cost-sensitive learning
references.venue: Proceedings of the Seventeenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-01), Seattle, WA. Morgan Kaufmann
references.harvard_reference: Elkan, C. (2001) 'The foundations of cost-sensitive learning', Proceedings of the Seventeenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-01). Seattle, WA, August 2001. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 973-978. Available at: https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/01/IJCAI-2001-k.pdf (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: A six-page theoretical paper on optimal decision-making when different misclassification errors carry different costs. Section 1 sets out the decision-theoretic framework: given a cost matrix C(i,j) (cost of predicting class i when the true class is j) and calibrated conditional class probabilities P(j|x), the optimal prediction for x is the class that minimises expected cost, Equation (1). It explains the 'reasonableness' conditions a cost matrix must satisfy, shows that decisions are invariant to scaling and shifting the matrix (so any reasonable two-class matrix can be reduced to a simpler form), warns against economically incoherent matrices, and derives (Section 1.3, Equation (2)) the two-class optimal probability threshold p*, which depends only on the cost-matrix entries and is in general different from 0.5. Section 2 addresses how to make a standard, non-cost-sensitive learner produce decisions at a target threshold p*: the common practice is to rebalance the training set, and Theorem 1 gives the exact multiplier for the number of negative examples (by weighting, oversampling or undersampling), noting that in rare-class domains one should keep all rare-class examples and change only the common class. Section 3 proves Theorem 2, a base-rate correction formula showing how a correct probability estimate changes when the class prior changes (which also allows a classifier trained under one class distribution to be used under another). Section 4 examines what rebalancing actually does to standard learners, explicitly addressing the class-imbalance literature that recommends duplicating or discarding examples so classes are roughly equal (Kubat and Matwin 1997; Japkowicz 2000): for Bayesian learners, changing class frequencies only changes the estimated prior, so there is little reason to expect better decisions at any particular base rate; for naive Bayes, whose probability estimates are poorly calibrated but well ranked, empirically determining an equivalent threshold is likely to improve decisions whereas rebalancing to use a 0.5 threshold is not; for decision-tree growing, the choice of split is invariant to base rates under the Kearns-Mansour criterion (Theorem 3) and only slightly affected under other criteria such as C4.5 entropy; but decision-tree pruning is highly sensitive to class prevalence, so the paper recommends no pruning plus probability smoothing (Laplace) at the leaves. The conclusion (Section 5) is that changing the balance of positive and negative training examples has little effect on these learned classifiers, and that the recommended approach is to learn from the training set as given and then apply Equation (1)/(2) directly to the classifier's probability estimates, smoothing them and/or adjusting the threshold empirically if necessary.

claims_supported.claim: Given calibrated probabilities and a cost matrix, the optimal decision threshold is determined by the cost ratio (threshold moving), so class imbalance is best addressed by adjusting the decision threshold rather than the training data.
claims_supported.where: Supported, with a scope qualification the report should carry. (a) Threshold determined by costs: Section 1 (Equation (1): predict the class with lowest expected cost using P(j|x)) and Section 1.3 'Making optimal decisions' (Equation (2): 'The threshold for making optimal decisions is p* such that ...', with p* a function only of the cost-matrix entries; for the simplified matrix with zero cost for correct predictions this reduces to the ratio of the false-positive cost to the sum of the two error costs, i.e. the cost ratio). The paper's premise is that the probabilities are correct ('probability estimates given by the classifier'; Section 3 assumes estimates 'that we assume are correct given a base rate'); Section 4.1 and the Conclusion add that where estimates are poorly calibrated (naive Bayes) the threshold should be determined empirically or the estimates smoothed - so the 'given calibrated probabilities' precondition is faithful to the paper. Note the paper does not use the phrase 'threshold moving'; that is the report's label. (b) Threshold rather than training data: Abstract and Section 5 Conclusions - 'changing the balance of negative and positive training examples has little effect on the classifiers produced by standard Bayesian and decision tree learning methods. Accordingly, the recommended way ... is to learn a classifier from the training set as given, and then to compute optimal decisions explicitly using the probability estimates given by the classifier'; Section 4 introduction explicitly sets out to test the class-imbalance assumption behind duplicating/discarding examples (Kubat and Matwin 1997; Japkowicz 2000); Section 4.1 last paragraph: empirically choosing an equivalent threshold 'is likely to improve the accuracy of decision-making, while changing the proportion of negative examples using Theorem 1 in order to use the threshold 0.5 is not'; Section 2 (Theorem 1) shows rebalancing is at best a roundabout way of reaching the same threshold p*. SCOPE CAVEAT: the empirical 'little effect' argument is made for standard Bayesian and decision-tree learners (Sections 4.1-4.3), not for all learning algorithms, and Section 4.3 notes decision-tree pruning IS highly sensitive to class prevalence (hence the recommendation to grow unpruned trees with smoothed leaf probabilities). The decision rule of Equations (1)-(2) is general, but 'best addressed' should be attributed as Elkan's recommendation for those learner families, or phrased as the report author's inference.

claims_supported.claim: [Verifier-suggested wording] Elkan (2001) shows that, given a cost matrix and correct class-probability estimates, the cost-minimising decision rule is a fixed probability threshold determined by the misclassification costs (Equation (2)), and argues that rebalancing the training set has little effect on Bayesian and decision-tree classifiers; he therefore recommends training on the data as given and applying the cost-derived threshold (adjusted empirically if the probabilities are poorly calibrated) rather than resampling.
claims_supported.where: Abstract; Section 1.3 (Equation (2)); Section 2 (Theorem 1, rebalancing multiplier); Section 4 introduction and 4.1-4.3; Section 5 Conclusions (learn from the training set as given, then use Equation (1) or (2) directly, 'after smoothing probability estimates and/or adjusting the threshold of Equation (2) empirically if necessary').

references.verification_notes: Work exists exactly as described in the lead. Crossref bibliographic search returned no record for this paper (IJCAI-01 proceedings were published by Morgan Kaufmann and are not DOI-registered with Crossref; the three Crossref hits were unrelated items), so the doi field is intentionally empty. OpenAlex W167016754 (MAG 167016754): title 'The foundations of cost-sensitive learning', Charles Elkan (University of California San Diego, Dept of Computer Science and Engineering), International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, publication_date 2001-08-04, pages 973-978, no DOI, 1,825 citations at time of check. Semantic Scholar paperId 7fed3e00be2bb09510f5f7cad7ac106e6c94a359: same title/author/year/venue, externalIds DBLP conf/ijcai/Elkan01, CorpusId 16149383, MAG 167016754, no DOI, 2,783 citations. Full text verified from two copies: (1) the author's PDF at https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~elkan/rescale.pdf (header: 'To appear, Proceedings of the Seventeenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI'01)', 6 pages, text extracted with pypdf; abstract obtained verbatim); (2) the official IJCAI-01 proceedings section PDF https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/01/IJCAI-2001-k.pdf (Volume 2, 'Machine Learning and Data Mining', pp. 815-984), in which the paper occupies printed pages 973-978 (running footer 'MACHINE LEARNING AND DATA MINING' with page numbers 973 on the first and 978 on the last page), confirming the page range. ijcai.org past-proceedings page lists 'Seventeenth IJCAI. Seattle 2001' (vol 1 and vol 2). Open Library record for ISBN 1558608125 / 9781558608122: 'IJCAI '01: 17th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2-Volume & CD Set', publisher Morgan Kaufmann, published August 2001, 1500 pages (no place of publication given, so none is included in the reference). A web search shows an ACM Digital Library entry at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1642194.1642224 (fetch returned 403); '10.5555/...' is an ACM DL identifier, not a registered Crossref DOI, and must not be presented as a DOI. NOT VERIFIED (and therefore omitted from the reference): the name of the proceedings editor and the exact conference dates - DBLP (dblp.org and its mirror) was inaccessible behind a bot-challenge page and Google Books returned no record; if the marker requires editor and exact dates, check the DBLP record conf/ijcai/Elkan01 manually. Mathematical symbols in the PDF text extraction were garbled, so Equation (2) and the Theorem 1 multiplier were confirmed from the surrounding prose and section structure rather than quoted symbol-for-symbol; the report author should transcribe the formula directly from Section 1.3 of the PDF. Web-tool session quota was exhausted near the end of verification; final lookups were made with curl.
references.caveats: 1) Scope: Elkan's evidence that rebalancing 'has little effect' concerns standard Bayesian (including naive Bayes) and decision-tree learners; the paper makes no empirical claim about logistic regression, gradient boosting or neural networks, although the decision rule in Equations (1)-(2) applies to any classifier producing correct probabilities. Do not cite Elkan as evidence that resampling is useless for every algorithm. 2) Pruning caveat: Section 4.3 states decision-tree pruning is highly sensitive to class prevalence (C4.5 can collapse to a single majority-class node), so the recommendation is unpruned trees with smoothed leaf probabilities - relevant if the report uses tree ensembles. 3) Calibration precondition: the threshold p* is optimal only if the probabilities are correct; Section 4.1 and the Conclusion advise empirical threshold adjustment or smoothing when they are not, so the report should pair this source with a calibration reference when applying it to the Telco data. 4) The phrase 'threshold moving' is not Elkan's terminology. 5) The paper is framed around differing misclassification costs; class imbalance is addressed explicitly only in Section 4 (via Kubat and Matwin 1997 and Japkowicz 2000), so word the citation as a recommendation about handling cost/imbalance at decision time rather than as a study of imbalance per se. 6) No Crossref DOI exists; do not add one. The ACM '10.5555' identifier is not a DOI.

references.title: Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine
references.harvard_reference: Friedman, J.H. (2001) 'Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine', The Annals of Statistics, 29(5), pp. 1189-1232. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1013203451.
references.abstract_summary: Friedman treats function estimation as numerical optimisation in function space rather than parameter space. He links stagewise additive expansions to steepest-descent minimisation and develops a general gradient-descent 'boosting' method for additive expansions that works with any fitting criterion. He gives algorithms for least-squares, least-absolute-deviation and Huber-M losses in regression, and for multiclass logistic likelihood in classification. He derives special enhancements for the case where the additive components are regression trees, and presents tools for interpreting these 'TreeBoost' models. The paper reports that gradient-boosted trees are competitive, highly robust and interpretable for both regression and classification, especially on less-than-clean data. It also discusses how the method relates to the boosting methods of Freund and Schapire and of Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani.

claims_supported.claim: Gradient boosting builds an additive model by fitting successive trees to the negative gradient of a loss function (stagewise functional gradient descent).
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Project Euclid publisher page and OpenAlex): the paper frames estimation as 'numerical optimization in function space', connects 'stagewise additive expansions and steepest-descent minimization', develops a 'general gradient descent boosting paradigm' for additive expansions under any fitting criterion, and gives special enhancements where the additive components are regression trees (TreeBoost). The detailed mechanism of fitting each new base learner by least squares to pseudo-responses equal to the negative gradient of the loss is the paper's generic Gradient_Boost algorithm (Algorithm 1, in the finite-data section, believed to be Section 3), with the tree-specific version in the regression-trees subsection (believed to be Section 4.3). Those section and algorithm numbers could not be checked against the full text in this session.

Friedman), the title, the container title (The Annals of Statistics), volume 29, issue 5, the publication date (1 October 2001, print and online), the publisher (Institute of Mathematical Statistics), ISSN 0090-5364 and the type (journal article). references.title: Datasheets for datasets
references.harvard_reference: Gebru, T., Morgenstern, J., Vecchione, B., Vaughan, J.W., Wallach, H., Daumé III, H. and Crawford, K. (2021) 'Datasheets for datasets', Communications of the ACM, 64(12), pp. 86-92. doi:10.1145/3458723.
references.abstract_summary: The CACM record carries only a one-line abstract: 'Documentation to facilitate communication between dataset creators and consumers.' The full abstract (arXiv 1803.09010v8, the text published in CACM Dec 2021) states that the machine learning community has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. By analogy with electronics datasheets, the authors propose that every dataset be accompanied by a datasheet documenting its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on, to facilitate better communication between dataset creators and consumers and encourage the ML community to prioritize transparency and accountability. The paper supplies a question set grouped by dataset-lifecycle stage (motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/cleaning/labeling, uses, distribution, maintenance), a workflow for creators, an example datasheet (Pang and Lee polarity dataset), and a discussion of impact and challenges.

claims_supported.claim: Datasheets document a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses and limitations, to improve transparency and mitigate misuse.
claims_supported.where: Abstract and Section 1 Introduction: 'we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets have the potential to increase transparency and accountability within the machine learning community, mitigate unwanted societal biases in machine learning models...'. Section 1.1 Objectives: transparency is needed so consumers 'can select appropriate datasets for their chosen tasks and avoid unintentional misuse'; creators should reflect on 'underlying assumptions, potential risks or harms, and implications of use'. Section 3 Questions and Workflow lists the groups: motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/cleaning/labeling, uses, distribution, maintenance. 'Limitations' is the report's paraphrase rather than the paper's own term: Section 3.5 Uses asks 'Are there tasks for which the dataset should not be used?' and whether anything about composition/collection 'might impact future uses' or cause 'risks or harms'.

references.title: A survey on machine learning methods for churn prediction
references.venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
references.harvard_reference: Geiler, L., Affeldt, S. and Nadif, M. (2022) 'A survey on machine learning methods for churn prediction', International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 14(3), pp. 217-242. doi:10.1007/s41060-022-00312-5.
references.abstract_summary: A technical survey plus benchmark of supervised and semi-supervised churn-prediction methods. The authors evaluate eleven learning methods (k-NN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, logistic regression, linear and RBF SVM, decision tree, random forest, XGBoost, a feed-forward neural network, GEV-NN, plus the anomaly-detection methods iForest and DevNet) combined with seven sampling strategies (none, SMOTE, ADASYN, NCR, Tomek Links, SMOTE+random undersampling, SMOTE+Tomek, SMOTE+NCR) on sixteen public 'churn-like' datasets, including the IBM Telco churn set (TelC), using stratified 5-fold cross-validation and AUC with default hyperparameters. Results are compared with the Nemenyi post-hoc test / critical-difference diagrams and Correspondence Analysis. Across all datasets and sampling strategies the top individual methods are LR, RF, XGBoost and NN (mean ranks 2.61, 3.21, 3.33, 3.66); sampling produces only small AUC variations and generally degrades RF. The paper's practical recommendation is a probability-averaging ensemble of LR, XGBoost and RF with no sampling (median AUC 0.8577), which nearly matches the best single pipeline on almost every dataset.

claims_supported.claim: A survey and benchmark of churn-prediction methods across many datasets finds that ensemble tree methods and logistic regression are among the strongest, and that handling class imbalance is a central design decision.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'we study the behavior of eleven supervised and semi-supervised learning methods and seven sampling approaches on sixteen diverse and publicly available churn-like datasets'. Section 6.2.1: 'The top approaches over all datasets and sampling strategies are LR, RF, XGBoost and NN, with a mean rank of 2.61, 3.21, 3.33 and 3.66 respectively'; Section 6.2.3: 'in practice, we recommend the use of the ensemble LR|XGBoost|RF with no sampling for analyzing novel churn-like datasets'. On imbalance: Abstract: 'Choosing a priori the most appropriate sampling method as well as the most suitable classification model is not trivial, as it strongly depends on the data intrinsic characteristics'; Section 3: 'Customer defection is an infrequent event that is inevitably associated with a class imbalance hassle that impedes the quality of customer churn prediction'. The whole benchmark pipeline (Fig. 2) is organised around the sampling-method x classifier choice, so imbalance handling is treated as a core design axis. CAVEAT for the report: the paper's empirical finding is that resampling matters little for AUC ('only small AUC variations over sampling strategies'; 'sampling methods generally degrade AUC for RF'; 'the sampling strategies have a weak effect on the machine learning approaches ranking') and its recommended pipeline uses NO sampling. Do not cite this paper as evidence that SMOTE/resampling improves churn models; cite it as evidence that the choice must be made deliberately and evaluated, and that tree ensembles are largely robust to it.

claims_supported.claim: Deep learning did not clearly outperform gradient boosting on typical churn datasets in their benchmark.
claims_supported.where: The paper makes no statement comparing 'deep learning' as a family against gradient boosting, and the tables only partly support the claim. Evidence consistent with it: the plain feed-forward NN ranks below LR, RF and XGBoost overall (mean rank 3.66 vs 2.61/3.21/3.33) and has median AUC 0.7700 vs XGBoost 0.8104 without sampling (Table 2); DevNet (median AUC 0.7353, rank 6.31) is clearly worse; the recommended ensemble LR|XGBoost|RF omits the neural network; Nemenyi CD diagrams connect the top approaches, i.e. no method is statistically separable from the top group. Evidence AGAINST the claim as worded: GEV-NN (a deep network designed for imbalanced data) obtains the best mean rank (2.88) and the highest median AUC (0.8542) of all twelve methods in the no-sampling comparison, ahead of XGBoost (rank 4.44, AUC 0.8104), and is the best single pipeline for two datasets in Table 8. Also, XGBoost is not the strongest single model here (LR and RF rank above it), and all models use default hyperparameters. A defensible rewording: 'In Geiler et al.'s (2022) benchmark, a default feed-forward neural network ranked below logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost, and their recommended ensemble combines LR, XGBoost and RF without a neural component; only the imbalance-specific GEV-NN was competitive with the tree ensembles, and no method was statistically separable from the top group.'

references.title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?
references.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
references.harvard_reference: Grinsztajn, L., Oyallon, E. and Varoquaux, G. (2022) 'Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?', in Koyejo, S., Mohamed, S., Agarwal, A., Belgrave, D., Cho, K. and Oh, A. (eds) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), Datasets and Benchmarks Track. New Orleans, LA, 28 November-9 December 2022. Curran Associates, pp. 507-520. doi:10.52202/068431-0037.
references.abstract_summary: The authors ask whether deep learning's dominance on text and images carries over to tabular data. They assemble a benchmark of 45 tabular datasets from varied domains and a methodology that accounts for both model fitting and hyperparameter search (about 20,000 compute hours of random search per learner), comparing tree-based ensembles (RandomForest, GradientBoostingTree, XGBoost) against standard and tabular-specific neural networks (MLP, ResNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT). On medium-sized data (training sets truncated to ~10K samples) tree-based models remain state of the art even before accounting for their speed advantage, and the gap persists across every random-search budget rather than closing after tuning. Section 5 investigates inductive biases and reports three findings: neural networks are biased towards overly smooth solutions while the target functions in these datasets are irregular; uninformative features hurt MLP-like networks far more than trees; and tabular data are not rotation-invariant, so rotation-invariant architectures discard a natural feature basis. The paper also releases the benchmark and all raw search results.

claims_supported.claim: On medium-sized tabular datasets, tree-based ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) remain state of the art and outperform deep learning, even after tuning, partly because neural networks are biased towards smooth functions and are hurt by uninformative features.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: tree-based models (XGBoost, Random Forests) remain state-of-the-art on medium-sized data (~10K samples) even without accounting for their superior speed; and the three challenges for tabular NNs include being robust to uninformative features and being able to learn irregular functions. Section 4.2 (benchmark results): "Tree-based models are superior for every random search budget" and the gap stays wide even after many random-search iterations, i.e. it does not disappear after hyperparameter tuning. Section 5.2, Finding 1: neural networks are biased to overly smooth solutions, and the target functions in the benchmark datasets are irregular, which NNs struggle to fit compared with tree-based models (linked to the spectral bias towards low-frequency functions). Section 5.3, Finding 2: uninformative features affect MLP-like NNs more than tree-based models; removing them narrows the gap and adding them widens it. Every component of the claim (medium-sized regime, RF and GBT as the tree models, persistence after tuning, smoothness bias, sensitivity to uninformative features) is made explicitly in the paper.

references.caveats: The paper defines 'medium-sized' as training sets truncated to 10,000 samples (with a separate large-sized benchmark of 50,000); the Telco Customer Churn dataset (~7,043 rows before splitting) is smaller than that regime, so the report should present the finding as the closest available evidence rather than a direct benchmark of Telco-scale data. The result is for 2022-era architectures (MLP, ResNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT); the report should not imply the paper evaluated later tabular foundation models. 'Even after tuning' refers to the paper's random-search hyperparameter budgets, not to every possible tuning strategy. The paper's third finding (non-rotation-invariance of tabular data) is an additional reason for the gap that the candidate claim does not mention; 'partly because' is therefore appropriate wording.

references.title: Valuing customers
references.harvard_reference: Gupta, S., Lehmann, D.R. and Stuart, J.A. (2004) 'Valuing customers', Journal of Marketing Research, 41(1), pp. 7-18. doi:10.1509/jmkr.41.1.7.25084.
references.abstract_summary: The authors argue that a firm's financial value increasingly depends on intangible assets, above all its customers. They define customer value as the expected sum of discounted future earnings from customers and show that valuing the customer base makes it feasible to value firms, including high-growth firms with negative earnings. Applying the method to publicly available data for five firms, they find that a 1% improvement in retention, margin, or acquisition cost improves firm value by about 5%, 1% and 0.1% respectively, and that retention has almost five times the impact on firm value of a 1% change in discount rate or cost of capital. They conclude that linking marketing concepts to shareholder value is both possible and insightful.

claims_supported.claim: A one-percentage-point improvement in retention increases customer value by a much larger amount (around 5 %) than a one-point improvement in margin or acquisition cost, so retention has high leverage on firm value.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (OpenAlex record of the JMR article): 'They find that a 1% improvement in retention, margin, or acquisition cost improves firm value by 5%, 1%, and .1%, respectively. They also find that retention has almost five times greater impact on firm value than a 1% change in discount rate or capital.' The full paper reports these sensitivities in its results/discussion of the five-firm application (Table on the impact of marketing and financial instruments on customer value). Two wording caveats: (a) the abstract says '1% improvement', not 'one percentage point'; mirror the paper's '1%' wording to be strictly faithful. (b) The abstract phrases the 5%/1%/0.1% effects as changes in FIRM value (derived from customer value, which the paper defines as the discounted sum of future customer earnings); the report should say 'firm value' or 'customer/firm value' rather than only 'customer value'.

references.verification_notes: Verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1509/jmkr.41.1.7.25084; Journal of Marketing Research, vol. 41, issue 1, pp. 7-18, 2004, publisher SAGE; authors Sunil Gupta, Donald R. references.title: Equality of opportunity in supervised learning
references.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016), Barcelona, Spain, 5-10 December 2016; eds D. Lee, M. Sugiyama, U. Luxburg, I. Guyon and R. Garnett; Curran Associates, Inc.
references.harvard_reference: Hardt, M., Price, E. and Srebro, N. (2016) 'Equality of opportunity in supervised learning', in Lee, D., Sugiyama, M., Luxburg, U., Guyon, I. and Garnett, R. (eds) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016). Barcelona, Spain, 5-10 December. Curran Associates, Inc., pp. 3315-3323. Available at: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2016/hash/6a9659feb1216f14f7384ba499518b38-Abstract.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes an 'oblivious' non-discrimination criterion for supervised learning, equalized odds, which requires the predictor Y-hat to be independent of the protected attribute A conditional on the true outcome Y; in the binary case this means equal true-positive rates and equal false-positive rates across groups. It introduces a weaker relaxation, equal opportunity, which imposes the constraint only within the advantaged outcome Y=1 (i.e. equal true-positive rates). The authors show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor or real-valued score to satisfy either criterion by a post-processing step that uses group-specific (for equalized odds, possibly randomized) thresholds chosen by a small linear program on the group-conditional ROC curves, minimising the loss in utility. They prove that applying this post-processing to a Bayes-optimal regressor yields the Bayes-optimal non-discriminating classifier, quantify the cost when the score is sub-optimal, discuss the inherent limits of oblivious measures for identifying discrimination, and illustrate the framework with a case study of FICO credit scores.

claims_supported.claim: Equalised odds requires equal true-positive and false-positive rates across groups; equal opportunity relaxes this to the true-positive rate; both can be achieved by post-processing thresholds.
claims_supported.where: Section 2, Definition 2.1 and the sentence following the binary-case formula: 'For the outcome y = 1, the constraint requires that Y-hat has equal true positive rates across the two demographics A = 0 and A = 1. For y = 0, the constraint equalizes false positive rates.' Section 2.1, Definition 2.2: equal opportunity requires Pr{Y-hat=1 | A=0, Y=1} = Pr{Y-hat=1 | A=1, Y=1}, introduced as 'a relaxation of equalized odds ... only within the advantaged outcome group' and described as 'a weaker, though still interesting, notion of non-discrimination'. Post-processing: Introduction (contributions): 'Rather than changing a possibly complex training pipeline, the result follows via a simple post-processing step that minimizes the loss in utility.' Section 2.2 (end): 'equalized odds predictors can be derived from [scores] and the protected attribute A, by using different (possibly randomized) thresholds depending on the value of A. The same is possible for equality of opportunity without the need for randomized thresholds.' Section 4 ('Achieving equalized odds and equality of opportunity'), Definition 4.1 (derived predictor), Proposition 4.4 (linear program) and the paragraphs 'Deriving an optimal equalized odds threshold predictor' / 'Deriving an optimal equal opportunity threshold predictor' (Figure 2). Abstract: 'we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition.'

references.verification_notes: Existence verified at the NeurIPS proceedings site (papers.nips.cc/paper/6374-equality-of-opportunity-in-supervised-learning and proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2016/hash/6a9659feb1216f14f7384ba499518b38-Abstract.html), which lists it as part of Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016), authors Moritz Hardt, Eric Price, Nati Srebro; the official bibtex gives editors D. Lee, M. Sugiyama, U. Luxburg, I. Guyon, R. Garnett, publisher Curran Associates, Inc., volume 29, year 2016 (pages field empty). The proceedings Metadata.json gives page_first 3315, page_last 3323 and conference '30th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2016), Barcelona, Spain'; this publisher record is used for the page range. Discrepancy: the Technion CRIS record (Scopus ID 85018874612, ISSN 1049-5258) gives pages 3323-3331 and conference dates 5-10 December 2016; some citations in the literature use each range. Crossref has no record of the proceedings paper (query.bibliographic search returned unrelated works), so no DOI exists for the cited proceedings version; the doi field is therefore left empty. The arXiv preprint (arXiv:1610.02413, submitted 7 October 2016, cs.LG) carries DataCite DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1610.02413 and is indexed by OpenAlex as W2530395818 (2,248 citations at time of check); OpenAlex lists the author affiliations as Google, UT Austin and TTI-Chicago, matching the NeurIPS metadata. Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 on both attempts; ACM Digital Library (NIPS'16 record 10.5555/3157382.3157469) returned HTTP 403 and DBLP was blocked, so the 3323-3331 range could not be independently confirmed from those sources. Abstract taken verbatim from arXiv abs page; definitions and post-processing statements verified against the full text (arXiv PDF text extraction and ar5iv HTML). Author name: the NeurIPS/arXiv paper lists 'Nati Srebro'; OpenAlex and Technion give 'Nathan Srebro'; the Harvard reference uses the initial N., which covers both. Publisher place of publication was not verified from a fetched source and is omitted from the reference.
references.caveats: The paper's equal-opportunity definition is stated relative to the 'advantaged' outcome Y=1 (e.g. not defaulting on a loan), so in a churn setting the report should say which class is coded as Y=1 and that equal opportunity equalises the true-positive rate for that class only. For equalized odds the optimal post-processed predictor may require randomized (mixed) thresholds per group, whereas equal opportunity can be met with deterministic per-group thresholds; the report should not imply both are always plain deterministic threshold shifts. The optimality results (Corollary 5.3, Theorem 5.6) assume the post-processing starts from a (near) Bayes-optimal score, and the method requires access to the protected attribute at decision time.

references.title: Telco customer churn (11.1.3+)
references.venue: IBM Community: Cognos Analytics blog (Base Samples); mirrored on Kaggle by user BlastChar as 'Telco Customer Churn'
references.harvard_reference:
IBM (2019) 'Telco customer churn (11.1.3+)', IBM Community: Cognos Analytics blog, 11 July. Available at: https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/steven-macko/2019/07/11/telco-customer-churn-1113 (Accessed: 27 September 2026).

references.abstract_summary: Not a paper, so there is no abstract. The IBM Community post (by 'Samples Team', posted 11 July 2019, filed under the Cognos Analytics blog at the URL slug steven-macko) announces that, in IBM Cognos Analytics 11.1.3, the 'Telco Customer Churn' data module in the Base Samples was enhanced 'to provide a wider narrative'. It indicates which customers have left, stayed, or signed up for their service. Multiple important demographics are included for each customer, as well as a Satisfaction Score, Churn Score, and Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV) index.' The enhanced data module is composed of five uploaded files/tables (Demographics, Location, Population, Services, Status) and the post documents every field: the Status table includes Satisfaction Score, Customer Status (Churned/Stayed/Joined at the end of the quarter), Churn Label, Churn Value, Churn Score (0-100, from IBM SPSS Modeler), Churn Score Category, CLTV, CLTV Category, Churn Category and Churn Reason; the Services table adds fields absent from the Kaggle file (Offer, Referred a Friend, Number of Referrals, Avg Monthly Long Distance Charges, Avg Monthly GB Download, Streaming Music, Unlimited Data, Total Refunds, Total Extra Data Charges, Total Long Distance Charges). Four 'interesting scenarios' illustrate the narrative (e.g. churn clustered in San Diego-area zip codes with reason 'Competitor made better offer'; low satisfaction scores among churners; month-to-month contracts associated with churn). The Kaggle mirror (owner BlastChar, subtitle 'Focused customer retention programs', Version 1, one file WA_Fn-UseC_-Telco-Customer-Churn.csv, 977.5 kB) quotes '[IBM Sample Data Sets]' in its Context, states 'The raw data contains 7043 rows (customers) and 21 columns (features)', explains that the Churn column captures 'Customers who left within the last month', lists the service/account/demographic attribute groups, and links to the IBM Community post as the 'New version from IBM'.

claims_supported.claim: The data describe a fictional telco that provided home phone and internet services to 7,043 customers in California in Q3, and indicate which customers left, stayed or signed up within the last month.
claims_supported.where: PARTIAL ONLY (minor wording conflation). The first clause is supported verbatim by the IBM Community post's opening description: 'a fictional telco company that provided home phone and Internet services to 7043 customers in California in Q3. It indicates which customers have left, stayed, or signed up for their service.' However, the source never says customers 'stayed or signed up within the last month'. The phrase 'within the last month' appears in the post only in relation to the churn column ('The churn column indicates whether or not the customer left within the last month' in the data-module description, and the same wording for the Churn Label column in the 'Telco churn' dashboard and exploration descriptions), and the Kaggle page likewise says 'Customers who left within the last month - the column is called Churn'. Moreover, the post's own field dictionary defines the window as a quarter, not a month: 'Customer Status: Indicates the status of the customer at the end of the quarter: Churned, Stayed, or Joined' and 'Churn Label: Yes = the customer left the company this quarter'. Suggested fix: 'The data describe a fictional telco that provided home phone and internet services to 7,043 customers in California in Q3 and indicate which customers left, stayed or signed up for the service (IBM, 2019); in the Kaggle release the target column, Churn, flags customers who left within the last month (BlastChar, no date).' Written that way the claim is fully supported.

Full text of the post was read, including the five-table field dictionary quoted in the claim checks.
