references.title: Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations
references.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
references.harvard_reference: Kaplan, E.L. and Meier, P. (1958) 'Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations', Journal of the American Statistical Association, 53(282), pp. 457–481. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452.
references.abstract_summary: In life-testing and medical follow-up, observation of the time to the event of interest ('death') may be prevented for some sample items by an earlier 'loss' (what is now called right-censoring), which may be accidental or controlled; lifetime is assumed independent of potential loss time. The paper estimates P(t), the proportion of the population whose lifetimes would exceed t, without assuming any functional form for P(t). It defines the product-limit (PL) estimate as a product of factors (N - r)/(N - r + 1) over ordered observed death times up to t, and shows that it is the distribution, unrestricted as to form, that maximises the likelihood of the observations. It also discusses actuarial (grouped) estimates and reduced-sample estimates, and notes that all reduce to the binomial proportion of survivors when no losses occur before t.

claims_supported.claim: The product-limit estimator gives a nonparametric estimate of the survival function from censored data.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: the paper sets out to estimate P(t), the proportion of items whose lifetimes would exceed t (the survival function), 'without making any assumption about the form of the function P(t)' (nonparametric), from data made incomplete by 'losses' (censoring), and defines the product-limit (PL) estimate for this purpose. The paper uses the terms 'losses' and 'incomplete observations', not 'censored'; calling these 'censored' data follows standard later usage and is an accurate description.

claims_supported.claim: The product-limit estimator presupposes a random sample in which each item is observed from its initial event (no left truncation).
claims_supported.where: Abstract (OpenAlex record of the JASA paper): observation of each item's initial event is presupposed and the PL estimate is defined for random samples; checked by an independent critic on 31 October 2026.

references.verification_notes: Metadata confirmed via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452): authors E. L. Kaplan (University of California Radiation Laboratory) and Paul Meier (University of Chicago); title 'Nonparametric Estimation from Incomplete Observations'; Journal of the American Statistical Association, vol. 53, issue 282, pp. 457-481; print publication June 1958 (online version on Taylor & Francis dated 12 April 2012); publisher Informa UK Limited (Taylor & Francis); type journal-article. OpenAlex matches all fields (1958, 53(282), 457-481) and supplied the full abstract. Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 404 for the DOI lookup and the Taylor & Francis landing page returned HTTP 403, so the abstract comes from OpenAlex only. JASA is a long-established peer-reviewed journal of the American Statistical Association, so this is not a predatory venue. The lead metadata (authors, year, title, journal, volume, issue, DOI) is correct; the page range 457-481 was added from Crossref. Title is given in sentence case per Cite Them Right. Strictness note: the original text says 'losses' and 'incomplete observations' rather than 'censored'; the claim is a faithful modern restatement.

references.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science
references.harvard_reference: Kapoor, S. and Narayanan, A. (2023) 'Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science', Patterns, 4(9), 100804. doi:10.1016/j.patter.2023.100804.
references.abstract_summary: The authors systematically investigate reproducibility problems in machine-learning-based science, focusing on data leakage. A literature survey across research communities that have adopted ML finds 22 papers in 17 fields reporting leakage, collectively affecting 294 papers and in some cases producing wildly overoptimistic conclusions. From this survey they build a taxonomy of eight leakage types grouped under three headings: (L1) lack of clean train/test separation, comprising no test set, pre-processing on training and test set, feature selection on training and test set, and duplicates in datasets; (L2) model uses illegitimate features; and (L3) test set not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest, comprising temporal leakage, non-independence between train and test samples, and sampling bias. They propose 'model info sheets', a 21-question template that requires researchers to argue explicitly that each type of leakage is absent, as a means to detect and prevent leakage. Finally, a reproducibility study of civil-war prediction shows that once leakage errors are corrected, complex ML models do not substantively outperform decades-old logistic regression.

claims_supported.claim: Data leakage (including pre-processing on the full dataset before splitting and duplicates across train and test) is a pervasive cause of over-optimistic results across many fields; they propose model info sheets to prevent it.
claims_supported.where: Abstract/Summary: leakage found in 17 fields, affecting 294 papers, 'in some cases, leading to wildly overoptimistic conclusions'; 'We propose that researchers test for each type of leakage by filling out model info sheets, which we introduce.' Taxonomy (Section 'A taxonomy of leakage', Table 1 / Figure 1): item [L1.2] 'Pre-processing on training and test set' and item [L1.4] 'Duplicates in datasets' are explicitly named leakage types under [L1] 'Lack of clean separation of training and test dataset'. Body text: 'leakage usually leads to inflated estimates of model performance' and 'We introduce model info sheets to detect and prevent leakage in ML-based science ... by answering 21 questions based on our taxonomy of leakage.'

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified via the Crossref REST API (DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100804; Elsevier BV; journal-article; Patterns; volume 4, issue 9, page/article-number 100804; issued 2023-09; authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan). Abstract retrieved from the Semantic Scholar Graph API (PMID 37720327; PMC10499856; Gold open access, CC BY). Full text checked on PubMed Central (PMC10499856), which confirms the eight-type taxonomy including [L1.2] pre-processing on training and test set and [L1.4] duplicates in datasets, the 17-field/294-paper finding, the statement that leakage inflates performance estimates, and the 21-question model info sheets. Date nuance: the article was published online 4 August 2023 and appears in the September 2023 issue (4(9)); the citation year 2023 is unaffected. The lead's citation details were accurate. The paper's exact wording is '17 fields' and '294 papers' rather than 'pervasive'; the report should keep the claim tied to those figures rather than implying the authors quantified prevalence across all of ML science. Note also that the paper does not study the Telco churn dataset; it is a general methodological source.

references.title: Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores
references.venue: 8th Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference (ITCS 2017), Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs), edited by Christos H. Papadimitriou. Schloss Dagstuhl - Leibniz-Zentrum fuer Informatik. Conference held Berkeley, CA, USA, 9-11 January 2017; volume published 28 November 2017.
references.harvard_reference: Kleinberg, J., Mullainathan, S. and Raghavan, M. (2017) 'Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores', in Papadimitriou, C.H. (ed.) 8th Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference (ITCS 2017). Berkeley, CA, USA, 9-11 January 2017. Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs), vol. 67. Dagstuhl: Schloss Dagstuhl - Leibniz-Zentrum fuer Informatik, pp. 43:1-43:23. doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.43.
references.abstract_summary: The paper responds to public debate (notably around the COMPAS recidivism tool) over what it means for a probabilistic risk score to be fair to different demographic groups. It formalises three fairness conditions for risk assignments across two groups: (A) calibration within groups, (B) balance for the negative class (equal average score for true negatives in each group) and (C) balance for the positive class (equal average score for true positives in each group). Its main theorem shows that no risk assignment can satisfy all three at once unless the instance admits perfect prediction (every feature vector has positive-class probability 0 or 1) or the two groups have equal base rates. A second theorem shows the impossibility is robust: approximately satisfying all three conditions forces the data to be approximately in one of those two special cases. The authors present this as a framework for reasoning about unavoidable trade-offs between fairness notions.

claims_supported.claim: Calibration within groups, balance for the positive class and balance for the negative class cannot all be satisfied simultaneously except in trivial cases (equal base rates or perfect prediction), so fairness definitions are mutually incompatible.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 43:1): 'except in highly constrained special cases, there is no method that can satisfy these three conditions simultaneously'. Section 1, 'The present work: Trade-offs among the guarantees' (p. 43:3): the conditions 'are in general incompatible with each other; they can only be simultaneously satisfied in certain highly constrained cases'. Section 1.1 (p. 43:5) defines (A) Calibration within groups, (B) Balance for the negative class, (C) Balance for the positive class. Section 1.2, Theorem 1.1 (p. 43:6): an instance with a risk assignment satisfying (A), (B) and (C) 'must either allow for perfect prediction (with p_sigma equal to 0 or 1 for all sigma) or have equal base rates'. Theorem 1.2 (p. 43:6) extends this to epsilon-approximate versions of the conditions. Caveat on wording: the paper calls the two exceptions 'highly constrained special cases' rather than 'trivial', and its incompatibility result concerns these three specific conditions (under a two-group model with known p_sigma); it does not claim that all fairness definitions in general are mutually incompatible, so the report should phrase the generalisation as 'these key fairness notions' rather than 'fairness definitions' at large.

references.verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-27. The Crossref bibliographic search returned only the 2023 ACM book-chapter reprints (DOIs 10.1145/3603195.3603206 and 10.1145/3603195.3603197 in 'The Societal Impacts of Algorithmic Decision-Making'); the ITCS 2017 LIPIcs version is registered with DataCite, not Crossref (Crossref /works/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.43 returns 404). DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.43 was confirmed via the DataCite API (creators Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan, Manish Raghavan; publisher Schloss Dagstuhl; year 2017; LIPIcs vol. 67, article 43, pp. 43:1-43:23; ISBN 978-3-95977-029-3; ISSN 1868-8969; CC BY 3.0), the DROPS landing page, the LIPIcs volume 67 page (editor Christos H. Papadimitriou; ITCS 2017, Berkeley, CA, USA, 9-11 January 2017; published 28 November 2017) and the published PDF itself, whose footer reads 'Editor: Christos H. Papadimitrou [sic]; Article No. 43; pp. 43:1-43:23'. Author affiliations from the PDF: Kleinberg and Raghavan (Cornell University), Mullainathan (Harvard University). Abstract and Theorems 1.1/1.2 confirmed from the published PDF text (pp. 43:1, 43:5-43:6) and cross-checked against the arXiv version (arXiv:1609.05807, v1 19 Sep 2016, v2 17 Nov 2016) via ar5iv. Semantic Scholar lists year 2016 (the arXiv date) and an incorrect venue string ('Information Technology Convergence and Services'); the correct venue is ITCS 2017 / LIPIcs 67 and the citation year should be 2017. OpenAlex (W2962922665) agrees on 2017 and the DOI, reporting 616 citations. The lead reference supplied was accurate. No 'issue' field applies to a LIPIcs volume, so it is left empty. The report should use the published spelling 'Trade-Offs' (hyphenated) in the title; the 2023 ACM reprint uses 'Tradeoffs'.

references.title: Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
references.harvard_reference: Kozodoi, N., Jacob, J. and Lessmann, S. (2022) 'Fairness in credit scoring: assessment, implementation and profit implications', European Journal of Operational Research, 297(3), pp. 1083-1094. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2021.06.023.
references.abstract_summary: The paper examines fair machine learning in credit scoring. It (1) reviews statistical group-fairness criteria (independence, separation, sufficiency) and assesses whether they suit credit scoring, (2) catalogues pre-, in- and post-processing algorithms for building fairness into the ML pipeline, and (3) benchmarks fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring setting on real-world data. The authors find that several fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once, and they recommend separation as the criterion for scorecard fairness. Fair in-processors give a good balance of profit and fairness, and algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at relatively low cost. Code is available on GitHub.

claims_supported.claim: Enforcing group-fairness constraints in a profit-driven scoring model costs profit, and the profit-fairness trade-off can be quantified; some fairness criteria are more compatible with profit than others.
claims_supported.where: Abstract ('clarify the profit-fairness trade-off'; discrimination reduced 'at a relatively low cost'). Section 6.1 and Table 4 (arXiv 2103.01907 preprint numbering): independence and separation have moderate negative rank correlations with profit (about -0.38 and -0.30), and adding fairness constraints 'decreases profit'. Sufficiency has a weak positive correlation with profit (about 0.16), so 'profit maximization is compatible with maximizing sufficiency'. That is the evidence for some criteria being more compatible with profit than others. Section 6.2 and Table 5: profit loss for each processor relative to the unconstrained scorecard (e.g. over 30% for reject option classification, under 5% for the prejudice remover, 23% for reweighing). Section 6.3, 'The Cost of Fairness', and Figure 2: Pareto frontiers put a number on the trade-off. Bringing separation below 0.2 costs under EUR 0.01 profit per EUR issued, an average profit reduction of 4.91%. Perfect separation (0) needs a profit sacrifice of more than 35%. Caveat: the evidence comes from credit scoring (profit is based on EMP), not churn. The criterion found compatible with profit is sufficiency, which the authors themselves consider a questionable fairness notion.

claims_supported.claim: Fairness processors (pre-, in- and post-processing) were empirically compared on real credit data.
claims_supported.where: Abstract ('we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data'). Section 1 (seven real-world credit scoring data sets). Section 5.1, Table 2 (data sets german, taiwan, pakdd, gmsc, homecredit, bene, uk). Section 5.2: eight processors were compared: pre-processors reweighing and disparate impact remover; in-processors prejudice remover, adversarial debiasing and meta fair algorithm; post-processors reject option classification, equalized odds processor and Platt scaling. They were tested against an unconstrained profit-maximising scorecard, using four base classifiers (LR, ANN, RF, XGB) with 5-fold cross-validation. Age was the sensitive attribute.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.ejor.2021.06.023) confirms the authors Nikita Kozodoi, Johannes Jacob and Stefan Lessmann, the title, and the journal European Journal of Operational Research (Elsevier BV). It also confirms volume 297, issue 3, pages 1083-1094, print issue March 2022 and online publication 18 June 2021. Crossref returned no abstract. The abstract comes from the Semantic Scholar Graph API, which gives year 2021 (the online-first date) and links the arXiv preprint 2103.01907. The reference uses 2022, the year of the issue, which matches the lead. EJOR is an established peer-reviewed Elsevier OR journal, not a predatory venue. Claims were checked against the full text of the arXiv preprint (text extracted locally from arxiv.org/pdf/2103.01907). Section, table and figure numbers follow the preprint and may differ slightly from the published version. Page-specific pinpoints in the published version could not be checked because the publisher PDF is paywalled. Relevance caveat for a telecom churn report: this is a credit scoring study. It supports points about the profit-fairness trade-off and fairness processors by analogy only. Its profit measure builds on the EMP framework of Verbraken et al. (2014), which parallels profit-based churn evaluation (EMPC). All lead metadata matched; no discrepancies were found.

references.title: Customer churn prediction system: a machine learning approach
references.harvard_reference: Lalwani, P., Mishra, M.K., Chadha, J.S. and Sethi, P. (2022) 'Customer churn prediction system: a machine learning approach', Computing, 104(2), pp. 271-294. doi:10.1007/s00607-021-00908-y.
references.abstract_summary: The paper presents a six-phase pipeline for telecom customer churn prediction: data pre-processing, feature analysis, feature selection with a gravitational search algorithm (GSA), an 80/20 train/test split, model fitting (logistic regression, naive Bayes, SVM with linear and polynomial kernels, decision tree, random forest, KNN, and boosting/ensemble variants including AdaBoost, AdaBoost with extra trees, AdaBoost-wrapped random forest/SVM/logistic regression, XGBoost and CatBoost), 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation on the test set with confusion-matrix metrics and AUC. The abstract reports that AdaBoost and XGBoost gave the highest accuracy (81.71% and 80.8%) and that both reached the highest AUC of 84%. The dataset is not named in the abstract, but Table 2 ('Feature vector and their types') lists the 21 fields of the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn file (customer id, gender, senior citizen, partner, dependents, tenure, phone service, multiple lines, internet service, online security, online backup, device protection, tech support, streaming TV, streaming movies, contract, paperless billing, payment method, monthly charges, total charges, churn). Table 6 ('Comparison of machine learning models', test set) gives accuracy / AUC of: logistic regression 80.45% / 82; decision tree 80.14% / 83; random forest 78.04% / 82; random forest (AdaBoost) 81.21% / 82; AdaBoost 81.71% / 84; AdaBoost (extra tree) 81.14% / 72; KNN 79.64% / 80; naive Bayes 77.07% / 80; SVM linear 79.14% / 79; SVM poly 80.21% / 80; SVM (AdaBoost) 74.07% / 80; logistic regression (AdaBoost) 76.57% / 78; XGBoost 80.8% / 84; CatBoost 81.8% / 82. Table 3 gives 5-fold CV accuracies (logistic regression 79.85, decision tree 79.56, random forest 79.28, AdaBoost 80.72, XGBoost 79.5, CatBoost 80.34, KNN 78.51, naive Bayes 75.86).

claims_supported.claim: On the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset, boosting methods (AdaBoost/XGBoost) reached about 81 % accuracy, with tree ensembles and logistic regression finishing close together.
claims_supported.where: Accuracy figures: Abstract ('Adaboost and XGboost Classifier gives the highest accuracy of 81.71% and 80.8% respectively'; both AUC 84%) and Table 6 'Comparison of machine learning models' (AdaBoost 81.71%, XGBoost 80.8%, CatBoost 81.8%, random forest (AdaBoost) 81.21%, AdaBoost (extra tree) 81.14%, logistic regression 80.45%, decision tree 80.14%, plain random forest 78.04%). Dataset: Table 2 'Feature vector and their types' lists exactly the 21 fields of the Kaggle/IBM Telco Customer Churn file; the accessible portions of the paper (abstract, tables, figure captions) do not print the words 'Kaggle' or 'IBM', so the attribution rests on that field-for-field schema match plus citing works (Jagini, 2025, Stockholm University MSc thesis, Table 2.1 labels the Lalwani results 'IBM Telco Customer Churn Dataset'; a 2025 citing paper indexed by Semantic Scholar describes the study as using 'the Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records, 21 attributes)'). 'Finishing close together' is the report's reading of Table 6, not a sentence in the paper: logistic regression (80.45%) sits within about 1.4 points of the boosted tree ensembles (80.8-81.8%), and a citing paper (Akan et al., 2022, IEEE UEMCON) summarises the conclusion as XGBoost and AdaBoost best 'with no significant difference'. Two qualifications: (i) plain random forest scored 78.04%, 2.4 points BELOW logistic regression, so the wording should be 'boosted tree ensembles' or should acknowledge random forest; (ii) CatBoost (81.8%) narrowly exceeded AdaBoost (81.71%) in Table 6, so do not describe AdaBoost/XGBoost as the single best models, only as reaching about 81%.

Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 233947001, DBLP journals/computing/LalwaniMCS22, 283 citations at check) and OpenAlex agree on authors/title/venue but both withhold the abstract and list year 2021 (online-first); the volume/issue version is 2022, which is the year used in the reference. Unpaywall: closed access, no OA copy. Verbatim abstract obtained from the Springer landing page (reached through the idp.springer.com cookie redirect); it states received 19 June 2020, accepted 12 January 2021, published 14 February 2021, all authors at VIT Bhopal University. Springer's per-table sub-pages were readable despite the paywall: Table 1 (GSA notation), Table 2 (feature vector, 21 Telco fields), Table 3 (5-fold CV accuracy), Table 4 (confusion-matrix layout), Table 5 (CV AUC), Table 6 (test-set comparison, transcribed in full); Table 7 returned a login page. Figures 1-3 captions: 'Gravitational Search Algorithm', 'Exploratory Data Analysis (Monthly Charges vs Churn ...)', 'System Architecture'. The full body text (dataset section naming Kaggle/IBM, 7,043 rows) could not be read; ResearchGate, ACM DL and scite returned HTTP 403. Secondary confirmation of dataset and per-model figures: Jagini, A. (2025) 'Improving customer churn prediction using machine learning', MSc thesis, Stockholm University DSV (diva2:2045966), Table 2.1, reproduces LR 0.8045/0.82, NB 0.7707/0.80, SVM 0.7914/0.79, DT 0.8014/0.83, AdaBoost 0.8171/0.84, XGBoost 0.808/0.84, CatBoost 0.818/0.82 labelled 'IBM Telco Customer Churn Dataset' (values match Table 6); Akan et al. (2022, IEEE UEMCON) and Semantic Scholar citation contexts from 2025-2026 papers agree on AdaBoost/XGBoost as top performers and on the Telco dataset. The lead's details (authors, year 2022, title, Computing 104) were accurate; issue 2 and pp. 271-294 added.
references.caveats: 1) Results come from a single 80/20 split with no confidence intervals or repeated runs; differences of about one accuracy point between logistic regression, decision tree and the boosted ensembles are within plausible sampling noise, so 'close together' should be stated as an observation, not a statistically tested finding. 2) The abstract's claim that AdaBoost and XGBoost give the highest accuracy is not exactly borne out by the paper's own Table 6, where CatBoost (81.8%) edges AdaBoost (81.71%); cite AdaBoost/XGBoost for about 81% accuracy and the joint-best AUC of 84%, not as the outright winners. 3) Plain random forest (78.04%) underperformed logistic regression; only AdaBoost-wrapped random forest (81.21%) was close to the top. 4) Accuracy on this dataset (about 26.5% churners) is a weak headline metric: a majority-class predictor scores about 73.5%; the paper's AUC figures (84% for AdaBoost/XGBoost) are the more informative comparison. 5) The 5-fold CV accuracies in Table 3 (e.g. AdaBoost 80.72%, XGBoost 79.5%) are lower than the test-set values in Table 6, so quote which table you are using. 6) Figures were obtained after gravitational-search feature selection and the paper's tuning, so they are not directly comparable to a plain scikit-learn baseline on the raw Kaggle file. 7) The words 'Kaggle' and 'IBM' were not visible in the accessible parts of the paper; the dataset identification rests on the exact schema match and citing works.

references.title: Imbalanced-learn: A Python Toolbox to Tackle the Curse of Imbalanced Datasets in Machine Learning
references.harvard_reference: Lemaître, G., Nogueira, F. and Aridas, C.K. (2017) 'Imbalanced-learn: a Python toolbox to tackle the curse of imbalanced datasets in machine learning', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 18(17), pp. 1-5. Available at: http://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-365.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: A five-page software paper introducing imbalanced-learn, an open-source Python toolbox (MIT licence, scikit-learn-contrib project) that implements state-of-the-art methods for imbalanced datasets in four groups: under-sampling, over-sampling, combinations of both, and ensemble learning. It depends only on numpy, scipy and scikit-learn and is described as fully compatible with scikit-learn. Section 3 (Implementation design) describes the sampler API (fit, sample, fit_sample), gives a SMOTE code example, lists the implemented methods (ADASYN, SMOTE, random over/under-sampling, CNN, ENN, NearMiss, NCL, OSS, Tomek links, SMOTE+ENN, SMOTE+TL, BalanceCascade, EasyEnsemble, etc.) and states that a Pipeline class inherited from scikit-learn combines samplers, transformers and estimators. Section 4 gives brief background on each strategy; Section 5 outlines future work.

claims_supported.claim: imbalanced-learn provides resampling methods (including SMOTE) that integrate with scikit-learn pipelines so resampling is applied only to training folds.
claims_supported.where: PARTIALLY supported only. Supported parts: (a) the toolbox provides under-/over-sampling methods including SMOTE - Abstract; Section 3 'Implementation design' Listing 1 ('Code snippet to over-sample a dataset using SMOTE') and Table 1 listing SMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTE+ENN, SMOTE+TL etc. (pp. 2-3); (b) integration with scikit-learn pipelines - Abstract ('fully compatible with scikit-learn and is part of the scikit-learn-contrib supported project') and Section 3, p. 3: 'A class Pipeline is inherited from the scikit-learn toolbox to automatically combine samplers, transformers, and estimators.' NOT supported: the paper nowhere states that resampling is applied only during fit / only to the training folds / not to test data, nor does it discuss cross-validation or data leakage. Section 3 only describes fit, sample and fit_sample methods. That training-only behaviour is documented in the imbalanced-learn user guide, 'Common pitfalls and recommended practices' (Data leakage section), https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html, which states that using a Pipeline avoids data leakage because resampling is delegated to imbalanced-learn. Recommended fix: cite Lemaître et al. (2017) for 'provides resampling methods including SMOTE and a scikit-learn-compatible Pipeline', and cite the imbalanced-learn documentation (a separate web reference) for 'the Pipeline applies resampling only when fitting, so only training folds are resampled'.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified against the JMLR article page (https://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-365.html), the JMLR BibTeX file (https://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-365.bib: volume 18, number 17, pages 1--5, year 2017) and the published PDF header ('Journal of Machine Learning Research 18 (2017) 1-5, Submitted 7/16; Published 1/17', editor Geoff Holmes). The full PDF text was read to check the claim. DOI: none exists for the JMLR article - JMLR does not register DOIs and the Crossref bibliographic query returned no match for this title/author (only unrelated works). The only DOI found (OpenAlex W2521200999) is 10.48550/arXiv.1609.06570, which belongs to the 2016 arXiv preprint (submitted 21 Sept 2016), not the 2017 JMLR version; it is therefore not placed in the doi field. Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 on all attempts, so its abstract record could not be retrieved; the abstract was taken directly from the JMLR page and PDF instead. The lead reference was accurate except that it omitted the page range (pp. 1-5). Author surname carries a circumflex: Lemaître.

references.title: Managing churn to maximize profits
references.harvard_reference: Lemmens, A. and Gupta, S. (2020) 'Managing churn to maximize profits', Marketing Science, 39(5), pp. 956-973. doi:10.1287/mksc.2020.1229.
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes a profit-based loss function for targeting proactive customer-retention campaigns. Instead of ranking customers by predicted churn probability (the conventional churn model) or by churn uplift (responsiveness to the offer), it predicts each customer's expected profit lift: the incremental effect of the retention intervention on churn and on post-campaign cash flows, net of the intervention cost. The loss function also weights prediction errors by each customer's expected profit lift, so the model is most accurate for the customers who matter most to campaign profit, and the authors add a procedure to optimise the campaign's target size. Estimation uses stochastic gradient boosting on data from randomised experiments (heterogeneous treatment effects on churn and cash flows). Two field experiments, a European interactive-TV subscription firm and a North American membership organisation, show that the profit-based approach yields significantly higher campaign profit than churn-classification, reordered-churn and uplift benchmarks.

claims_supported.claim: Optimising the targeting model with a profit-based loss function, rather than a classification-accuracy loss, increases campaign profit.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'Two field experiments affirm that our approach leads to significantly more profitable campaigns than competing models.' Section 7.3.1 / Table 1 (accepted manuscript pp. 22-23): in Study 1 the campaign profit for the profit-based loss is 168% higher than for the 'classic loss' (a stochastic-gradient-boosting churn model trained with the standard churn-classification loss, Section 6.1.1), 300% higher than the reordered classic loss and 23% higher than the uplift model; in Study 2 only the profit-based approach yields a positive campaign profit. The authors state the classic loss 'produces the lowest profit, because it is the only estimation method that optimizes a non-profit-related criterion' and that firms 'need to align their estimation method, and in particular their loss function, with their evaluation criterion'. Section 7.3.9 replicates with logistic regression vs profit-weighted regression: EUR 3,331 vs EUR 4,907 (Study 1) and minus USD 1,112 vs USD 416 (Study 2), p < .01. Caveat from Section 7.3.8 / Table 3: the classic loss remains the most accurate at predicting churn itself (Gini, top-decile lift), so the paper's claim is about campaign profit, not predictive accuracy.

claims_supported.claim: Customer heterogeneity in value and response should drive retention targeting decisions.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: conventional churn-probability and responsiveness approaches 'ignore that some customers contribute more to the profitability of retention campaigns than others'; the method ranks customers on 'the incremental impact of the intervention on churn and post-campaign cash flows, after accounting for the cost of the intervention'. Introduction (manuscript pp. 1-2): 'not all customers are equally valuable, and incorrectly predicting the churn risk or lift would be costlier for some customers than others'; targeting on churn lift alone may select customers whose profit lift is negative. Section 5.1 estimates heterogeneous treatment effects of the intervention on churn and on cash flows separately. Section 7.3.5 shows that target-size rules based on aggregate metrics that 'do not reflect customer heterogeneity in profit lift' yield 93% and 84% less profit. Nuance: the paper's own construct is heterogeneity in profit lift (response to the offer in churn and cash flows, net of cost); 'value and response' is a fair paraphrase, but the report should not attribute a customer-lifetime-value framing to the paper.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified from the Crossref record for DOI 10.1287/mksc.2020.1229 (journal-article, Marketing Science, vol. 39, issue 5, pp. 956-973, INFORMS, published-print September 2020, ISSN 0732-2399 / 1526-548X) and from OpenAlex (W2115769109; online publication date 2020-08-27; affiliations Erasmus University Rotterdam and Harvard Business School). Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 404 for the DOI lookup and 429 for title search; INFORMS, SSRN and HBS landing pages returned HTTP 403, so the abstract was confirmed on the Erasmus University Pure repository page and the full text was checked in the author-hosted accepted manuscript (aurelielemmens.com, dated 6 Dec 2019, marked 'Forthcoming at Marketing Science', 56 pages). Section numbers and page references above refer to that manuscript, not to the published pagination. The lead reference was accurate in every field it gave. Earlier versions exist as HBS Working Paper 14-020 (2013) and SSRN 2964906 (2017); cite the 2020 Marketing Science version.
references.caveats: The report's Telco Customer Churn (Kaggle) dataset has no randomised treatment/control assignment, no intervention cost and no post-campaign cash flows, so Lemmens and Gupta's profit-lift method cannot be replicated on it; cite the paper for the principle that the loss function should be aligned with the business (profit) objective and that customers differ in retention value, not as a method the report implements. Do not cite it as evidence that a profit-based loss improves churn-classification accuracy: Table 3 shows the opposite. Percentage figures (168%, 300%, 23%) come from the accepted manuscript and should be checked against the published version before quoting them verbatim.

references.title: A unified approach to interpreting model predictions
references.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017), Long Beach, CA, USA. Curran Associates, Inc.
references.harvard_reference: Lundberg, S.M. and Lee, S.-I. (2017) 'A unified approach to interpreting model predictions', in Guyon, I. et al. (eds) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017). Long Beach, CA, USA. Curran Associates, Inc., pp. 4765-4774. Available at: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/8a20a8621978632d76c43dfd28b67767-Abstract.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that understanding why a model makes a prediction matters as much as accuracy, but the most accurate models (ensembles, deep networks) are hard to interpret, and the many post-hoc explanation methods proposed have unclear relationships. It introduces SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a unified framework that assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its two novel components are (1) identifying a new class of additive feature attribution methods and (2) theoretical results showing a unique solution in that class with desirable properties. The class unifies six existing methods (LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values and Quantitative Input Influence), several of which lack those properties. Building on this, the authors propose new estimation methods (e.g. Kernel SHAP, Deep SHAP) with better computational performance and/or closer agreement with human intuition.

claims_supported.claim: SHAP values unify several additive feature-attribution methods under Shapley-value axioms (local accuracy, missingness, consistency) and provide per-prediction explanations.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP ... SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction ... The new class unifies six existing methods'. Section 2 (Additive Feature Attribution Methods) shows LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values and Quantitative Input Influence all fit Definition 1. Section 3 (Simple Properties Uniquely Determine Additive Feature Attributions) states Property 1 (Local accuracy), Property 2 (Missingness) and Property 3 (Consistency), and Theorem 1 proves the Shapley-value formula (Eq. 8) is the only explanation model satisfying all three. Section 4 defines SHAP values as this unique solution. Note the paper calls these 'properties' (from cooperative game theory) rather than 'axioms'; the substance of the claim is accurate.

references.verification_notes: Crossref bibliographic search returned only unrelated works (NeurIPS proceedings are not Crossref-registered), so the work was verified directly at the official proceedings site (papers.nips.cc / proceedings.neurips.cc abstract page and bibtex), via Semantic Scholar (arXiv:1705.07874; CorpusId 21889700; venue Neural Information Processing Systems; pages 4765-4774) and via OpenAlex. The official NeurIPS PDF was downloaded and its text extracted: the running header reads '31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017), Long Beach, CA, USA'; embedded metadata gives Book = 'Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30', firstpage 4765, lastpage 4774, Publisher = Curran Associates, Inc., Editors = I. Guyon, U.V. Luxburg, S. Bengio, H. Wallach, R. Fergus, S. Vishwanathan, R. Garnett, EventType = Oral. The official bibtex lists volume 30, the same editors and publisher, but leaves the pages field empty; the page range 4765-4774 comes from the PDF metadata and Semantic Scholar. Section 2, Section 3 (Properties 1-3, Theorem 1) and the abstract sentence on per-prediction importance were confirmed verbatim in the extracted text and independently in the ar5iv rendering of the arXiv version. DOI field left empty because the proceedings paper has no registered DOI; the arXiv preprint carries the arXiv-assigned DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1705.07874 (OpenAlex), which identifies the preprint rather than the NeurIPS version. Issue field is not applicable. Conference dates and publisher place were not verified in this session and are therefore omitted from the reference.
references.caveats: No DOI exists for the NeurIPS proceedings version; if the report's reference list requires a DOI, cite the arXiv preprint separately as Lundberg, S.M. and Lee, S.-I. (2017) 'A unified approach to interpreting model predictions', arXiv. doi:10.48550/arXiv.1705.07874 - but be aware the arXiv text lacks the NeurIPS header and pagination. The paper itself uses the term 'properties' rather than 'axioms' for local accuracy, missingness and consistency. The lead's 'NeurIPS 30' is fine in substance, but the 2017 conference was branded 'NIPS 2017' at the time; the proceedings series is 'Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30'.

references.title: From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees
references.harvard_reference: Lundberg, S.M., Erion, G., Chen, H., DeGrave, A., Prutkin, J.M., Nair, B., Katz, R., Himmelfarb, J., Bansal, N. and Lee, S.-I. (2020) 'From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees', Nature Machine Intelligence, 2(1), pp. 56-67. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0138-9.
references.abstract_summary: The paper improves the interpretability of tree-based models (random forests, decision trees, gradient boosted trees) via TreeExplainer, with three contributions: (1) the first polynomial-time algorithm to compute optimal game-theoretic (Shapley value) explanations for trees; (2) SHAP interaction values, a new explanation type that directly measures local feature interaction effects; and (3) tools for understanding global model structure by combining many local explanations (e.g. SHAP summary plots, dependence plots, global importance from aggregated SHAP values). Applied to three medical datasets, the tools identify rare high-magnitude non-linear mortality risk factors, population subgroups with shared risk characteristics, non-linear interaction effects in chronic kidney disease risk, and features degrading a deployed hospital model's performance over time.

claims_supported.claim: TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles in polynomial time, and local explanations can be aggregated into global feature importance and dependence plots.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (contribution 1: 'first polynomial time algorithm to compute optimal explanations based on game theory'; contribution 3: global tools 'based on combining many local explanations'); main text states TreeExplainer enables the exact computation of Shapley values in low-order polynomial time; Methods (Tree SHAP) gives worst-case complexity O(TLD^2) (T trees, L leaves, D max depth); section 'Local explanations as building blocks for global insights' and Fig. 4 describe global feature importance from aggregated (mean absolute) SHAP values, SHAP summary plots and SHAP dependence plots.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s42256-019-0138-9): 10 authors in the order given, title, Nature Machine Intelligence, vol. 2, issue 1, pp. 56-67, published online 17 January 2020, publisher Springer Science and Business Media LLC, type journal-article. Abstract and external IDs cross-checked via Semantic Scholar (PMID 32607472, PMCID PMC7326367). Full text (author manuscript) checked on PubMed Central for the claim. Nature Machine Intelligence is a peer-reviewed Springer Nature journal; not predatory. The lead's metadata is correct; issue number (1) added from Crossref. Note: the paper names the method TreeExplainer and the underlying algorithm Tree SHAP; exactness refers to exact Shapley values of the tree model's (path-dependent or interventional) conditional-expectation value function, which is how the paper frames it. Crossref did not list a published-print date; year 2020 taken from the online publication date and the volume.

references.title: Utilizing data sampling techniques on algorithmic fairness for customer churn prediction with data imbalance problems
references.harvard_reference: Maw, M., Haw, S.-C. and Ho, C.-K. (2022) 'Utilizing data sampling techniques on algorithmic fairness for customer churn prediction with data imbalance problems', F1000Research, 10, p. 988. Available at: https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.72929.2.
references.abstract_summary: The paper examines whether applying data sampling techniques (DSTs) to address class imbalance in customer churn prediction (CCP) affects algorithmic fairness between male and female customers. Three versions of a real-world telecom dataset with different churn rates (5%, 15%, 30%) were prepared, four DSTs (Random Over Sampler, Random Under Sampler, SMOTE, ADASYN) were applied, and six classifiers were evaluated on both predictive performance and fairness metrics (statistical parity difference and disparate impact, with gender as the protected attribute). Random Forest performed best on all three datasets; SMOTE and ADASYN produced more discrimination against the female group; and unintentional discrimination appeared higher in the original (unsampled) data of the extremely imbalanced dataset under Logistic Regression, LightGBM and XGBoost.

claims_supported.claim: Applying resampling techniques (SMOTE, ADASYN) to imbalanced churn data can change group fairness outcomes (e.g. gender disparity) in churn prediction.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Results): 'using SMOTE and ADASYN techniques causes more discrimination in the female group'; Methods define gender as the protected attribute (female = protected group) with statistical parity and disparate impact (0.8 threshold) as fairness metrics; Results/Discussion fairness tables compare original vs resampled data (for the 5% churn dataset, the reported statistical parity difference moves from about -0.0056 on original data to about 0.14 under SMOTE/ADASYN). Caveat: evidence comes from a single proprietary Telekom Malaysia dataset, not the Kaggle Telco data, so cite it as evidence that resampling can alter fairness, not as a result on the Telco dataset.

claims_supported.claim: The study uses the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset (state which dataset it actually uses).
claims_supported.where: Methods (dataset) and Data availability: the study uses a proprietary real-world telecom dataset from the Business Intelligence and Analytics department of Telekom Malaysia Bhd (1,265,535 customer records, January-December 2011, 22 features incl. gender). A random sample of 100,000 records was drawn, and three imbalanced versions were prepared (5%, 15% and 30% churn). The IBM Cognos 'Telco Customer Churn' sample and Kaggle Telco Customer Churn datasets appear only in the Data availability statement as representative alternative datasets for readers, and are not analysed in the paper.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.12688/f1000research.72929.2) confirms: authors Maw Maw (Crossref given='Maw', family='Maw'; a mononymous Burmese name, so 'Maw, M.' is correct Harvard form), Su-Cheng Haw (ORCID 0000-0002-7190-0837), Chin-Kuan Ho; title as above; container F1000Research; volume 10; article/page 988; no issue number; version 2 published online 27 June 2022; publisher F1000 Research Ltd; CC-BY 4.0. Version 1 (doi:10.12688/f1000research.72929.1) was published 30 Sep 2021, so volume 10 is the 2021 volume, but the year of the cited version 2 is 2022. Semantic Scholar lists year 2021 (the v1 date), PMID 36071889 and PMCID PMC9428497. The abstract was taken from the Crossref record. Dataset and review details were checked on the F1000Research v2 landing page and the PMC full text. F1000Research peer-review status (post-publication open peer review): Version 1 had two reports, Chu Kiong Loo (University of Malaya, 11 Jan 2022) and Prabu P (CHRIST University, 24 Feb 2022), both 'Approved with reservations'. Version 2 had one report, Kok-Chin Khor (Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman, 30 Aug 2022), 'Approved'. The overall status is 1 approved and 2 approved with reservations, which meets F1000Research's indexing threshold; the article is indexed in PubMed/PMC. The venue is not predatory, but it uses post-publication peer review, so it is less rigorous than conventional pre-publication review. The specific fairness values in claim 1 (SPD about 0.14 vs -0.0056; a reported DI of about 1.32) were extracted via page summarisation of the PMC full text and should be checked against the paper's tables before quoting exact numbers.
references.caveats: Does NOT use the Kaggle/IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset; it uses a proprietary Telekom Malaysia dataset (2011), so it cannot be cited as prior work on the Telco dataset. The abstract's 'three real-world datasets' are three imbalance-rate versions (5%, 15%, 30%) of one source dataset, not three independent datasets. The findings come from one operator's data and may not generalise. F1000Research uses post-publication peer review: v1 was 'Approved with reservations' by two reviewers and v2 was 'Approved' by one. Cite version 2 (2022) with its DOI.

references.title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
references.harvard_reference: Mehrabi, N., Morstatter, F., Saxena, N., Lerman, K. and Galstyan, A. (2021) 'A survey on bias and fairness in machine learning', ACM Computing Surveys, 54(6), pp. 1-35. doi:10.1145/3457607.
references.abstract_summary: A broad survey of bias and fairness in machine learning. The authors motivate the topic with real-world cases of discriminatory algorithmic outcomes (Section 2, e.g. the COMPAS recidivism tool's higher false-positive rate for African-American defendants and facial-recognition benchmarks skewed by skin colour and gender). Section 3 organises sources of bias into a feedback loop between data, algorithms and users (Figure 1): 3.1.1 'Data to Algorithm' (measurement, omitted-variable, representation, aggregation, sampling, longitudinal-data and related biases in data), 3.1.2 'Algorithm to User' (algorithmic, user-interaction, presentation, ranking, popularity, emergent and evaluation bias) and 3.1.3 'User to Data' (historical, population, self-selection, social, behavioural, temporal and content-production bias in user-generated data). It then distinguishes types of discrimination (direct vs indirect, explainable vs unexplainable, systemic vs statistical). Section 4 gives a taxonomy of fairness definitions (equalised odds, equal opportunity, demographic parity, fairness through awareness, fairness through unawareness, treatment equality, test fairness, counterfactual fairness, subgroup fairness, conditional statistical parity) and Table 1 classifies them as group, subgroup or individual notions. Later sections review bias-mitigation methods (pre-, in- and post-processing), the unfairness observed across AI subdomains, and open challenges. The abstract states the aim is to list sources of bias affecting AI applications, create a taxonomy of fairness definitions, and motivate researchers to address bias.

claims_supported.claim: Bias can enter ML systems through data, algorithms and user interaction; the survey catalogues sources of bias and fairness definitions and notes that removing protected attributes does not remove bias because of proxies.
claims_supported.where: Composite claim; each component is verified separately below (1a, 1b, 1c). Components 1a and 1b are stated explicitly by the paper. Component 1c is supported in substance by the paper's treatment of indirect discrimination (Section 3.3.2) and its discussion of proxy discrimination, but the paper does not use the exact wording 'removing protected attributes does not remove bias' and does not critique the fairness-through-unawareness definition directly; see 1c for recommended phrasing.

claims_supported.claim: 1a. Bias can enter ML systems through data, algorithms and user interaction (a feedback loop between the three).
claims_supported.where: Introduction (Section 1): 'biased algorithmic outcomes might impact user experience, thus generating a feedback loop between data, algorithms and users that can perpetuate and even amplify existing sources of bias.' Section 3 and Figure 1: 'Examples of bias definitions placed in the data, algorithm, and user interaction feedback loop... We use this loop to categorize definitions of bias.' Section 3.1: 'we will introduce a different categorization of these definitions in the paper according to the data, algorithm, and user interaction loop', with subsections 3.1.1 'Data to Algorithm', 3.1.2 'Algorithm to User' ('Algorithms modulate user behavior. Any biases in algorithms might introduce biases in user behavior') and 3.1.3 'User to Data' ('Any inherent biases in users might be reflected in the data they generate').

claims_supported.claim: 1b. The survey catalogues sources of bias and fairness definitions.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'we listed different sources of biases that can affect AI applications. We then created a taxonomy for fairness definitions that machine learning researchers have defined to avoid the existing bias in AI systems.' Section 3.1 'Types of Bias' lists and defines over twenty named biases (measurement, omitted variable, representation, aggregation, Simpson's paradox, longitudinal data fallacy, sampling, algorithmic, user interaction, presentation, ranking, popularity, emergent, evaluation, historical, population, self-selection, social, behavioural, temporal, content production). Section 4 'Algorithmic Fairness' gives numbered Definitions 1-10 (equalized odds, equal opportunity, demographic parity, fairness through awareness, fairness through unawareness, treatment equality, test fairness, counterfactual fairness, subgroup fairness, conditional statistical parity) and Table 1 'Categorizing different fairness notions into group, subgroup, and individual types'.

claims_supported.claim: 1c. Removing protected attributes does not remove bias because of proxies.
claims_supported.where: Section 3.3.2 (Types of Discrimination), item (2) Indirect Discrimination: 'individuals appear to be treated based on seemingly neutral and non-protected attributes; however, protected groups, or individuals still get to be treated unjustly as a result of implicit effects from their protected attributes (e.g., the residential zip code of a person can be used in decision making processes such as loan applications. However, this can still lead to racial discrimination, such as redlining, as despite the fact that zip code appears to be a non-sensitive attribute, it may correlate with race because of the population of residential areas.)' (citing [130, 164]). The paper also reproduces Kilbertus et al.'s causal-graph notion of 'proxy discrimination' (a path from the protected attribute A to a variable V that passes through a proxy variable) in its discussion of causal fairness methods. This is the substance of the claim: a decision rule that uses only non-protected attributes can still discriminate because those attributes act as proxies for protected ones. CAVEATS ON WORDING: (i) the paper does not use the phrase 'removing protected attributes does not remove bias'; it frames the point as indirect discrimination via correlated attributes. (ii) It presents 'Fairness Through Unawareness' (Definition 5: 'An algorithm is fair as long as any protected attributes A are not explicitly used in the decision-making process') neutrally as one definition in its taxonomy and does not explicitly criticise it in the text; do not cite Mehrabi et al. as arguing against that definition. (iii) The word 'proxy' in Section 3.1.1 (measurement bias in COMPAS, 'prior arrests... used as proxy variables to measure riskiness') refers to mismeasured proxies for the target variable, a different sense; do not conflate. Recommended phrasing for the report: 'Mehrabi et al. (2021) note that decisions based on seemingly neutral attributes can still discriminate indirectly because those attributes correlate with protected characteristics (e.g. postcode and race), so simply omitting protected attributes from a model does not by itself guarantee fairness.'

references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes 'model cards': short documents that accompany released machine learning models to encourage transparent model reporting. A model card gives benchmarked evaluation under a variety of conditions, including across cultural, demographic or phenotypic groups (e.g. race, geographic location, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type) and intersectional groups relevant to the intended application domain, and discloses the context in which the model is intended to be used, details of the evaluation procedure, and other relevant information. Section 4 sets out nine card sections: Model Details; Intended Use (primary intended uses, primary intended users, out-of-scope use cases); Factors; Metrics; Evaluation Data; Training Data; Quantitative Analyses (unitary and intersectional results); Ethical Considerations; and Caveats and Recommendations. Two worked examples are given (a smiling-face detector and a toxic-comment classifier). The authors frame model cards as a step towards the responsible democratisation of ML and as 'an approach for responsible transparent and accountable practices in machine learning'.

claims_supported.claim: Model cards document a model's intended use, evaluation across demographic groups and conditions, and limitations, to support transparent and responsible model reporting.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: model cards are proposed 'to encourage such transparent model reporting'; they 'provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups ... and intersectional groups' and 'disclose the context in which models are intended to be used'; proposed 'as a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning'. Section 4.2 'Intended Use' (primary intended uses, primary intended users, out-of-scope use cases); Section 4.3 'Factors' (demographic/phenotypic groups, environmental conditions); Section 4.7 'Quantitative Analyses' (unitary and intersectional results); Section 4.8 'Ethical Considerations'; Section 4.9 'Caveats and Recommendations'. Section 2 (p. 2): model reporting is 'an approach for responsible transparent and accountable practices in machine learning'. references.title: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Survival Analysis Framework for Churn Prediction in the Telecom Sector
references.harvard_reference: Mlambo, F.F., Musuphi, M. and Letsela, K. (2026) 'A hybrid machine learning and survival analysis framework for churn prediction in the telecom sector', Information, 17(7), 680. Available at: https://doi.org/10.3390/info17070680.
references.abstract_summary: The authors build and compare three-stage hybrid models that predict telecom customer churn within a set timeframe and estimate how covariates affect time until churn. The data come from an Iranian telecommunications company, not the IBM/Kaggle Telco dataset. Stage 1 segments customers with K-means (KM) or agglomerative clustering. Stage 2 classifies churn with logistic regression (LR), an artificial neural network or a decision tree. Stage 3 fits a Cox proportional hazards model to estimate hazard rates and covariate effects on churn time. Models are evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, specificity and AUC-ROC. The hybrid models generally beat standalone Cox models on most metrics. The best model, KM + LR + Cox, reports accuracy 88.24%, precision 93.18%, specificity 63.64% and F1 93.01%. KM with two clusters (churners and non-churners) was the best segmentation, and cluster membership changed survival length. The authors say the framework offers insights for targeted retention strategies. According to search-indexed full-text snippets, class imbalance was handled with SMOTE and random oversampling.

claims_supported.claim: Combining survival analysis (time-to-churn) with machine-learning classification can improve churn prediction and support timing of retention interventions in telecom.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: the study aims at 'accurately predicting customer churn within a specified timeframe' and assessing 'how various factors influence the time until churn'. It combines clustering, ML classification (LR/ANN/DT) and a Cox PH model, and reports that 'hybrid models generally outperformed individual Cox models across most predictive performance metrics'. It ends by 'offering valuable insights for targeted retention strategies'. A full-text snippet surfaced by search describes the framework as predicting 'customer churn and its timing in a unified manner'. Caveats: (a) the improvement is measured against standalone Cox models, not against standalone ML classifiers; (b) the evidence comes from one Iranian telecom dataset; (c) 'timing of retention interventions' is a reasonable inference from the time-to-churn and retention-strategy framing, but the paper does not evaluate any intervention. Word the claim as 'can', citing one study, not as an established result.

claims_supported.claim: The study uses the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset (state which dataset it actually uses and the reported performance).
claims_supported.where: NOT SUPPORTED. The abstract says 'a dataset from an Iranian telecommunications company was utilised', not the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset. Search-indexed full-text snippets describe the data as a random sample collected over 12 months from an Iranian telecom company's database. That matches the public UCI 'Iranian Churn Dataset' (3,150 customer records over 12 months), but the paper's own naming of the UCI repository and its record count could not be read directly because the MDPI full text returned HTTP 403. A search snippet reports that both standalone Cox models (oversampling vs SMOTE) scored Accuracy 84.42%, Precision 84.95%, Recall 100%, F1 91.86% and AUC-ROC 80.51%, but this was not checked against the full text. references.title: Inference for the Generalization Error
references.harvard_reference: Nadeau, C. and Bengio, Y. (2003) 'Inference for the generalization error', Machine Learning, 52(3), pp. 239-281. doi:10.1023/A:1024068626366.
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that significance tests used to compare learning algorithms usually account only for test-example variability and ignore the variability due to the choice of training set, which can lead to gross underestimation of the variance of the cross-validation estimator and to false claims that a new algorithm is better. The authors analyse the variance of a cross-validation-type estimator (J independent random train/test splits of sizes n1/n2, with the split-level errors averaged) that accounts for both training-set and test-example randomness. They prove that no variance estimator based only on the cross-validation results can be unbiased, and propose two new estimators: the 'corrected resampled t-test', which multiplies the sample variance of the J split scores by (1/J + n2/n1) instead of 1/J, and the 'conservative Z'. Simulations (Section 5) show that the ordinary resampled t-test and pseudo-bootstrap are far too liberal, while the new tests have approximately correct size and good power compared with the tests catalogued by Dietterich (1998). The authors recommend J around 15 and note the corrected resampled t-test costs nothing beyond the usual cross-validation runs.

claims_supported.claim: Because cross-validation folds share training data, the naive t-test on fold scores underestimates variance; the corrected resampled t-test adjusts the variance by a factor accounting for the train/test proportion.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 239): ignoring training-set variability 'could lead to gross underestimation of the variance of the cross-validation estimator'. Section 3.1 'First method: Approximating rho' (pp. 247-248): E[S^2_muhat_j] = sigma1(1-rho), so (1/J + rho/(1-rho)) S^2 is unbiased for Var[muhat_J]; rho (the correlation between the J split estimates) is unknown, and under the simplifying assumption that the loss depends only on the test example and n1 the correlation becomes rho0 = n2/(n1+n2), giving the estimator (1/J + n2/n1) S^2. Section 4, statistic 2 'Resampled t-test statistic' (p. 252): the naive statistic uses S^2/J, its 'political ratio' Var[muhat]/E[sigmahat^2] = 1 + J rho/(1-rho) > 1, 'so this approach leads to liberal inference, a phenomenon that grows worse as J increases. Dietterich (1998) observed this empirically'. Section 4, statistic 6 'Corrected resampled t-test statistic' (pp. 254-255): 'The resampled t-test boldly puts rho = 0. We propose here to proceed as if rho = rho0 = n2/(n1+n2) ... So we use sigmahat^2 = (1/J + n2/n1) S^2_muhat_j', with critical value t_{J-1,1-alpha/2}. Table 1 (p. 250) summarises both statistics. Section 5 simulations (pp. 264-266): the resampled t-test's actual size is 'far away from the nominal size 10%', while the corrected resampled t-test's size is close to nominal. Section 6 (p. 281): the corrected resampled t-test 'appears to be a good choice' and 'requires little computing'. Caveats on wording: (a) the source's estimator is J independent random train/test splits (random subsampling), which the authors say is 'close to the popular K-fold cross-validation estimator' (p. 242) but explicitly 'contrasts with the most standard cross-validation estimator for which the testing sets are mutually exclusive' (p. 281); the paper does not analyse K-fold folds per se. (b) The source attributes the variance underestimate to the split scores being correlated (rho > 0) because the splits are drawn from the same data; the rho0 = n2/(n1+n2) derivation formally comes from overlap of the test sets across splits under the assumption that the loss does not depend on the particular training examples, so 'share training data' is a loose paraphrase of the dependence rather than the paper's exact derivation. (c) 'Naive t-test on fold scores' corresponds to the paper's 'resampled t-test' (statistic 2), not its 't-test' (statistic 1, a single-split McNemar-type test). The substance of the claim - dependence between split scores makes the S^2/J variance estimate too small, and the correction replaces 1/J with (1/J + n2/n1), i.e. a term set by the test/train size ratio - is exactly what the source states.

references.title: Defection Detection: Measuring and Understanding the Predictive Accuracy of Customer Churn Models
references.harvard_reference: Neslin, S.A., Gupta, S., Kamakura, W., Lu, J. and Mason, C.H. (2006) 'Defection detection: measuring and understanding the predictive accuracy of customer churn models', Journal of Marketing Research, 43(2), pp. 204-211. doi:10.1509/jmkr.43.2.204.
references.abstract_summary: Descriptive meta-analysis of a churn-modelling tournament run by the Teradata Center for CRM at Duke University, in which 33 academics and practitioners submitted 44 entries built on an anonymous US wireless carrier's data (100,000-customer calibration set with 171 predictors; two validation sets of 51,306 and 100,462 customers, 1.8% churners). Entries were scored on top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient on both a current and a three-months-later validation set. Three findings: (1) methods matter - top-decile lift ranged from 1.07 to 3.01 and, via a profit model linking lift to campaign profitability, such differences are worth hundreds of thousands of dollars; (2) models have staying power, with negligible decay over three months; (3) a factor analysis of survey responses identified five modelling 'approaches' (logit, tree, practical, discriminant, explain) defined by estimation technique, variable-selection method and time allocation; logit and tree approaches performed best, discriminant and explain worst.

claims_supported.claim: Methodological choices (estimation technique, variable selection, time allocation) materially affect churn-model accuracy, and logistic regression and decision trees performed well in the churn tournament.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 204): 'methods do matter' and approaches are 'characterized by variables such as estimation technique, variable selection procedure, number of variables included, and time allocated to steps in the model-building process'. Results, 'Regression Results of Performance' and Table 3 (pp. 207-208): 'Logit and tree approaches are positively associated with predictive performance ... both tend to do well' (logit factor coefficient .527, p = .001; tree .293, p = .042 on current lift), while discriminant and explain approaches carry consistently negative signs. Conclusions (p. 209): 'Logistic and tree approaches perform relatively well, the practical approach has average performance, and discriminant and explain approaches have the lowest performance', holding across both criteria and both validation sets. Implications (pp. 209-210): 'logit and tree approaches are good techniques with which to begin'. Caveat to state in the report: 'logit' and 'tree' are factor-analytic bundles that combine the technique with variable-selection and time-allocation habits, and the authors warn that 'the approaches mean more than just the statistical technique'; the winning entry used gradient tree boosting of small trees (p. 210), not a single decision tree.

claims_supported.claim: Top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient are appropriate business-facing metrics for churn models, and small accuracy differences can translate into large profit differences.
claims_supported.where: Tournament structure, 'Data' (p. 206): the two scoring criteria were top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient; 'Lift is probably the most commonly used prediction criterion in predictive modeling, and its relevance is demonstrated by the direct link between lift and profitability we demonstrated previously. The Gini coefficient represents the area between the cumulative lift curve and random prediction, so it is a broader measure than top-decile lift.' Overall Performance (p. 206): the criteria correlate above .9, so 'top-decile lift can be used by itself as a measure of predictive performance'. Equations 1-4 (p. 205) express campaign profit as a linear function of lift; 'Profit Impact of Results' (pp. 207-209): under the most conservative assumptions a one-unit change in lift is worth $1.71 per customer, a half-unit (one standard deviation) change $0.85 per customer, i.e. $427,500 for a firm with 5 million customers contacting 10%; the variation observed 'can easily amount to changes in profit in the hundreds of thousands of dollars by using one method rather than another'; Table 4 and p. 209 give $230,000 for a one-SD move toward the logit approach. Nuance: the paper's wording is 'managerially meaningful' rather than 'business-facing', and the accuracy gaps it monetises are one SD of lift (about 0.5) on a range it calls 'a wide spread'; 'small' is defensible only in the sense that a difference worth cents per customer becomes large at scale, so the report should phrase it that way.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1509/jmkr.43.2.204), OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all agree on title, five authors, Journal of Marketing Research 43(2), pp. 204-211, 2006, DOI 10.1509/jmkr.43.2.204, publisher SAGE (originally American Marketing Association), ISSN 0022-2437 / 1547-7193; Crossref gives issued 2006-04-07 and print issue May 2006. The lead's author list, year and volume/issue were correct; the issue and page range were confirmed and added. The verbatim abstract was reconstructed from OpenAlex's inverted index and matches the full text. The SAGE landing page, SSRN, HBS and the CORE API returned HTTP 403 and the UNC Carolina Digital Repository copy (cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/pn89dg80z, listed by OpenAlex) could not be reached; the full text used for the claim checks was a third-party hosted PDF (2lvw.nl) whose masthead reads 'Journal of Marketing Research Vol. XLIII (May 2006), 204-211, (c) 2006 American Marketing Association' and whose content matches the abstract and page numbering exactly. Kamakura's given name appears as 'Wagner' in the article and Crossref (OpenAlex adds a middle initial 'A.'); initials used: W. Semantic Scholar reports about 604 citations.
references.caveats: The tournament data are a 2000s US wireless carrier's proprietary dataset (171 predictors, 1.8% monthly churn, oversampled to 50% churners for calibration), not the Kaggle IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, so results are transferable as methodological lessons rather than as benchmarks. The 'logit' and 'tree' findings are about factor-analytic approaches (technique plus variable selection plus time allocation), not head-to-head technique comparisons; regression sample size was n = 35 and the design was not factorial, which the authors acknowledge. The winning entry used gradient tree boosting. The profit figures rest on assumed parameters (delta = $50 incentive, CLV $500-$2,500, success rate 10-50%, base churn 1.8%) and scale with firm size. The paper predates modern ensembles, class-imbalance methods and uplift modelling, and its own discussion notes that targeting on churn risk and targeting on response to retention offers 'need not be the same'.

references.title: Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
references.venue: Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML '05), Bonn, Germany, 7-11 August 2005. New York: ACM Press
references.harvard_reference: Niculescu-Mizil, A. and Caruana, R. (2005) 'Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning', Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML '05). Bonn, Germany, 7-11 August 2005. New York: ACM Press, pp. 625-632. doi:10.1145/1102351.1102430.
references.abstract_summary: The authors compare the probability estimates produced by ten supervised learning algorithms (SVMs, neural nets, decision trees, k-NN, bagged trees, random forests, boosted trees, boosted stumps, naive Bayes, logistic regression) against true posterior probabilities on eight binary classification problems, using reliability diagrams and prediction histograms. Maximum-margin methods (boosted trees, boosted stumps, SVMs) push predicted probabilities away from 0 and 1, producing a characteristic sigmoid-shaped distortion; naive Bayes has the opposite distortion; neural nets, bagged trees and logistic regression are well calibrated without post-processing. Two calibration methods are evaluated, Platt scaling (sigmoid fit) and isotonic regression (monotone piecewise-constant fit via PAV), including a learning-curve analysis of how much calibration data each needs. Platt scaling wins with small calibration sets (below roughly 200-1000 cases) because isotonic regression overfits; with 1000+ cases isotonic regression is as good or better. After calibration, boosted trees, random forests and SVMs predict the best probabilities.

claims_supported.claim: Boosted trees and SVMs produce distorted (sigmoid-shaped) probability estimates that benefit from Platt scaling or isotonic regression, whereas logistic regression and bagged trees are naturally well calibrated; isotonic regression needs larger samples than Platt scaling.
claims_supported.where: All three parts are stated explicitly. (a) Sigmoid distortion of boosted trees and SVMs and benefit from calibration: Abstract ('maximum margin methods such as boosted trees and boosted stumps push probability mass away from 0 and 1 yielding a characteristic sigmoid shaped distortion'); Section 1 names SVMs, boosted trees and boosted stumps; Section 4 (pp. 3 and 6) says boosted stumps and SVMs 'exhibit distinctive sigmoid-shaped reliability plots' and 'Both Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression are effective at fitting this sigmoidal shape'; Section 6 / Figure 8 reports boosted trees, SVMs, boosted stumps and naive Bayes are 'dramatically improved by calibration'. (b) Logistic regression and bagged trees well calibrated: Section 4 (pp. 4-5): logistic regression and bagged trees 'are well calibrated initially and post-calibration does not help them on most problems'; Section 5 lists 'neural nets, bagged trees, and logistic regression' as methods for which neither calibration method helps much; Section 6: 'Calibration does not help bagged trees'. (c) Isotonic regression needs more data: Section 5 (learning-curve analysis, Figure 7): with calibration sets 'less than about 200-1000 cases, Platt Scaling outperforms Isotonic Regression with all nine learning methods' because isotonic regression 'is less constrained ... so it is easier for it to overfit'; with '1000 or more points' isotonic regression is 'as good as, or better than' Platt scaling. Section 7: 'Platt Scaling is most effective when the data is small, but Isotonic Regression is more powerful when there is sufficient data to prevent overfitting.' Note the abstract itself names only neural nets and bagged trees as well calibrated; logistic regression is confirmed in the body (Sections 4 and 5), so cite the paper generally rather than the abstract alone for that element.

references.title: Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python
references.harvard_reference: Pedregosa, F. et al. (2011) 'Scikit-learn: machine learning in Python', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 12(85), pp. 2825-2830. Available at: https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/pedregosa11a.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: Short (6-page) software paper introducing scikit-learn, a BSD-licensed Python module that integrates a wide range of supervised and unsupervised machine-learning algorithms for medium-scale problems, aimed at non-specialists. The abstract stresses ease of use, performance, documentation and API consistency, with minimal dependencies (numpy, scipy). The body describes the project vision, underlying technologies (numpy, scipy, Cython), the code design (estimators with fit/predict/transform/score, cross-validation iterators, GridSearchCV, Pipeline) and benchmark timings against other Python ML toolkits on the Madelon dataset.

claims_supported.claim: Scikit-learn provides the estimator/pipeline API used for the models and cross-validation in this report.
claims_supported.where: Section 4 'Code Design', pp. 2827-2828 (verified from the publisher PDF). The paper states that the central object is an estimator implementing a fit method, that supervised estimators implement predict, transformers implement transform, and estimators may provide score; it describes the cross-validation iterator (K-fold, leave-one-out, stratified), the GridSearchCV object for selecting parameters by cross-validation, and the Pipeline object that combines several transformers and an estimator into a combined estimator that GridSearchCV can tune end-to-end.
