references.title: Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models
references.harvard_reference: Devriendt, F., Berrevoets, J. and Verbeke, W. (2021) 'Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models', Information Sciences, 548, pp. 497-515. doi:10.1016/j.ins.2019.12.075.
references.abstract_summary: The authors note that uplift modelling (estimating the net effect of a retention action on a customer's churn probability) is promoted as better than predictive churn modelling, but no study had compared the two directly, and the two are normally scored with different metrics. They propose the maximum profit uplift (MPU) measure, which extends the maximum profit (MP) measure used for churn-prediction (CCP) models. They also propose the liftup curve and liftup measure as the uplift versions of lift. They test logistic-regression and random-forest CCP and churn-uplift (CCU) models on one retention campaign from a European financial institution: 200,903 customers, 162 variables, and three-month churn of 25.52% in the untargeted control group against 13.25% in the treatment group. Scored with MP on control-group data only, CCP models earn more profit. Scored with MPU on treatment and control data, CCU models do better. CCP models rank 'lost causes' (customers who churn whether targeted or not) near the top, while CCU models pick out 'persuadables' (customers who stay only if targeted), cut churn further and make campaigns more profitable.

claims_supported.claim: 1. Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Abstract ('uplift models outperform predictive models and lead to improved profitability of retention campaigns'); Sec. 1.2 and 2.2.1 (sure things / lost causes / persuadables / do-not-disturbs; churn models only predict the gross outcome); Sec. 4.3.1-4.3.3; Sec. 5. Rankings differ a lot: Spearman correlation between CCP and CCU rankings is 0.17-0.52, and the overlap in the top 5% is as low as 21%. Limits for a strict reader: the evidence is one offline case study (a European financial institution, not telecom) using only LR and RF. Cost and benefit figures were assumed from the literature, because the institution did not supply them. The advantage shows up only under MPU; under the classic MP measure (Scenario 1) CCP beats CCU. The method needs a randomised treatment/control group.

claims_supported.claim: 2. Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. Sec. 2.1 has one literature-review sentence saying survival analysis 'can be used to analyze and estimate the time until a customer's defection' (citing Backiel et al.). The paper says nothing on when to intervene, censoring or truncation. Cite a primary survival-analysis source instead.

claims_supported.claim: 3. Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The full text does not mention SMOTE, resampling, class imbalance, class weighting or probability calibration. The nearest point is Sec. 3.1: the MP measure picks the profit-maximising share of customers to target instead of a fixed top-decile cut-off. That is a cost-based choice of cut-off on a ranking, not threshold moving after resampling.

claims_supported.claim: 4a. Case-study data: 200,903 customers of a European financial institution (118,809 control, 82,094 treatment), 162 variables; three-month churn 25.52% in the untargeted control group vs 13.25% in the treated group, a baseline uplift of 12.27 percentage points.
claims_supported.where: Sec. 4.1.1 and Table 2

claims_supported.claim: 4b. The verdict depends on the evaluation metric. Under MP (control-group test data, constant retention rate assumed) CCP profit curves beat CCU for both LR and RF. Under MPU (treatment + control test data, retention rate varies with the targeted fraction) CCU beats CCP. MPU can only be computed when a randomised control group exists, which standard churn datasets do not have.
claims_supported.where: Sec. 3.1-3.2 (Eqs. 3-13; MP assumes a constant retention rate); Sec. 4.3.1

claims_supported.claim: 4c. Churn-probability models tend to target 'lost causes' (and, for RF, 'sure things'); uplift models target 'persuadables' and cut the churn rate by more.
claims_supported.where: Sec. 4.3.2 (Figs. 7-10; the liftup curve of the CCP RF model rises around 20-40% of customers targeted); Sec. 5

claims_supported.claim: 4d. Feedback loop: a churn model retrained on data collected while a model-driven retention campaign was running learns from behaviour the campaign changed. Retained would-be churners are labelled non-churners, so the new model is biased.
claims_supported.where: Sec. 1.2 and Figure 1

claims_supported.claim: 4e. Judging churn models by top-decile lift at an arbitrary cut-off can pick a suboptimal model; the maximum profit measure scores a model at its profit-maximising targeted fraction (from Verbeke et al., 2012).
claims_supported.where: Sec. 1.3 and Sec. 3.1

claims_supported.claim: 4f. Random forests beat logistic regression for both CCP and CCU in this case. The logistic-regression CCP and CCU models barely beat random targeting on the Qini curve, and the LR CCP model falls below random from 50% targeted onwards. Results were stable over five repeated random 2/3-1/3 train/test splits.
claims_supported.where: Sec. 4.3.1, Sec. 4.3.2 (Fig. 9), end of Sec. 4.3.3

Crossref's issue value 'C' is Elsevier's placeholder for a continuous volume, so the issue is left empty. Semantic Scholar gives the abstract, venue Information Sciences, year 2021, publicationDate 2021-02-01, and DBLP key journals/isci/DevriendtBV21. OpenAlex gives publication_date 2019-12-31, 90 citations, not retracted, all three authors at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Data Analytics Laboratory / Solvay Business School). DOI resolves to ScienceDirect PII S0020025519312022; ScienceDirect returned 403, so the version of record was not opened directly. Full text was read from the KU Leuven Lirias copy, which is the 'Journal Pre-proof' (accepted manuscript) with an article history of received 22 March 2018, revised 8 November 2019, accepted 27 December 2019, which confirms peer review. Page numbers and volume come from Crossref and Semantic Scholar, not the pre-proof. Venue: Information Sciences is an established Elsevier journal, not predatory. It meets the 2021-2026 requirement only through its 2021 volume year (vol. 548, Feb 2021). Cite Them Right uses the volume year (2021), but if the report's recency rule means 'first published', this is a 2019 paper. The same DOI may already be in the reference list as devriendt2021.json, so do not cite it twice. The evidence comes from one financial-services case study (not telecom) with assumed cost/benefit parameters and only LR and RF. It is an offline evaluation on held-out data from one past campaign, not a new field test. Uplift modelling and MPU need a randomised treatment/control indicator. The Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset has none, so this paper supports a critical or limitations discussion (churn probability does not tell you whom a campaign will retain), not a method that can be applied to that dataset. It does not support claims about survival analysis, censoring, SMOTE/resampling, class weighting, calibration or threshold moving.

references.title: Uplift modeling and its implications for B2B customer churn prediction: A segmentation-based modeling approach
references.harvard_reference: De Caigny, A., Coussement, K., Verbeke, W., Idbenjra, K. and Phan, M. (2021) 'Uplift modeling and its implications for B2B customer churn prediction: a segmentation-based modeling approach', Industrial Marketing Management, 99, pp. 28-39. doi:10.1016/j.indmarman.2021.10.001.
references.abstract_summary: The paper presents uplift modelling as a prescriptive analytics tool for B2B customer retention. It proposes the uplift logit leaf model (uplift LLM), a two-step, segmentation-based method. An uplift decision tree (Kullback-Leibler divergence splitting) first splits customers into segments. A separate uplift logistic regression (Lo, 2002 interaction approach) is then fitted in each segment. The data are 6,432 contracts from a European B2B process-automation software provider: 1,399 treated with a retention campaign (17.58% churn) and 5,033 controls (19.29% churn), a baseline uplift of 1.71%. There are 144 predictors, and the evaluation uses stratified 5-fold cross-validation with the Qini metric. Uplift LLM beat uplift decision tree, uplift logistic regression and uplift random forest on the overall, top-30% and top-10% Qini (for example, overall Qini 4.56 against 3.25 for uplift RF; all differences significant by paired t-tests). The paper also shows interpretable global and segment-level outputs: a decision table, incremental-gains curves by segment and partial dependence plots. The findings support uplift modelling for B2B retention decisions.

claims_supported.claim: Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Supported, with a qualification. Introduction (manuscript pp. 2-3) and section 2.1 (p. 5): 'customers who are most likely to churn are not necessarily those that will respond positively to retention campaigns'. The paper cites Devriendt et al. (2020) and Ascarza (2018) for the finding that ranking by churn probability is less effective than ranking by sensitivity to the intervention. Section 2.2 and Figure 1 (p. 6) set out the persuadables / sure things / do-not-disturbs / lost causes typology. Section 6.2 (p. 27) says traditional churn models target the gross outcome, so they include customers who cannot be retained. The paper's own evidence is limited: every model compared is an uplift model, and the only comparison is against random targeting (Qini, Table 6; Figure 4, where all models beat random targeting except uplift LR at 10%). It never runs a churn-probability-ranking model on its own data. The first half of the claim is argued here and shown empirically only in the cited Ascarza (2018) and Devriendt et al. (2020). Evidence that uplift targeting beats churn-probability targeting should be cited to those papers. It also comes from B2B software, not telecom. One further caveat: Segment 4 has negative uplift (-9.36%; Table 7, p. 23), so a campaign can raise churn for some customers.

claims_supported.claim: Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no survival or hazard modelling and does not mention censoring or truncation (full-text keyword search of the HAL accepted manuscript). Churn is defined as a binary outcome: non-renewal within a six-month window after a contract renewal date (section 4.1, p. 14). The only point about timing is that contractual settings have a 'two-clock nature' (Ascarza and Hardie, 2013): usage is daily but renewal is yearly, so churn can be predicted at the renewal point (section 2.1, p. 4). It also cites the Ascarza et al. (2018) framework question 'When do we target?' (p. 1) but does not address it. Do not cite this paper for survival analysis.

claims_supported.claim: Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The only reference to class imbalance is methodological: 'Due to the typically imbalanced class distribution, the folds are stratified' (section 4.1, p. 15). SMOTE, resampling, class weighting, calibration, threshold moving and cost-sensitive thresholds are not discussed (full-text keyword search).

claims_supported.claim: Additional precise finding 1: in a randomised B2B retention campaign (6,432 customers; 1,399 treated, 5,033 control), treated customers churned at 17.58% and controls at 19.29%, so the campaign's average effect (baseline uplift) was only 1.71 percentage points.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.1 and Table 3 (manuscript p. 14). Useful for a critical point: the average treatment effect of a retention campaign can be small, so knowing who to target matters. The paper states that uplift models use randomised experiments with treatment and control groups (p. 2).

claims_supported.claim: Additional precise finding 2: the segment-based uplift logit leaf model gave the highest Qini at every targeting depth (overall Qini 4.5646 against 3.2543 for uplift random forest, 2.1869 for uplift logistic regression and 1.9344 for uplift decision tree; all differences significant). All models reached their best cumulative uplift when targeting about 60-80% of customers.
claims_supported.where: Section 5.1, Table 6 and Figure 4 (manuscript pp. 18-19). Section 5.2 (p. 19) reports that uplift LLM's biggest gain comes from targeting about 60-70% of customers, for an uplift of about 6%.

claims_supported.claim: Additional precise finding 3: uplift models cannot be evaluated per customer, because each customer is observed only as treated or as control. Evaluation therefore uses group-based metrics such as the Qini curve or coefficient rather than accuracy or AUC.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2 (manuscript pp. 16-17). Relevant to critiquing accuracy- or AUC-only evaluation of churn classifiers when the goal is a retention decision.

claims_supported.claim: Additional precise finding 4: a retention campaign can increase churn for some customers. The model found a segment (managerial contact with a long contract duration, n = 864) with negative uplift of -9.36%: 15.64% churn in control against 25.0% when treated.
claims_supported.where: Section 5.2 (pp. 20-21) and Table 7 (p. 23). The authors link this to Ascarza et al. (2016): targeting may make past usage more salient and prompt customers to reconsider the contract. Section 6.3 (p. 28) names this as motivation for multi-treatment extensions.

claims_supported.claim: Additional precise finding 5: interpretable, segment-level models are valued by managers. Uplift LLM produced 4 segments, each with an uplift logistic regression averaging about 3 variables, whereas a global uplift logistic regression used 34 variables and an uplift decision tree had 8 leaves (first fold).
claims_supported.where: Section 5.2 (pp. 19-20) and section 6.2, third implication (p. 27). Cross-fold means in section 5.1 (p. 18): 4.00 segments (sd 3.08) against 6.00 for uplift DT, and 10.80 variables per segment model against 37.00 for uplift LR.

claims_supported.claim: Limitation statement: the results come from one proprietary B2B dataset. The authors call for validation on multiple datasets and in B2C settings.
claims_supported.where: Section 6.3 (manuscript p. 28). Relevant when comparing with the B2C telecom Telco Customer Churn dataset, which is also cross-sectional and has no treatment or control group, so uplift modelling cannot be applied to it directly. (That last point is the verifier's inference, not a statement in the paper.)

references.caveats: Peer-reviewed article in Industrial Marketing Management (Elsevier, ISSN 0019-8501), an established journal; not a predatory venue. Published online 7 October 2021 in volume 99 (November 2021). The setting is B2B contractual software, not telecom, so findings may not transfer to the B2C Telco dataset. The Telco dataset has no randomised treatment or control, so this paper supports a critical or future-work discussion (predictive vs prescriptive targeting), not a method that can be run on the Telco data. The paper does not itself benchmark churn-probability targeting against uplift targeting; that comparison is cited from Ascarza (2018) and Devriendt et al. (2020). Page numbers in claims_supported are the accepted-manuscript pagination (HAL hal-03599615, CC BY-NC), not journal pages 28-39. The Elsevier version of record could not be accessed (HTTP 403).
references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.indmarman.2021.10.001) confirms: journal-article; title as given; authors in order Arno De Caigny, Kristof Coussement, Wouter Verbeke, Khaoula Idbenjra, Minh Phan; Industrial Marketing Management; volume 99; no issue number (Elsevier continuous volume); pages 28-39; published in print November 2021; publisher Elsevier BV; 77 references; is-referenced-by 48. OpenAlex confirms the same metadata, online date 2021-10-07, 48 citations, and gives the fifth author's fuller name as 'Vu Minh Hieu Phan'. The abstract was taken from the HAL API record and from the full-text accepted manuscript (hal.science/hal-03599615/file/S0019850121001930.pdf, downloaded and read in full), and matches the OpenAlex reconstructed abstract. references.title: Partial counterfactual identification and uplift modeling: theoretical results and real-world assessment
references.harvard_reference: Verhelst, T., Mercier, D., Shrestha, J. and Bontempi, G. (2024) 'Partial counterfactual identification and uplift modeling: theoretical results and real-world assessment', Machine Learning, 113(3), pp. 1043-1067. doi:10.1007/s10994-023-06317-w.
references.abstract_summary: This is a methods paper on causal inference from ULB (Machine Learning Group) and Orange Belgium's Data Science Team. It asks what can be said about unobservable counterfactual customer types when all you have is uplift (CATE) estimates. For a retention campaign the types are: sure thing (does not churn either way), persuadable (churns only if not contacted), do-not-disturb (churns only if contacted) and lost cause (churns either way). The authors derive new bounds on the probability of each type, written in terms of the two uplift-model scores S0(x) and S1(x). They show these bounds are never looser than the classical Fréchet bounds and become tighter as the features carry more information about the uplift. They also propose a point estimator that assumes the two potential outcomes are conditionally independent. The estimators are tested first on simulated data from a hierarchical Bayesian model. They are then applied to Orange Belgium data from 6 randomised churn-prevention campaigns run over 6 months in 2019-2020: 11,268 customers and 145 features, with the target group phoned and offered an adapted tariff plan. The model is an uplift random forest with EasyEnsemble balancing, a probability-calibration correction and 5-fold cross-validation. Estimated shares of the campaign population are 91.12% sure things, 4.29% persuadables (bounds 0.52-4.49%), 4.39% do-not-disturbs and 0.20% lost causes. That is at most about 505 persuadable customers, against 7,500 actually called. A simplistic profit analysis (EUR 1 per call, EUR 120 lifetime value) puts the campaign as run at a net loss of about EUR 130, against a possible profit of up to EUR 57,477 if only the persuadables could have been called. The uplift bounds were only slightly tighter than the Fréchet bounds on real data, which the authors read as showing that counterfactual probabilities are hard to estimate in real churn settings.

claims_supported.claim: 1 (as stated). Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Only partly supported, so it is marked false under strict reading. The paper supports the conceptual difference. Sect. 3, p. 1048 says an effective campaign 'should then only reach out to persuadable customers', because sure things and lost causes would not change their behaviour and do-not-disturbs would react negatively. Sect. 7.1, pp. 1061-1062 shows the real campaigns contacted the riskiest customers ranked by a churn-prediction model. Sects. 7.3-7.4, pp. 1063-1064 estimate that only about 4.29% of them were persuadable (at most 505, against 7,500 called) and that the campaign roughly broke even or lost money. However, the paper does NOT show empirically that uplift-based targeting improves outcomes. Sect. 7.5, p. 1064 says outright that these results 'do not indicate which customers should be targeted'. It also cites Fernández-Loría and Provost (2022a, 2022b), who show uplift models can be sub-optimal and that proxy targets such as outcome probability are sometimes more effective. The EUR 57,477 figure is a hypothetical upper bound that assumes the persuadables could be identified perfectly.

claims_supported.claim: 1a (narrower, supportable). Orange Belgium ran randomised retention campaigns that phoned customers ranked highest by a churn-risk model. Only an estimated 4.29% of that campaign population was persuadable (uplift bounds 0.52-4.49%; about 483 customers, bounded 58-505, against 7,500 called), and about as many were do-not-disturb (4.39%). The overall campaign uplift was about 0.8 percentage points (control churn 4.85% against target churn 4.03%). A simplistic profit analysis puts the campaign as run at a net loss of about EUR 130, against up to EUR 57,477 had only persuadables been called.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.1, pp. 1061-1062 (campaign design, 11,268 customers, churn rates 4.85%/4.03%, control group 33%); Table 4 and Sect. 7.3, p. 1063 (counterfactual shares and bounds, 483 [58-505] persuadables against 7,500 called); Sect. 7.4, pp. 1063-1064 (profit analysis assuming EUR 1 per call and EUR 120 CLV, uplift about 0.8%, net loss about EUR 130 against up to EUR 57,477). The authors themselves call the profit analysis 'simplistic'.

claims_supported.claim: 2. Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Not supported anywhere. A full-text search of the published version found no mention of survival analysis, hazard models, time-to-churn, censoring or truncation. Churn is treated as a binary outcome within the campaign window. Cite a survival-analysis source instead.

claims_supported.claim: 3 (as stated). Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Only partly supported. Sect. 7.2, p. 1062 says that balancing the data with a resampling strategy (EasyEnsemble undersampling, k = 10) changes the prior probability of churn, so the predicted scores are biased. The authors correct this with the calibration formula of Dal Pozzolo et al. (2015) and cite Batista et al. (2004). SMOTE, class weighting, threshold moving and cost-sensitive thresholds are not discussed. This is a methodological remark that cites other work, not a finding of the paper.

claims_supported.claim: 3a (narrower, supportable). Undersampling-based class balancing (EasyEnsemble) shifts the churn prior, so a model trained on the balanced data gives biased scores that need a calibration correction before they are used as probabilities.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.2, p. 1062. Secondary support only: for a primary source, cite Dal Pozzolo et al. (2015), 'Calibrating probability with undersampling for unbalanced classification', as listed in the paper's references.

claims_supported.claim: 4a. The paper's assessment data: 6 randomised churn-prevention campaigns at Orange Belgium (monthly, Sept 2019-Feb 2020), with 11,268 customers and 145 features. The riskiest customers by a churn model were randomly split into target (phoned with an adapted tariff-plan offer) and control (33%). The treatment indicator records a call attempt, not whether the customer answered or accepted.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.1, pp. 1061-1062; the campaign months come from Fig. 8, p. 1063.

claims_supported.claim: 4b. On the Orange Belgium data, the uplift bounds were consistently tighter than the Fréchet bounds, but not by a large margin. The authors conclude that uplift terms, and so counterfactual probabilities, are difficult to estimate in real-world churn settings, and that more informative features or stronger uplift models are needed.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.3, p. 1063 (Fig. 7, Table 4) and Sect. 7.5, p. 1064.

claims_supported.claim: 4c. The authors acknowledge an open debate: uplift modelling is not always the best approach for causal decision-making. They cite Fernández-Loría and Provost (2022a, 2022b) as showing that outcome-probability proxies (i.e. churn-risk scores) are sometimes more effective, in line with the large churn literature that uses predictive rather than uplift models.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.5, p. 1064. This reports other authors' results; cite Fernández-Loría and Provost directly for the substantive claim.

claims_supported.claim: 4d. Stated limitations: the estimators assume unconfoundedness (randomised treatment), depend on an unbiased and accurate uplift model, and need separate estimates of S0(x) and S1(x). That rules out single-model learners such as the X-learner and restricts them to approaches such as uplift random forest or T-learner. The point estimator also assumes conditional independence of the potential outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Sect. 7.2, p. 1062; Sect. 8 (Conclusion), pp. 1064-1065.

claims_supported.claim: 4e. Companion resource: the same authors released an anonymised Orange Belgium churn/uplift dataset. It is published as a benchmark in 'A churn prediction dataset from the telecom sector: a new benchmark for uplift modeling' (doi:10.1007/978-3-031-74640-6_21), whose abstract calls it the first publicly available dataset for evaluating uplift modelling on churn prediction.
claims_supported.where: Journal article, 'Availability of code, data and material' statement, p. 1065 (anonymised data and code on GitHub). The companion chapter's abstract is on SpringerLink. Metadata verified via Crossref and SpringerLink: Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2136, pp. 292-299, 2025, in the International Workshops of ECML PKDD 2023 volume (Part IV), eds. Meo, R. and Silvestri, F., Springer, Cham.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (query and DOI record) confirms: DOI 10.1007/s10994-023-06317-w; authors Théo Verhelst, Denis Mercier, Jeevan Shrestha, Gianluca Bontempi; Machine Learning (Springer, ISSN 0885-6125/1573-0565), vol. 113, issue 3, pp. 1043-1067; published online 14 Mar 2023, print issue March 2024; journal-article.
