The published version is 'under exclusive licence to Springer', not open access; the arXiv preprint is freely available and its Sect. 7 numbers match. Year choice: I used 2024 (volume/issue year) because the reference gives vol. 113(3) pagination. The lead's '2023' is the online-first year. Use one year consistently. If the report cites the online-first version, write (2023) and drop the volume/issue/pages. Currency symbols were lost in the PDF text extraction; the arXiv text shows them as euros. Scout's note: mostly accurate. Crossref and the S2 abstract do not by themselves say 'Orange Belgium', but the full text does. Corrections to the companion paper details: (i) it is a workshop paper in the 'International Workshops of ECML PKDD 2023 ... Revised Selected Papers, Part IV' volume, not the main ECML PKDD conference proceedings; (ii) it was published in 2025, not 2023; (iii) Crossref and SpringerLink spell the third author 'Shestha', a metadata typo for Shrestha. CCIS vol. 2136, pp. 292-299 and DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-74640-6_21 are confirmed. I did not verify the workshop's review process. Suggested Harvard entry for the companion: Verhelst, T., Mercier, D., Shrestha, J. and Bontempi, G. (2025) 'A churn prediction dataset from the telecom sector: a new benchmark for uplift modeling', in Meo, R. and Silvestri, F. (eds) Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases: International Workshops of ECML PKDD 2023. Cham: Springer (Communications in Computer and Information Science, 2136), pp. 292-299. doi:10.1007/978-3-031-74640-6_21.
references.caveats: This is a methods paper on causal inference, not a churn-classifier benchmarking study. It does not compare churn prediction algorithms or use the Kaggle/IBM Telco dataset. Its main contribution is bounds and point estimates for counterfactual customer types. The profit figures come from a deliberately simplistic calculation (assumed EUR 1 per call, EUR 120 CLV), and the persuadable count is an estimate with wide bounds (58-505), so neither should be presented as measured campaign results. The paper does not show that uplift-targeted campaigns beat churn-risk-targeted ones, and it explicitly flags evidence that churn-probability targeting can sometimes be better. Pair it with Ascarza (2018) or Devriendt et al. for the 'risk is not responsiveness' argument. Inference by the verifier, not stated in the paper: the Kaggle Telco dataset has no treatment/control indicator, so uplift and counterfactual types cannot be estimated from it. That makes this paper most useful in the report's critical discussion and limitations sections, not for its methods. It says nothing about survival analysis, censoring, SMOTE, class weights or threshold moving; claims 2 and 3 need other sources.

references.title: Customer churn prediction for fixed wireless access: The case of a regional internet service provider
references.harvard_reference: Pflughoeft, K.A., Butz, N.T. and Corbley, A. (2025) 'Customer churn prediction for fixed wireless access: The case of a regional internet service provider', Telecommunications Policy, 49(4), article 102929. doi:10.1016/j.telpol.2025.102929.
references.abstract_summary: The paper studies customer churn at a fixed wireless access (FWA) internet service provider. It argues that churn is a major problem in telecoms and that competition in FWA is growing, partly because 5G now serves both cellular and FWA customers. The authors model the risk factors behind churn with three survival-analysis methods: random survival forests, Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier survival plots. The abstract says fiber, sales zone (brand presence), age, speed and discounts are among the more important variables for the cumulative hazard ratio. Discounts worked in many sales zones, but their effect was weaker for more expensive internet services. The authors present the findings as a basis for providers' retention strategies in the FWA market. The publisher keywords are fixed wireless access, telecommunications, Cox regression model, random survival forests, Kaplan-Meier survival plots, concordance index, data augmentation and customer churn. Secondary sources, not read in full, add that the case firm is Bug Tussel, a regional ISP based in Green Bay, Wisconsin, that the data cover customers with an active account at some point between 1 January 2018 and 1 March 2023, and that the analysis used JMP Pro and R with cross-validation tuning.

claims_supported.claim: Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The abstract and keywords never mention uplift, causal or treatment-effect modelling, or campaign targeting. The one related finding is that discounts had a weaker observed association with churn for more expensive services, and that is an observational survival-model result, not an uplift or causal targeting comparison.

claims_supported.claim: Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Only partly supported, so it is marked false as worded. The abstract supports the narrower point that survival methods (Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression, random survival forests) were used to model time-to-churn risk and rank risk factors by cumulative hazard, and it says the insights help providers 'curtail customer churn over time'. I could not check whether the paper explicitly argues for timing interventions or discusses censoring or truncation limits of cross-sectional tenure snapshots, because the full text is closed access (ScienceDirect, ResearchGate and Academia.edu all returned HTTP 403). Do not cite it for the censoring/truncation part.

claims_supported.claim: Survival-analysis methods (Kaplan-Meier, Cox proportional hazards regression and random survival forests) have been applied to real telecom (FWA ISP) subscriber data to model churn hazard and rank churn risk factors, with model fit assessed by the concordance index.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: the three methods are named ('Random Survival Forests, the Cox regression model, and Kaplan-Meier Survival Plots'), and variables are ranked 'with regard to the cumulative hazard ratio'. The publisher keyword list includes 'Concordance index'.

claims_supported.claim: Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The abstract does not mention class imbalance, SMOTE, class weighting, calibration or decision thresholds. 'Data augmentation' is one of the publisher keywords, but I could not read what it refers to in the paper, so it must not be cited as evidence about resampling or calibration.

claims_supported.claim: In a regional FWA ISP, fiber, sales zone (brand presence), customer age, speed and discounts were among the more important variables for the cumulative hazard of churn.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (verbatim on RePEc/IDEAS): 'fiber, sales zone (i.e., brand presence), age, speed, and discounts are some of the more important variables with regard to the cumulative hazard ratio.'

claims_supported.claim: Discounts were associated with reduced churn in many sales zones, but their effect was diminished for more expensive (premium) internet services, so retention incentives have heterogeneous effects.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: discounts 'were effective in many sales zones' but 'their impact was diminished for more expensive internet services'. Note that this is an observational association from survival models, not a randomised or uplift estimate.

claims_supported.claim: Fibre competition was the top predictor with about 18% importance, and churn risk peaks within the first 10 to 20 months after activation (scout's note).
claims_supported.where: Not verified. The abstract lists fiber first among 'some of the more important variables' but gives no ranking percentages and does not say fiber is the single top predictor. It also says nothing about the months when hazard peaks. The full text could not be accessed, so neither figure should be cited unless the student checks it in the full paper.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (queried by title and first author) confirms the metadata: DOI 10.1016/j.telpol.2025.102929; authors Kurt A. Pflughoeft, Nikolaus T. Butz and Alick Corbley; journal Telecommunications Policy (Elsevier BV); volume 49, issue 4; article number 102929; issue dated May 2025; type journal-article. OpenAlex agrees on the metadata. It gives an online publication date of 3 March 2025, lists all three authors at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point, shows 5 citations and marks the paper closed access. Semantic Scholar confirms the title, venue, year and authors but has a null abstract, and OpenAlex also has no abstract. I took the abstract and keywords verbatim from the RePEc/IDEAS record (ideas.repec.org/a/eee/telpol/v49y2025i4s0308596125000266.html). The PII S0308596125000266 comes from the doi.org redirect. ScienceDirect, ResearchGate, Academia.edu and the ACM DL all returned HTTP 403, so I could not read the full text. Telecommunications Policy is an established, peer-reviewed Elsevier journal indexed in SSCI and Scopus, not a predatory venue, and the 2025 date falls inside the required 2021-2026 window. Details I could not check first-hand, all taken from web search snippets or a university blog: the case firm is Bug Tussel of Green Bay, Wisconsin; the study window is 1 January 2018 to 1 March 2023; the software was JMP Pro and R; and a related conference talk was given in Amsterdam in 2024 (UWSP blog, 9 July 2024). The scout's specific figures (fibre about 18% importance as the top predictor; churn risk peaking at 10 to 20 months) are not verified.
references.caveats: The work is a single-firm case study of a rural fixed-wireless ISP in the US Midwest, not the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset, so its variables (fibre availability, sales zone, tower speed) have no direct equivalents in the Telco data and results may not generalise. The findings on discount effects are observational hazard associations, not causal or uplift estimates. The full text is paywalled, so only abstract-level and keyword-level statements are verified; cite the paper for the method choice (survival analysis for time-to-churn) and the headline risk factors, not for specific numbers. Use the article number (102929), not page numbers, in the reference.

references.title: Predictability & explainability of survival analysis in churn prediction
references.harvard_reference: Kimitei, S., Agiro, D., Ni, S. and Ni, H. (2025) 'Predictability & explainability of survival analysis in churn prediction', Journal of Marketing Analytics, pp. 1-17 [advance online publication, 22 December]. doi:10.1057/s41270-025-00450-2.
references.abstract_summary: Kimitei et al. (Kennesaw State University) apply survival analysis to churn in contractual utility services. The main aims are to compare the Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) and Aalen Additive (AA) hazards models for finding churn drivers, and to show that the models can be read clearly when predicting when churn happens. The data come from one US gas utility and cover 3,667 monthly customer-product rows, 69 columns and 2016-2023. Churn is 75% of rows, the real rate rather than the result of resampling. Churn is defined as early cancellation, internal switching at renewal or leaving the company, and all three are pooled. Feature selection by domain experts, p<0.05 tests and VIF left 11 predictors, including heating degree days, daily usage, product (price) switch count, automatic contract renewal and tariff or NYMEX prices at enrolment. The authors used an 80:20 split with five-fold cross-validation, a ridge-regularised AA model, and the concordance index (C-index) as the only metric. Models were fitted to the full data and to segments by product (6- or 12-month contract) and by time (before or after contract expiry). Test C-index for CPH (Table 1) was 73.3% on the full data, 78.5% and 60.1% for 6-month contracts before and after expiry, and 79.1% and 71.8% for 12-month contracts before and after expiry. Test C-index for AA (Table 3) was 72.20%, 73.99%, 70.19% and 80.70% in the same order. Survival drops sharply at the 6- and 12-month renewal points, and customers on automatic renewal had lower survival. AA cumulative-coefficient plots show when each predictor matters. The authors argue that separate product-level models work better than one pooled model and that hazard-based segments (for example 'critical risk: likely to churn within 30 days') support retention offers timed around contract renewal.

claims_supported.claim: 1. Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. Uplift appears only once in the text, in the last sentence of the Conclusion, as a 'broader application' of survival models ('uplift modeling, propensity scoring, and customer lifetime value analysis'). An uplift paper (Carla et al. 2024, EJOR) appears in the reference list. The paper does no causal or uplift analysis and never contrasts risk-based with uplift-based targeting. It actually recommends targeting by predicted risk and timing ('Customer segmentation guided by survival risk analysis': Critical/High/Moderate/Low risk bands), which is the practice uplift critics question. Cite Ascarza (2018) or Devriendt et al. (2021) for this claim instead.

claims_supported.claim: 2a. Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support the timing of interventions.
claims_supported.where: Supported. The abstract says the models forecast 'not only ... whether customers are at risk but also when churn is likely', which supports 'timely, tailored strategies'. The Introduction says fixed-time classifiers 'fail to capture the dynamic changes in the likelihood of customer churn over time'. Literature review gap (i): 'fixed-horizon classifiers rank who will churn but not when, limiting the timing of outreach'. The Results (Fig. 3) and the Discussion subsection 'Contract time critical intervention program' show sharp survival drops at the 6- and 12-month contract points and suggest campaigns about 60 days before contract end. Caveat: this rests on one gas-utility dataset, and the timing benefit is shown by description only. No field test of intervention timing was run.

claims_supported.claim: 2b. Cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Only partly supported, so marked false under strict reading. The Introduction defines censoring as 'a defining feature' of time-to-event data: a customer still subscribed at 180 days 'is censored at 180'. It says survival methods 'handle both event times and censored observations without bias', and the Literature review says survival analysis models hazards 'while handling censoring'. The paper does not discuss truncation (left truncation or delayed entry) or the limits of cross-sectional tenure snapshots such as the Telco dataset. The closest point is in the Discussion: CPH 'after-contract' models 'lose substantial data on customers who have already churned'. That is really a conditioning/truncation effect, but the authors call it a data-availability problem. You can cite this paper for 'survival models handle right-censoring'. You cannot cite it for truncation or snapshot-bias claims.

claims_supported.claim: 3. Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. SMOTE, class weighting, calibration, Brier score and decision thresholds do not appear anywhere in the paper. The only related sentence is in Materials and methods: the 75% churn / 25% non-churn split 'is not the result of re-sampling or labeling but reflects the business reality'. Cite Chawla et al. (2002), Elkan (2001) or a calibration source instead.

claims_supported.claim: 4a. On this utility dataset, churn is much harder to predict after the contract term ends. CPH test C-index falls from 78.5% to 60.1% for 6-month contracts and from 79.1% to 71.8% for 12-month contracts (73.3% on the full dataset).
claims_supported.where: Results, 'Cox proportional hazard (CPH) model', Table 1 (CPH test-set concordance index), with the text 'churn behavior becomes significantly more unpredictable once contractual obligations end'.

claims_supported.claim: 4b. The Aalen additive model, which relaxes the proportional-hazards assumption and allows time-varying covariate effects, keeps performance high after contract expiry. Test C-index was 72.20% and 73.99% for 6-month contracts before and after expiry, and 70.19% and 80.70% for 12-month contracts. CPH did better before expiry.
claims_supported.where: Results, 'Aalen additive model', Table 3 (testing C-index), and Discussion ('the CPH model better predicts customer churn before the contract expires, while the AA model performs well across all product contract periods'). The authors warn this 'may be specific to the scenario presented by the dataset being used'. Note that the Conclusion gives different AA figures (60.96%, 74.45%, 58.85%, 78.65%) and a CPH 6-month figure of '72%', which do not match Tables 1 and 3. Cite the table values.

claims_supported.claim: 4c. Churn hazard is concentrated at contract renewal points (6 and 12 months), and separate product-level (contract-type) churn models outperform a single pooled model.
claims_supported.where: Results, 'Full Dataset' (Fig. 3): survival 'declines more sharply' for 6-month products, with 'significant drops' at the 6- and 12-month marks. Discussion: 'building product-level churn models can be more effective than relying solely on one model for all customers'. Conclusion: 'product renewal dates are especially high-risk periods'. For the Telco dataset this is analogous to the Contract (month-to-month / one-year / two-year) variable, but that link is ours, not the authors'.

claims_supported.claim: 4d. The Cox proportional-hazards assumption is often assumed rather than tested in churn studies. Unchecked violations can bias effect sizes and mis-time interventions.
claims_supported.where: Literature review: 'the proportional-hazards (PH) assumption ... is often assumed rather than tested', and 'unexamined PH violations can bias effect sizes and mis-time interventions', citing Grambsch and Therneau 1994. Caveat: the authors say they 'explicitly run PH diagnostics', but the results do not report any Schoenfeld-residual test.

claims_supported.claim: 4e. The paper empirically shows survival models outperforming standard (non-survival) churn classifiers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported, despite the scout's note and the paper's own wording. The Conclusion claims 'survival models outperform traditional churn prediction approaches', and the Discussion says they are 'outperforming traditional models'. However, no logistic regression, tree-ensemble or other classifier is fitted as a baseline. The only metric is the C-index for CPH and AA. The claim is an assertion about extra capability (timing and interpretability), not a measured result.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1057/s41270-025-00450-2) confirms the title, the four authors in order (Symon Kimitei, ORCID 0009-0008-5112-0500; Don Agiro; Sherri Ni; Huan Ni) and the journal (Journal of Marketing Analytics, ISSN 2050-3318 print / 2050-3326 online, Springer Science and Business Media LLC). It records type journal-article, published online 22 December 2025, and a CC BY 4.0 licence. Crossref still lists NO volume, issue, page or published-print date, so the article is online-first and has not yet been assigned to an issue. Semantic Scholar gives the same abstract, year 2025 and venue. The Springer landing page (fetched in full; open access) gives publisher 'Palgrave Macmillan UK', article type 'Original Article', Received 10 May 2025, Accepted 28 October 2025, Published / Version of record 22 December 2025, and online-first pagination 1-17 (citation_firstpage/lastpage meta tags). The volume and issue fields are left empty because no source has assigned them yet. The pages '1-17' are online-first pagination and may change when the article goes into an issue, so re-check volume, issue and pages before submission. All four authors are affiliated with the School of Data Science and Analytics, Kennesaw State University, USA. Peer review is shown by the received and accepted dates in an established Palgrave Macmillan / Springer Nature marketing journal (running since 2013). It is not a predatory venue. Indexing (Scopus/ESCI) was not re-checked in this session. It falls within 2021-2026. The claims were checked against the full article text and Tables 1-3 on the publisher page, not only the abstract. The Harvard reference follows Cite Them Right for an advance-online article; if your marker prefers it, the 'pp. 1-17' can be dropped until final pagination exists.
references.caveats: (1) Domain: the data come from one US contract-based gas utility, not a telecom provider. The scout's note is right that it fits the subscription/contract framing, but transfer to the Telco dataset is by analogy. (2) Class balance: the data are unusual, at 75% churn / 25% non-churn, over 3,667 monthly rows. (3) No classifier baseline and no calibration or Brier score: the only metric is the concordance index. So it does NOT show survival models beating plain classifiers, even though the Discussion and Conclusion say so. (4) The paper contradicts itself: the Conclusion's C-index figures (CPH '72%' for 6-month; AA 60.96/74.45/58.85/78.65%) differ from Table 1 (78.5/60.1/79.1/71.8%) and Table 3 (72.20/73.99/70.19/80.70%). The optimal tau for 12-month after-expiry customers is 20 in Table 2 but 100 in Table 3. Cite the table values and treat the numbers with caution. (5) Our own inference, not stated by the authors: customer IDs repeat across monthly rows and the paper reports only a plain 80:20 split. No grouping by customer is mentioned, so leakage across train and test may have inflated the C-index. (6) The authors say they ran PH diagnostics but report no results for them. (7) The 'after-contract' subsets only include customers who survived to contract end. This conditions on survival, a form of left truncation, and it complicates the before/after comparison. (8) The paper is online-first, with volume, issue and pages not yet assigned as of 2026-09-28. Best used as a recent example that time-to-event models add 'when' to 'who' for timing retention, not as evidence on uplift, imbalance handling or calibration.

references.title: Dynamic Survival Analysis of Customer Churn in Poland's Telecommunications Industry
references.venue: Emerging Challenges in Intelligent Management Information Systems: Proceedings of 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence ECAI 2025 - IMIS Workshop, Volume 1 (Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, vol. 1767), eds. M. Hernes, E. Walaszczyk and A. Rot
references.harvard_reference: Deja, R., Przybyła-Kasperek, M. and Sulikowski, P. (2026) 'Dynamic survival analysis of customer churn in Poland's telecommunications industry', in Hernes, M., Walaszczyk, E. and Rot, A. (eds) Emerging Challenges in Intelligent Management Information Systems: Proceedings of 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence ECAI 2025 - IMIS Workshop, Volume 1. Bologna, Italy, 25-30 October 2025. Cham: Springer (Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, 1767), pp. 187-199. doi:10.1007/978-3-032-13869-9_15.
references.abstract_summary: The authors present churn as a major telecom problem because retaining existing users is cheaper than acquiring new ones. Using eight years of data on more than 8,000 customers of a Polish telecom provider, they fit a Cox proportional hazards model with time-dependent variables to follow how churn risk changes over time. They contrast this with most churn studies, which use fixed or aggregated data. The contribution they claim is combining static demographic variables with detailed service usage that varies over time, which they say is rarely done in churn modelling. Results: more calls, more minutes and more MMS use lower churn risk, while more SMS use slightly raises it. Customers from more populated areas tend to stay longer. The authors present the method as a framework for churn analysis that supports data-driven retention and business intelligence decisions. The abstract gives no predictive-performance metrics (for example a C-index) and no hazard ratios. It also says nothing about censoring handling, checks of the proportional hazards assumption or any comparison with classification models.

claims_supported.claim: 1. Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The abstract (Springer chapter page) never mentions uplift modelling, causal or treatment-effect targeting, retention campaigns or campaign outcomes. The study estimates observational hazard associations with a Cox model. Its only link to retention is the general closing statement that the method 'supports more effective, data-driven decisions in customer retention'. The chapter is behind a paywall and the full text was not seen. Nothing in the available abstract, keywords or visible reference titles suggests the chapter covers uplift. Cite Ascarza (2018) or Devriendt et al. (2021) for this claim instead.

claims_supported.claim: 2. Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Partly supported, and not supported as worded. Abstract sentence 3 supports the idea behind the first half: 'Unlike most studies that rely on fixed or aggregated data, we apply the Cox proportional hazards model with time-dependent variables to track how churn risk changes over time.' Sentence 4 adds that combining static demographics with time-varying usage is 'rarely used in churn modeling'. Sentence 8 says the method 'supports more effective, data-driven decisions in customer retention'. However, the abstract does not say the model is used to predict when an individual customer will churn, and it does not discuss timing retention interventions. It does not mention censoring, left truncation or any limitation of cross-sectional tenure snapshots such as the Kaggle Telco data. So the source supports only the narrower point in the next item. The full text was not accessible to check whether censoring is discussed in the methods.

claims_supported.claim: 2a (narrowed, verifier-added). A Cox proportional hazards model with time-dependent covariates can be used to track how customer churn risk changes over time, as an alternative to churn studies that rely on fixed or aggregated (static) data.
claims_supported.where: Abstract sentences 3-4 (Springer chapter page, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-13869-9_15): the Cox proportional hazards model with time-dependent variables is applied 'to track how churn risk changes over time'. The authors contrast this with 'most studies that rely on fixed or aggregated data'. They combine 'static demographic data with detailed, time-varying service usage'. Keywords: customer churn, survival analysis, Cox proportional hazards model, telecommunications.

claims_supported.claim: 3. Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The study is a survival (time-to-event) analysis with a Cox model, not a binary classifier. The abstract does not mention class imbalance, SMOTE, class weighting, calibration, decision thresholds or cost-sensitive learning. Cite Chawla et al. (2002), van den Goorbergh et al. (2022) or Elkan (2001) instead.

claims_supported.claim: 4. Precise finding: in eight years of data on more than 8,000 customers of a Polish telecom provider, a Cox proportional hazards model with time-dependent variables found that more calls, minutes and MMS use lowered churn risk, more SMS use slightly raised it, and customers from more populated areas tended to stay longer.
claims_supported.where: Abstract sentences 2, 3, 6 and 7 (Springer chapter page). The data are 'eight years of data from over 8,000 customers of a Polish telecom provider'. The results show that 'increased use of calls, minutes, and MMS lowers churn risk, while more SMS usage slightly raises it', and 'Customers from more populated areas also tend to stay longer.' These are hazard associations from an observational Cox model, not causal effects, and the abstract gives no hazard ratios or confidence intervals. The data are proprietary and differ from the Kaggle Telco dataset: they are longitudinal and include time-varying usage.

claims_supported.claim: 4b (critical-discussion point). Static, single-snapshot churn datasets (such as the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn data, with one tenure value and current charges per customer) cannot support time-dependent-covariate survival models of the kind used here. The authors present their combination of static demographics with time-varying usage as rare in churn modelling.
claims_supported.where: Supported only for the authors' own characterisation. Abstract sentence 3 says most studies 'rely on fixed or aggregated data'. Sentence 4 describes the static-plus-time-varying combination as 'an approach rarely used in churn modeling'. Sentence 5 claims this 'allows for a deeper and more accurate understanding of customer behavior'. The source does not mention the Kaggle Telco dataset. Applying the point to that dataset is the student's own inference and should be written as such. The claim of being 'more accurate' is not backed by any metric in the abstract.

references.verification_notes: Crossref record for DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-13869-9_15 (fetched directly by DOI; a bibliographic query returned HTTP 429, so the DOI lookup was used): book-chapter; title as above; authors Rafał Deja (ORCID 0000-0002-1006-2454), Małgorzata Przybyła-Kasperek (ORCID 0000-0003-0616-9694) and Piotr Sulikowski (ORCID 0000-0002-8704-8925); container titles 'Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems' and 'Emerging Challenges in Intelligent Management Information Systems'; pp. 187-199; published online 2 January 2026, print 2026; publisher Springer Nature Switzerland; ISBN 9783032138682 (print) and 9783032138699 (electronic); series ISSN 2367-3370/2367-3389; event: 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence (ECAI), Bologna, Italy, 25-30 October 2025. The Springer chapter page confirms the series volume (LNNS vol. 1767), the editors (Marcin Hernes, Ewa Walaszczyk and Artur Rot), the affiliations (WSB University, Dąbrowa Górnicza; University of Silesia in Katowice and Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra; West Pomeranian University of Technology in Szczecin), the keywords and the full abstract. The Springer book page gives the subtitle 'Proceedings of 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence ECAI 2025 - IMIS Workshop, Volume 1'. So this is a paper in the proceedings of the IMIS workshop held at ECAI 2025, not the ECAI main-track proceedings, which the lead did not make clear. Semantic Scholar (Corpus ID 289315311; DBLP key conf/imis2/DejaPS25) lists the venue as IMIS@ECAI with year 2025, but the publication year is 2026. Its abstract field is 'elided by the publisher'. OpenAlex lists the type as conference paper with 0 citations and no abstract. The abstract used here comes from the Springer landing page (link.springer.com), not from Crossref, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar. The lead's note that no abstract was available is therefore out of date, and the lead's guess about the model is now confirmed: a Cox PH model with time-dependent variables. Peer review: according to search-result text from the IMIS 2025 call for papers (imis.ue.wroc.pl), 'All papers will be reviewed by members of the International Programme Committee' before acceptance and Springer publication. That page itself could not be fetched because of a TLS certificate error, so this rests on the search-engine snippet. The Springer book page has no explicit peer-review statement. Venue: Springer Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, an established publisher series, and not predatory. Place of publication 'Cham' is inferred from the publisher (Springer Nature Switzerland AG is based in Cham). Crossref gives the publisher but no city. The full text is paywalled and was not read, so the methods, censoring handling, PH-assumption checks and performance metrics could not be verified. Among the visible reference titles are 'A time-dependent discrimination index for survival data' and 'Applying survival analysis to telecom churn data'. These suggest, but do not confirm, that a time-dependent concordance index was used for evaluation. Date range check: 2026, within 2021-2026.
references.caveats: This is a 13-page workshop-proceedings chapter (IMIS Workshop at ECAI 2025), not a journal article and not an ECAI main-track paper. It has no citations yet. The data are proprietary: eight years of records on more than 8,000 customers of one Polish provider, longitudinal with time-varying usage. That makes the data structurally different from the cross-sectional Kaggle Telco dataset, so the findings do not transfer directly. The findings are observational hazard associations from a Cox model and must not be described as causal effects of usage on churn. The abstract gives no effect sizes and no discrimination or calibration metrics. Its claim of being 'more accurate' is not backed by numbers in the abstract. The full text was not accessed, so use this source only for what the abstract states: the method (Cox PH with time-dependent covariates), the data scale and the direction of effects. If a journal article is required, the scout's runner-up, Mlambo, Musuphi and Letsela (2026), Information 17(7):680 (MDPI), was not verified in this run.

references.title: Predict-then-optimize or predict-and-optimize? An empirical evaluation of cost-sensitive learning strategies
references.harvard_reference: Vanderschueren, T., Verdonck, T., Baesens, B. and Verbeke, W. (2022) 'Predict-then-optimize or predict-and-optimize? An empirical evaluation of cost-sensitive learning strategies', Information Sciences, 594, pp. 400-415. doi:10.1016/j.ins.2022.02.021.
references.abstract_summary: The paper frames cost-sensitive classification as a two-stage problem. Under predict-then-optimize, a model is first trained for accuracy and costs enter only at the decision (threshold) stage. Under predict-and-optimize, the model is trained with a task-specific, cost-aware loss. The authors sort existing methods into cost-sensitive training (before or during training) and cost-sensitive decision-making (thresholding after training). They then benchmark both approaches on nine public datasets from fraud detection, direct marketing, customer churn and credit scoring. Two of the datasets are churn sets: Kaggle Telco Customer Churn (n = 7,032, 26.58% churners) and TV Subscription Churn. Three losses (cross-entropy, cost-weighted cross-entropy and average expected cost) are each combined with logistic regression, a one-hidden-layer MLP and gradient boosting. Each model is paired with nine threshold rules: instance- and class-dependent cost-sensitive thresholds with and without isotonic calibration, empirical thresholds tuned for cost or F1, the class-imbalance prior and 0.5. The authors test both instance-dependent and class-dependent costs, using 2x5-fold stratified cross-validation with Friedman/Nemenyi and Wilcoxon tests. Their main finding is that the decision-making (thresholding) strategy generally matters more for cost than training with a task-specific loss, or than combining the two. The best average savings came from a cost-insensitive model combined with an instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold.

claims_supported.claim: 1. Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Not addressed anywhere in the paper. A full-text search of the author manuscript for 'uplift', 'causal' and 'treatment' found nothing relevant. The paper covers cost-sensitive classification and thresholding of predicted probabilities, not treatment effects or uplift modelling.

claims_supported.claim: 2. Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Not addressed. The paper has no survival analysis, time-to-event modelling, censoring or truncation. All tasks, including Telco churn, are treated as static binary classification.

claims_supported.claim: 3a. Class weighting (reweighting the training loss) changes predicted probabilities and damages calibration.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.2 and Table 7 (averaged over all nine datasets). The authors used cost-weighted cross-entropy, i.e. training examples weighted by misclassification cost, which Section 2.2.1 calls equivalent to oversampling in proportion to misclassification costs. Before calibration, these models had Brier scores of 0.16 (wlogit), 0.16 (wnet) and 0.13 (wboost), against 0.07 for the unweighted cross-entropy models. Isotonic calibration brought them back to 0.07-0.08. Unweighted cross-entropy models were unchanged by calibration (0.07 to 0.07), which the authors read as a sign that their probabilities were already calibrated. Caveat: in the main experiment the weights are cost-based (instance-dependent), not plain inverse-class-frequency weights. Class-weighted calibration results are not shown in the main text.

claims_supported.claim: 3b. Resampling such as SMOTE changes predicted probabilities/calibration.
claims_supported.where: SMOTE and synthetic oversampling are not tested or discussed. The only link to resampling is one sentence in Section 2.2.1 saying cost-weighted cross-entropy is equivalent to oversampling in proportion to misclassification costs. That does not support a claim about SMOTE.

claims_supported.claim: 3c. Threshold moving / cost-sensitive thresholds on an unmodified model are an effective alternative to changing the training objective.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.2 (Table 6), Section 5 and Section 6. For cross-entropy models, average savings with the instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold (IDCS) were 0.36 (logit), 0.41 (net) and 0.41 (boost), against 0.06, 0.12 and 0.13 at the default 0.5 threshold. The authors say it is 'absolutely crucial' not to use 0.5 for such models. The best savings overall came from a cost-insensitive model with IDCS thresholding. A cost-sensitive loss helped only for logistic regression, provided an appropriate threshold was used. The conclusion recommends training a cost-insensitive model and adding costs only at the thresholding stage.

claims_supported.claim: 4a. Cost-optimal thresholds depend on calibrated probabilities; the paper examines calibration directly but its evidence on whether calibration improves thresholding is inconclusive.
claims_supported.where: Section 2.2.2 says the Bayes-optimal instance-dependent threshold needs calibrated probabilities or a prior calibration step. Calibration is tested explicitly (RQ2, hypotheses 2.2 and 2.4) using isotonic regression and the Brier score. Results: calibration improved savings only for cost-weighted models or class-dependent thresholds, and the two best savings were obtained without calibration (Section 4.2.2). Table 11 marks the calibration hypothesis '?' (inconclusive) for both costs and errors.

claims_supported.claim: 4b. Minimising errors and minimising costs are different objectives: cost-sensitive models score lower on AUROC/AP but achieve lower expected cost, and the F1-optimal threshold is not the cost-optimal threshold.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.1 (Figs 3-4): cross-entropy models had the best AUROC and AP (significant at 5% only against cslogit), while average-expected-cost models had the lowest AEC, significant at 5% in almost all cases. Section 4.2.2 (Table 8): thresholds tuned for F1 gave the best F1 but not the lowest cost. Section 5 calls errors and costs two fundamentally different objectives at both the training and decision stages. This supports a critique of reporting only AUC, accuracy or F1 for churn models.

claims_supported.claim: 4c. The study includes the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset with an instance-dependent cost matrix based on monthly charges.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.1, Table 4 and Appendix A: KTCC with n = 7,032, 19 features and 26.58% positives. The churn cost parameters are set at 2 and 12 times the customer's monthly amount, following Petrides et al. [34] (Table 5c). Caveat: the paper reports results averaged across all nine datasets and puts per-dataset results in a digital appendix. The main text therefore gives no Telco-specific performance figures, so it should not be cited for Telco-only results.

claims_supported.claim: 4d. Instance-dependent costs improve cost-based metrics but can reduce error-based metrics compared with class-dependent costs.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.3 (Tables 9-10) and Section 5. Training with class-dependent costs gave better AUROC, AP and F1 in almost all cases. Training with instance-dependent costs gave consistently lower AEC (not always significant) and better Spearman correlation between scores and costs, and better savings on average though not consistently. Summary from the authors: using no costs is best for errors, instance-dependent costs are best for costs, and class-dependent costs fall in between.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.ins.2022.02.021; journal-article; Information Sciences, Elsevier BV; vol. 594, pp. 400-415; issue print date May 2022), Semantic Scholar (full abstract; venue Information Sciences, ISSN 0020-0255; 81 citations; DBLP journals/isci/VanderschuerenV22) and OpenAlex (published online 22 February 2022; not retracted; 79 citations). Crossref gives the issue as 'C', which is an Elsevier placeholder rather than a real issue number, so the issue is left blank and omitted from the Harvard reference. Information Sciences is an established peer-reviewed Elsevier journal, not a predatory venue, and the year (2022) is within the 2021-2026 window. The full text was checked from the authors' green open-access manuscript on KU Leuven Lirias (marked 'Preprint submitted to Elsevier', 18 pages). All section, table and numeric citations above come from that version, so check page-level details against the typeset version if quoting exactly. The scout's note is confirmed: (i) the paper compares cost-sensitive training with cost-sensitive decision-making under both class- and instance-dependent costs; (ii) its key finding is that the decision-making strategy generally matters more than a task-specific loss; (iii) Telco Customer Churn and TV Subscription Churn are among the nine datasets (Table 4, Appendix A); (iv) the paper covers four domains, not only churn. On calibration, it does examine calibration directly (isotonic regression, Brier score, Table 7, hypotheses 2.2/2.4), but it finds calibration beneficial only for cost-weighted models or class-dependent thresholds and calls the overall hypothesis inconclusive. Suitable to cite for cost-sensitive thresholding and the effect of weighted training on calibration. Not suitable for uplift or causal targeting, survival or timing of churn, or SMOTE specifically. The authors also caution that cost-sensitive training can be preferable under model misspecification (Section 6), which is worth noting in a critical discussion.

references.title: Investigating the impact of undersampling and bagging: an empirical investigation for customer attrition modeling
references.venue: Annals of Operations Research (Springer; ISSN 0254-5330 print, 1572-9338 online)
references.harvard_reference: De Caigny, A., Coussement, K., Meire, M. and Hoornaert, S. (2025) 'Investigating the impact of undersampling and bagging: an empirical investigation for customer attrition modeling', Annals of Operations Research, 346(3), pp. 2401-2421. doi:10.1007/s10479-025-06516-9.
references.abstract_summary: The authors note that undersampling and bagging are both popular in customer churn prediction (CCP). Undersampling tackles class imbalance and bagging improves model stability. However, the CCP literature is unclear about how undersampling affects model stability and predictive performance, and bagging on its own struggles with class imbalance. The paper therefore benchmarks 'underbagging', which combines the two. Each bag passes an undersampled, more balanced training set to the classifier, and using many bags recovers majority-class customer data that plain undersampling would discard. In an experiment on 11 real-life churn datasets, underbagging is compared with its constituents (undersampling alone, bagging alone) and with other popular CCP classifiers on predictive performance, profit and operational efficiency. The authors conclude that underbagging is 'a valid and reliable alternative framework for CCP prediction'. Springer keywords: Underbagging, Logistic regression, Business analytics, Customer relationship management, Data science.

claims_supported.claim: Targeting retention offers by predicted churn probability is not the same as targeting by expected uplift; uplift/causal targeting improves campaign outcomes.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The abstract and keywords do not mention uplift, treatment effects or causal targeting. The paper is a predictive-classifier benchmark that measures profit alongside predictive performance, not a study of who responds to a retention offer. The full text is paywalled and was not read, but nothing in the abstract, keywords or visible reference list suggests an uplift analysis.

claims_supported.claim: Survival models can estimate when customers are likely to churn and support timing of interventions; cross-sectional tenure snapshots have censoring/truncation limitations.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The abstract and keywords do not mention survival analysis, time-to-churn, censoring or truncation. The study frames CCP as binary classification (undersampling, bagging, underbagging, other classifiers).

claims_supported.claim: Resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or class weighting changes predicted probabilities/calibration; threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds are an alternative.
claims_supported.where: Not supported as stated. The paper is about resampling: the abstract says undersampling 'helps in tackling the class imbalance problem' and that the effect of undersampling on 'model stability and predictive performance' is unclear in the CCP literature. It says nothing about predicted probabilities, calibration, class weighting, threshold moving or cost-sensitive thresholds. SMOTE (Chawla et al., 2002) and cost-sensitive learning (Coussement, 2014) appear in the visible reference list, but whether and how the text discusses them could not be checked because the full text is paywalled. Cite it only for the point that resampling choices (undersampling vs underbagging) affect predictive performance, profit and operational efficiency in churn models, not for calibration or thresholding.

claims_supported.claim: Other precise finding (a): Undersampling and bagging are popular in churn prediction for different reasons. Undersampling addresses class imbalance and bagging improves model stability. The CCP literature is unclear on how undersampling affects model stability and predictive performance, and bagging has difficulty handling class imbalance.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Springer landing page, RePEc/IDEAS record). This is the paper's stated motivation.

claims_supported.claim: Other precise finding (b): Plain undersampling throws away majority-class (non-churner) data. Underbagging recovers it by drawing a different undersampled, more balanced training set for each of multiple bags.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: combining the techniques lets the authors recover customer data that undersampling would lose by using it in multiple bags, each passing an undersampled, more balanced training set to the classifier.

claims_supported.claim: Other precise finding (c): Across 11 real-life churn datasets, underbagging was benchmarked against undersampling alone, bagging alone and other popular CCP classifiers on predictive performance, profit and operational efficiency, and was found to be a valid and reliable alternative framework for churn prediction.
claims_supported.where: Abstract. Caveat: the abstract does not say that underbagging wins on every metric or dataset. It does not name the profit measure, the base learner(s) (though 'Logistic regression' is a keyword), the number of bags or the effect sizes. These details are only in the paywalled full text and must not be stated without reading it. The paper evaluates profit and operational efficiency as well as AUC-type performance, which makes it useful when critiquing accuracy-only churn evaluation.

references.verification_notes: Existence and metadata verified on 2026-09-28. Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s10479-025-06516-9): journal-article in Annals of Operations Research, publisher Springer Science and Business Media LLC, authors in order Arno De Caigny, Kristof Coussement, Matthijs Meire, Steven Hoornaert, volume 346, issue 3, pages 2401-2421, published online 11 Feb 2025, print issue March 2025. A Crossref bibliographic search on title plus first author returned this DOI as the top hit. OpenAlex agrees (vol 346, issue 3, pp. 2401-2421, 2025, closed access, no abstract index), and so does the HAL record hal-05114891 (a bibliographic notice only, no full text). Semantic Scholar returns the record but the publisher has elided the abstract. The abstract, keywords and publication history (received 11 Dec 2023, accepted 29 Jan 2025, published 11 Feb 2025, issue date March 2025) come from the Springer landing page (link.springer.com), whose article body is paywalled; only the abstract and reference list were visible. The lead gave no issue number; Crossref and OpenAlex confirm issue 3. Crossref gives the surname as 'De Caigny' (HAL uses 'de Caigny'), and the capitalised form is used here. Venue check: Annals of Operations Research is a long-running peer-reviewed Springer journal (OpenAlex source record: earliest works 1984, 9,861 works, 288,764 citations, h-index 187, two-year mean citedness 3.97; subscription/hybrid, APC USD 3,090, not in DOAJ). It is a mainstream, well-established operations research journal, not a predatory venue. Rankings such as the ABS/AJG grade or JCR impact factor were not checked in this session and are not asserted. Publication year 2025 falls within the requested 2021-2026 window. The authors are an established churn-modelling group (IESEG School of Management), consistent with the scout's note. The full text could not be read, so every claim judgement rests on the abstract, keywords and visible reference list. The scout's statement that the paper 'does not look at probability calibration' fits the abstract, which never mentions calibration, but could not be confirmed against the full text.
references.caveats: Full text paywalled, so the profit metric, base classifiers, number of bags, statistical tests and effect sizes are unverified; do not quote specific results without reading the article (for example via institutional access). The conclusion is qualitative ('valid and reliable alternative'), not a claim that underbagging beats all rivals. It covers only undersampling-based rebalancing combined with bagging. It does not support claims about calibration, threshold moving, uplift or survival modelling. Whether the 11 datasets include the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset is unknown, so do not imply the paper tested that dataset.

references.title: Explaining customer churn prediction in telecom industry using tabular machine learning models
references.harvard_reference: Poudel, S.S., Pokharel, S. and Timilsina, M. (2024) 'Explaining customer churn prediction in telecom industry using tabular machine learning models', Machine Learning with Applications, 17, 100567. doi:10.1016/j.mlwa.2024.100567.
references.abstract_summary: An applied benchmark-plus-explainability study on the public Kaggle telco churn dataset (7,043 customers, 30 attributes, 26.54% churners; the attribute list in Table 1 - CustomerID, Lat_Long, CLTV, Churn_Label, etc. - matches the IBM Telco Customer Churn data, although the paper only cites kaggle.com). Seven classifiers (SVC, logistic regression, random forest, GBM, neural network, AdaBoost, XGBoost) were tuned (Table 2) and compared by 10-fold cross-validation on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-score and PR-score (Table 4). GBM ranked first (accuracy 0.81 +/- 0.02, ROC 0.86 +/- 0.01, PR 0.68 +/- 0.03, recall 0.55), followed by XGBoost (ROC 0.85) and random forest (ROC 0.84); the neural network was weakest and least stable (accuracy 0.74 +/- 0.06, recall 0.43 +/- 0.31). A Wilcoxon signed-rank test against GBM (Table 5) found significant differences only for the neural network and logistic regression (p = 0.03125 each); AdaBoost (p = 0.05), XGBoost (0.07), SVC (0.0625) and random forest (0.156) were not significantly different. SHAP beeswarm and interaction plots for the GBM identify month-to-month contract, tenure and monthly charges as the dominant drivers, with fibre-optic internet and electronic-check payment also pushing towards churn; the month-to-month x fibre-optic and short-tenure x high-monthly-charge interactions are highlighted. The authors conclude GBM is 'notably better' and that SHAP explanations make churn drivers actionable for telecom operators. No class-imbalance treatment, calibration, threshold or profit-based evaluation is performed.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data.
claims_supported.where: Table 4 (10-fold CV on the Kaggle telco dataset, n = 7,043, 26.54% churn): ROC-score GBM 0.86 +/- 0.01, XGBoost 0.85 +/- 0.02, Random Forest 0.84 +/- 0.01, AdaBoost 0.82 +/- 0.01, versus Neural network 0.83 +/- 0.02, Logistic Regression 0.81 +/- 0.03 and SVC 0.77 +/- 0.02. Section 6.2: 'The ROC-score follows a similar trend, with GBM having the highest score.' The three tree ensembles (GBM, XGBoost, RF) occupy the top three ROC-AUC positions, and GBM also leads on accuracy and PR-score. Note the ranking in the paper is by accuracy, with ROC reported alongside.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles' ROC-AUC on telecom churn data is often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: This paper does not support the 'close to logistic regression' qualifier and frames the opposite. In Table 4 LR's ROC-score (0.81 +/- 0.03) is 0.03-0.05 below the tree ensembles (0.84-0.86), and the authors state that GBM 'significantly outperforms Neural Networks and Logistic Regression' (Section 6.2 and Discussion, Section 7; Wilcoxon p = 0.03125 in Table 5). LR is within 0.02 of the ensembles on accuracy only (0.79 vs 0.80-0.81), but the claim concerns ROC-AUC. Cite this paper only for the ensemble ranking; support the 'close to LR' point from a multi-dataset benchmark such as Geiler et al. (2022) instead.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 6.2.1 (Fig. 2, SHAP beeswarm plot for the GBM model): the 'Contract_Month-to-month', 'Tenure_Months' and 'Monthly Charges' features 'exert the most substantial impact on the model's output, with the Contract_Month-to-month feature, in particular, strongly pushing predictions towards churn'; 'Internet_Service_Fiber optic' and 'Payment_Method_Electronic check' also 'predominantly contribute positively to churn predictions'. Discussion (Section 7): 'features like month-to-month contracts, tenure, and monthly charges were identified as key drivers of churn. Customers with short-term contracts or higher monthly charges were predisposed to churn'. Section 6.2.2 (Figs 3-4) adds two interactions: month-to-month contract combined with fibre-optic service amplifies churn, and short tenure with high monthly charges carries the highest risk, with the charge effect fading beyond roughly 20 months of tenure. Caveat: the evidence is a single beeswarm plot for one model (GBM); no numeric mean |SHAP| values or rankings for other models are reported, and no individual-level (local) explanation is actually shown despite the paper's framing.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: The paper does not make this claim and contains no such evaluation. Models are compared only on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-score and PR-score (Table 4; 'The models are ranked by their Accuracy') plus a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Table 5). There is no cost-sensitive, profit or expected-maximum-profit metric, no decision-threshold analysis, and the preferred model is never re-examined under a business criterion. The nearest passage is the confusion-matrix discussion (Table 6: TN 466, FP 51, FN 84, TP 103), which remarks qualitatively that overlooked churners 'could lead to substantial customer loss' and that improving sensitivity is 'a critical focus for advancing its utility in practical business scenarios', but no alternative threshold or model is selected on that basis. For this claim cite Verbraken et al. (2013), Verbeke et al. (2012) or Lemmens and Gupta (2020) instead.

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for critical discussion (dataset, imbalance, testing, tuning, scope).
claims_supported.where: (1) Dataset (Table 3, Table 1): Kaggle telco data, 7,043 samples, 30 features, 26.54% churn / 73.46% non-churn; the attribute list (CustomerID, Count, Country, State, City, Zip_Code, Lat_Long, ..., Tenure_Months, Contract, Monthly Charges, Total_Charges, CLTV, Churn_Label) matches the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, so results are directly comparable with the student's report, though the paper never names IBM. (2) Full metric table (Table 4, mean +/- SD over 10 folds): GBM acc 0.81/prec 0.67/rec 0.55/F1 0.60/ROC 0.86/PR 0.68; XGBoost 0.80/0.68/0.55/0.61/0.85/0.67; RF 0.80/0.71/0.43/0.53/0.84/0.64; AdaBoost 0.79/0.65/0.50/0.57/0.82/0.63; LR 0.79/0.64/0.47/0.54/0.81/0.61; SVC 0.78/0.68/0.34/0.45/0.77/0.57; NN 0.74/0.58/0.43/0.41/0.83/0.64 with very large fold-to-fold variance (precision +/- 0.26, recall +/- 0.31) - i.e. a tuned MLP did not beat tree ensembles on this tabular data. (3) Imbalance: the 26.5% churn rate is reported and class imbalance is discussed in Related Work (citing Zhu et al., 2017), but no resampling, class weighting or cost-sensitive learning is applied; the consequence is visible in GBM's recall of 0.55 and the confusion matrix (84 of 187 churners missed, about 45%), which the authors themselves call 'a notable challenge' and say improving sensitivity 'emerges as a critical focus'. (4) Statistical testing (Table 5, Wilcoxon signed-rank vs GBM): NN p = 0.03125, LR p = 0.03125, SVC 0.0625, AdaBoost 0.05, XGBoost 0.07, RF 0.15625 - so GBM is statistically separable only from NN and LR, not from the other ensembles; the paper does not say which metric the test compares or how many paired observations were used, p-values of exactly 1/32 suggest very few pairs, and no multiple-comparison correction is applied, so the abstract's 'GBM is notably better' is overstated relative to XGBoost/RF/AdaBoost (the authors concede AdaBoost is 'on the threshold' and suggest ensembling). (5) Tuning (Table 2): search ranges are given (e.g. GBM max-depth 5-29, min-samples-leaf 5-10, max-leaf-nodes 3-7; RF max-depth 9-20 with n-estimators only 14-20; XGBoost n-estimators 100-1000, learning-rate 0.01-0.3) but the paper does not state whether tuning was nested inside the 10-fold CV, so the reported CV scores may be optimistically biased (cf. Cawley and Talbot, 2010). (6) Feature engineering (Section 5): an 'engagement score' (from tenure, monthly and total charges) and a 'service utilisation' count were created, yet Table 3 still reports 30 features and neither engineered feature appears in the SHAP plot, so their contribution is unreported. (7) Novelty and writing: the claim 'our approach is the first to generate global and/or local explanations for churn prediction' (Introduction) is contestable given the Leung et al. (2021) XAI-for-churn paper they cite; the Conclusion refers to 'call duration, plan type' which are not attributes of this dataset. (8) Not addressed at all: probability calibration, threshold selection, profit/cost metrics, uplift or treatment-effect modelling (Ascarza, 2018 is cited only in Related Work), survival/time-to-event models (Related Work only), fairness, and deployment/monitoring. (9) Table 7 benchmarks GBM's ROC 0.86 against 0.98-0.99 figures from other papers on different datasets, which is not like-for-like; the one comparable entry (Ebrah and Elnasir, 2019, SVM on the IBM dataset, ROC 0.83) is close to the present GBM result.

references.caveats: Cite this paper for (i) the ranking of tuned tabular classifiers on the IBM/Kaggle Telco data (GBM > XGBoost > RF > AdaBoost/LR > SVC on ROC-AUC, with a neural network unstable and weakest) and (ii) SHAP-identified drivers (month-to-month contract, tenure, monthly charges, fibre-optic, electronic check).
