The venue is a reputable but young (2020) gold-OA Elsevier journal, not a flagship marketing/OR journal.

references.title: A data-driven approach with explainable artificial intelligence for customer churn prediction in the telecommunications industry
references.harvard_reference: Asif, D., Arif, M.S. and Mukheimer, A. (2025) 'A data-driven approach with explainable artificial intelligence for customer churn prediction in the telecommunications industry', Results in Engineering, 26, 104629. doi:10.1016/j.rineng.2025.104629.
references.abstract_summary: Proposes XAI-Churn TriBoost, a soft-voting ensemble of XGBoost, CatBoost and LightGBM (weights 2:1:3) for telecom churn prediction. The data are NOT the IBM/Kaggle Telco file: the paper uses train.csv from the Expresso Churn Prediction Challenge on Zindi (Senegalese prepaid operator), 2,154,048 records and 17 stated variables, with churn defined as the customer becoming inactive with no transactions for 90 consecutive days; 19% of records are churners. Preprocessing: drop zone1/zone2 (>90% missing), MRG (one value), user_id, region (dropped 'to avoid introducing location-based bias' and to generalise across countries), top_pack and freq_top_pack (140 categories); ordinal encoding; iterative imputation with a Bayesian ridge estimator (median initialisation, converged after 15 iterations); sequential robust -> standard -> min-max scaling; a new feature off_net = tigo + orange; Boruta with random forest (100 trees, percentile 90, alpha 0.05) leaving nine features (montant, frequence_rech, revenue, arpu_segment, frequence, data_volume, on_net, regularity, off_net). Stratified 60/40 split (random_state 42); SMOTE applied to the training set only with k=5 and sampling_strategy 0.5, raising the minority share from 19% to 33% (1,575,055 training rows; 861,620 test rows). Hyperparameters tuned by RandomizedSearchCV. Reported test results: accuracy 0.9644, precision 0.9282, recall 0.8782, F1 0.9025, AUC-ROC 0.9828, PR-AUC 0.9601. Table 9 baselines (same preprocessing): decision tree 0.9395 acc / 0.8468 F1; logistic regression 0.8200 / 0.6338; Gaussian NB 0.5682 / 0.4565 (recall 0.9672); Bernoulli NB 0.7952 / 0.5519; ridge classifier 0.8011 / 0.6164; SGD 0.7993 / 0.6146. A 27-combination ablation of ensemble weights (Table 8) spans only accuracy 0.9635-0.9644 and F1 0.8999-0.9025. LIME gives local explanations for a 53%-churn and a 78%-no-churn instance (revenue, regularity, arpu_segment); SHAP force/waterfall plots (regularity +0.21, revenue +0.06, arpu_segment -0.03), a beeswarm plot and a mean-|SHAP| ranking identify regularity (number of activities over the last three months) and montant (top-up amount) as the top drivers, followed by arpu_segment and revenue. Future work only: multi-industry datasets, a web app with real-time monitoring, a feedback loop and periodic retraining.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Partly contradicted. The boosting ensemble is the top model on accuracy, precision and F1 (Section 5, Table 9: TriBoost 0.9644 / 0.9282 / 0.8782 / 0.9025) and Section 4.2.5 / Fig. 10 report AUC-ROC 0.9828 and PR-AUC 0.9601 for the ensemble, but no ROC-AUC is reported for ANY baseline, so the paper contains no ROC-AUC comparison at all. Random forest is not evaluated as a classifier (it is only the base learner inside Boruta feature selection). The 'close to logistic regression' half is directly contradicted on this dataset: logistic regression scores accuracy 0.8200, precision 0.5125, recall 0.8304, F1 0.6338 (Table 9), i.e. about 14 accuracy points and 27 F1 points below the ensemble, and even a single decision tree (0.9395 / 0.8468) beats it by a wide margin. Note this is the 2.15-million-row Expresso prepaid usage dataset, not the IBM Telco data on which the near-parity pattern is usually reported, so this paper is evidence AGAINST parity on large usage-count data, not for it.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported as phrased. SHAP mean-|SHAP| ranking (Section 4.4, Fig. 16), the Discussion and the Conclusion name 'regularity' (number of activities over the last three months) and 'montant' (top-up amount) as the most important features, followed by 'arpu_segment' and 'revenue'; the abstract states 'Key factors impacting churn include regularity and montant'. The dataset is prepaid and has no contract-type variable at all. No tenure variable appears in the final feature set (Table 2). The Zindi source data does contain a TENURE column (subscription duration band; confirmed from a third-party data dictionary of the Expresso challenge, not from the paper), and the paper's own counts - 11 features retained after cleaning (Section 3.2.1), 10 after merging tigo+orange, 9 after Boruta (Section 5) - imply that the single feature Boruta eliminated was tenure, although the paper never names it. The only loose 'equivalent' is that spend features (montant, revenue, arpu_segment) play the role monthly charges play in the IBM Telco data. Also note the paper says (Section 4.4, beeswarm) that HIGH regularity pushes predictions toward churn, which is counter-intuitive and should be checked against Fig. 15 before being cited.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not addressed. Section 4.2 defines the evaluation as accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC and PR-AUC only; there is no cost matrix, profit measure, expected-value analysis, uplift or threshold optimisation anywhere in the paper. The default 0.5 decision rule is implied (the LIME example with 53% churn probability is classed as churn, Section 4.3.1). Ensemble weights were chosen in the ablation (Table 8) by accuracy/F1. The Discussion's statement that the ensemble is 'the most reliable and practical choice for businesses focused on customer retention strategies' is argued from precision and F1, not from any business metric.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (a) Imbalance handling (Section 3.6): SMOTE is applied to the training set only, with an explicit statement that resampling the whole dataset 'would alter the real-world distribution', and only PARTIAL rebalancing is used (sampling_strategy 0.5: minority share 19% -> 33%, not 1:1). (b) Ensemble weighting adds almost nothing measurable: across all 27 weight combinations in Table 8 accuracy ranges 0.9635-0.9644 and F1 0.8999-0.9025, differences at the third or fourth decimal with no confidence intervals or repeated runs; evaluation is a single 60/40 hold-out (Section 3.5), with cross-validation used only inside RandomizedSearchCV (folds not stated). (c) Linear models cluster together (LR 0.8200, ridge 0.8011, SGD 0.7993 accuracy; F1 0.61-0.63) while a single decision tree reaches 0.9395, indicating strong non-linearity in prepaid usage-count features after the authors' scaling pipeline (Table 9). (d) Gaussian naive Bayes illustrates the recall/precision trade-off: recall 0.9672 but precision 0.2988 and accuracy 0.5682 (Table 9, Section 5). (e) Missing data: iterative imputation with Bayesian ridge (median initialisation, tolerance 1e-5, converged after 15 of 20 iterations) rather than deletion or mean fill, because some columns exceed 50% missing (Section 3.2.3). (f) Feature selection by Boruta with a random-forest base (Table 1) is presented as a bias-reducing alternative to threshold- or domain-driven manual selection (Section 3.4). (g) Fairness/generalisability gesture only: the region feature is dropped 'to avoid introducing location-based bias' and to keep the model applicable across countries (Section 3.2.1); there is no formal fairness, calibration, uplift or survival analysis. (h) Deployment is future work only: a web application with real-time data links, monitoring, customer segmentation, a user feedback loop and periodic retraining to cope with drift such as 'economic turmoil or changes in the market' (Sections 5-6). (i) Compute: the whole pipeline on 2.15 million rows ran on a single HP ZBook laptop (i9-9880H, Quadro T2000, 32 GB RAM) (Section 4.1.2). (j) The authors themselves position IBM-Telco-scale studies (7,043 samples, 20 features) as small-data contrasts (Section 5, Table 10).

references.verification_notes: Crossref (query.bibliographic, 3 rows): first hit DOI 10.1016/j.rineng.2025.104629, type journal-article, 'A data-driven approach with explainable artificial intelligence for customer churn prediction in the telecommunications industry', Results in Engineering, Elsevier BV, ISSN 2590-1230, volume 26, article 104629, issue date 2025-06, licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 from 2025-03-12, 57 citing works; authors Daniyal Asif, Muhammad Shoaib Arif, Aiman Mukheimer. Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 277092256): same title/venue/year 2025, publicationTypes JournalArticle, 60 citations, isOpenAccess true (GOLD), publicationDate 2025-06-01, but no abstract returned. OpenAlex: same metadata, publication_date 2025-03-17 (online), gold OA, volume 26, pages 104629, 56 citations, affiliations Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology (Asif) and Prince Sultan University (Arif, corresponding; Mukheimer); OpenAlex abstract matches the ScienceDirect abstract. Full text read directly from the open-access ScienceDirect article page (PII S2590123025007066) in the built-in browser; the Highlights, abstract, Sections 1-6, all tables (1-10), CRediT, funding ('no specific grant'; APC paid by Prince Sultan University) and data-availability statement were read in full. Venue legitimacy: DOAJ API record for ISSN 2590-1230 lists Results in Engineering, publisher Elsevier (Netherlands), review process 'Single anonymous peer review', DOAJ seal, added 10 June 2019, APC up to 2,160 USD, CC BY / BY-NC / BY-NC-ND; OpenAlex source record: Elsevier BV, is_in_doaj true, is_core true, 13,050 works, h-index 99. The ScienceDirect journal page, DOAJ web page and Scimago returned HTTP 403, so Scopus/CiteScore figures were not directly checked, but Elsevier ownership plus DOAJ listing with a stated peer-review process is sufficient to rule out a predatory venue; it is a broad-scope, high-volume APC journal rather than a specialist ML or marketing-science venue. Publication year 2025 satisfies the 2021-2026 window. Author name: the article byline and Crossref give 'Aiman Mukheimer'; OpenAlex and the lead give 'Aiman A. Mukheimer'; the byline form is used in the reference. No issue number exists (article-number journal), so the issue field is empty. Dataset identification in the paper is explicit (Expresso Churn Prediction Challenge on Zindi, train.csv, 2,154,048 samples); the existence of a TENURE column in the source data was confirmed from a third-party data dictionary (github.com/aymanibrahim/telecom_churn_pipeline, docs/expresso.md), which the paper does not cite. The authors provide no code repository (data-availability statement: 'The manuscript included all required data and implementing information'); a GitHub reimplementation by a third party (BraveVahid/telecom-customer-churn-prediction) exists but is not the authors' code. The lead's title, authors, year, venue and DOI were all accurate; volume 26 and article number 104629 added.
references.caveats: 1) Dataset mismatch: this is the Expresso (Zindi, Senegal, prepaid) dataset with 2.15 million rows and nine usage/spend features, not the IBM/Kaggle Telco file; there is no contract, tenure, payment-method or monthly-charges variable in the model, so its feature-importance findings do not transfer to a Telco report and its 0.96 accuracy / 0.98 AUC must not be compared with the ~0.80 accuracy / ~0.84 AUC typical of Telco studies. 2) The paper reports no AUC for any baseline and never evaluates random forest as a classifier, so it cannot support statements about ensemble versus logistic-regression ROC-AUC. 3) Logistic regression is run on heavy-tailed count features after ordinal encoding and a robust/standard/min-max scaling chain with no interaction or log terms, so its weak result is partly a specification artefact. 4) Single 60/40 hold-out, no confidence intervals, no repeated seeds; the ablation shows weight choices differ only at the third or fourth decimal, so the claimed superiority of the 2:1:3 weighting is not meaningful. 5) SMOTE is partial (to 33% minority) and applied after scaling; no comparison with class weights or no-resampling is given, so the paper cannot show that SMOTE helped. 6) Accuracy is inflated by the 81% non-churn base rate; the PR-AUC of 0.9601 and F1 of 0.9025 are the more informative figures. 7) Section 4.4 states that high 'regularity' values push predictions toward churn, the opposite of the intuitive direction (and of what Zindi community analyses report: low activity -> churn); the paper does not reconcile this, so cite the ranking, not the direction, unless Fig. 15 is checked. 8) Internal inconsistencies: Highlights give precision 92.80% and F1 90.24% while the abstract and Table 8 give 92.82% and 90.25%; Section 5 text credits reference [47] (7,043 samples) with 0.981 accuracy but Table 10 lists [47] at 0.79 accuracy / 0.84 AUC; the '1.58 million' training records quoted in the Conclusion is the post-SMOTE count (original training set 1,292,428); the feature 'arpu_segment' is misspelt 'apru_segment' in Table 4 and Section 4.4. 9) No calibration, uplift, survival, cost-sensitive or fairness analysis; deployment is described only as future work. 10) The venue is a broad-scope, APC-funded Elsevier mega-journal (single-anonymous review); treat it as legitimate but give its methodological claims less weight than a specialist journal would carry.

references.title: Explainable AI-driven customer churn prediction: a multi-model ensemble approach with SHAP-based feature analysis
references.harvard_reference: El Attar, A. and El-Hajj, M. (2026) 'Explainable AI-driven customer churn prediction: a multi-model ensemble approach with SHAP-based feature analysis', Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, 9, article number 1748799. doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1748799.
references.abstract_summary: Applied study on the public IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset (n = 7,043). Pipeline: feature engineering (46 model features after encoding, including derived AvgMonthlyCharge), stratified 80/20 split (5,634 train / 1,409 test, random_state 42), SMOTE (k_neighbors = 5) applied only to the training portion of each fold, Optuna hyperparameter tuning with stratified 5-fold CV, and seven learners: Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Logistic Regression and an MLP (no SVM). Test-set results (Table 7): XGBoost, LightGBM and Gradient Boosting all reach accuracy/precision/recall/F1 of 0.84 with AUC-ROC 0.932, 0.930 and 0.926; Random Forest 0.81 / AUC 0.887; AdaBoost 0.79 / 0.872; Logistic Regression 0.78 / 0.864; MLP 0.76 / 0.848; a soft-voting ensemble of the top models gives F1 0.84 and AUC 0.918. SHAP (TreeExplainer for tree models, KernelExplainer for LR and MLP) is used for global and local explanation; Section 4.2 names Contract_Twoyear, MonthlyCharges and tenure as the three largest contributors (mean |SHAP| 0.85, 0.86, 0.72), while the abstract instead names contract type, tenure and technical support. A cost-sensitive framework (C_FP = 1, C_FN = 5) is used to fine-tune the decision threshold to 0.528 after an initial F1-based step; the abstract reports precision 0.90 / recall 0.91 and a 15% reduction in false negatives at that threshold. Probability calibration (isotonic regression via CalibratedClassifierCV for tree ensembles, Platt scaling for LR) is reported with Brier scores and ECE. An autoencoder (46 to 16 latent dimensions) plus K-means (k = 3) segments customers into a 'stable middle' cluster (n = 2,586, 21% churn), a 'high-risk' cluster (n = 2,478, 42% churn, mean tenure 22.9 months, about $73/month) and a 'loyal core' (n = 1,979, 15% churn, mean tenure 46.4 months). The authors conclude with actionable retention guidance and caveat that SHAP attributions are not causal.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: FIRST HALF SUPPORTED, SECOND HALF CONTRADICTED, so the claim as worded is not supported. Table 7 (Section 4.1, test set) shows gradient boosting models at the top: XGBoost AUC-ROC 0.932, LightGBM 0.930, Gradient Boosting 0.926; Random Forest is fourth at 0.887. Logistic Regression is 0.864 (F1 0.78) - i.e. 0.062-0.068 AUC and 0.06 F1 below the boosters, and the text ranks it below Random Forest and AdaBoost ('Random Forest showed solid but lower performance (F1-score: 0.81, AUC: 0.887) ... followed by AdaBoost, Logistic Regression, and the MLP'). The paper therefore presents a clear gap between boosted trees and logistic regression, not near-parity. The only sense in which LR is 'close' is Random Forest (0.887) vs LR (0.864), a 0.023 AUC gap, but the paper does not frame it that way. Note that the LR here is a scikit-learn logistic regression trained after SMOTE; the paper does not report how carefully the linear baseline was tuned relative to the boosters. Use this paper as evidence that boosted trees top the AUC ranking on the Telco data; do NOT cite it for 'close to logistic regression'.

claims_supported.claim: [Verifier-proposed replacement] On the IBM Telco Customer Churn data, gradient-boosted tree ensembles (XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting) achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.926-0.932), ahead of Random Forest (0.887) and logistic regression (0.864).
claims_supported.where: Table 7 and Section 4.1 (model performance comparison); abstract ('XGBoost attaining the best discriminative ability (AUC-ROC: 0.932)'); soft-voting ensemble F1 0.84 / AUC 0.918 also in Table 7 and abstract.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2 (SHAP global importance) and Figure 4 ('Top 10 features ranked by mean absolute SHAP value'): 'The SHAP analysis identified Contract_Twoyear, MonthlyCharges, and tenure as the three features making the largest contributions to the model's churn predictions, with mean absolute SHAP values of 0.85, 0.86, and 0.72, respectively.' Also: 'higher MonthlyCharges and use of electronic check payment methods were associated with increased likelihood of churn.' CAUTION: the abstract and a later results passage instead list 'contract type, tenure, and technical support' as the top three (with contract type mean |SHAP| 0.284, TechSupport 0.147, OnlineSecurity 0.134, electronic check 0.122 - a different scale, apparently from a different model/explainer run). So the paper is internally inconsistent about the third driver; contract type and tenure are consistently top-ranked, monthly charges is top-ranked in the Figure 4 / Section 4.2 analysis only. Cite Section 4.2 / Figure 4 specifically if you rely on monthly charges.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: NOT DEMONSTRATED. What the paper does: Section 3.7.2 ('Cost-sensitive evaluation') defines TotalCost = FP x C_FP + FN x C_FN with C_FP = 1, C_FN = 5, justified by acquisition costs being 5-10 times retention costs; Section 3.7.3 ('Threshold selection methodology') describes 'a two-step process' - F1-score optimisation followed by cost-sensitive fine-tuning 'to minimize expected business cost' - and the abstract reports the resulting threshold of 0.528 'balanced precision (0.90) and recall (0.91) while reducing false negatives by 15%'. What the paper does NOT do: it never reports the accuracy-optimal or F1-optimal threshold for comparison, never shows that the cost-based criterion moved the operating point relative to that intermediate value, never re-ranks the models under the cost function (model selection is made on F1/AUC in Table 7 and the cost analysis does not alter it), and does not compute profit, EMP or expected maximum profit. The precision 0.90 / recall 0.91 figures appear only in the abstract, with no table, model or class specified, and are arithmetically inconsistent with the Table 7 F1 of 0.84. The claimed 15% false-negative reduction has no baseline stated. Therefore the paper provides an example of adopting a cost-sensitive threshold, not evidence that business evaluation changes the preferred model or threshold versus accuracy-only evaluation.

claims_supported.claim: [Verifier-proposed replacement] The paper selects the decision threshold in two steps - F1 maximisation followed by fine-tuning to minimise an asymmetric business cost (C_FN = 5, C_FP = 1) - arriving at 0.528 rather than the default 0.5, but it does not report the intermediate F1-optimal threshold, a profit metric, or any change in model ranking under the cost criterion.
claims_supported.where: Sections 3.7.2 and 3.7.3 (cost function and two-step threshold procedure); abstract (threshold 0.528, precision 0.90, recall 0.91, false negatives reduced 15%); Table 7 (model ranking by F1/AUC, unchanged by the cost analysis).

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for a critical discussion (imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness, deployment).
claims_supported.where: (1) IMBALANCE: SMOTE (k_neighbors = 5, sampling_strategy = 'auto', random_state = 42) 'was applied exclusively to the training data, while the test set remained untouched', and within CV 'SMOTE was applied only to the training portion of the fold' - a leakage-aware protocol worth citing as good practice (Sections 3.4-3.6). (2) TUNING/PROTOCOL: Optuna with stratified 5-fold CV; single 80/20 stratified split (5,634/1,409); no confidence intervals or repeated splits reported for Table 7, so differences such as 0.932 vs 0.926 AUC are not shown to be significant. (3) CALIBRATION: CalibratedClassifierCV with isotonic regression (5-fold) for tree ensembles and Platt scaling for LR; 'Logistic regression exhibited near-perfect calibration initially, with Platt scaling providing marginal improvement'; Figure 9 reports XGBoost ECE falling from 0.042 to 0.018 after calibration. However Table 8 Brier scores WORSEN after isotonic calibration (XGBoost 0.106 to 0.110; Random Forest 0.137 to 0.187; LightGBM 0.107 to 0.113) even though the table labels isotonic as 'Best' - an internal inconsistency you can use critically (isotonic regression can overfit on ~1,100-sample folds). (4) EXPLANATION STABILITY: 1,000-iteration bootstrap - 'top 5 features maintaining 98% ranking consistency', coefficient of variation of SHAP values < 5%, presented as evidence of 'deployment readiness despite cross-sectional data limitations'. (5) SEGMENTATION: autoencoder (46 to 16 dims) + K-means k = 3; clusters n = 2,586 (21% churn, tenure 30.7 mo, $50.4/mo), n = 2,478 (42% churn, tenure 22.9 mo, ~$73/mo) and n = 1,979 (15% churn, tenure 46.4 mo); silhouette 0.3495, Calinski-Harabasz 3,757.51, Davies-Bouldin 1.1123 (weak-to-moderate cluster separation). (6) BUSINESS IMPACT CLAIMS ARE ASSERTED, NOT MEASURED: 'organizations can achieve estimated cost savings of 35%-45% in retention marketing expenditures while improving overall retention rates by 18%-25%' is not derived from any calculation in the paper; likewise the SHAP-based counterfactual that 'converting to a one-year contract would reduce churn by 0.35, with technical support providing an additional 0.08 reduction' is an attribution-based estimate, and the authors themselves state SHAP values 'explain feature contributions to the model's predictions, not necessarily real-world causal relationships'. (7) NOT ADDRESSED: uplift modelling, survival/time-to-event analysis, fairness/bias auditing, temporal validation, and real deployment; 'deployment' is limited to a suggestion that force plots be integrated into CRM systems. (8) LIMITATIONS acknowledged: reliance on the single public Telco benchmark, cross-sectional data, market-specific generalisability, SHAP not causal. (9) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES to flag: abstract's precision 0.90 / recall 0.91 vs Table 7 F1 0.84; abstract's 'technical support' vs Section 4.2's 'MonthlyCharges' as a top-three driver; Table 8 Brier scores vs 'Best' labels.

references.verification_notes: DOI 10.3389/frai.2026.1748799 resolves; Crossref record (journal-article, Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Frontiers Media SA, vol. 9, article 1748799, published online 10 February 2026, eISSN 2624-8212, CC-BY 4.0, 31 references, 9 citing works at time of check) matches the lead exactly. Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 285513128; DBLP journals/frai/AttarE26; PubMed 41743649; PMC12929532) and OpenAlex (gold OA, published 2026-02-10) agree on title, authors, venue, volume and year; the verbatim abstract was taken from Semantic Scholar. Full text read via the Frontiers article page and PubMed Central (PMC12929532). Authors: Ali El Attar and Mohammed El-Hajj (corresponding), Faculty of Computer Studies, Arab Open University, Beirut, Lebanon (OpenAlex records the second author as Mohammed Ibrahim El-Hajj; the byline uses 'Mohammed El-Hajj'). Dates: received 18 Nov 2025, revised 26 Dec 2025, accepted 20 Jan 2026, published 10 Feb 2026; section 'AI in Business'; edited by Ernesto Leon-Castro with two named reviewers, so it is peer reviewed (Frontiers single-anonymised model). Venue check: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (Frontiers Media SA, Lausanne) is indexed in Scopus, Web of Science ESCI, PubMed Central and DOAJ; Frontiers is a COPE/OASPA member. It is an established, non-predatory open-access venue, though Frontiers' APC model and fast review cycles have attracted criticism (the publisher was briefly on Beall's list in 2015 and later removed), and the 2-month submission-to-acceptance time here is fast; the journal page states an Impact Factor of 6.7 and CiteScore of 8.0, which I could not independently verify. Frontiers volumes carry no issue numbers, so 'issue' is left empty and the article number is given in place of pages. The lead's scout note is accurate except that the top SHAP drivers named ('contract type, tenure and tech support') follow the abstract, whereas the body (Section 4.2/Figure 4) names Contract_Twoyear, MonthlyCharges and tenure. The seven models are RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, LR and MLP (no SVM). All numbers quoted in this record were checked against the full text; where two full-text passes disagreed (threshold section, SHAP ranking) a third verbatim pass was used to resolve them.
references.caveats: 1) Applied benchmark paper with notable internal inconsistencies (abstract vs Section 4.2 on the third SHAP driver; abstract precision/recall 0.90/0.91 vs Table 7 F1 0.84; Table 8 Brier scores worsening under 'best' isotonic calibration) - cite specific tables/sections rather than the abstract, and consider mentioning the inconsistencies in a critical discussion. 2) Single 80/20 split with no confidence intervals; AUC differences among the three boosters (0.926-0.932) and between the ensemble (0.918) and XGBoost (0.932) are not shown to be statistically meaningful. 3) The 35-45% cost-saving and 18-25% retention-improvement figures are unsupported assertions, not results; do not cite them as findings. 4) The cost-sensitive threshold (0.528) is not compared against an accuracy- or F1-optimal threshold, and no profit/EMP metric is computed, so the paper cannot support claims about business evaluation changing model choice. 5) Same public IBM Telco dataset as the student report, so results are directly comparable but carry the same limitations (cross-sectional, ~26.5% churn base rate, no behavioural/usage data). 6) Uplift, survival, fairness and temporal validation are absent - useful as a gap to critique rather than a source for those topics.

references.title: Explainable churn prediction in telecom with tabular ML five model benchmark and SHAP analysis
references.venue: Discover Artificial Intelligence (Springer Nature; Crossref publisher string 'Springer Science and Business Media LLC'; eISSN 2731-0809)
references.harvard_reference: Zerine, I., Islam, M.M., Khan, M.A.U., Chy, M.A.R., Saimon, A.S.M., Manik, M.M.T.G. and Wata, C. (2026) 'Explainable churn prediction in telecom with tabular ML five model benchmark and SHAP analysis', Discover Artificial Intelligence, 6(1), 263. doi:10.1007/s44163-026-00983-0.
references.abstract_summary: Benchmarks five tabular learners (elastic-net logistic regression, RBF SVC, random forest, XGBoost, and a small MLP) on a Kaggle Telco Customer Churn snapshot using nested cross-validation (5 stratified outer folds, 3 inner folds; PR-AUC as the tuning objective; F1-optimal threshold chosen on inner validation). The MLP is reported best on every metric (accuracy 0.92, precision 0.88, recall 0.82, F1 0.85, ROC-AUC 0.95, PR-AUC 0.82); XGBoost is the best classical baseline (accuracy 0.89, F1 0.69, ROC-AUC 0.91), random forest 'followed closely', logistic regression had lower recall (F1 0.64) and SVC was weakest (F1 0.59). Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the five folds are at trend level two-sided (p = 0.0625-0.1875) and significant one-sided only against LR and SVC. SHAP, PDP and ICE show churn risk falling monotonically with tenure with a tipping point near three years, rising steeply from zero to about five technical tickets then saturating, and amplified by high monthly charges, month-to-month contracts and fibre-optic service. Recommended interventions: contract migration, rapid ticket resolution, and targeted credits for early-life, high-charge customers.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Section 4 (Results) and Section 5 (Conclusion). The paper reports the compact MLP as the top model on ROC-AUC (0.95 +/- 0.01) and XGBoost as the best NON-neural baseline (ROC-AUC 0.91 +/- 0.01), i.e. the MLP 'improved ... ROC AUC by 4 points' over XGBoost; random forest 'followed closely' behind XGBoost (accuracy 0.87, F1 0.66). Logistic regression's ROC-AUC is not stated in the text (Table 3 is only an image link); LR is described as the 'lower bound for performance' with F1 0.64 and recall 0.58 versus XGBoost F1 0.69. So this paper supports only the narrower point that tree ensembles were the strongest classical baselines; it contradicts the framing that tree ensembles achieve the top ROC-AUC, and gives no evidence that they are close to logistic regression. Cite it as a counter-example to the 'tree ensembles win on tabular churn' consensus, with the caveats noted.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.3 (Fig. 4 global SHAP beeswarm): 'Contract type, Monthly Charges, and Tenure are the dominant global drivers, with month-to-month contracts, higher charges, and shorter tenure increasing churn risk'; Section 4.4 repeats that the beeswarm 'identifies contract type, Monthly Charges, and tenure as the dominant global drivers'. Also supported by the abstract (tenure tipping point near three years; risk 'amplified by higher monthly charges and month to month contracts with fiber users most sensitive') and Section 4.3 SHAP dependence/PDP/ICE for tenure and technical tickets.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not demonstrated. Model selection and thresholding are statistical, not profit-based: the tuning objective is PR-AUC (Section 3.4) and 'the decision threshold is chosen on the inner validation data to maximize the F1 score' (Sections 3.4, 3.5). Section 4.5 states 'While this study reports threshold-independent metrics, the predicted probabilities enable cost-based threshold selection by minimizing expected misclassification cost or maximizing expected monetary value (EMV)' and Section 4.4 recommends sequencing outreach by 'expected business value, defined as the product of predicted churn probability and customer value net of treatment cost' - but no profit/EMV evaluation is actually run and no change in model or threshold preference is shown. The Conclusion explicitly lists 'cost sensitive learning and explicit thresholding tied to treatment budgets' as future work. The paper can be cited for the argument that cost-sensitive thresholding is needed, not for evidence that it changes the preferred model.

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for critical discussion: (a) imbalance handled by class weighting and XGBoost scale_pos_weight rather than SMOTE; (b) probabilities calibrated with Platt/isotonic when it improves PR-AUC, MLP Brier score 0.11 +/- 0.01; (c) the Wilcoxon tests use only five paired folds, so the smallest attainable two-sided exact p is 0.0625 - the 'significance' rests on one-sided tests (p = 0.03125 vs LR and SVC; RF p = 0.0625 and XGBoost p = 0.09375 remain non-significant); (d) tenure tipping point 'near the late third year', technical-ticket risk rising from 0 to ~5 tickets then saturating, fibre subscribers most sensitive; (e) authors state SHAP 'explains associations, not causes', results come from a single public dataset, and uplift, survival (time-to-churn), causal what-if, drift monitoring and fairness auditing are deferred to future work.
claims_supported.where: (a) Section 3.5: 'Class imbalance is addressed with class weighting for learners that support it and with a positive class scaling term for boosting'; (b) Section 3.5 and Section 4.5 ('mean Brier score of 0.11 +/- 0.01'); (c) Section 4.1: 'Exact p-values were computed because there are five paired observations per comparison', W = 0.0, two-sided p = 0.0625 vs LR and SVC; RF W = 1.0, p = 0.1250; XGBoost W = 2.0, p = 0.1875; one-sided p = 0.03125, 0.0625, 0.09375; (d) Sections 4.3 and 4.4; (e) Section 4.6 (Limitations) and Section 5 (Conclusion, final sentence).

references.verification_notes: Existence and metadata confirmed independently by Crossref (DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-00983-0; journal-article; Discover Artificial Intelligence; vol. 6, issue 1, article 263; published online 2026-02-22; eISSN 2731-0809; licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 285977799; DBLP journals/dai/ZerineIKCSMW26; 7 citations; gold OA) and OpenAlex (same title, authors, venue, year). The Springer Nature article page (fetched via curl; the WebFetch tool was bounced by Springer's cookie gate) confirms: Received 02 October 2025, Accepted 04 February 2026, Published 22 February 2026, Version of record 27 March 2026; authors and affiliations (Trine University, BRAC University, International American University, Washington University of Science and Technology, University of the Cumberlands, Bule Hora University). Peer review: DOAJ lists Discover Artificial Intelligence (Springer, Switzerland) with 'Single anonymous peer review', in DOAJ since 17 Nov 2021, APC EUR 1,390 / GBP 1,190; OpenAlex lists it as a Springer Nature journal, in DOAJ, flagged 'core', 2,108 works, h-index 40, 2-year mean citedness 3.07. It is an established-publisher, indexed, peer-reviewed venue and not predatory, though it is a young (2021) broad-scope APC mega-journal of the Springer 'Discover' series rather than a high-prestige specialist journal. Publication year 2026 is within the 2021-2026 window. Claims tested against the full open-access text (Introduction, Methods 3.1-3.6, Results 4-4.7, Conclusion). Author name: Springer's page renders 'Md Asikur Rahman Chy' with some Cyrillic look-alike characters; the Latin spelling from Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex is used here. Crossref/Springer give 'Mia Md. Tofayel Gonee Manik' (with a full stop); initials are unaffected.
references.caveats: (1) Internal inconsistencies the student should note if citing the numbers: the abstract gives a class ratio of 'approximately two point seven seven to one' but Section 3.1 gives 28%/72% = 'about two point five seven to one'; Sections 3.1-3.2 describe an 'expanded snapshot' of 8,093 customers and 34 input features including technical-ticket counts, whereas the Data Availability statement points to the standard Kaggle blastchar dataset (7,043 rows, 21 columns, no ticket fields). Ticket-count features exist only in the IBM Cognos 'Telco customer churn (11.1.3+)' variant, where numTechTickets is known to be extremely predictive; this likely explains the reported 92% accuracy / 0.95 ROC-AUC, which are far above the ~80-82% accuracy and ~0.84-0.86 ROC-AUC typically reported on the standard 7,043-row dataset. Results are therefore NOT directly comparable with studies on the standard Kaggle dataset. (2) Tables 3-6 are not in the HTML text (image/link only), so per-model ROC-AUC for LR, RF and SVC could not be read; only MLP (0.95) and XGBoost (0.91) are quoted in prose. (3) The statistical testing is under-powered by construction (n = 5 folds); the authors themselves describe two-sided results as 'trend level'. (4) The reproduction pack is described but no repository URL appears in the text. (5) Section 4.5 is mis-headed as a second 'Business implications' section (it actually covers robustness, calibration and fairness checks). (6) The 'Scout' lead listed six models; the paper benchmarks five - 'Logistic Regression with Elastic Net' is one model, not two.

references.title: Explainable AI-driven triple adaptive feature selection model for enhanced telecom churn prediction
references.harvard_reference: Javed, D., Jhanjhi, N.Z. and Ali, N.I. (2026) 'Explainable AI-driven triple adaptive feature selection model for enhanced telecom churn prediction', Results in Engineering, 31, 111361. doi:10.1016/j.rineng.2026.111361.
references.abstract_summary: Proposes 'Churn-Explainer', a modular telecom churn pipeline: preprocessing (median imputation, label encoding, z-scoring), Random Minority Oversampling (RMO) for class imbalance, a 'triple adaptive' hybrid feature-selection controller that iterates Mutual Information, RFE and Boruta under three feedback metrics (noise, redundancy, stability), then seven classifiers (Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, AdaBoost, TabNet, FT-Transformer) with SHAP (beeswarm, waterfall, force) and LIME explanations. Evaluated with 5-fold CV on Cell2Cell and the 28-column IBM Telco Kaggle variant. Random Forest with adaptive feature selection is best: 88.16% accuracy / F1 0.878 / AUC-ROC 0.934 on Cell2Cell and 89.60% / 0.901 / 0.971 on IBM Telco, with feature counts cut from 57 to 15 and 28 to 12. Friedman and Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon tests show the adaptive selector beats some single selectors but not all. SHAP fidelity (Pearson r = 0.978 vs permutation importance) and stability (Jaccard 0.858 across folds) are quantified. SHAP names Tenure Months, Contract and Monthly Charges as the main IBM Telco drivers and PercChangeMinutes, MonthlyMinutes and MonthlyRevenue for Cell2Cell.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only the first half is supported. Table 5 (Section 4.3): Random Forest has the highest AUC-ROC on both datasets (0.934 Cell2Cell; 0.971 IBM Telco) and the text says 'Random Forest consistently achieved the highest overall performance across both datasets'. However (i) logistic regression is not among the seven classifiers compared (DT, RF, XGBoost, SVM, AdaBoost, TabNet, FT-Transformer), so the paper makes no LR comparison at all; (ii) gradient boosting is not near-top on Cell2Cell: XGBoost AUC 0.860 is below a single Decision Tree (0.887) and far below RF (0.934), and AdaBoost is the weakest ML model (0.764 / 0.862). Cite this paper only for the narrower statement that RF achieved the highest AUC-ROC of the models tested, not for the LR comparison.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.4.1 (SHAP beeswarm, Fig. 3): on IBM Telco 'features such as Tenure Months, Contract, and Monthly Charges exhibit wide SHAP value distributions', i.e. a strong and consistent influence; higher tenure lowers predicted churn. Section 4.6: 'TenureMonths, Contract, and MonthlyCharges are the primary factors for the IBM telecom dataset'. Conclusion: PercChangeMinutes, MonthlyMinutes, TenureMonths and Contract are 'the most significant factors influencing customer attrition'. Force plot (Fig. 5): shorter contract and lower tenure push the prediction toward churn. Cell2Cell equivalents are usage/revenue variables (PercChangeMinutes, MonthlyMinutes, MonthlyRevenue). Note the IBM data are the 28-column Kaggle 'Telco customer churn (IBM dataset)' variant (yeanzc), not the 21-column blastchar file, though the named drivers map directly to Contract, tenure and MonthlyCharges.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not tested. Evaluation uses only accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC (Table 3, Section 4.2) and 'the best models for each dataset' are chosen 'based on their total metric ratings'. No profit, cost-sensitive, expected-value or threshold analysis is performed and the default 0.5 threshold is never varied. The only business remark is qualitative (Section 4.3): the RF's excess of false positives over false negatives 'makes sense from a business point of view, as excess targeting costs less than not recognizing potential clients' - an assertion, not an evaluation, and it did not alter the model or threshold chosen. Cannot be cited for this claim.

claims_supported.claim: Adaptive hybrid feature selection (MI + RFE + Boruta under a feedback controller) cut dimensionality by 57% (28 to 12 features, IBM Telco) and 74% (57 to 15, Cell2Cell) while accuracy improved only marginally (87.42% to 89.60% and 85.53% to 88.16%); the authors concede 'the improvement in the classification accuracy is small' and that the main benefit is dimensionality reduction.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.5 and Table 6 (ablation study); restated in Section 4.6 and the Conclusion ('marginally improves predictive performance and compresses the feature space ... reducing dimensionality by up to 74%').

claims_supported.claim: Statistical testing shows the adaptive selector is not uniformly better than single feature-selection methods: on IBM Telco it beats MI (p = 0.000061) and Boruta (p = 0.003357) but not RFE (p = 0.136); on Cell2Cell it beats RFE (p = 0.00072) and Boruta (p = 0.00558) but not MI (p = 0.446) (Friedman chi-square 17.20, p = 0.00064; Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank).
claims_supported.where: Section 4.5, paragraphs on the Friedman test and post-hoc Wilcoxon tests.

claims_supported.claim: SHAP explanation quality was quantified: Pearson r = 0.978 between SHAP feature importance and permutation importance (fidelity) and Jaccard similarity J = 0.858 for the top-K SHAP features across the five CV folds (stability).
claims_supported.where: Sections 4.4.3 (Quantitative explainability fidelity analysis) and 4.4.4 (Explanation stability analysis).

claims_supported.claim: Deep tabular models (TabNet, FT-Transformer) underperformed tree-based models on both datasets: Cell2Cell AUC 0.768 / 0.769 versus RF 0.934 and a single Decision Tree 0.887; IBM Telco 0.864 / 0.875 versus RF 0.971 and XGBoost 0.917.
claims_supported.where: Table 5 (Section 4.3). Useful for a critical discussion of whether deep learning is warranted on small tabular churn data.

claims_supported.claim: Imbalance handling: Random Minority Oversampling (random duplication of minority-class rows), stated to be applied to training folds only, with feature selection performed inside each CV training fold to avoid leakage; on IBM Telco the RF reached 95% churner recall with more false positives than false negatives.
claims_supported.where: Sections 3.1-3.2 (preprocessing and 5-fold protocol), 4.1 ('oversampling is only done on the training data'), 4.3 and Fig. 2 (confusion matrices). Caveat: Section 3.2 says rebalancing is done on 'the refined dataset' before feature selection, so the exact placement of oversampling relative to the CV split is not stated unambiguously.

claims_supported.claim: Deployment trade-off: feature-selection runtime rises (IBM Telco 24.9 s versus 0.35 s for MI alone; Cell2Cell 155.65 s versus 8.09 s) but is argued to be acceptable because telecom models are trained offline and served in real time; worst-case complexity O(d^2 * n log n).
claims_supported.where: Section 4.5 (complexity paragraph, Table 6 FS-time columns) and Section 4.6 ('In industrial telecom systems, where models are trained offline but deployed for real-time inference, this trade-off is favourable').

claims_supported.claim: The paper evaluates probability calibration, uplift modelling, survival analysis or fairness.
claims_supported.where: None of these is performed. 'Calibration' appears only as sklearn SVC probability=True in Table 4 (Platt scaling as a model option, never assessed) and loosely in a highlight bullet about oversampling. No uplift, survival, or fairness content anywhere. Future work (Conclusion) is multimodal/temporal data and continuous-learning feature selection.

references.verification_notes: Publisher: Elsevier B.V. (Results in Engineering, ISSN 2590-1230, gold open access, CC BY). Crossref record for 10.1016/j.rineng.2026.111361 confirmed: type journal-article, container-title Results in Engineering, publisher Elsevier BV, volume 31, article number 111361, issue date September 2026, 42 references, CC BY licence. OpenAlex confirms the same title/venue/volume, online date 6 June 2026, gold OA, and author affiliations (Javed - University of Management and Technology, Pakistan; Jhanjhi - Asia University, Taiwan and Taylor's University, Malaysia, corresponding; Ali - Technical University of Malaysia Malacca). Semantic Scholar has the record (CorpusId 288994491, JournalArticle, open access) but its abstract field is null. The full text was read from the open-access ScienceDirect page (PII S2590123026023790) via the built-in browser because ScienceDirect returns 403 to automated fetches; article history there: Received 13 February 2026, Revised 26 April 2026, Accepted 1 June 2026, Available online 6 June 2026, Version of Record 17 June 2026. Venue legitimacy: DOAJ lists the journal (added 10 June 2019) with 'single anonymous peer review' and an APC of up to USD 2,160; it is Scopus-indexed (CiteScore 7.9, SJR 1.24, SNIP 1.52 per third-party metric sites). It is an established, non-predatory Elsevier mega-journal, although broad-scope and less selective than specialist venues. The paper is therefore peer-reviewed, published in 2026, in an established venue. Title capitalisation normalised from Crossref's 'Explainable ai-driven' to 'AI-driven'. The journal uses continuous volumes with no issue numbers, so issue is left empty and the pages field carries the article number. Claims were assessed against the complete full text (all sections read), not only the abstract.
references.caveats: Reporting-quality issues a critical discussion should note: (1) F1 is almost equal to accuracy on both datasets (0.901 vs 89.60%; 0.878 vs 88.16%), a pattern typical of evaluation on class-balanced data; Section 3.2 says rebalancing precedes feature selection on 'the refined dataset' while Section 4.1 says oversampling is applied to training data only, and the paper never states explicitly that test folds were left imbalanced, so treat the headline metrics with caution. (2) The IBM Telco AUC-ROC of 0.971 is far above the roughly 0.83-0.86 usually reported for this dataset (the paper's own Table 7 cites 0.84 for stochastic gradient boosting). (3) Table 6's Cell2Cell F1 column contains feature counts (57, 18, 19, 16, ...) instead of F1 values for most rows. (4) Table 4 gives n_estimators=200 and learning_rate=0.03 for a single Decision Tree, which are not Decision Tree hyperparameters. (5) Cell2Cell is described as 71,047 rows but 14,711 churners + 36,336 non-churners = 51,047. (6) The Data availability statement says no datasets were analysed, contradicting the use of two Kaggle datasets. (7) No standard deviations or confidence intervals across the five folds are reported. (8) The Highlights mention Particle Swarm Optimization and an indexed version of the abstract mentions SMOTE, but the published body uses neither (it uses Random Minority Oversampling) - evidence of version drift. (9) No logistic regression or other linear baseline. (10) Two of three authors are frequent co-authors and 6 of 44 references are self-citations; peer review is single-anonymous. (11) The IBM dataset is the 28-column Kaggle variant (with City, Tenure Months, etc.), so results are not directly comparable with work on the 21-column blastchar file.

references.title: Prediction of Customer Churn Behavior in the Telecommunication Industry Using Machine Learning Models
references.harvard_reference: Chang, V., Hall, K., Xu, Q.A., Amao, F.O., Ganatra, M.A. and Benson, V. (2024) 'Prediction of customer churn behavior in the telecommunication industry using machine learning models', Algorithms, 17(6), article 231. doi:10.3390/a17060231.
references.abstract_summary: The authors frame churn as the telecom sector's largest annual attrition problem (over 30%) and apply a CRISP-DM workflow to a publicly available Telecom Customer Churn dataset (from Maven Analytics; 7,043 rows, 38 attributes) with a 75/25 train/test split. Five classifiers are compared (Logistic Regression, KNN, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest) using confusion matrices, accuracy, error rate, sensitivity, specificity and ROC-AUC. Random Forest performs best in the body of the paper (Table 3: accuracy 0.8694, AUC 0.95, sensitivity 0.8547, specificity 0.8839), followed by Naive Bayes (AUC 0.88), Logistic Regression (AUC 0.84), KNN (0.81) and Decision Tree (0.80). LIME is used for local explanations of two individual customers and SHAP summary plots for global feature importance of the Random Forest; the SHAP top five are Contract, Number of Referrals, Tenure in Months, Monthly Charge and Online Security. The paper positions 'explainable ensemble learning' as a way for CRM decision-makers to trust and act on churn predictions. Note: the abstract's headline numbers (91.66% accuracy, 82.2% precision, 81.8% recall) do not correspond to the study's own reported results.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only the first half is supported. Section 4.2 and Table 3 (Section 4.3): Random Forest had the highest AUC-ROC of 0.95, 'followed closely by Naive Bayes, with a score of 0.88'; Logistic Regression scored 0.84, KNN 0.81, Decision Tree 0.80 (Figure 6 ROC curves). So RF does achieve the top AUC. However, the paper contradicts the 'often close to logistic regression' part: the RF-LR gap is 11 AUC points (0.95 vs 0.84) and the authors describe LR and Naive Bayes as only 'moderate' performers. No gradient boosting model is implemented (Section 3.3 lists LR, RF, Naive Bayes, KNN and Decision Tree only, despite the abstract mentioning 'Boosted Trees'). Cite this paper for RF obtaining the top AUC, or as a counterexample where LR is clearly behind, not for LR being competitive.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.4.2 (SHAP) and Figure 9 (SHAP summary plot for the Random Forest classifier): 'Contract', 'Number of Referrals', 'Tenure in Months', 'Monthly Charge', and 'Online Security' are the five factors that make the most contribution to the prediction outcomes. Section 4.4.1 (LIME, Figure 8) also lists 'Contract' as the most significant factor for the first customer and 'Monthly Charge' among the top five for the second customer, with increases in 'Payment Method' and 'Monthly Charge' raising churn likelihood. Caveat: the SHAP section's direction statements (that high Contract, Tenure in Months and Online Security values increase churn probability while low Monthly Charge increases it) are inconsistent with the LIME section and with the usual domain findings, so cite the feature ranking rather than the stated directions.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper's evaluation is limited to confusion-matrix counts, accuracy, error rate, sensitivity, specificity and AUC-ROC at the default decision threshold (Sections 3.4, 4.2, 4.3, Table 3). There is no cost-sensitive, profit-based (e.g. EMP), lift/TDL or threshold-tuning analysis of its own, and the model choice (Random Forest) is made purely on accuracy and AUC. The nearest statements are qualitative: Section 4.2 notes the Decision Tree's high false-positive count means telecom companies 'may want to carefully assess the accuracy of the algorithm's positive predictions before taking any retention action', and Sections 1, 5.2 and 6 repeat the generic claim that acquisition costs 5-10 times (or 'eight times') retention. Only the literature review (Section 2.3) mentions AUC and TDL(10%) results from De Caigny et al. (2018).

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: (a) Dataset: Section 3.2 states the data is the 'Telecom CUSTOMER Churn dataset from the Maven Analytics website platform', 7,043 rows and 38 attributes (a richer derivative of the IBM Telco data with features such as Number of Referrals, Avg Monthly GB Download, Total Refunds), so results are not directly comparable with the 21-column Kaggle Telco file. (b) Reporting inconsistencies useful for a critical discussion: the abstract's 'Random Forest ... 91.66% predictive accuracy, 82.2% precision, and 81.8% recall' and the conclusion's 'accuracy of around 90%' do not match the paper's own Table 3 (RF accuracy 0.8694); precision and recall are not among the metrics the paper defines or reports; the 91.66% figure is the Random Forest accuracy the paper attributes to Mishra and Reddy's earlier study and the 81.8%/82.2% figures are those attributed to Lalwani et al.'s CatBoost model in Section 2.3. (c) Imbalance handling is undocumented and internally inconsistent: Section 3.2 mentions a '2:1 (non-churner: churner)' ratio 'based on Wei and Chiu' and says no rows were deleted from the 7,043; Section 4.1 (Figure 3) says the data is 'unbalanced, with almost twice as many churning samples than not churning samples'; Table 2 reports n = 4,601; and the confusion matrix in Figure 5 (RF: TP 670, FN 88, TN 641, FP 109) implies a near 50/50 test set of 1,508 customers. No SMOTE, class weighting or resampling method is described. (d) Model behaviour (Section 4.2): KNN was the worst performer (specificity 0.5805, 318 false negatives); the Decision Tree had the second-highest true positives (614) but the highest false positives (157) and lowest true negatives (593), which the authors say could lead to wasted retention spend; Naive Bayes and LR performed similarly. (e) XAI method critique (Section 3.5): the authors state that LIME 'only predicts how the present prediction will change in response to minute changes in the input values' and 'acts more like a sensitivity study' rather than explaining why a prediction was made, which motivates adding SHAP for global importance; Section 4.4 reports LIME and SHAP explanations as consistent. (f) Section 2.4 motivates XAI with GDPR's requirement for meaningful information about automated decision logic. (g) No calibration, uplift modelling (only cited via De Caigny et al. 2021 in Section 2.2), survival analysis, fairness assessment, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning or deployment evaluation is performed, although 'deploy a cost-effective system' is stated as an aim in Section 3. (h) Limitations (Section 5.3): no access to billing/credit information and a stated lack of demographic data, which sits oddly with Table 2 including Age and Number of Dependents.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified against Crossref (DOI 10.3390/a17060231, journal-article, Algorithms, MDPI AG, vol. 17, issue 6, article 231, published 2024-05-27, ISSN 1999-4893, CC BY 4.0), Semantic Scholar (DBLP id journals/algorithms/ChangHXAGB24, CorpusId 270079202) and OpenAlex (gold OA, in DOAJ, 89 citations at time of check). Received 21 April 2024, revised 19 May 2024, accepted 22 May 2024, published 27 May 2024 (a 32-day review cycle, typical of MDPI); academic editors Mateus Mendes and Balduino Mateus; authors affiliated with Aston Business School (Aston University) and Teesside University. Author names as printed: Victor Chang, Karl Hall, Qianwen Ariel Xu, Folakemi Ololade Amao, Meghana Ashok Ganatra, Vladlena Benson (OpenAlex lists the first author as Victor I. C. Chang). Venue check: Algorithms (MDPI, est. 2008) is peer-reviewed and, per Wikipedia and OpenAlex, indexed in Scopus, Web of Science Emerging Sources Citation Index, Ei Compendex, Inspec, MathSciNet and DOAJ (since 2008), with a 2022 JCR impact factor of 2.3 and an OpenAlex 2-year mean citedness of 3.46 (h-index 76); it is an established, non-predatory venue, though MDPI's rapid review times are sometimes criticised. Scimago and DOAJ pages returned HTTP 403 so the Scopus quartile could not be confirmed directly. The MDPI site blocked automated access (HTTP 403), so the full text was read from the publisher-version PDF (CC BY) deposited in the Aston University repository (publications.aston.ac.uk/id/eprint/46410), which OpenAlex lists as an OA location; that PDF contains overlaid 'FOR PEER REVIEW' proof text in some sections, so figures were cross-checked against the clean Table 3 and the cleaned text extraction. Claims were tested against the full text, not just the abstract. Important caveat for citation: the abstract's headline results (91.66% accuracy, 82.2% precision, 81.8% recall, 'Boosted Trees') are not borne out by the paper's own experiments; cite Table 3 (RF accuracy 0.8694, AUC 0.95) and note that the dataset is the Maven Analytics Telecom Customer Churn dataset rather than the Kaggle Telco file.
references.caveats: Do not quote the abstract's 91.66% / 82.2% / 81.8% figures as this study's results; they match numbers the paper attributes to prior work in Section 2.3. No boosting model is actually implemented. The dataset is the Maven Analytics telecom churn dataset (7,043 rows, 38 attributes), a variant of the IBM Telco data, not the Kaggle 21-column file. Sample size (7,043 vs 4,601), class balance and split descriptions are internally inconsistent, and no imbalance-handling method is documented. SHAP direction statements conflict with the LIME section; cite the feature ranking only.

references.title: Profit-driven weighted classifier with interpretable ability for customer churn prediction
references.venue: Omega (The International Journal of Management Science), Elsevier, ISSN 0305-0483 / eISSN 1873-5274
references.harvard_reference: Jiang, P., Liu, Z., Abedin, M.Z., Wang, J., Yang, W. and Dong, Q. (2024) 'Profit-driven weighted classifier with interpretable ability for customer churn prediction', Omega, 125, 103034. doi:10.1016/j.omega.2024.103034.
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that churn models built on a single classifier leave profit on the table and proposes a profit-driven weighted classifier (PWC). Nine heterogeneous base learners (CatBoost, CART, Gaussian naive Bayes, KNN, L1 logistic regression, LightGBM, MLP, random forest, XGBoost) are each tuned by grid search to maximise the expected maximum profit criterion (EMPC); an artificial hummingbird algorithm then finds the ensemble weights that maximise EMPC on a validation set. Interpretability is obtained by combining the members' SHAP values with those weights to give weighted SHAP values. On eight Kaggle churn datasets (e-commerce, three telecom, bank, newspaper, insurance, Uber), evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation with AUC, top-decile lift and EMPC and with Friedman/Holm tests, the PWC yields significantly higher EMPC than every individual classifier and than 16 alternative ensembles (stacking, selection, average/rank/probability weighting, profit-conscious ensemble selection, AUC-driven weighting and a GA-weighted variant), while remaining interpretable via SHAP.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Partly supported by the data, not as worded. Table 6 (Section 5.1, accepted manuscript pp. 21-22) reports AUC on three telecom datasets. Dataset 2 (Kaggle telecom, 7,043 customers, 26.54% churn - the same size and churn rate as the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, though the paper does not name it): CatBoost 0.8604, LightGBM 0.8599, XGBoost 0.8597, RF 0.8571, MLP 0.8520, ProfLogit 0.8482, L1-logistic regression 0.8451, GNBC 0.8424, KNN 0.8410, CART 0.8390, PWC 0.8605. So gradient-boosted trees and RF are top/near-top and LR trails by only about 0.015 AUC on that dataset. However, on the two larger telecom datasets (Datasets 7 and 8, Duke/Cell2Cell data obtained via Kaggle, 51,047 and 71,047 customers) L1-logistic regression collapsed to AUC 0.5000 (chance) while LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost scored about 0.67-0.68 and RF about 0.66. The paper therefore supports 'tree ensembles achieve top or near-top AUC on telecom churn data', but it does not support 'often close to logistic regression': that holds on only one of the three telecom datasets, and the paper never makes this comparison in words. A reworded claim restricted to the first half, citing Table 6, would be supported.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Only the tenure element is supported, and not on telecom data. Section 5.3 and Figure 2 (accepted manuscript pp. 27-28) present SHAP values for Dataset 1 only, an e-commerce dataset (5,630 customers), 'owing to space limitations'. There, 'Tenure' is the most important feature (shorter tenure -> higher churn probability), followed by 'Complain' (a complaint in the previous month raises churn), 'NumberOfAddress' and 'SatisfactionScore'. Contract type and monthly charges are not features of that dataset and are never discussed; SHAP results for the telecom datasets (2, 7, 8) are not reported. A narrower claim - 'SHAP applied to a profit-driven ensemble identified tenure as the dominant churn driver in an e-commerce dataset' - would be supported.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Supported for model choice; the threshold point is supported only at the level of the metric's definition. (a) Section 4 (p. 19): the authors build an AUC-optimised twin of their model (PWC-AUC) explicitly 'to verify the necessity of constructing a PWC to achieve profit'. Section 5.2 and Table 9 (pp. 22-25): PWC-AUC attains higher AUC than PWC on several datasets (e.g. Dataset 7: 0.6787 vs 0.6742; Dataset 8: 0.6813 vs 0.6791; Dataset 5: 0.9361 vs 0.9348) while PWC attains higher EMPC (Dataset 7: EUR 9.0568 vs 9.0528; Dataset 8: EUR 9.1913 vs 9.1888), and Table 10 shows PWC significantly out-ranks PWC-AUC on EMPC (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0000). The authors state that 'the AUC and TDL (10%) values of the PWC were not optimal in most scenarios' but that 'achieving a satisfactory profit metric value (EMPC) is more important than achieving good AUC and TDL values'. (b) Among individual classifiers (Table 6) the best-AUC and best-EMPC model differ on several datasets (e.g. Dataset 1: LightGBM best AUC 0.9955 but PWC best EMPC; Dataset 6: XGBoost best AUC 0.9452 but PWC best EMPC). (c) Threshold: Section 3.1, Eqs (2)-(4) define MPC/EMPC as profit at the profit-maximising classification threshold t*(gamma) rather than at a fixed accuracy-based cut-off, and the paper notes accuracy metrics are 'unrealistic' for imbalanced churn problems where the minority class is the focus; however the paper does not empirically compare thresholds chosen under the two regimes. Note that the EMPC differences between PWC and PWC-AUC are small in absolute terms.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (1) Imbalance: churn rates of the eight datasets range from 11.70% to 53.54%; the authors say this imbalance 'adversely affected the predictive results' (Section 4, p. 17) but apply no resampling or cost-sensitive learning - they address imbalance only through evaluation, arguing that accuracy metrics are unrealistic for CCP 'which is an imbalanced classification problem where the minority class (i.e., churners) is the primary focus' (Section 3.1, p. 10). (2) EMPC parameterisation: CLV = EUR 200, incentive cost d = EUR 10, contact cost f = EUR 1, acceptance probability gamma ~ Beta(6,14) (Section 3.2, p. 13), taken from prior research; Section 6.3 concedes these must be re-set for each business and that assuming a constant return per customer 'overlooks the diversity in customer values'. (3) Profit gains are modest in absolute terms: on the Telco-sized dataset the PWC's EMPC is EUR 10.82 per customer versus EUR 10.42 for L1-logistic regression and EUR 10.66 for RF (Table 6). (4) Top-decile lift on that dataset was highest for RF among individual models (TDL(10%) 2.9154 vs 2.8940 CatBoost and 2.7370 LR), so the winner changes even between accuracy-type metrics. (5) Statistical testing: Friedman test plus Holm post-hoc over 80 fold-level EMPC values; PWC vs individual classifiers Friedman statistic 474.49 (p < 0.001), vs ensemble benchmarks 47.66 (p < 0.001) (Tables 7 and 10). (6) Ensemble weights (Table 12): boosted trees (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost) received the largest weights in most datasets; RF got the lowest weight on Dataset 1, which the authors attribute to its predictions being redundant with other members. (7) Runtime (Table 11): AUC-driven weight optimisation is faster than EMPC-driven because EMPC is costlier to compute. (8) Deployment: Section 6.2 gives only managerial implications (target predicted churners with offers/messages); no live deployment, calibration, uplift modelling, survival analysis or fairness analysis is reported - these topics are absent from the paper.

references.title: e-Profits: a business-aligned evaluation metric for profit-sensitive customer churn prediction
references.venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics (Springer; ISSN 2364-415X print, 2364-4168 online)
references.harvard_reference: Manzoor, A., Qureshi, M.A., Kidney, E. and Longo, L. (2026) 'e-Profits: a business-aligned evaluation metric for profit-sensitive customer churn prediction', International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 22(1), 75. doi:10.1007/s41060-026-01044-6.
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that AUC and F1 do not reflect the financial outcome of a retention campaign and proposes e-Profits, a per-customer profit metric: for each customer flagged as a churner the model earns CLV_i minus offer and contact costs if the customer is a true churner, loses the offer and contact costs if a false positive, and earns nothing otherwise. CLV_i = R_i x M / (1 - min(r_i, 0.995)) uses the customer's monthly revenue R_i, a margin M (0.3 in experiments) and a retention probability r_i estimated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, either tenure-conditioned per customer (TRR: S(T_i + 1)/S(T_i)) or averaged over the population (ARR). Offer cost is 0.1 x CLV_i and contact cost is max(c0, c1 x offer cost). Unlike Expected Maximum Profit (EMP), which assumes fixed population-level CLV, costs and a Beta-distributed acceptance rate, e-Profits gives total and segment-level (e.g. top-20% most valuable customers) profit. Six classifiers (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Explainable Boosting Machine) are benchmarked on the IBM Telco (7,043 rows, 19 features, 26.5% churn) and Maven Telecom (7,043 rows, 32 features, 27% churn) datasets, with hyperparameters tuned by 5-fold cross-validation under five objectives (AUC, Accuracy, F1, EMP, e-Profits) and a fixed 0.5 decision threshold. e-Profits re-ranks the models relative to AUC/F1, reveals financial advantages in models that AUC/F1 overlook, and supports segment-level insight into which model maximises return on high-value customers; code is released on GitHub.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only partly borne out and the key comparison is absent. Tables 3-4 (arXiv v2 full text) report AUC of 83.5-86.2% on IBM Telco and 91.9-94.3% on Maven for the six tree-based models, with the Explainable Boosting Machine highest (86.16% and 94.16% when tuned on AUC) and RF/XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost within roughly 1-2 points. However, the paper benchmarks ONLY tree ensembles and EBM; logistic regression (or any linear/neural baseline) is not run or discussed anywhere, so it cannot support the statement that tree ensembles are 'top' relative to other model families or 'close to logistic regression'. Cite it for the AUC levels of tree ensembles on these datasets only, and take the LR comparison from another source.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no SHAP, permutation-importance or other feature-attribution analysis and reports no ranking of churn drivers; contract type is never analysed. EBM is included because it offers 'a compelling balance between model accuracy and interpretability' (classifier-selection section), but its explanations are not examined. Tenure and monthly revenue appear only as inputs to the metric (tenure conditions the Kaplan-Meier retention probability; monthly revenue feeds CLV), not as identified predictors of churn.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Strongly supported for MODEL choice (not threshold). Abstract: e-Profits 'reshapes model rankings compared to traditional metrics, revealing financial advantages in models previously overlooked by AUC or F1-score'. Results (arXiv v2 Tables 3-4): with AUC-tuned models, EBM has the best AUC/F1 on both datasets, yet Random Forest yields the highest full-population e-Profits (IBM: 9,104,621 vs EBM 7,894,896 under TRR; Maven: 996,582 vs 880,083) and the authors state 'Random Forest achieves higher e-Profits on both the full-population and the top 20% segment, indicating that AUC-optimised models do not necessarily prioritise customers with the highest financial value'. When hyperparameters are tuned on e-Profits instead, XGBoost becomes best (IBM 10,991,460; Maven 1,063,393). Spearman rank correlation between AUC and e-Profits rankings on Maven is only about 0.49 (full population) and 0.45 (top-20%); paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests reject concordance (p<1e-23 Maven, p<1e-18 IBM) and models selected by e-Profits significantly outperform AUC/Accuracy-tuned ones in e-Profits (p<<0.001). Conclusion: 'traditional predictive metrics are insufficient proxies for business value in churn prediction'. Caveat: the paper uses a fixed 0.5 threshold throughout and does not study threshold selection, so it evidences model re-ranking and re-tuning, not threshold change.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (1) Survival + profit: retention probability is estimated with a non-parametric Kaplan-Meier curve on tenure (churn = event, non-churners right-censored, non-informative censoring assumed); the tenure-conditioned one-month probability S(T_i+1)/S(T_i) gives customer-level CLV instead of the single population value assumed by EMP (which the paper parameterises as CLV=200, offer cost 10, contact cost 1). (2) Tuning objective matters: models tuned on EMP 'do not consistently maximise e-Profits', and tuning directly on e-Profits lifts the best IBM model from 9,104,621 (AUC-tuned RF) to 10,991,460 (XGB) and the best Maven model from 996,582 to 1,063,393. (3) Segment-level targeting: evaluating on the top-20% most valuable customers changes the winner again (LightGBM 'consistently outperforms other classifiers on top-segment e-Profits when tuned on F1-score, EMP, and e-Profits', e.g. 340,635 on Maven), and in the AUC-tuned IBM block several models record zero top-segment profit, i.e. they flag no profitable high-value customers; the authors argue this makes e-Profits suited to 'resource-constrained retention campaigns'. (4) Explicit limitations (Section 5.2): it is 'a decision-oriented evaluation and model-selection metric rather than a causal treatment-effect estimator'; it assumes every contacted churner is retained and does not model heterogeneous response, so 'integrating causal uplift or treatment-effect modelling' is left to future work; Kaplan-Meier captures heterogeneity 'only through customer tenure using a single population-level survival curve', with Cox proportional hazards (time-varying covariates), Weibull and BG/NBD models suggested as extensions; intervention is binary; results are telecom-only. (5) Methodological choices relevant to critique: fixed 0.5 threshold, no probability calibration, no resampling or class weighting despite 26-27% churn (imbalance addressed only via metric choice), 5-fold CV for hyperparameter selection on the training set followed by refit, profit margin 0.3 and cost-per-offer 0.1 set by assumption. Fairness is not discussed at all.

references.verification_notes: Existence and metadata verified on 2026-09-27 via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s41060-026-01044-6: type journal-article, container International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, publisher Springer Science and Business Media LLC, volume 22, issue 1, article-number 75, published online 2026-02-25, print issue dated 2026-12, CC BY 4.0, 37 references), OpenAlex (same volume/issue, hybrid OA, affiliations: Manzoor and Qureshi - Enable Ireland / Technological University Dublin; Kidney - TU Dublin; Longo - University College Cork) and Semantic Scholar (abstract, ArXiv 2507.08860, DBLP journals/corr/abs-2507-08860). Crossref stores the title in lower case ('e-profits'); the authors' own styling 'e-Profits' is used here. Semantic Scholar lists year 2025 (arXiv v1, 9 July 2025); the journal version is 2026 and that is the year cited. Received/accepted dates could not be read because the Springer article, PDF and journal pages sit behind a cookie-gated redirect (idp.springer.com) that WebFetch cannot follow; these fields are therefore left out.
