Full-text findings, table values and quotations were taken from arXiv v2 (Jan 2026), the version closest to the Feb 2026 journal article; two independent extractions of the tables agreed on all numbers quoted here (one extractor mislabelled the IBM full-population winner as LightGBM, but its own numbers show RF 9,104,621 > LightGBM 7,944,468, consistent with the authors' sentence quoted above). The student should still check the quoted table values against the published Springer version before citing specific figures. Venue check: IJDSA is a Springer journal established in 2015, peer reviewed, indexed in Scopus, Emerging Sources Citation Index, EI Compendex and Inspec (Wikipedia entry; Springer pages gated), JCR impact factor 2.4 (2022); OpenAlex source record shows 1,275 works, 13,441 citations, h-index 53, two-year mean citedness 3.54, APC USD 3,390 (hybrid). Nothing suggests a predatory venue. Publication date (Feb 2026) falls within the requested 2021-2026 window.
references.caveats: Only tree-ensemble and EBM classifiers are compared (no logistic regression, SVM or neural baseline), so the paper cannot be used to rank model families. Decision threshold is fixed at 0.5 and probability calibration is not examined, so profit differences partly reflect how many customers each model flags rather than ranking quality alone. Profit figures depend on assumed parameters (margin 0.3, cost-per-offer 0.1, contact-cost floor) and on the strong assumption that every contacted churner is retained (no uplift/treatment effect). Both benchmark datasets are 7,043-record telecom samples (IBM Telco and Maven Telecom) that appear closely related; check their independence before treating results as two independent benchmarks. The extraction inconsistency on LightGBM's IBM top-20% TRR value means that particular cell should not be quoted without checking the published table.

references.title: Extreme gradient boosting trees with efficient Bayesian optimization for profit-driven customer churn prediction
references.venue: Technological Forecasting and Social Change (Elsevier; ISSN 0040-1625)
references.harvard_reference: Liu, Z., Jiang, P., De Bock, K.W., Wang, J., Zhang, L. and Niu, X. (2024) 'Extreme gradient boosting trees with efficient Bayesian optimization for profit-driven customer churn prediction', Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 198, 122945. doi:10.1016/j.techfore.2023.122945.
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes BO-XGBT, an XGBoost churn classifier whose structural hyperparameters (learning rate, min_child_weight, max_depth) and, unusually, its class-weight parameter (scale_pos_weight, searched in [0.0001, 50]) are tuned by Bayesian optimisation (Probability-of-Improvement acquisition) directly on the Expected Maximum Profit criterion for churn (EMPC; Verbraken et al., 2013) rather than on accuracy, F1 or AUC. It is benchmarked on eight public Kaggle churn datasets from six sectors (e-commerce, telecom x3 including the IBM Telco set, bank, newspaper, insurance, Uber) against twelve BO-tuned comparators (CART, KNN, LASSO, MLP, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forest, grid-searched XGBoost variants, and the profit-driven B2Boost) using 10-fold cross-validation with a held-out validation fold and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over 80 estimates. XGBoost variants yield the highest EMPC on every dataset; BO-tuned XGBoost significantly beats grid-searched XGBoost on EMPC (p = 5.5e-8) and is much faster when several hyperparameters are searched; optimising the class weight adds profit over both the default weight (CW=1) and a deterministic cost-based 'balanced' weight. The profit advantage does not carry over to AUC or top-decile lift. Sensitivity analyses over BO iteration counts and over CLV assumptions (EUR 100/200/300) show the results are stable.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Supported for the first part; only indirectly for the 'close to logistic regression' part. Tables 5-6 (Section 5.1, pp. 19-20 of the preprint) report AUC on three telecom datasets: on the IBM Telco dataset (Dataset 2, n = 7,040, churn 26.55%) the XGBoost variants have the top AUC (GS-XGBT 0.8601; BO-XGBT 0.8544) with BO-random forest at 0.8565, and the text states 'all XGBT variants ... consistently outperform the other classifiers considered'. However, the paper has NO plain logistic regression benchmark; the nearest linear model is BO-LASSO (a LASSO-penalised linear model), which scores 0.8460 on the IBM Telco data (within 0.014 of the best tree ensemble) but about 0.06 lower on the two larger Cell2Cell-type telecom sets (Datasets 7-8: LASSO 0.616-0.617 vs XGBoost 0.674-0.678). Also, on the IBM Telco data even Gaussian naive Bayes reaches 0.8424, so all models are within 0.02 AUC there. Cite this paper for 'tree ensembles top the AUC ranking' but not for a direct comparison with logistic regression.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no SHAP, LIME, feature-importance or any feature-level analysis; no feature (contract, tenure, charges) is ever discussed as a churn driver. A full-text search of the preprint finds 'SHAP' only in the title of a cited reference (Chehreh Chelgani et al., 2021) and 'contract' only in the phrase 'multiple contractual settings' describing dataset selection (Section 4.1). The scout's note is correct that the paper offers no XAI content.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Supported. The abstract and Introduction argue that classifiers 'optimized for accuracy-based performance measures ... may not always fulfill the critical business objective of profit maximization', and Section 2.2 says selecting hyperparameters on statistical indicators 'ignored the primary objective of the learning process'. Empirically, Section 5.1 states that XGBoost's EMPC superiority 'does not translate to other metrics, i.e., top-decile lift and AUC', and Tables 5-6 show the metric changes the winning model: e.g. Dataset 1 (GS-XGBT CW=balanced tops AUC at 0.9944 but BO-XGBT tops EMPC at EUR 9.10), Dataset 3 (GS-XGBT CW=1 tops AUC 0.8652, BO-XGBT tops EMPC EUR 7.38), Dataset 6 (GS-XGBT tops AUC 0.9464, BO-XGBT tops EMPC EUR 28.05); on the IBM Telco set BO-random forest has higher AUC than BO-XGBT (0.8565 vs 0.8544) but lower EMPC (EUR 10.64 vs 10.72). On thresholds/weights: EMPC is evaluated at the profit-optimal cut-off T (Eq. 3) and the profit-optimised class weight beats both the default (CW=1) and the 'balanced' cost-ratio weight, with the authors concluding that 'simply and deterministically setting class weight may degrade CCP performance'. Caveat: the paper does not report an explicit accuracy-chosen threshold versus a profit-chosen threshold side by side; the threshold effect is embedded in the EMPC/class-weight results.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (a) Imbalance handling: treating the class weight (scale_pos_weight) as a profit-tuned hyperparameter outperforms both no weighting and the deterministic cost-based 'balanced' weight of Eq. 8; on most datasets the 'balanced' weight actually LOWERS EMPC relative to CW=1 (e.g. IBM Telco: BO-XGBT CW=balanced EUR 10.63 vs CW=1 EUR 10.67; insurance: 4.33 vs 4.45), i.e. naive re-weighting can hurt profit (Section 5.1, Tables 5-8). (b) On the IBM Telco dataset all 13 models fall in a very narrow band (EMPC EUR 10.36-10.75 per customer; AUC 0.842-0.860), so model choice matters little on that benchmark compared with the larger Cell2Cell-type sets. (c) EMPC parameterisation used: CLV = EUR 200, retention-offer cost d = EUR 10, contact cost f = EUR 1, acceptance probability c ~ Beta(6,14) (Verbraken et al., 2013 defaults); robustness checked at CLV 100/200/300 (Section 5.4, Tables 11-12). (d) Efficiency: BO with 100 iterations per hyperparameter (400 total) versus a 500-point grid; on the IBM Telco set BO-XGBT trained in 74.8 s versus 234.9 s for GS-XGBT, and 257.5 s vs 2,464.8 s on Dataset 7 (Table 9); BO-XGBT beats GS-XGBT on EMPC with Wilcoxon p = 5.5e-8 and beats BO-random forest with p = 1.2e-13 (Table 7). (e) Evaluation protocol worth emulating: 10-fold CV with a separate validation fold for tuning and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across 8 datasets x 10 folds. (f) Gaps the student can critique: no probability calibration, uplift modelling, survival analysis, fairness or deployment/monitoring analysis; no interpretability; no plain logistic regression baseline; and the authors' own stated limitation (Section 6.4) that the CLV-to-retention-cost relationship is assumed rather than measured, so EMPC rankings depend on untested cost assumptions.

references.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for predictive customer churn modeling in telecommunications: a framework for enhanced customer relationship management
references.harvard_reference: Abdelhady, M.G. and Mohamed, K.A. (2025) 'Leveraging artificial intelligence for predictive customer churn modeling in telecommunications: a framework for enhanced customer relationship management', Scientific Reports, 15(1), 43826. doi:10.1038/s41598-025-30108-z.
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes an AI-driven churn-prediction framework embedded in a CRM workflow. A Random Forest classifier (scikit-learn; Gini impurity) was trained on a publicly available telecom dataset the authors attribute to the UCI Machine Learning Repository (N = 2,668 customer profiles, 19 features, 14.6% churn = 389 churners; no missing values; LabelEncoder for categoricals, StandardScaler for numerics; stratified train/test split described as 70/30; 10-fold cross-validation on the training set, although no CV figures are printed). Class imbalance was handled with SMOTE and, as a comparison, class weighting inside the Random Forest; SMOTE was kept because it gave minority-class recall 0.74 versus 0.70 for class weighting ('SMOTE improved recall from 0.68 to 0.74'). Headline test-set results: accuracy 95.13%, AUC 0.89, churn-class precision 0.98, churn-class recall 0.68 (67.9%); confusion matrix Fig. 9 on N = 534 test rows: TP 53, FN 25, FP 1, TN 455. Table 1 (benchmark, values recovered from the publisher's cell images; columns Model / Accuracy / Recall (Churn) / AUC): Random Forest 0.951 / 0.74 / 0.89; XGBoost 0.943 / 0.71 / 0.87; ANN (feed-forward) 0.935 / 0.69 / 0.86; SVM (RBF kernel) 0.926 / 0.65 / 0.84. Logistic regression, gradient boosting other than XGBoost, SHAP and LIME were not used. Gini (mean-decrease-in-impurity) importance ranked total day minutes 14.2%, total day charge 13.8%, customer service calls 12.1%, international plan 9.8% (Figs 6-7; the top three account for over 40% of importance); evening/night/international usage ranked lower. EDA notes r = 1.00 collinearity between each minutes variable and its charge variable (Fig. 8), a higher median and IQR of total day charge among churners (Fig. 1), and a monotonic rise in churn proportion with the number of customer-service calls with 'a critical threshold observed at 4+ calls' (Fig. 10). The Discussion interprets the precision-recall profile in business terms (the model is 'calibrated for high precision', 'minimizing false alarms at the cost of missing some true churn events') and proposes a CRM workflow: data ingestion -> scoring that returns a churn probability plus a feature-importance 'reason code' -> flagging customers above a pre-defined risk threshold -> automated retention actions. Further figures on retention-offer adoption (Fig. 11), AI-generated service recommendations (Fig. 12) and recommended price tiers (Fig. 13) are presented without any description of where that data came from. Stated limitations: single public dataset (external validation needed); churn recall could be improved, with ensemble sampling and cost-sensitive learning as future work; structured data only; no live deployment, with A/B testing needed to measure the causal effect on churn and customer lifetime value.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only the first half of this claim is supported. Table 1 ('Bechmark algorithms', values read from the publisher's table-cell images; text in 'Comparative models' says Random Forest 'achieved the best balance of accuracy, recall, and AUC') gives AUC: Random Forest 0.89, XGBoost 0.87, ANN 0.86, SVM (RBF) 0.84, so the two tree ensembles are the top two on ROC-AUC. However, logistic regression is never trained or mentioned anywhere in the paper (the only benchmarks are XGBoost, RBF-SVM and a feed-forward ANN), so the paper provides no evidence for 'often close to logistic regression'. Cite it only for the narrowed statement 'on a public telecom churn dataset a random forest (AUC 0.89) and XGBoost (0.87) out-performed an RBF-SVM (0.84) and a feed-forward ANN (0.86)', and note that the differences (0.02-0.05 AUC) come from a single split with no confidence intervals or significance tests, and that the dataset is not the IBM/Kaggle Telco file.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported as worded. (a) Method: the paper uses Random Forest Gini importance (mean decrease in impurity), not SHAP or LIME; the strings 'SHAP' and 'LIME' do not occur in the full text, and 'explainable AI (XAI) techniques' are named only as future work. (b) Drivers: the dataset has no contract-type variable and no 'tenure'/'monthly charges' fields; the reported top predictors (Results, Figs 6-7) are total day minutes 14.2%, total day charge 13.8%, customer service calls 12.1% and international plan 9.8%. 'Account length' (the nearest tenure analogue) exists in the data but is not reported among the top features, and 'total day charge' is a usage-based charge rather than a monthly subscription charge. The paper therefore supports only 'usage-based charges and customer-service contact frequency are the strongest importance-ranked churn drivers in this (non-IBM) telecom dataset'. Useful critical point: the authors note r = 1.00 collinearity between minutes and charge variables (Fig. 8), which splits impurity importance between them, and they do not discuss the known bias of Gini importance toward continuous/high-cardinality features (Strobl et al., 2007).

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: The paper contains no profit, cost or expected-value metric, no cost matrix, no threshold sweep and no comparison of model rankings under different criteria. Random Forest is chosen on accuracy, churn recall and AUC (Table 1); SMOTE is chosen over class weighting on minority recall alone (0.74 vs 0.70, Methods), which is a metric-choice effect, not a business evaluation. The Discussion only re-describes the fixed precision 0.98 / recall 0.68 profile in business language ('calibrated for high precision, ensuring that customers flagged as high-risk are very likely to churn, thereby optimizing the cost-efficiency of retention campaigns'; the missed churners are 'a limitation that should be considered based on the specific cost-benefit analysis of retention actions'), and lists cost-sensitive learning as future work. The CRM workflow refers to 'a pre-defined churn risk threshold' but gives no value or selection rule. Note that the word 'calibrated' is used loosely (strategic emphasis) and does not refer to probability calibration; no reliability diagram or Brier score is reported. The paper can be cited as an example of a study that acknowledges the business trade-off but does not evaluate it.

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for critical discussion of churn-prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: (1) Imbalance handling (Methods, 'Imbalance Handling' and 'Predictive model specification'): SMOTE vs class weighting inside Random Forest evaluated on minority recall only (0.74 vs 0.70); no report of the effect on precision, AUC or calibration. (2) Precision-recall trade-off (Results/Discussion): precision 0.98 but recall 0.68, i.e. 'approximately 32% of actual churners' missed (FN 25 of 78 churners in the N = 534 test set, Fig. 9); on this 14.6%-churn data a majority-class baseline already scores 85.4% accuracy, and the authors concede that 'the AUC of 0.89 provides a more robust evaluation metric'. (3) Internal inconsistencies worth flagging in a critical review: Table 1 lists RF churn recall 0.74 while the text and confusion matrix give 0.68/67.9%; one sentence states '53 True Positives and 11 False Negatives' while Fig. 9 gives FN = 25; the split is described as 70/30 but the test set is N = 534 (20% of 2,668); the 10-fold CV results are never reported; the authors call the data 'UCI' but the schema (state, account length, area code, international plan, voicemail messages, day/evening/night/international minutes-calls-charge, customer service calls) and size (2,668 rows, 14.6% churn) match the BigML/Kaggle 'Telecom Churn' file (churn-bigml-80.csv: 2,666 rows, 20 columns; parent dataset 3,333 rows, 14.5% churn). (4) Customer-service calls: churn proportion rises monotonically with call count with 'a critical threshold observed at 4+ calls' (Fig. 10). (5) Deployment: proposed workflow of scoring -> churn probability plus feature-importance 'reason code' -> threshold flag in CRM dashboard -> automated actions (Discussion, 'Conceptual workflow'); hypotheses H2/H3 (accuracy enables interventions; integrated AI-CRM reduces churn) are stated but never tested, and the offer-adoption/recommendation/pricing figures (Figs 11-13) have no described data source. (6) Causal effect: the authors state that 'longitudinal A/B testing in a live environment' is required 'to quantitatively validate its impact on churn reduction and customer lifetime value', an admission that predictive accuracy is not evidence of retention impact (supports an uplift-modelling critique, although 'uplift' is never used). (7) Not covered at all: probability calibration, survival analysis, fairness, uplift modelling; cost-sensitive learning and ensemble sampling are future work only.

references.title: Profit-Sensitive Benchmarking of Post-hoc Explainability in Customer Churn
references.venue: Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science: 33rd Irish Conference, AICS 2025, Dublin, Ireland, December 1-2, 2025, Revised Selected Papers (Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2950). Publisher: Springer Nature Switzerland (Springer, Cham).
references.harvard_reference: Manzoor, A., Mazhar Qureshi, M.D., Yousuf, B., Kidney, E. and Atif Qureshi, M. (2026) 'Profit-sensitive benchmarking of post-hoc explainability in customer churn', in Mai, T.T. et al. (eds) Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science: 33rd Irish Conference, AICS 2025, Dublin, Ireland, December 1-2, 2025, Revised Selected Papers. Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2950. Cham: Springer, pp. 348-360. doi:10.1007/978-3-032-25809-0_28.
references.abstract_summary: The paper benchmarks post-hoc explainability for churn prediction by applying LIME and SHAP to high-performing tree ensembles and comparing them with inherently interpretable baselines (logistic regression and a decision tree) on two public telco datasets (footnotes identify them as the Kaggle IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, blastchar/telco-customer-churn, and the Maven Analytics telecom churn dataset). Models are assessed with standard predictive metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC) and with business/profit-sensitive measures (top-decile lift, Expected Maximum Profit (EMP) and customer-level e-Profits), while explanation quality is scored on fidelity, robustness, simplicity and consistency. SHAP, especially on boosted ensembles, reaches near-perfect fidelity and stable robustness, whereas LIME gives simpler but less faithful explanations. Profit-based metrics reorder the model rankings produced by accuracy and F1: ensembles that do not lead on F1 still deliver higher e-Profits. Gradient Boosting is presented as the balanced choice across predictive and profit-sensitive criteria, with SHAP offering dependable explanations for it, so the authors argue this is a practical alternative to relying only on inherently interpretable classifiers. The paper is framed as a compact benchmark that reports model performance and explanation quality side by side.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Abstract only (full text is paywalled). The abstract says churn models on tabular data 'often favour boosted ensembles for predictive performance' and that Gradient Boosting 'emerges as a balanced choice across predictive and profit-sensitive measures', but it reports no ROC-AUC values, does not say which model tops AUC, and makes no comparison of ensemble AUC with logistic regression. The only ranking statement is that some ensembles 'do not lead on F1'. The specific claim (near-top AUC, close to logistic regression) therefore cannot be attributed to this source; at most it supports the weaker statement that boosted ensembles are the conventional performance choice and that Gradient Boosting balanced predictive and profit criteria in this benchmark.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported by any accessible part of the source. The abstract evaluates the quality of LIME/SHAP explanations (fidelity, robustness, simplicity, consistency) but names no individual features and makes no statement about which variables drive churn. The full text could not be accessed (Springer paywall; the linked GitHub repository Awaismanzoor/aics-xai was empty on 2026-09-27), so this claim must be sourced elsewhere.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'Profit-based metrics reorder model rankings relative to accuracy and F1, with ensembles that do not lead on F1 still delivering higher e-Profits, underscoring profitability as a key selection criterion.' This directly supports the model-preference half of the claim. The abstract says nothing about thresholds, so cite it for model selection only, not for threshold choice.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: Abstract. Usable findings: (a) SHAP applied to boosted tree ensembles 'achieves near-perfect fidelity and stable robustness, whereas LIME yields simpler but less faithful explanations' - a quantified explanation-quality comparison using fidelity, robustness, simplicity and consistency; (b) SHAP on Gradient Boosting is presented as 'a practical alternative to relying solely on inherently interpretable classifiers', which speaks to the interpretable-vs-post-hoc debate (the paper cites Rudin 2019) and to deployment of black-box churn models; (c) the benchmark jointly reports predictive metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC), top-decile lift, EMP and customer-level e-Profits alongside explanation metrics, and argues these perspectives should be reported 'side-by-side ... without conflation'; (d) one of the two datasets is the same Kaggle IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (blastchar) used in the student's report, the other being the Maven Analytics telecom churn dataset. The abstract does not address class-imbalance handling, calibration, uplift modelling, survival analysis or fairness, so the paper should not be cited for those topics.

references.title: A predict-and-optimize approach to profit-driven churn prevention
references.publisher: Elsevier BV (on behalf of the Association of European Operational Research Societies, EURO)

dates.issue: 16 July 2025 (Crossref issued July 2025; Universidad de los Andes Pure portal: Published - 16 Jul 2025)

references.harvard_reference: Gómez-Vargas, N., Maldonado, S. and Vairetti, C. (2025) 'A predict-and-optimize approach to profit-driven churn prevention', European Journal of Operational Research, 324(2), pp. 555-566. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2025.02.008.
references.abstract_summary: The paper proposes PnOcp, a profit-driven churn-prevention classifier that frames retention-campaign targeting as a regret-minimisation problem inside a predict-and-optimize (decision-focused learning) framework, described as the first such model for churn prevention. Instead of the average or segment-level customer lifetime value (CLV) used by maximum-profit / expected-maximum-profit (MP/EMP) and multi-segment (MSP) approaches, the loss uses each customer's individual CLV so that only the most valuable at-risk customers are targeted, and it explicitly charges a cost for failing to target a would-be churner, which conventional profit metrics treat as costless. A sigmoid smooth surrogate makes the regret loss differentiable, so a shallow neural network can be trained by stochastic gradient descent (Adam). On churn datasets from an investment (Chilean mutual-fund) company, 13 in the published version (12 monthly 2017 datasets in the preprint), the method achieved the best average rank and the highest average campaign profit against ProfLogit, MSP-based classifiers and standard classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, CART, KNN, SVM).

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The experiments use no telecom data (Section 4.1: datasets from a Chilean mutual-fund company; Section 5 lists telecommunications only as future work). ROC-AUC is never reported; performance is measured as campaign profit and accuracy (Tables 5-7). No gradient boosting model is evaluated (baselines: logistic regression, random forest, CART, KNN, SVM, ProfLogit, MSP variants). Random forest does obtain the best accuracy ('For the statistical measure (accuracy), random forest achieves the best overall performance', Section 4.3) but ranks near the bottom on profit (Table 7: RF avg rank 7.88, avg profit EUR 92.33, versus logistic regression 7.71 / EUR 295.00 and PnOcp 2.79 / EUR 592.00). The paper cannot be cited for telecom ROC-AUC rankings.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. A keyword sweep of the full preprint finds no SHAP, Shapley, feature-importance or explainability analysis; the only use of 'interpretability' refers to normalising the optimality gap (Section 4.4, Eq. 13). The 24 features are mutual-fund variables (customer demographics, redemption/repurchase behaviour, fund financial indexes; Section 4.1), so no contract-type, tenure or monthly-charge variables exist, and no churn drivers are identified.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Supported. Section 4.3 and Table 7: random forest is the best model on accuracy, but PnOcp is best on profit (avg rank 2.79, EUR 592.00; best on 7 of 12 datasets) while RF is second-worst on profit (EUR 92.33); Friedman test p < 0.0001 and the Holm post-hoc test rejects equality between PnOcp and every classifier validated with traditional statistical measures. Section 4.4: 'relying solely on traditional statistical measures does not guarantee the optimization of the specific objective at hand - in our context, the total profit from a retention campaign'. On thresholds, Section 3 replaces the single profit-maximising cut-off t of the MP/EMP framework with an individual, CLV-dependent decision threshold m^i per customer, so the preferred targeting rule itself changes. Caveat: the statistical benchmark is accuracy (not AUC) and the data are financial, not telecom.

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: (a) Cost of missed churners: the regret loss assigns a strictly positive cost -f - gamma(d - CLV_i) to leaving out a customer who should have been targeted (Table 2 / Section 3), whereas the MP/EMP framework assumes that failing to target potential churners incurs no cost (Section 1). (b) Individual vs aggregated CLV: profit gains do not come from targeting more people; in the December dataset PnOcp earns more while contacting fewer than half as many customers as ProfLogit (Figure 4, Section 4.4). (c) Imbalance handling: PnOcp and ProfLogit 'leverage profit metrics to address the class imbalance issue', while the standard classifiers are trained with SMOTE (Section 4.2); churn rates are 16.3-21.5%. (d) Profit-trained models (PnOcp, ProfLogit) are the two top performers, but the Holm test does not separate PnOcp from ProfLogit or from the MSP-SVM, MSP-RF and MSP-logistic variants (Table 7). (e) Sensitivity: as the retention incentive d grows, every method's profit converges towards zero because fewer customers are valuable enough to cover the cost (Section 4.4, Figures 2-3). (f) Limitations stated by the authors: acceptance probability gamma fixed at 0.3 rather than stochastic; single financial-sector source because public datasets with individual CLVs are scarce; no campaign-response data, so uplift-style evaluation and personalised incentives could not be assessed; shallow network only. Calibration, survival analysis, fairness and deployment are not discussed at all.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified from Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.ejor.2025.02.008: type journal-article, EJOR, Elsevier BV, vol. 324 issue 2 pp. 555-566, issued July 2025, ISSN 0377-2217) and OpenAlex (publication_date 2025-02-13, ISSN 0377-2217 / 1872-6860, not open access, cited_by_count 5, 60 references). The verbatim published abstract was taken from the Universidad de los Andes Pure research portal (investigadores.uandes.cl), which also states 'Published - 16 Jul 2025'; the ScienceDirect page and Scimago returned HTTP 403 and the Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 on every attempt, so neither was used. The published full text is paywalled; claim checks were therefore made against the complete text of the arXiv preprint v2 (2310.07047v2, 15 Dec 2023, 15 pages) plus the published abstract. Known differences between preprint and published version: the preprint reports 12 monthly datasets and says it was submitted to Information Sciences, whereas the published abstract reports 13 datasets sourced from an investment company; section numbers, table numbers and exact figures quoted here are from the preprint and may differ slightly in the EJOR version. Venue check: EJOR is a long-established peer-reviewed journal (founded 1977, published by Elsevier for EURO, Scopus and MathSciNet indexed, 2024 impact factor 6.0 per the Wikipedia infobox); not predatory. Publication year 2025 lies within the required 2021-2026 window. No conference version exists; item_type is journal-article. All requested bibliographic fields were verifiable; none left empty.
references.caveats: The paper is about financial-services (mutual-fund) churn, not telecom, and it reports accuracy and campaign profit rather than ROC-AUC, so it cannot support claims about telecom model rankings or churn drivers (claims 1 and 2 are unsupported). It is best cited for (i) the profit-vs-accuracy model-ranking reversal and the individual-threshold argument (claim 3) and (ii) decision-focused / cost-sensitive learning as a critique of EMP-style evaluation. Test sets are small (roughly 200 customers per dataset), the incentive-acceptance rate is a fixed assumption (gamma = 0.3), and the preprint used for full-text checks differs from the published version (12 vs 13 datasets).

references.title: Predict-then-optimize or predict-and-optimize? An empirical evaluation of cost-sensitive learning strategies
references.venue: Information Sciences (Elsevier BV; ISSN 0020-0255 print, 1872-6291 online)
references.harvard_reference: Vanderschueren, T., Verdonck, T., Baesens, B. and Verbeke, W. (2022) 'Predict-then-optimize or predict-and-optimize? An empirical evaluation of cost-sensitive learning strategies', Information Sciences, 594, pp. 400-415. doi:10.1016/j.ins.2022.02.021.
references.abstract_summary: The paper contrasts two ways of making classification cost-aware: the conventional two-stage 'predict-then-optimize' route (train a standard classifier, then apply a cost-sensitive decision threshold) and the integrated 'predict-and-optimize' route (train the classifier with a task-specific, cost-weighted or expected-cost loss). It uses this two-stage framing to organise the cost-sensitive learning literature into training-stage and decision-stage methods, then benchmarks combinations of three classifiers (logistic regression, one-hidden-layer neural network, gradient boosting), three objectives (cross-entropy, cost-weighted cross-entropy, average expected cost) and nine thresholding rules on nine public datasets from fraud, direct marketing, churn (including Kaggle Telco Customer Churn) and credit scoring, with both instance-dependent and class-dependent costs and with cost-sensitive and cost-insensitive metrics. The headline result is that how the decision threshold is set matters more for cost outcomes than which loss the model was trained with; the best savings came from a cost-insensitive model combined with an instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold.

claims_supported.claim: 1. Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: NOT supported as worded. (a) Random forests are not in the study; the classifiers are logistic regression, a one-hidden-layer MLP and gradient boosting (Section 3.1.1, Table 3). (b) No per-model AUROC is reported for the Telco dataset in the paper body: Figure 3a (critical-difference diagram) ranks models on AUROC averaged across all nine datasets (net > boost > logit > csnet > wboost > wnet > csboost > wlogit > cslogit; only the gap to cslogit is significant at 5%), and Table B1 gives one pooled AUC of 0.82 for KTCC across cost-sensitive models, not a per-classifier comparison. Per-dataset, per-model results are only in a digital appendix. The most the paper supports is a weaker, aggregate statement: across nine datasets, gradient boosting and logistic regression trained with plain cross-entropy rank adjacently on AUROC with no significant difference, and 'neither logistic regression, neural networks nor gradient boosting consistently outperform another category' (Section 4.2.1). Cite it for that weaker claim only, and not for random forests or for telecom-specific AUC.

claims_supported.claim: 2. Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: NOT supported. The paper contains no SHAP, feature-importance or other explainability analysis and never discusses contract type, tenure or monthly charges as churn drivers. The only appearance of monthly charges is in the cost matrix design: for the Telco data the false-positive cost is set to 2x and the false-negative cost to 12x the customer's monthly amount A_i (Section 4.1, Table 5c, following Petrides and Verbeke 2021). Do not cite this source for claim 2.

claims_supported.claim: 3. Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Strongly supported, for both model choice and threshold choice. Model choice: Section 4.2.1 and Figures 3-4 show the cost-insensitive models (net, boost, logit) rank best on AUROC and average precision while the cost-sensitive models (cslogit, csboost, csnet) rank best on average expected cost; cslogit is worst on AUROC/AP but best on AEC and logit is the reverse; the authors conclude that 'minimizing errors or minimizing costs are two fundamentally different objectives'. Threshold choice: Section 4.2.2, Tables 6 and 8 - for gradient boosting the best savings (0.41) come from the instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold whereas the best F1 (0.48) comes from t = 0.5; the authors state that the best thresholding strategies in terms of F1 'do not necessarily achieve the lowest costs' and that t = 0.5 gives good F1 'even though it does not result in large cost savings'. Discussion (Section 5): the differences in best-performing thresholds under savings vs F1 show that minimising errors and costs are different objectives in the decision stage too. Conclusion (Section 6): optimising for accuracy can be detrimental when the real objective is cost minimisation, 'which is the case in a large variety of business applications'.

claims_supported.claim: 4a. Headline finding: the decision-making (thresholding) strategy matters more for costs than the training objective; a cost-insensitive model plus an instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold gave the best overall savings.
claims_supported.where: Highlights; Abstract (final sentence); Section 4.2.2 (Table 6: net and boost with IDCS threshold both reach mean savings of 0.41, the highest in the table); Section 5 (RQ3: 'the best savings were obtained by training with a cost-insensitive objective function and using the instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold'); Section 6 ('a conceptually simple yet well-performing strategy is to first train a cost-insensitive model and only introduce costs in a second stage through instance-dependent thresholding'). The authors note this agrees with Nikolaou et al. (2016) and Zheng (2010) in the class-dependent setting.

claims_supported.claim: 4b. For models trained with ordinary cross-entropy, using the default 0.5 threshold is costly; cost-sensitive thresholding is essential, and cost-sensitive training only helped savings for the least flexible model (logistic regression).
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.2: for cost-insensitive models 'it is absolutely crucial to not use the default threshold 0.5 and instead use the instance-dependent cost-sensitive threshold' (Table 6: logit savings 0.36 with IDCS vs 0.24 at t = 0.5; boost 0.41 vs 0.29). 'Given that an appropriate threshold is used, it is only beneficial in terms of savings to use a cost-sensitive objective function for the simplest model: logistic regression. For neural networks and gradient boosting, the cost-insensitive models also achieve good results given that the optimal threshold is used.'

claims_supported.claim: 4c. Calibration: cross-entropy-trained models were already well calibrated (isotonic calibration left Brier unchanged at 0.07), whereas cost-weighted and expected-cost objectives distort probabilities (Brier 0.13-0.24 before calibration) and calibration only improved savings for the weighted-cross-entropy models or when class-dependent thresholds were used; the hypothesis that calibration makes thresholding more effective was left inconclusive.
claims_supported.where: Section 3.1.2 (isotonic regression used for IDCS*/CDCS*); Section 4.2.2 and Table 7 (Brier before/after: logit 0.07/0.07, wlogit 0.16/0.07, cslogit 0.24/0.08, boost 0.07/0.07, csboost 0.19/0.08); 'the two best savings are obtained without calibration'; Section 5 and Table 11 (hypotheses 2.2 and 2.4 marked inconclusive). Section 2.2.2 also states the theoretical optimal threshold t* = (cFP - cTN)/(cFP - cTN + cFN - cTP) requires calibrated probabilities.

claims_supported.claim: 4d. Imbalance handling: cost-weighted cross-entropy is equivalent to oversampling proportional to misclassification cost, class-dependent cost-sensitive learning is 'intertwined' with the class-imbalance literature, and the popular class-imbalance threshold heuristic (t = P(Y=1)) can produce very poor cost outcomes for cost-weighted models.
claims_supported.where: Section 2.1.1 (cost-sensitive and imbalance literatures intertwined; refers to Leevy et al. 2018 survey); Section 2.2.1 ('this approach is equivalent to oversampling proportional to misclassification costs'); Section 2.2.2 (class-imbalance threshold defined); Table 6 (savings with CI threshold: wlogit -1.33, wnet -0.66, i.e. worse than the trivial default classifier) and Section 4.2.2 ('empirical thresholding with the F1-score, the class imbalance heuristic or t = 0.5 can obtain bad results'). Note: no SMOTE or resampling experiments are run; the point is conceptual plus the CI-threshold result.

claims_supported.claim: 4e. Telco-specific details usable in a report: the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn data are used with N = 7,032, 19 features and 26.58% churners; costs are instance-dependent with cFP = 2x and cFN = 12x the customer's monthly charge (cTP = cTN = 0); categorical features are WoE-encoded and features standardised; evaluation is 2x5-fold stratified CV with Friedman/Nemenyi and Wilcoxon tests; on this dataset the pooled AUC was 0.82 and cost savings from cost-sensitive thresholding were modest (about 0.20-0.26 versus 0.10 when the threshold is tuned for F1).
claims_supported.where: Table 4 (KTCC: N 7,032, D 19, 26.58% positive); Section 4.1 and Table 5c (2A_i / 12A_i cost matrix, following Petrides and Verbeke 2021); Algorithm 1 (WoE encoding, z-standardisation, 2x5-fold stratified CV); Section 3.2 (statistical tests); Table B1 (KTCC AUC 0.82 ID / 0.82 CD; F1 0.54-0.61); Table B2 (KTCC savings: IDCS 0.21, IDCS* 0.26, CDCS* 0.26, empirical ID/CD 0.26, empirical F1 0.10, t=0.5 0.20). Caveat: Tables B1/B2 average over the six cost-sensitive models, not per classifier. N = 7,032 rather than the raw 7,043 is consistent with dropping the 11 rows with blank TotalCharges, but the paper does not say so (my inference).

claims_supported.claim: 4f. Instance-dependent vs class-dependent costs: training with instance-level costs improves cost metrics (lower AEC, higher Spearman correlation between scores and cost) but worsens error metrics (AUROC, AP, F1); no costs at all is best for minimising errors.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.2.3, Tables 9 and 10; Section 5 (RQ4): 'not using costs at all is preferential for minimizing errors, using instance-dependent costs is optimal for minimizing costs, and using class-dependent costs lies somewhere between these two.'

claims_supported.claim: 4g. Topics absent from this paper: uplift modelling, survival analysis, fairness, deployment/monitoring, random forests, SHAP/explainability, and resampling methods such as SMOTE are not studied.
claims_supported.where: Confirmed by reading the full accepted manuscript (Sections 1-6 and appendices). The paper explicitly scopes out cost-sensitive feature selection, model selection, ensembles, semi-supervised and PU learning (Section 2). Code is public under MIT licence at https://github.com/toonvds/CostSensitiveLearning (Section 1 and repository README).
