references.title: Profit-driven pre-processing in B2B customer churn modeling using fairness techniques
references.predatory_check: Not predatory. Journal of Business Research is a long-established Elsevier journal (ISSN 0148-2963, confirmed via Crossref and OpenAlex), widely indexed and recognised in business-school journal lists; the article carries a registered Crossref DOI, an Elsevier volume/article number, and a green open-access accepted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's institutional repository.
references.harvard_reference: Rahman, S., Janssens, B. and Bogaert, M. (2025) 'Profit-driven pre-processing in B2B customer churn modeling using fairness techniques', Journal of Business Research, 189, article 115159. doi:10.1016/j.jbusres.2024.115159.
references.abstract_verbatim: This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance the profitability of business-to-business (B2B) customer retention campaigns through profit-driven pre-processing techniques, deviating from the traditional focus on in- and post-processing methods. Our study explores the effectiveness of three pre-processing techniques-massaging, reweighing, and resampling-derived from fairness literature. We evaluate these techniques alongside a baseline model and three state-of-the-art in- and post-processing methods using the EMPB and a newly introduced metric, the Area Under the Expected Profit Curve (AUEPC). Our findings demonstrate that reweighing and resampling consistently outperform baselines up to a 49% profit increase. Furthermore, compared to state-of-the-art algorithms, reweighing and resampling methods surpass in-processing techniques and perform favorably against post-processing methods, particularly at optimal customer contact rates. However, post-processing methods are preferred under budget constraints. This study contributes to the current literature by offering a simpler, model-agnostic, and less computationally expensive framework for profit-driven churn modeling in B2B contexts.
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that because churn propensity is inversely related to customer lifetime value (CLV), propensity-ranked retention campaigns are biased towards low-value customers, which matters most in B2B settings with highly heterogeneous CLV. It repurposes three bias-mitigation pre-processing techniques from the algorithmic-fairness literature (Kamiran and Calders' massaging, reweighing and resampling), treating high-CLV customers as the under-represented 'sensitive' group, and applies them to five classifiers (LASSO logistic regression, random forest, SVM, AdaBoost, XGBoost) on two proprietary B2B datasets (a North American beverage retailer, n = 41,739, churn 3.77%; a European construction-material wholesaler, n = 30,199, churn about 55%). Evaluation uses the Expected Maximum Profit measure for B2B churn (EMPB) plus a newly proposed Area Under the Expected Profit Curve (AUEPC), which integrates expected profit over all contact fractions so models can be compared under campaign-budget constraints. Reweighing and resampling significantly outperform the baseline and massaging on AUEPC (p < 0.001), with up to a 49% profit gain when only 30% of customers can be contacted, although differences vanish at EMPB's optimal contact rate (82-87% of customers). Against state-of-the-art methods, XGBoost with resampling beats the in-processing ProfLogit and B2Boost and the post-processing 'expected CLV at loss' ranking on EMPB (all p = 0.006), but expected-CLV-at-loss is preferable under tight budgets (below roughly a 47% contact rate). The authors highlight the much lower computational cost and knowledge barrier of pre-processing versus EMP-based in-processing methods, and release open-source code.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The study uses two proprietary B2B datasets (beverage retailer, construction-material wholesaler), not telecom data, and it never reports ROC-AUC for its own models; all model comparison is by EMPB and AUEPC (Sections 3.4-3.6, Tables 2-3). AUC is mentioned only in the literature review (manuscript p.12: B2Boost 'sacrifices predictive accuracy (as measured by the AUC)', citing Janssens et al., 2022; and profit differences 'not reflected by traditional metrics such as AUC', citing Sanchez Ramirez et al., 2024). The only adjacent evidence is that, on the profit metric EMPB, random forest and XGBoost rank first/second for both datasets, well ahead of LASSO logistic regression on the beverage data (Table 3: XGBoost 16.06k vs LASSO 1.46k), and XGBoost is chosen as the best baseline for Experiment 2 (Section 4.2.1). That is a profit ranking on B2B data, not ROC-AUC on telecom data, so the claim cannot be attributed to this paper.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no SHAP, Shapley, feature-importance or other explainability analysis (zero occurrences in the full text; 'interpretable' appears only in a cited reference title). Its features are B2B RFM, relationship-length, credit-score, product-mix and buyer-supplier interaction variables (Appendix A), with no contract-type, tenure or monthly-charges analogue discussed as a driver. The only driver-type finding is the negative point-biserial correlation between churn and CLV (-12.4% beverage, -22.5% construction; Section 3.3, Figure 2).

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not supported as literally stated, because the paper never runs an accuracy-only (accuracy/AUC) evaluation of its own models to contrast with the profit evaluation; the accuracy-versus-profit divergence appears only as cited prior work (manuscript p.12, citing Janssens et al., 2022 and Sanchez Ramirez et al., 2024). What the paper DOES demonstrate, and what could be cited instead, is that the choice of profit-based evaluation changes the preferred method and contact threshold: (a) at EMPB's optimal contact rate (82-87% of customers) no pre-processing method differs significantly from the baseline (p = 0.916, 0.170, 0.375), yet across budget-constrained contact rates (AUEPC) resampling and reweighing are significantly better (p < 0.001) and deliver a 49% profit gain at a 30% contact rate (Section 4.1.1: 'Evaluating classifiers solely at this threshold might yield misleading conclusions'); (b) optimal contact fractions differ widely by method (expected CLV at loss 67.75%, massaging 85.05%, B2Boost 86.75%, ProfLogit 96.6%; Section 4.2.1); (c) resampling wins on EMPB but the post-processing expected-CLV-at-loss method is preferable below about a 47% contact rate (Section 4.2.1, Figure 8; Conclusion).

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: Several precise, citable findings: (1) Fairness pre-processing repurposed for profit: high-CLV customers are treated as the discriminated group, statistical parity (P(Y=+|high) - P(Y=+|low)) is the bias measure, and the high/low-CLV cut-off is tuned as a hyperparameter (Section 3.3). (2) Inverse churn-value relationship: point-biserial correlation of churn with CLV is -12.4% (beverage) and -22.5% (construction), so 'CCP models are biased towards low-value customers' (Section 3.3, Figure 2). (3) Imbalance handling: the datasets are deliberately NOT resampled for class imbalance (3.77% and about 55% churn) because the reweighing/resampling methods exploit the class distribution; customers above the 95th CLV percentile are excluded as key-account-managed (Section 3.1). (4) Evaluation metric: AUEPC is the integral over contact fractions of EP(eta|C)/EP(eta|C*), the ratio of a model's expected-profit curve to that of a perfect ranking, integrated up to the last profitable fraction eta*; introduced because firms 'cannot suddenly double their sales force' to reach EMPB's optimal contact rate (Section 3.6). (5) Low-churn instability: on the 3.77%-churn retailer, EMPB standard deviations are very large, optimal contact rates are 0-0.05% and some models target nobody; with default parameters no profitable campaign exists, and even in the most lenient sensitivity scenario the best AUEPC is only 0.13 (Section 4.1.2). (6) Benchmark: XGBoost + resampling beats ProfLogit, B2Boost and expected-CLV-at-loss on EMPB (all p = 0.006); resampling and expected CLV at loss beat both in-processing methods on AUEPC (p = 0.010) with no significant difference between the two (p = 0.064); 'the in-processing techniques currently suggested by academic literature never achieve superior performance' (Sections 4.2, 6). (7) Deployment/computation: ProfLogit hyperparameter trials take 5.5-5.7x longer than LASSO, 98% of its time is spent in the EMP fitness function, and running ProfLogit with the EMPB would take 'two to three years', while churn models lose predictive performance after about three months (citing Neslin et al., 2006) (Section 5.1). (8) Uplift: uplift models 'require randomized controlled trials to identify causal effects', which is challenging and risky in B2B firms with small customer bases (Section 2.2). (9) Telecom contrast, directly relevant to the student's dataset: 'B2C firms, particularly in industries such as telecommunication, experience much less inequality in customer value, as price differentiation is limited' (price spread $40-$100 versus near-zero to over $1M in the B2B cases), so value bias may matter less there and 'churn propensity could outweigh value discrepancies' (Section 5.2). (10) Limitation acknowledged: the expected-CLV-at-loss post-processing trains the CLV regressor only on non-churners and does not correct for Heckman self-selection bias; CLV uses a status-quo assumption (Sections 3.1, 6). (11) Methodology exemplar: 5x2 nested stratified cross-validation, TPE Bayesian optimisation (Optuna), Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, weight-of-evidence encoding and median imputation (Sections 3.2, 3.4). Nothing on calibration or survival analysis.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.jbusres.2024.115159) confirms DOI, title, authors Shimanto Rahman, Bram Janssens, Matthias Bogaert, container Journal of Business Research, volume 189, article/page 115159, no issue number, publisher Elsevier BV, ISSN 0148-2963, type journal-article, issued 2025-02 (print), 7 citing works. OpenAlex confirms volume 189, page 115159, online ISSN 1873-7978, publication date 2024-12-24 (online first) and green OA. Semantic Scholar returned the record (JournalArticle, Journal of Business Research, 2025) but with a null abstract; the abstract was therefore taken verbatim from the accepted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's repository (biblio.ugent.be, 52-page author manuscript, 2.3 MB PDF, text extracted locally), and it matches the biblio.ugent.be record summary. Discrepancy noted: OpenAlex lists the first author as 'S.M. Kawshik Rahman', but both Crossref and the manuscript itself print 'Shimanto Rahman' (UGent), so the OpenAlex name is treated as an author-disambiguation error. The ScienceDirect landing page and journal page returned HTTP 403, so publisher-side received/accepted dates were not verified and are left out. All section/page references in claims_supported refer to the accepted-manuscript pagination, not the typeset journal version. Year 2025 is used for the reference because the version of record sits in the February 2025 issue (Crossref 'issued' 2025-02), consistent with the search lead. Peer-review status: Journal of Business Research is a long-established Elsevier subscription journal (established 1973; described as peer-reviewed and indexed in Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus per its Wikipedia entry, ISSN 0148-2963 matching Crossref); Scimago and ScienceDirect journal pages returned HTTP 403 so quartile/CiteScore were not independently verified. The paper is within the required 2021-2026 window and there is no indication of predatory publishing.
references.caveats: This is a B2B study on proprietary retail/wholesale datasets, not telecom and not the Kaggle Telco dataset; it reports no ROC-AUC, accuracy, calibration, SHAP or survival results, so it must not be cited for claims 1-3 as worded. Its value for the report is (a) the profit-driven/budget-constrained evaluation argument (EMPB vs AUEPC), (b) reweighing/resampling as cheap model-agnostic alternatives to in-processing profit models, and (c) its explicit statement that value heterogeneity, and hence value bias, is much smaller in B2C telecom, which is a useful critical counterpoint when discussing whether profit-weighting matters for the Telco dataset. The 49% profit gain applies to one dataset at a 30% contact rate and is not significant at the EMPB-optimal contact rate. Open-source implementation: github.com/ShimantoRahman/churn-preprocessing.

references.title: Zero defections: quality comes to services
references.harvard_reference: Reichheld, F.F. and Sasser, W.E., Jr. (1990) 'Zero defections: quality comes to services', Harvard Business Review, 68(5), pp. 105-111.
references.abstract_summary: Reichheld (Bain & Company) and Sasser (Harvard Business School) argue that service companies should treat lost customers as their equivalent of manufacturing scrap and manage towards 'zero defections', i.e. keeping every customer they can profitably serve. Drawing on Bain client case data rather than a formal study, they report that as companies cut customer defection rates 'amazing things happen to their financials': although 'the magnitude of the change varies by company and industry, the pattern holds: profits rise sharply'. The abstract gives three worked cases in which reducing the defection rate by 5% produced 85% more profit in one bank's branch system, 50% more in an insurance brokerage and 30% more in an auto-service chain, plus MBNA America, a credit-card issuer whose profits rose 125% after it halved a 10% defection rate. The mechanism is that long-standing customers generate rising profit over time (base profit, growth in purchases, lower servicing cost, referrals and price premiums), so defection destroys a stream of future value. The authors also present defection rates as a diagnostic: interviewing defectors shows where service falls short (Staples uses such feedback to find over-priced products), and retention targets should be reinforced through incentives (Great-West Life pays a 50% commission premium to brokers who hit retention targets; MBNA pays departmental bonuses).

claims_supported.claim: Reducing defections by 5 % can increase profits by 25-85 %; this is the origin of popular retention-economics multipliers, which are based on case examples rather than a general law.
claims_supported.where: Supported in substance, with two qualifications on wording. (i) The 5%-defection / large-profit-gain figure: the PubMed-indexed abstract states verbatim 'Reducing the defection rate just 5% generates 85% more profits in one bank's branch system, 50% more in an insurance brokerage, and 30% more in an auto-service chain', and 'when MBNA America ... cut its 10% defection rate in half, profits rose a whopping 125%'. The abstract therefore directly verifies a 30-85% range across three named cases. The commonly quoted '25% to 85%' range is the heading of the article's bar-chart exhibit covering nine service industries (the lowest bar, credit insurance, is 25%); that exhibit sits inside the paywalled full text and could not be opened in this session, so the 25% lower bound is verified here only via standard secondary attribution (Wikipedia, 'Loyalty business model': 'It is claimed by Reichheld and Sasser (1990) that a 5% improvement in customer retention can cause an increase in profitability between 25% and 85%', citing HBR Sept-Oct 1990, pp. 105-111). Either phrase the figure as 'between roughly 25% and 85% depending on industry' (standard attribution) or use the abstract-verifiable '30% to 85%' with the three named cases. (ii) 'Based on case examples rather than a general law': directly supported by the abstract's own hedging, 'Although the magnitude of the change varies by company and industry, the pattern holds', and by the fact that every figure is tied to a single named company or client case (one bank, an insurance brokerage, an auto-service chain, MBNA). The article is a practitioner piece built on Bain consulting case data, not a statistical study, so it is fair to say the multipliers are illustrative rather than a general law. (iii) 'This is the origin of popular retention-economics multipliers' is a statement about the article's influence on later practice, which the source does not and cannot make about itself; see the separate sub-claim entry below for how to word it.

claims_supported.claim: Sub-claim (attribution): Reichheld and Sasser (1990) is the origin of the popular retention-economics multipliers (the '5% retention = 25-85% profit' rule of thumb).
claims_supported.where: Not a claim the source makes: the article presents its case figures but says nothing about its own subsequent influence. The attribution is nevertheless well corroborated externally: OpenAlex records 5,279 citing works (W1594945480), Wikipedia's 'Loyalty business model' article attributes the 25-85% figure specifically to this paper, and it is the standard citation for the rule of thumb in the churn and CRM literature. Recommended wording: 'the widely repeated rule of thumb that a 5% improvement in retention raises profits by 25-85% originates in case examples reported by Reichheld and Sasser (1990)' - the citation then supports the figures and their case-based nature, while the 'widely repeated' / 'origin' framing is the report's own (defensible) observation, ideally backed by one secondary source that says so.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (query.bibliographic) did not return the HBR article itself - HBR did not assign DOIs to 1990 magazine articles - and instead returned only the German translation reprinted as a chapter ('Zero-Migration: Dienstleister im Sog der Qualitaetsrevolution') in Handbuch Kundenbindungsmanagement (Springer/Gabler, DOIs 10.1007/978-3-322-99638-1_6 [1998], 10.1007/978-3-322-99714-2_6 [1999], 10.1007/978-3-322-99464-6_6 [2003]); these are not the cited work and must not be used as its DOI. The doi field is therefore left empty: no DOI exists for the original article. Bibliographic details were verified from three independent sources that agree: (1) the publisher page hbr.org/1990/09/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services, which shows the title, authors 'Frederick F. Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser, Jr.' and 'From the Magazine (September-October 1990)'; (2) the PubMed record PMID 10107082 fetched via NCBI E-utilities XML: Harv Bus Rev, ISSN 0017-8012, 1990 Sep-Oct, Vol 68, Issue 5, pages 105-11 (i.e. 105-111), authors Reichheld FF and Sasser WE Jr, with the full abstract, which is quoted verbatim in claims_supported; (3) OpenAlex W1594945480: same title, authors, 'Harvard business review' 68(5): 105-11, PMID 10107082, DOI none, 5,279 citations. The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 (rate-limited) on every attempt, so OpenAlex was used as the fallback the task allows; the Semantic Scholar web page for the paper (3cf9e452adceb66ead134d9377ae8155016aa259) exists but rendered empty to the fetcher. The HBS faculty listing (hbs.edu item 9151) and HBSP product pages (90508-PDF-ENG, 519X-PDF-ENG) were blocked or empty (403 / bot-check). The Bain reprint page shows only an excerpt; its fetcher summary of 'almost 100%' should be ignored as it is not the article's own number. The full text behind the HBR paywall was not accessed, so the nine-industry exhibit (source of the 25% lower bound) is verified only via secondary attribution, as stated above. Two search hits offering the article as a downloadable PDF from unfamiliar mirror domains were deliberately not opened. Cite Them Right note: HBR is a magazine with volume/issue/pages, so it is referenced like a print journal article; if the student read it online, 'Available at: https://hbr.org/1990/09/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services (Accessed: 27 September 2026).' may be appended. The suffix 'Jr.' appears in the publisher's and PubMed's author listing; 'Sasser, W.E.' without it is also commonly used and acceptable.
references.caveats: (1) Source type: HBR is a practitioner magazine, not a peer-reviewed journal, and the profit figures come from Bain & Company client cases rather than a designed study; present them as illustrative multipliers, not as an empirical law - which is exactly the framing the candidate claim adopts. (2) Meaning of '5%': in the article a 5% reduction in the defection rate refers to moving the annual defection rate by about five percentage points (cf. MBNA halving a 10% rate), not a 5% relative change; avoid re-expressing it in a way the source does not. (3) Range: the abstract verifies 30-85%; the 25-85% range is the article's exhibit heading known via secondary attribution, so quote it as 'between roughly 25% and 85%, depending on industry'. (4) Reichheld himself later warned that such cross-sectional profit-vs-tenure comparisons can mislead (Carroll and Reichheld, 1992, 'The fallacy of customer retention', Journal of Retail Banking, 13(4) - cited by Wikipedia; not verified in this session), which would strengthen a critical paragraph if independently checked. (5) The examples are banking, insurance, auto service and credit cards from around 1990, not telecoms; the Kaggle Telco dataset contains no profit or margin data, so the multipliers cannot be tested on it - use the source only to motivate why churn reduction matters economically.

references.title: The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets
references.harvard_reference: Saito, T. and Rehmsmeier, M. (2015) 'The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets', PLoS ONE, 10(3), e0118432. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0118432.
references.abstract_summary: The paper argues that ROC plots, although standard for evaluating binary classifiers, can be deceptive on imbalanced datasets where negatives greatly outnumber positives, because specificity (and hence the false positive rate) is intuitively but wrongly interpreted: the same absolute rise in false positives yields only a small change in FPR when negatives are numerous, so the ROC curve looks essentially unchanged. Precision-recall (PRC) plots, which evaluate the fraction of true positives among positive predictions, expose this deterioration and therefore give a more accurate picture of expected classification performance. Using simulated classifiers on balanced (1000:1000) and imbalanced (1000:10000) data, the authors show ROC curves remain identical across the two conditions while PRC curves change; a survey of 58 genome-wide SVM studies found ROC used in 66.7% versus PRC in 6.0%; and a re-analysis of the MiRFinder microRNA study showed tools that appeared adequate under ROC performed near the random baseline under PRC.

claims_supported.claim: ROC plots can be misleadingly optimistic under class imbalance, whereas precision-recall plots reflect performance on the minority class more informatively.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: ROC plots on imbalanced datasets 'can be deceptive with respect to conclusions about the reliability of classification performance, owing to an intuitive but wrong interpretation of specificity', while PRC plots 'can provide the viewer with an accurate prediction of future classification performance due to the fact that they evaluate the fraction of true positives among positive predictions'. Results/simulation section: identical ROC curves for balanced and imbalanced data despite false positives rising from 160 to 1,600 at the same operating point ('The ROC curves fail to explicitly show this performance difference'), whereas only the PRC curves changed. MiRFinder re-analysis: ROC suggested consistent performance across test sets, PRC revealed near-random precision on the second set. The 'minority class' in the paper is the positive class (positives outnumbered by negatives), and precision is defined over positive predictions, so the claim's framing matches the paper.

references.caveats: The paper's evidence and framing are bioinformatics-specific (genome-wide SVM literature survey, microRNA discovery tools) and its simulations use a strong 1:10 imbalance; the argument is general to any binary classifier but the source itself makes no reference to churn, telecom or the Telco Customer Churn dataset (~26.5% churn, a milder imbalance). The paper compares ROC and PRC plots/curves; it does not evaluate every threshold-based metric, so it should not be cited for claims about F1, cost-sensitive metrics or resampling. Journal name appears as 'PLOS ONE' in Crossref and the publisher's site and as 'PLoS ONE' in Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex; either spelling is acceptable in a reference list.
references.verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-27. Crossref (query.bibliographic) returned DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0118432, type journal-article, authors Takaya Saito and Marc Rehmsmeier, container-title PLOS ONE, volume 10, issue 3, article e0118432, year 2015. Semantic Scholar (DOI endpoint) confirmed the same title, year, venue, authors and gave PubMed 25738806, PMC 4349800 and the full abstract. OpenAlex confirmed volume 10, issue 3, pages e0118432, PMID 25738806. PLOS landing page confirmed publication date 4 March 2015 and the same abstract; body passages on the balanced-vs-imbalanced simulation, the literature survey (58 studies) and the MiRFinder re-analysis were read from the publisher page. All metadata in the lead was accurate. No fields left unverified.

references.title: Tabular data: Deep learning is not all you need
references.harvard_reference: Shwartz-Ziv, R. and Armon, A. (2022) 'Tabular data: deep learning is not all you need', Information Fusion, 81, pp. 84-90. doi:10.1016/j.inffus.2021.11.011.
references.abstract_summary: The authors ask whether recently proposed deep-learning models for tabular data (TabNet, NODE, DNF-Net and a 1D-CNN) should replace tree ensembles such as XGBoost. They benchmark the deep models against XGBoost on 11 tabular datasets, including the datasets the deep models' own papers used plus two new Kaggle datasets (Shrutime churn-modelling and Blastchar, i.e. the Telco Customer Churn dataset), using a common hyperparameter-tuning protocol. XGBoost outperformed the deep models on most datasets (8 of 11) and needed much less tuning, converging to good performance in fewer and shorter optimisation iterations. No single deep model was consistently best; each did well mainly on the datasets from its own paper. A weighted ensemble of the deep models plus XGBoost gave the best results overall (2.32% average relative error increase vs 3.4% for XGBoost alone), and beat ensembles of classical models or of deep models without XGBoost.

claims_supported.claim: Across several tabular datasets, XGBoost outperformed recent deep-learning models designed for tabular data, and deep models required more tuning; an ensemble of both performed best.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'XGBoost outperforms these deep models across the datasets, including the datasets used in the papers that proposed the deep models. We also demonstrate that XGBoost requires much less tuning. On the positive side, we show that an ensemble of deep models and XGBoost performs better on these datasets than XGBoost alone.' Section 3.2 'Do the deep models generalize well to other datasets?': XGBoost outperformed the deep models on 8 of the 11 datasets; the ensemble of all models was best (2.32% average relative increase) with XGBoost second (3.4%). Section 3.2 'How difficult is the optimization?': XGBoost converged to good performance more quickly, in fewer and shorter iterations, and the hyperparameter search was much shorter. Section 3.2 'Do we need both XGBoost and deep networks?' and Section 4 'Discussion and Conclusions': the ensemble of XGBoost with deep models yielded the best results.

references.verification_notes: Verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.inffus.2021.11.011; Information Fusion, vol. 81, pp. 84-90, publisher Elsevier BV, ISSN 1566-2535; issued/published-print May 2022; record created 26 Nov 2021), Semantic Scholar (title, authors, abstract, arXiv 2106.03253), OpenAlex (W3172701880; authors affiliated with Intel), and the arXiv v2 full text (23 Nov 2021), which matches the abstract of the journal version. Year: the journal issue is May 2022, so 2022 is correct for the published article; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list 2021 because the article appeared online on 26 Nov 2021 and the arXiv preprint dates from June 2021. Issue: Crossref shows 'C', an Elsevier placeholder rather than a real issue number, so the issue field is left empty and the Harvard reference cites volume 81 only. The ScienceDirect landing page returned HTTP 403, so the 'Received/Accepted' dates were not checked, but no cited field depends on them. Caveats for the report: the benchmark is from 2021 and covers four deep models (TabNet, NODE, DNF-Net, 1D-CNN) against XGBoost only; newer tabular deep models (e.g. FT-Transformer, TabPFN) are not included. Relevance: one of the 11 benchmark datasets is Blastchar, the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset used in the student's report, though per-dataset figures for it were not extracted here.

references.harvard_reference: Platt, J.C. (2000) 'Probabilities for SV machines', in Smola, A.J., Bartlett, P., Schölkopf, B. and Schuurmans, D. (eds) Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers. Cambridge, MA: The MIT Press, pp. 61–74. doi:10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008.
references.title: Probabilities for SV Machines
references.venue: Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers (edited book, eds A.J. Smola, P. Bartlett, B. Schölkopf and D. Schuurmans), The MIT Press
references.abstract_summary: Platt argues that a classifier's output should be a calibrated posterior probability so that it can be post-processed (e.g. combined with other classifiers or used with asymmetric costs), but standard SVMs give only an uncalibrated decision value. One alternative is to train a kernel classifier directly with a logit link and a regularised maximum-likelihood objective, but that produces non-sparse kernel machines. Platt instead trains an ordinary SVM and then fits the two parameters (A, B) of an additional sigmoid, P(y=1|f) = 1/(1+exp(Af+B)), that maps the SVM output f to a probability; A and B are fitted by maximum likelihood (minimising cross-entropy) on held-out or cross-validated SVM outputs, with a Laplace-style smoothing of the targets to limit over-fitting. Classification error rate and likelihood scores of SVM+sigmoid are compared against a regularised-likelihood kernel machine on three data-mining-style datasets (Reuters, Adult, Web). The SVM+sigmoid produces probabilities of comparable quality to the regularised-likelihood method while retaining the sparseness of the SVM. Published chapter sections: Introduction; Fitting a Sigmoid After the SVM; Empirical Tests; Conclusions; Appendix: Pseudo-code for Training Sigmoid.

claims_supported.claim: Platt scaling fits a sigmoid to classifier scores to produce calibrated probabilities.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (preprint text via OpenAlex W1618905105): 'The output of a classifier should be a calibrated posterior probability ... Standard SVMs do not provide such probabilities ... we train an SVM, then train the parameters of an additional sigmoid function to map the SVM outputs into probabilities.' The published chapter's Section 2 is titled 'Fitting a Sigmoid After the SVM' and its appendix gives pseudo-code for training the sigmoid (section list from OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar records of DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008). The sigmoid form P(y=1|f) = 1/(1+exp(Af+B)) with A, B fitted by maximum likelihood is confirmed by scikit-learn's calibration guide (which cites section 2.1 of Platt 1999) and by a Cornell CS678 (2007) lecture summary of the paper. Caveat: Platt's own text describes fitting the sigmoid to SVM decision values; the name 'Platt scaling' and its application to the scores of arbitrary classifiers are later usage (e.g. Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005), so the report should not attribute the general term or a claim of generality to this source.

references.verification_notes: The lead is imprecise. Two versions of this work exist. (1) A 1999 preprint/technical report from Microsoft Research titled 'Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines and Comparisons to Regularized Likelihood Methods' (OpenAlex W1618905105; primary location CiteSeerX, raw source research.microsoft.com/~jplatt/SVMprob.ps.gz; no DOI; 4,852 OpenAlex citations). This is the form scikit-learn's calibration documentation cites as '[4] J. Platt, 1999' and links to www.cs.colorado.edu/~mozer/Teaching/syllabi/6622/papers/Platt1999.pdf. (2) The published book chapter, retitled 'Probabilities for SV Machines', in Smola, Bartlett, Schölkopf and Schuurmans (eds) Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers, The MIT Press, published 29 September 2000, pp. 61-74, DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008, e-book ISBN 9780262283977 (Crossref record; the edited book itself is Crossref DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.001.0001; print ISBN 9780262194488 and 422 pages per MIT Press/Amazon/Waterstones search results). OpenAlex records the chapter with 1,112 citations; Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 64295966) records it with the abstract elided by the publisher and, erroneously, the book editors listed as authors. The Harvard reference above uses the published, DOI-bearing chapter (year 2000, not 1999). Fields not verifiable: volume/issue (none; book chapter). Place of publication 'Cambridge, MA' is The MIT Press's imprint location and is not stated in the Crossref record. Not reachable during verification: mitpress.mit.edu and direct.mit.edu (HTTP 403 to automated fetch), Microsoft Research publication page (404), Google Books API (429), Open Library (fetch quota exhausted). The paper's full text could not be read directly: the Cornell copy fetched (cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs678/2007sp/platt.pdf) is a 2007 lecture presentation summarising the paper, not the paper itself; claim assessment therefore rests on the abstract, the chapter section titles, scikit-learn's description, and that summary. If the report prefers to cite the form used by scikit-learn, an acceptable alternative is: Platt, J.C. (1999) Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods. Preprint. Microsoft Research. Available at: https://www.cs.colorado.edu/~mozer/Teaching/syllabi/6622/papers/Platt1999.pdf (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.caveats: Cite as 2000 (published chapter) rather than 1999 unless deliberately citing the preprint; the chapter title differs from the preprint title. The evidence in the paper is limited to SVMs (linear and quadratic kernels) on three datasets (Reuters, Adult, Web); scikit-learn notes the sigmoid assumption was justified for SVMs in Platt's section 2.1 but 'does not necessarily hold in general', and that the logistic model works best when calibration error is symmetric, which can be a problem for imbalanced problems such as churn. Lin, Lin and Weng (2007, Machine Learning, 68(3), pp. 267-276, doi:10.1007/s10994-007-5018-6) report numerical problems in Platt's original pseudo-code and give a corrected algorithm (the one scikit-learn implements).

references.title: Bias in random forest variable importance measures: illustrations, sources and a solution
references.harvard_reference: Strobl, C., Boulesteix, A.-L., Zeileis, A. and Hothorn, T. (2007) 'Bias in random forest variable importance measures: illustrations, sources and a solution', BMC Bioinformatics, 8(1), 25. doi:10.1186/1471-2105-8-25.
references.abstract_summary: The paper examines random forest variable importance measures as a tool for variable selection and shows, via simulation studies, that they are unreliable when predictor variables differ in scale of measurement or number of categories: suboptimal predictors can be artificially preferred. Two mechanisms are identified - biased variable selection in the individual CART-style trees (favouring variables with many possible split points) and effects induced by bootstrap sampling with replacement. The authors propose using an alternative random forest implementation built on conditional inference trees (cforest in the R party package), which provides unbiased variable selection in the individual trees; combined with subsampling without replacement, its permutation importance can be used reliably for variable selection even with mixed-type predictors. The approach is illustrated with a re-analysis of RNA editing data.

claims_supported.claim: Impurity-based (Gini) variable importance in random forests is biased towards variables with more categories or continuous scales; permutation importance with unbiased trees is preferable.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Results and Conclusion paragraphs): importance measures are 'not reliable in situations where potential predictor variables vary in their scale of measurement or their number of categories'; the authors 'propose to employ an alternative implementation of random forests, that provides unbiased variable selection in the individual classification trees'. Full text, Results section on the simulation studies (null and power cases): the Gini importance 'shows a strong preference for variables with many categories and the continuous variable' and the authors 'conclude that the Gini importance cannot be used to reliably measure variable importance in this situation'. Conclusion: recommends cforest (conditional inference trees, unbiased split selection) with the permutation importance and subsampling without replacement.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified against Crossref (DOI 10.1186/1471-2105-8-25; authors Carolin Strobl, Anne-Laure Boulesteix, Achim Zeileis, Torsten Hothorn; BMC Bioinformatics, vol. 8, issue 1, article number 25, 2007, Springer Science and Business Media LLC, type journal-article) and Semantic Scholar (title, abstract, year 2007, venue BMC Bioinformatics, PubMed 17254353, PMC1796903). Full text checked at PMC (PMC1796903) for the Gini-specific finding, because the abstract itself does not use the word 'Gini' - it refers generically to 'random forest variable importance measures'. Lead reference was accurate; the only correction is that '25' is an article number, not a page number (BMC Bioinformatics is article-numbered, so there is no page range). The publisher landing page (biomedcentral.com -> link.springer.com) redirected to a cookie-authorisation endpoint and was not followed; Crossref (publisher-deposited metadata) was used instead.
references.caveats: The paper's evidence is from simulation studies and an RNA-editing bioinformatics application, not customer churn data, so the report should present it as a general methodological finding. The paper also shows that the permutation importance of the ORIGINAL randomForest (Breiman/CART) implementation is affected by the same two biases (variable selection bias plus bootstrap-with-replacement effects), so the claim should not be paraphrased as 'permutation importance alone fixes the problem' - the recommendation is specifically permutation importance computed on unbiased (conditional inference) trees with subsampling WITHOUT replacement. Cite Them Right formatting of article-numbered journals varies; '8(1), 25' is used here, with 25 being the article number.

authors: on behalf of Topic Group 'Evaluating diagnostic tests and prediction models' of the STRATOS initiative
references.title: Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics
references.harvard_reference: Van Calster, B., McLernon, D.J., van Smeden, M., Wynants, L. and Steyerberg, E.W. (2019) 'Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics', BMC Medicine, 17(1), 230. doi:10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7.
references.abstract_summary: A position/review paper from the STRATOS initiative topic group arguing that assessment of calibration (agreement between predicted risks and observed outcome frequencies) receives far too little attention compared with discrimination (AUC). The authors argue this must change because poorly calibrated algorithms, whether from regression or flexible machine learning methods, can be misleading and potentially harmful for decision-making. They describe a hierarchy of calibration (mean, weak, moderate, strong), recommend flexible calibration curves (loess/spline) over the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, discuss how to avoid poor calibration at development (balancing model complexity against sample size, penalisation), note that calibration curves at external validation need sufficiently large samples (roughly 200 events and 200 non-events), and recommend algorithm updating (intercept adjustment, slope recalibration, or full refitting) when miscalibration is found. The stated aim is to optimise the utility of predictive analytics for shared decision-making.

claims_supported.claim: Calibration is often neglected; poorly calibrated risk predictions can be misleading and harmful for decision making even when discrimination is good, so calibration should be assessed (e.g. calibration plots) and models recalibrated when necessary.
claims_supported.where: Neglect: Abstract (Background: calibration assessment 'receives little attention') and section 'Discrimination is important, but are the risk estimates reliable?' (systematic reviews find calibration is assessed far less often than discrimination). Misleading/harmful: Abstract (Main text: 'poorly calibrated algorithms can be misleading and potentially harmful for clinical decision-making') and section 'How can inaccurate risk predictions be misleading?'. Even when discrimination is good: same section states poor calibration may make an algorithm less useful than a competitor with a lower AUC that is well calibrated, illustrated by the QRISK2-2011 (AUC 0.771, well calibrated) vs NICE Framingham (AUC 0.776, overestimating risk) example. Calibration plots: section 'How to assess calibration?' recommends flexible calibration curves (loess/spline) and recommends against the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Recalibration: Abstract ('Algorithm updating should be considered'; Conclusion: 'update models when indicated') and section 'How to prevent or correct poor calibration?' (intercept updating for calibration-in-the-large, slope recalibration, full refitting when the validation sample is large).

references.verification_notes: DOI and metadata confirmed via Crossref (journal-article, BMC Medicine, vol 17, issue 1, article number 230, 2019). Abstract retrieved from Semantic Scholar (PubMed 31842878, PMC6912996). Full text checked via PubMed Central and Europe PMC, which allowed section-level verification of every component of the claim. Crossref and OpenAlex also list the STRATOS initiative topic group as a collective author; the Harvard reference uses the five named individual authors, which is standard practice. The article has an article number (230) rather than a page range; Cite Them Right style places the article number where pages would go. One caveat for the churn report: the paper's framing is clinical/medical ('clinical decision-making', 'patient counseling'); the general principles about calibration transfer directly to churn probability scoring, but the student should not imply the paper discusses churn or business decisions specifically.
references.caveats: Source is written for medical risk prediction; its harm argument is about clinical decisions and patient counselling. Applying it to telecom churn is a reasonable extension of the general principle but is the student's inference, not something the paper states. The paper also recommends against the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, so the report should not cite it in support of that test.

references.title: The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression
references.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
references.harvard_reference: van den Goorbergh, R., van Smeden, M., Timmerman, D. and Van Calster, B. (2022) 'The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression', Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 29(9), pp. 1525-1534. doi:10.1093/jamia/ocac093.
references.abstract_summary: Simulation study plus an ovarian-cancer case study examining how four approaches to class imbalance (no correction, random undersampling, random oversampling, SMOTE) affect standard and ridge logistic regression models, evaluated on discrimination, calibration and classification while varying training-set size, number of predictors and event fraction. Undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE produced poorly calibrated models in which the probability of belonging to the minority class was strongly overestimated, and they did not yield higher AUCs than uncorrected models. Although corrections improved the sensitivity/specificity balance, the same effect was obtained simply by shifting the probability threshold. The authors conclude that outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself and that imbalance correction may even worsen model performance, reducing clinical utility because treatment decisions are ill-informed by inaccurate probabilities.

claims_supported.claim: Imbalance corrections such as random undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE lead to strongly miscalibrated models that overestimate the probability of the minority class, without improving discrimination (AUC); they recommend against them for risk prediction models.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (Results): 'The use of random undersampling, random oversampling, or SMOTE yielded poorly calibrated models: the probability to belong to the minority class was strongly overestimated. These methods did not result in higher areas under the ROC curve when compared with models developed without correction for class imbalance.' Abstract (Conclusion): 'Outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself, imbalance correction may even worsen model performance.' Discussion (full text, PMC9382395): 'We therefore warn researchers for the limitations of imbalance corrections when developing a prediction model.' The title itself frames these corrections as harmful for risk prediction models. Note: the source's own wording is a warning/caution ('warn researchers', 'may even worsen model performance') rather than a formal sentence saying 'we recommend against'; phrasing such as 'caution against' or 'warn against' is the most faithful paraphrase. The findings are also specific to standard and ridge logistic regression (the authors' stated scope), so the report should not present them as demonstrated for all model classes.

references.verification_notes: Verified via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/jamia/ocac093), Semantic Scholar (DOI:10.1093/jamia/ocac093; PubMed 35686364; PMC9382395; arXiv 2202.09101) and the PMC full text. All fields in the lead were confirmed except the title, which the lead gave imprecisely as 'illustrated using logistic regression'; the correct title is '...illustration and simulation using logistic regression'. Author order and name capitalisation (van den Goorbergh, van Smeden, Timmerman, Van Calster) follow Crossref. Published online 10 June 2022; Crossref lists the print issue date as 16 August 2022 for volume 29, issue 9, pages 1525-1534; publisher Oxford University Press; ISSN 1527-974X. Claim 1 is supported by the abstract and discussion, with the caveat about wording ('warn' rather than 'recommend against') and scope (logistic regression) noted in the claim entry.
references.caveats: The study's empirical scope is logistic regression (standard and ridge) in a clinical risk-prediction setting, with Monte Carlo simulations and one ovarian-cancer case study; extrapolation to tree ensembles or gradient boosting on the Telco churn dataset should be presented as an inference, not a finding of this paper. The authors' conclusion is phrased as a warning about the limitations and potential harm of imbalance corrections rather than an explicit formal 'recommendation against'; the report should paraphrase accordingly (e.g. 'caution against'). Published online June 2022; issue dated 2022 (vol. 29, no. 9).

references.title: New insights into churn prediction in the telecommunication sector: A profit driven data mining approach
references.harvard_reference: Verbeke, W., Dejaeger, K., Martens, D., Hur, J. and Baesens, B. (2012) 'New insights into churn prediction in the telecommunication sector: a profit driven data mining approach', European Journal of Operational Research, 218(1), pp. 211-229. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2011.09.031.
references.abstract_summary: Churn models exist to cut the cost of attrition, yet are usually judged with statistical measures, which the authors argue leads to sub-optimal model selection. Part one develops a profit-centric performance measure: the maximum profit (MP) obtainable by targeting the optimal fraction of customers with the highest predicted churn probabilities in a retention campaign; this measure picks both the model and the fraction of customers to contact, and the authors report a significant profit gain relative to statistical measures. Part two is an extensive benchmark of many classification techniques on eleven real-life datasets from telecom operators worldwide, scored with both MP and statistical measures. Findings: a small number of variables suffices to predict churn with high accuracy; oversampling generally does not improve performance significantly; and a large group of classifiers yields comparable performance.

claims_supported.claim: Churn models should be evaluated on profit rather than accuracy or AUC alone; the maximum profit criterion can change model ranking.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (first part): statistically based measures give 'suboptimal model selection'; the MP measure 'selects the optimal model and fraction of customers to include, yielding a significant increase in profits compared to statistical measures'. Lead author's own summary of this study (Verbeke PhD thesis, KU Leuven Lirias, Chapter 4): applying the MP criterion 'leads to substantially different outcomes' versus top-decile lift/AUC and can have a profound impact on campaign profits. Section 3 of the paper introduces the MP measure; Section 5 reports results under MP, AUC and lift.

claims_supported.claim: In a benchmark across many telecom datasets, complex models did not consistently outperform simpler ones, and comprehensibility matters for practitioners.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (second part): benchmark of 'various classification techniques' on 'eleven real-life data sets from telecom operators worldwide'; 'a large group of classifiers is found to yield comparable performance'. Author's thesis summary of this chapter: Alternating Decision Trees had the best overall performance but 'a large number of other techniques were not significantly outperformed', so comprehensibility, justifiability and operational efficiency should drive technique choice; logistic regression, Naive Bayes, rule and tree learners are recommended as powerful yet comprehensible. Caveat: the paper does say technique choice significantly affects predictive power and that the top performer (ADT, a boosting-based tree) is not the simplest model, so phrase the claim as 'many techniques were statistically indistinguishable' rather than 'simple models won'.

claims_supported.claim: Oversampling did not generally improve performance in their benchmark.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (second part), verbatim finding: 'oversampling generally does not improve the performance significantly'. 'Oversampling' is also a paper keyword. Author's thesis summary adds nuance: the effect of oversampling depends on the dataset and technique and can be positive or negative, so it should be tested empirically in each case.

references.verification_notes: Metadata verified against Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.ejor.2011.09.031): journal-article, Elsevier BV, EJOR vol. 218 issue 1 pp. 211-229, print issue April 2012 (first online 26 Sept 2011, which is why OpenAlex/Unpaywall list 2011; cite as 2012 per the printed issue and Crossref 'issued'). Author names confirmed by Crossref and KU Leuven Lirias (handle 123456789/316841); Semantic Scholar renders 'Hur' as 'Joonyoung Hur' and OpenAlex as 'Joon Moo Hur' but the article byline is 'Joon Hur'. ISSN 0377-2217 / eISSN 1872-6860. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex return no abstract (publisher-elided); RePEc/IDEAS/EconPapers carry only the first paragraph. The complete two-paragraph abstract was retrieved verbatim from the KU Leuven Lirias DSpace record. Paper keywords (from RePEc): Data mining; Churn prediction; Profit; Input selection; Oversampling; Telecommunication sector. Full text is paywalled (ScienceDirect 403, no open-access copy via Unpaywall or Lirias), so section-level checks rest on the full abstract plus the lead author's summary of this exact study in his KU Leuven PhD thesis record (also on Lirias). Google Scholar/S2 citation count approx. 465 (S2), Crossref 375.
references.caveats: Claim 1: the abstract establishes that MP selects a different (better-profit) model than statistical measures; the specific wording 'changes model ranking' is consistent with this and with the author's summary but was not checked against a results table in the paywalled full text. Claim 2: the benchmark's best single technique was Alternating Decision Trees (not a simple model); the defensible statement is that a large group of techniques, including logistic regression and Naive Bayes, was not significantly outperformed, and that the authors argue comprehensibility should therefore inform technique choice. Claim 3: fully supported by the abstract, but the authors' fuller conclusion is that oversampling's effect is dataset- and technique-dependent and should be tested empirically. The lead may be cited with the truncated title 'a profit driven data mining approach' but the published title capitalises 'A'; either is acceptable in Harvard style with sentence-case titles. The publication year 2012 is correct despite some databases giving 2011.

references.title: A novel profit maximizing metric for measuring classification performance of customer churn prediction models
references.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
references.harvard_reference: Verbraken, T., Verbeke, W. and Baesens, B. (2013) 'A novel profit maximizing metric for measuring classification performance of customer churn prediction models', IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 25(5), pp. 961-973. doi:10.1109/TKDE.2012.50.
references.abstract_summary: The paper formalises a cost-benefit analysis framework for defining classifier performance measures that are aligned with the end user's objective of profit maximisation, and defines a new measure, the expected maximum profit (EMP) criterion. The general framework is then applied to customer churn prediction with its particular cost-benefit structure (customer lifetime value, cost of the retention offer, cost of contact, and the probability that a targeted would-be churner accepts the offer, the latter modelled with a beta distribution). The authors argue the measure lets companies select the classifier that maximises profit and, as a practical by-product, gives guidance on the fraction of the customer base that should be included in a retention campaign.

claims_supported.claim: The expected maximum profit (EMP) measure evaluates churn classifiers by expected profit, incorporating offer cost, customer lifetime value and probability of acceptance, and determines the optimal fraction of customers to target.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (via OpenAlex, verbatim): defines 'the expected maximum profit criterion', applies it to churn 'with its particular cost-benefit structure', states it 'assists companies with selecting the classifier which maximizes the profit' and 'provides guidance about the fraction of the customer base that should be included in retention campaign'. The specific parameters (CLV per retained customer, retention-offer cost d, contact cost f, acceptance probability gamma ~ Beta(6,14)) and the profit-maximising fraction eta are the paper's churn profit function (its eqs for P_C(t; gamma, CLV, delta, phi), MPC and EMPC), as reproduced with attribution to Verbraken et al. (2013) in Hoppner et al., arXiv:1712.08101, Section 2, eqs (14)-(18), and exposed as the alpha/beta/clv/d/f arguments and EMPfrac output of the CRAN 'EMP' R package co-authored by Verbraken. Note the model also includes a contact cost, which the claim omits but does not contradict.

references.verification_notes: DOI 10.1109/TKDE.2012.50 verified via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/<doi>): authors Thomas Verbraken, Wouter Verbeke, Bart Baesens; container IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering; vol. 25, issue 5, pp. 961-973; publisher IEEE; issued 2013. doi.org resolves (302) to ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6165289. Semantic Scholar (DOI lookup) confirms title, venue, year 2013 and authors but withholds the abstract; the abstract was reconstructed verbatim from OpenAlex's abstract_inverted_index. OpenAlex and the Edinburgh Research Explorer record give 2012 because the article appeared online (early access) on 2012-03-06; the print issue (25(5)) is May 2013, so 2013 is used in the reference, matching Crossref and how the paper is normally cited (e.g. in the CRAN EMP package citation). The full text is paywalled (IEEE Xplore page is JavaScript-rendered; Southampton ePrints 336464 and CORE returned 403; no open-access PDF listed by Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex), so the claim's parameter details were checked against two secondary sources that reproduce the paper's formulas with explicit attribution: Hoppner, Stripling, Baesens, vanden Broucke and Verdonck, 'Profit driven decision trees for churn prediction' (arXiv:1712.08101, later EJOR 2020) and the CRAN EMP package documentation (Bravo, vanden Broucke and Verbraken). Crossref's query.bibliographic endpoint returned HTTP 429 on the first attempt; the direct DOI endpoint succeeded.
references.caveats: Year is 2013 (print issue) although some databases list 2012 (online-first date 2012-03-06). Full text not accessed directly; the abstract supports the general claim and the specific parameters were confirmed through secondary sources that quote the paper. The EMP churn model also includes a cost of contact (f) alongside offer cost, CLV and acceptance probability; the report should not imply the list in the claim is exhaustive.

references.title: Nonparametric estimation from cross-sectional survival data
references.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
references.harvard_reference: Wang, M.-C. (1991) 'Nonparametric estimation from cross-sectional survival data', Journal of the American Statistical Association, 86(413), pp. 130–143. doi:10.1080/01621459.1991.10475011.
references.abstract_summary: Wang considers follow-up studies in which survival data are gathered by cross-sectional sampling, so that the observations are left-truncated as well as right-censored. The paper revisits the product-limit estimate for left-truncated, right-censored data as a conditional maximum-likelihood estimate; derives the nonparametric MLE of the truncation distribution, with uses including testing the stationarity assumption and estimating the proportion of truncated data in prevalent cohort studies; develops asymptotic results through nonparametric score functions; derives the nonparametric MLE of the joint distribution of truncation and censoring variables; and uses these estimates to extend Efron's simple bootstrap for right-censored data to data that are both left-truncated and right-censored.

claims_supported.claim: Survival data collected by cross-sectional sampling (a snapshot of current customers) are left-truncated as well as right-censored.
claims_supported.where: Abstract, opening sentences (OpenAlex W2103527136, the publisher abstract): the paper states that follow-up data gathered by cross-sectional sampling are left-truncated as well as right-censored. Independently corroborated by the zbMATH Open review Zbl 0739.62026 (reviewer B. K. Kale), which describes the setting the same way.

references.verification_notes: Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/01621459.1991.10475011): type journal-article; title 'Nonparametric Estimation from Cross-Sectional Survival Data'; sole author Mei-Cheng Wang; Journal of the American Statistical Association, vol. 86, issue 413, pp. 130-143; issued March 1991; publisher Informa UK Limited (Taylor & Francis); no abstract deposited. Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 123323004, MAG 2103527136) gives JASA 86, pp. 130-143, abstract elided by the publisher. OpenAlex W2103527136 matches (published 1991-03-01, vol. 86, issue 413) and supplies the abstract. zbMATH Open (Zbl 0739.62026, via api.zbmath.org) records the JSTOR DOI 10.2307/2289722, MSC 62G05/62G20/62G09 and a reviewer summary consistent with the abstract. The Taylor & Francis landing page returned HTTP 403 and JSTOR failed to load, so the full text was not read. JASA is the peer-reviewed journal of the American Statistical Association, not a predatory venue. Title given in sentence case per Cite Them Right. Checked again by an independent critic on 31 October 2026: Kaplan and Meier (1958), abstract via https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452: observing each item's initial event is presupposed, and the PL estimate is defined for random samples. Wang (1991) is verified: Crossref gives JASA 86(413), pp. 130-143, March 1991, and the OpenAlex abstract (https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1080/01621459.1991.10475011) says cross-sectionally sampled survival data are left-truncated as well as right-censored. src/eda.py fits the lifelines KM (lines 100-101) and Cox (129-130) models with no entry times. results/km_contract.json gives S(12) = 0.703, which implies 2.9% a month (1 - 0.703^(1/12)). churn_by_category.csv gives 42.7% month-to-month churn in one window, so the clash holds whether the window is a month or a quarter. The contract ordering matches 2.8%, 11.3% and 42.7%. 'Overstate retention' rests on the report's own numbers, not on Wang's abstract, which is how the sentence is built. Cox (1972) stays cited in Table 1. Word delta -3 raw and counted (Part 2 486 to 483, inside ±5%). No new numbers; the number-check simulation finds 0 unmatched.
references.caveats: 1) The paper's motivating applications are prevalent-cohort (biomedical) studies, not customer churn; applying it to the Telco snapshot is the report's own step. 2) The abstract does not state that a naive Kaplan-Meier fit overstates survival; in the report that conclusion rests on the 70.3% versus 42.7% inconsistency in results/, not on Wang. 3) A left-truncation correction needs each subject's entry (truncation) time; for the Telco file that depends on the label window, which IBM's documentation describes both as a month and as a quarter. 4) Only the abstract and an independent review were checked, not the full text. 5) The JSTOR DOI 10.2307/2289722 is an alternative identifier for the same article; cite the Taylor & Francis DOI.

references.title: Fairlearn: Assessing and Improving Fairness of AI Systems
references.harvard_reference: Weerts, H., Dudík, M., Edgar, R., Jalali, A., Lutz, R. and Madaio, M. (2023) 'Fairlearn: assessing and improving fairness of AI systems', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24(257), pp. 1-8. Available at: https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
references.abstract_summary: An eight-page JMLR 'Machine Learning Open Source Software' paper by the current maintainers of Fairlearn (Eindhoven University of Technology and Microsoft). Fairlearn is an MIT-licensed open-source project (started at Microsoft in 2018, under independent governance since 2021) consisting of the Python library fairlearn plus learning resources. The abstract states that the library supports evaluation of a model's output across affected populations and includes several algorithms for mitigating fairness issues, and that the project treats fairness as a sociotechnical challenge. Section 2 (Fairness Assessment) describes disaggregated evaluation via the MetricFrame class in fairlearn.metrics (metric functions plus y_true, y_pred and sensitive_features; results returned as pandas Series/DataFrame; group comparison by differences or ratios), scalar fairness metrics such as demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference (derived from a MetricFrame), make_derived_metric, and plot_model_comparison. Section 3 covers mitigation algorithms: preprocessing (CorrelationRemover), reductions-based in-processing (ExponentiatedGradient, GridSearch, following Agarwal et al. 2018), adversarial mitigation, and postprocessing (ThresholdOptimizer, following Hardt et al. 2016), all with scikit-learn-compatible APIs. Section 4 describes the learning resources (user guide, example notebooks) that encourage practitioners to consider a system's broader societal context rather than treating fairness metrics as a purely technical fix.

claims_supported.claim: Fairlearn provides MetricFrame for disaggregated metrics by sensitive feature and standard group-fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equalised odds differences.
claims_supported.where: Section 2, 'Fairness Assessment', p. 2 of the JMLR PDF. Paragraph 'MetricFrame class': 'The primary tool for disaggregated evaluation in the fairlearn library is the MetricFrame class in the fairlearn.metrics module ... MetricFrame is initialized by providing one or more metric functions together with input arrays y_true, y_pred, and sensitive_features ... the sensitive_features array is used to split the data into slices for disaggregated evaluation. Once a MetricFrame is constructed, the disaggregated metrics can be accessed as a pandas Series ... or a pandas DataFrame ... MetricFrame also enables a comparison of metric values across groups, for example, in terms of differences or ratios.' Paragraph 'Fairness Metrics': 'functions demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference quantify how much the predictions of a given classifier depart from the fairness criteria known as demographic parity and equalized odds (see, e.g., Hardt et al., 2016). These two metrics are derived from a MetricFrame with a specific choice of input arguments.' Every element of the claim (MetricFrame, disaggregation by sensitive feature, demographic parity difference, equalized odds difference) is stated explicitly in the paper's own text, not merely in the documentation.

references.verification_notes: Crossref query.bibliographic did NOT return this paper (only unrelated Packt book chapters and an IEEE paper), which is expected because JMLR does not register Crossref DOIs for its articles; the doi field is therefore left empty rather than invented. The article was verified directly on the publisher's site: the JMLR landing page https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.html gives the title, the six authors in order (Hilde Weerts, Miroslav Dudík, Richard Edgar, Adrin Jalali, Roman Lutz, Michael Madaio), the citation '24(257):1-8, 2023' and the abstract; the JMLR BibTeX file (https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.bib) confirms journal, year 2023, volume 24, number 257, pages 1--8. The official PDF (https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume24/23-0389/23-0389.pdf, 8 pages) was downloaded and its text extracted; the header reads 'Journal of Machine Learning Research 24 (2023) 1-8 Submitted 3/23; Published 7/23', editor Alexandre Gramfort, affiliations Eindhoven University of Technology (Weerts) and Microsoft (Dudík, Edgar, Lutz, Madaio; Madaio's listed e-mail is at google.com). The claim was checked against the extracted full text of Section 2. OpenAlex (W4361806824) indexes the work as JMLR vol. 24, issue 257, 2023, with the same six authors, but the only DOI it attaches is the arXiv/DataCite DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2303.16626, which belongs to the preprint (arXiv:2303.16626, submitted 29 March 2023, verified on arxiv.org) rather than to the JMLR version; hence the Harvard reference uses the JMLR URL with an access date, per Cite Them Right for online articles without a DOI. The earlier work mentioned in the lead is confirmed by the paper's own reference list and footnote 3: Bird, S., Dudík, M., Edgar, R., Horn, B., Lutz, R., Milan, V., Sameki, M., Wallach, H. and Walker, K. (2020) Fairlearn: a toolkit for assessing and improving fairness in AI, Technical Report MSR-TR-2020-32, Microsoft, May 2020, https://aka.ms/fairlearn-whitepaper (also indexed by OpenAlex as W3030081171). The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 and was not used. The lead's metadata was accurate apart from omitting the page range (pp. 1-8).
references.caveats: This is a short software paper, not an empirical study on churn or telecom data; cite it for what the Fairlearn library provides (MetricFrame, fairness metrics, mitigation algorithms), not for any finding about fairness in churn models. The paper describes the API as of 2023 (fairlearn ~0.8); function names such as demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference match the current library, but any specific version-dependent behaviour should be cited to the Fairlearn documentation. The paper's own framing (Section 4) cautions against treating fairness metrics as a purely technical fix, which the report should reflect when interpreting parity gaps on the Telco dataset (e.g. by SeniorCitizen or gender). If the report also cites the 2020 Microsoft technical report (Bird et al., 2020), that is a separate grey-literature reference (MSR-TR-2020-32) and should be listed separately.

references.title: Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates
references.venue: Proceedings of the eighth ACM SIGKDD international conference on Knowledge discovery and data mining (KDD '02), Edmonton, Alberta, Canada
references.harvard_reference: Zadrozny, B. and Elkan, C. (2002) 'Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates', in Proceedings of the eighth ACM SIGKDD international conference on knowledge discovery and data mining (KDD '02). Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. New York: ACM, pp. 694-699. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1145/775047.775151.
references.abstract_summary: Argues that many data-mining applications need accurate class-membership probabilities (e.g. for example-dependent misclassification costs or combining with other classifiers), and that earlier calibration methods only handled two-class problems. The paper (i) proposes a new two-class calibration method, isotonic regression computed with the pair-adjacent violators (PAV) algorithm, applicable to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples, and (ii) shows how to obtain multiclass probability estimates by calibrating and then combining binary estimates (normalisation, least-squares, coupling). Experiments use naive Bayes, SVM and boosted naive Bayes on direct marketing (KDD-98), Adult, text categorisation (20 Newsgroups) and digit recognition (Pendigits); PAV-calibrated scores give lower MSE (and higher profit on KDD-98) than raw scores and are comparable to or better than sigmoid fitting and binning.

claims_supported.claim: Isotonic regression (pair-adjacent violators) can calibrate classifier scores into accurate probability estimates and is applicable to boosted and naive Bayes models.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (new calibration method 'can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples'; experiments with naive Bayes and SVM); Section 3 (isotonic regression proposed as intermediary between sigmoid fitting and binning, computed with the pair-adjacent violators (PAV) algorithm; Figure 5 applies PAV to naive Bayes and SVM scores on Adult); Section 5.1, Tables 1-3 (PAV naive Bayes improves MSE/profit over raw NB); Section 5.2, Tables 4-5 (naive Bayes and boosted naive Bayes used as binary learners on Pendigits, calibrated with PAV, lowering MSE and error rate); Section 6 Conclusions (recommends PAV for two-class calibration). Caveat: 'boosted' in this paper means boosted naive Bayes (Elkan's boosting of NB), not boosted decision trees/gradient boosting such as XGBoost; do not cite it as evidence for calibrating gradient-boosted trees.

references.verification_notes: Metadata confirmed via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/775047.775151): authors Bianca Zadrozny and Charles Elkan (UC San Diego); title as given; container 'Proceedings of the eighth ACM SIGKDD international conference on Knowledge discovery and data mining'; event KDD02, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada; publisher ACM, New York, NY, USA; published 23 July 2002; pages 694-699; type proceedings-article; no volume or issue (left empty, not applicable to this proceedings). OpenAlex confirmed same metadata and supplied the abstract; Semantic Scholar confirmed title/year/venue/authors (abstract elided there; DBLP conf/kdd/ZadroznyE02). Full text was read from a PDF copy (cs.columbia.edu course handout) whose copyright notice gives 'SIGKDD '02 Edmonton, Alberta, Canada' and ISBN 1-58113-567-X. Peer-reviewed ACM SIGKDD conference paper; not predatory. Conference day-range not given by Crossref, so it was omitted from the reference. Note the paper uses the name 'pair-adjacent violators'; the algorithm is also widely called 'pool-adjacent violators'. Claim 1 is supported, with the caveat that the boosted model evaluated is boosted naive Bayes only (multiclass Pendigits experiments), and the two-class experiments use naive Bayes and SVM.

legal.status_summary: The current BCS Code of Conduct is 'Code of Conduct for BCS Members', issued as Schedule 3 to the BCS Trustee Board Regulations, Version 8. The members'-area control sheet records: Responsible Body Trustee Board; Version 8; Date Approved 2 February 2022 (Trustee Board paper TB/2022/007 Appendix 3); Date Issued 4 February 2022; Date of last review 4 June 2025 (version number unchanged). The public PDF on bcs.org is headed 'Version 8 last reviewed and approved by Trustee Board 8 June 2022'. The public web page ('BCS Code of Conduct for members - Ethics for IT professionals') carries the same four sections and clause wording as v8 but no version or date. The Code is not legislation and is not amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; it binds BCS members contractually via Bye-law 18(a) of the BCS Bye-laws (as amended by Order in Council 8 June 2022), which requires members at all times to act in accordance with the Code of Conduct, and breaches are handled under the Institute's disciplinary procedures (Trustee Board Regulations Section VIII). The Code has four sections: 1 Public Interest (clauses a-d); 2 Professional Competence and Integrity (a-g); 3 Duty to Relevant Authority (a-e); 4 Duty to the Profession (a-e), plus Appendix 1 (interpretation and definitions of 'Legislation', 'Third Parties' and 'Relevant Authority'). A Code of Conduct Review Working Group (Terms of Reference, 2024) reviews the Code annually and recommends changes via the Community Board to the Trustee Board; no Version 9 or later revision was found as at 2026-09-28.
legal.in_force: Yes. Version 8 is the current and operative version as at 2026-09-28 (approved 2 February 2022, issued 4 February 2022, last reviewed by Trustee Board 4 June 2025 with no change of version). It is a professional-body code binding on BCS members as a condition of membership (Bye-law 18(a)), not a statutory instrument, so 'commencement' does not apply and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 does not amend it.

current_version.title: Code of Conduct for BCS Members (Trustee Board Regulations Schedule 3, Version 8)
current_version.publisher: BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT
current_version.public_pdf_header_date: Version 8 last reviewed and approved by Trustee Board 8 June 2022

four_sections.heading: Public Interest
four_sections.paraphrase: Members must have due regard for public health, privacy, security and the wellbeing of others and the environment; respect the legitimate rights of Third Parties; carry out professional activities without discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation, marital status, nationality, colour, race, ethnic origin, religion, age or disability; and promote equal access to the benefits of IT and inclusion of all sectors of society.

four_sections.heading: Professional Competence and Integrity
four_sections.paraphrase: Members must only undertake work within their professional competence; not claim competence they do not possess; keep knowledge, skills and competence up to date; know and comply with applicable Legislation when carrying out professional responsibilities; respect alternative viewpoints and seek, accept and offer honest criticism of work; avoid injuring others (property, reputation, employment) by false, malicious or negligent action or inaction; and reject and never offer bribery or unethical inducement.

four_sections.heading: Duty to Relevant Authority
four_sections.paraphrase: Members must carry out responsibilities with due care and diligence to the Relevant Authority's requirements while exercising professional judgement; avoid conflicts of interest with the Relevant Authority; accept professional responsibility for their own work and that of people under their supervision; not disclose or misuse confidential information without permission (or unless required by Legislation); and not misrepresent or withhold information on the performance of products, systems or services, nor exploit others' lack of knowledge or inexperience.

four_sections.heading: Duty to the Profession
four_sections.paraphrase: Members must uphold the reputation of the profession and avoid bringing it into disrepute; seek to improve professional standards through participation in their development, use and enforcement; uphold the reputation and good standing of BCS; act with integrity and respect towards BCS members and members of other professions; and encourage and support fellow members' professional development.
