key_points: Current version: 'Code of Conduct for BCS Members', Trustee Board Regulations Schedule 3, Version 8. Approved by Trustee Board 2 February 2022 (TB/2022/007 Appendix 3), issued 4 February 2022; the public bcs.org PDF is headed 'Version 8 last reviewed and approved by Trustee Board 8 June 2022'; the members'-area control copy records a further review on 4 June 2025 with the version number unchanged.

Cite the public PDF URL https://www.bcs.org/media/2211/bcs-code-of-conduct.pdf (5 pages) and/or the web page https://www.bcs.org/membership-and-registrations/become-a-member/bcs-code-of-conduct/. The web page carries the same four headings and clause wording as v8 but shows no version number or date.

Warning: the mirror URL https://cdn.bcs.org/bcs-org-media/2211/bcs-code-of-conduct.pdf (same path on the CDN host) serves an OUTDATED Version 5 (approved 3 June 2015, last reviewed 5 June 2019), which still contains a former clause 4(e) requiring members to notify BCS of criminal convictions, bankruptcy or director disqualification. That clause was removed in Version 7 (Trustee Board 9 June 2021, on legal advice of 16 April 2021). Do not cite the cdn.bcs.org copy.

Version 8 changes (2 February 2022) were to Appendix 1 only, following the Engineering Council Licence Review 2021: added guidance to assess the need for and hold appropriate indemnity insurance, and to support a colleague or other person who in good faith raises concerns about danger, risk, malpractice or wrongdoing (whistleblowing).

Structure: introduction; breaches section; scope statement (applies to all members regardless of grade, role or jurisdiction; governs the individual's conduct, not the ethics of the Relevant Authority); four numbered sections with lettered clauses; Appendix 1 (interpretation) including definitions of 'Legislation' (any applicable laws, statutes and regulations), 'Third Parties' and 'Relevant Authority' (normally employer or client; for student members normally the academic institution).

Section 1 Public Interest (a-d): due regard for public health, privacy, security, wellbeing and the environment; legitimate rights of Third Parties; non-discrimination across protected characteristics; promotion of equal access to IT and inclusion.

Section 2 Professional Competence and Integrity (a-g): work only within competence; do not overclaim competence; continuing professional development; know and comply with applicable Legislation; respect alternative viewpoints and honest criticism; avoid injuring others by false, malicious or negligent action or inaction; reject bribery and unethical inducements.

Section 3 Duty to Relevant Authority (a-e): due care and diligence with professional judgement; avoid conflicts of interest; accept responsibility for own and supervised work; keep confidential information confidential (save with permission or as required by Legislation); do not misrepresent or withhold information on performance of products, systems or services, nor exploit others' inexperience.

Section 4 Duty to the Profession (a-e): uphold the profession's reputation; improve professional standards; uphold BCS's reputation and standing; act with integrity and respect towards BCS members and other professionals; encourage and support fellow members' development.

Legal basis: Bye-law 18(a) of the BCS Bye-laws (as amended by Order in Council 8 June 2022) obliges all members to safeguard the public interest and act at all times in accordance with the Code of Conduct; Bye-law 18(b)-(c) require the Trustee Board to make disciplinary and appeal regulations. The Bye-laws define 'Code of Conduct' as the code for members approved and prescribed by the Trustee Board from time to time. Breaches are considered under the Institute's disciplinary procedures (Trustee Board Regulations Section VIII) and can result in expulsion from membership; the web page invites reports of breaches to customerservice@bcs.uk.

Currency mechanism: the Community Board must review the Code annually; the Code of Conduct Review Working Group (ToR copyright 2024) benchmarks it against the Engineering Council's Statement of Ethical Principles, legal and regulatory requirements and member feedback, and submits recommendations via the Community Board and Registration and Standards Committee to the Trustee Board. As at 2026-09-28 no Version 9 or post-2025 revision was located on bcs.org.

Relationship to legislation: the Code is not a statute and is not amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Its relevance to a churn-prediction project is indirect: clause 2(d) requires members to know and comply with applicable Legislation (for personal-data processing that means UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, plus PECR for marketing contact), clause 1(a) requires due regard for privacy and security, clause 1(c) prohibits discriminatory professional conduct (relevant to model fairness), clause 3(d) protects confidential customer data, and clause 3(e) prohibits misrepresenting the performance of systems (relevant to honest reporting of model metrics).
legal.quotable: Clause 1(a) requires members to "have due regard for public health, privacy, security and wellbeing of others" (BCS, 2022, s.1(a)).
legal.uncertainties: 1) Two dates circulate for Version 8: the public bcs.org PDF header states 'last reviewed and approved by Trustee Board 8 June 2022', whereas the members'-area control sheet records approval on 2 February 2022, issue on 4 February 2022 and a last review on 4 June 2025; all refer to the same Version 8 text, so the safest citation is 'version 8, 2022' with the public PDF URL, noting the 2025 review. 2) The members'-area copy (mybcs.bcs.org) is marked 'Confidential to BCS Members' though it was openly retrievable without login; prefer the public PDF for citation and treat the mybcs copy as corroboration. 3) The cdn.bcs.org mirror of the same path serves an obsolete Version 5 (2015/2019); search engines index it under the current title, so anyone citing from it would reproduce a removed clause. 4) The public web page has no version or date, so a citation to it should be '(no date)' and paired with the dated PDF. 5) The Code is reviewed annually (typically at the Trustee Board's June meeting); a June 2026 review could have occurred, but no evidence of any change or a Version 9 was found on bcs.org as at 2026-09-28. 6) The disciplinary regulations themselves (Trustee Board Regulations Section VIII) were not retrieved; the summary of enforcement relies on the Code's own breaches section, Bye-law 18 and the breach web page.

legal.status_summary: Verified on 2026-09-28 against gov.uk, legislation.gov.uk, ofcom.org.uk and the Citizens Advice primary document. Citizens Advice submitted the super-complaint 'Excessive prices for disengaged consumers: A super-complaint to the Competition and Markets Authority' under s.11 Enterprise Act 2002; the CMA records it as received on 28 September 2018 (the Citizens Advice page is dated 27 September 2018). It estimated a loyalty penalty of GBP 4.1bn a year (table total GBP 4,122,000,000) across mobile (handset-inclusive), broadband, home insurance, mortgages and savings. The CMA published 'Tackling the loyalty penalty: Response to a super-complaint made by Citizens Advice on 28 September 2018' on 19 December 2018, putting the penalty at around GBP 4bn a year, including 'nearly GBP 1 billion in broadband and GBP 0.3 billion in mobile (for handset inclusive contracts)', and making 8 cross-market recommendations plus market-specific recommendations to Ofcom and the FCA. The CMA published progress updates on 19 June 2019, 21 January 2020, 13 July 2020 and 1 December 2020. The gov.uk case page shows 'Case state: Closed', last updated 1 December 2020, and no later CMA loyalty-penalty update was found. In telecoms, Ofcom's statement of 15 May 2019 introduced end-of-contract notifications (ECNs) and annual best tariff information/notifications (ABTNs), in force from 15 February 2020. They remain in force today, renumbered, as General Conditions C1.21-C1.29 (ECN) and C1.30-C1.36 (ABTN) in the consolidated General Conditions with effect from 8 April 2026. The 10-40 day timing now sits in Ofcom's January 2025 C1 guidance rather than in the condition text. Ofcom also secured voluntary out-of-contract pricing commitments from mobile providers in July 2019 (all major providers except Three) and from broadband providers in September 2019 and July 2020. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 does not amend any of these instruments. Its Part 1 smart-data powers (in force 20 August 2025) and the DMCC Act 2024's CMA direct-enforcement powers (in force 6 April 2025) act on two of the CMA's 2018 recommendations.
legal.in_force: Mixed: policy documents plus regulatory conditions that are in force. (1) The Citizens Advice super-complaint, the CMA response of 19 December 2018 and the CMA updates (June 2019 to December 2020) are policy and regulatory publications, not legislation. The CMA case is recorded as 'Closed' (last updated 1 December 2020). (2) The statutory basis, Enterprise Act 2002 s.11 (super-complaints; 90-day CMA response duty), is in force in its latest revised form, and legislation.gov.uk lists no outstanding effects. (3) Ofcom's ECN and ABTN rules were made by the 15 May 2019 statement and took effect on 15 February 2020. They are IN FORCE as General Conditions C1.21-C1.29 and C1.30-C1.36 (consolidated version with effect from 8 April 2026). The ABTN scope was changed by Ofcom's EECC statement of 27 October 2020. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 does not affect them. (4) The 2019-2020 provider pricing commitments were voluntary, not legal obligations. (5) Related legislation: DMCC Act 2024 Part 3 (CMA direct consumer enforcement and fines) and Part 4 Chapter 1 have been in force since 6 April 2025 (SI 2025/272). DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Chapter 2 (subscription contracts) is NOT yet in force. Government has announced commencement in January 2027 (No 10 press release, 9 August 2026), but no commencement regulations were identified. Once in force, Sch. 22 para 5 will exclude contracts bound by Ofcom general conditions from the regime. (6) Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 Part 1 (smart data) has been in force since 20 August 2025 (SI 2025/904). No telecoms smart-data scheme regulations were identified as of 28 September 2026.

key_points: SUPER-COMPLAINT (Citizens Advice, 2018): 'Excessive prices for disengaged consumers: A super-complaint to the Competition and Markets Authority', made under s.11 Enterprise Act 2002. The CMA records receipt on 28 September 2018 and its press release 'CMA to investigate 'loyalty penalty' super-complaint' is dated the same day. The s.11 duty requires a published response within 90 days. The five markets were mobile (handset-inclusive), broadband, home insurance, mortgages and savings. Headline estimate: GBP 4.1bn a year (Table 3 total GBP 4,122,000,000). Polling: 8 in 10 bill-payers pay a loyalty penalty in at least one market (mobile 34%, broadband 43%). A household paying it in all five markets pays up to GBP 877 a year more.

CITIZENS ADVICE TELECOMS FIGURES: mobile handset contracts: 3,965,000 adults, GBP 473.3m a year, GBP 264 per person per year. Broadband: 11,300,000 households, GBP 1,277m a year, GBP 113 per household per year.

CMA RESPONSE (19 December 2018): 'Tackling the loyalty penalty: Response to a super-complaint made by Citizens Advice on 28 September 2018', with a gov.uk executive summary and the press release 'CMA tackles loyalty penalty charges'. The CMA put the penalty at around GBP 4bn a year across the five markets: nearly GBP 1bn in broadband, GBP 0.3bn in mobile (handset-inclusive), GBP 1.1bn in savings, GBP 0.7bn in home insurance and GBP 0.8bn in mortgages. The number of people paying it ranged from under 1 million (mortgages) to over 12 million (home insurance).

CMA TABLE 4.1, TELECOMS: Mobile (handset-inclusive): Ofcom 2018 estimate of 1.5 million people (6%), GBP 330m a year, GBP 222 average; Citizens Advice estimate of 4 million (34%), GBP 473m, GBP 264. Broadband: CMA calculations of 8.7 million (37% of dual-play and 41% of triple-play customers), GBP 990m a year, GBP 112 average (GBP 72 dual-play, GBP 156 triple-play); Citizens Advice estimate of 11 million (43%), printed as 'GBP 1,1280 million', GBP 113. The CMA judged the Citizens Advice mobile estimate implausible, because Ofcom data showed only about 3.7 million handset-inclusive customers beyond their initial contract period at all.

CMA RECOMMENDATIONS (December 2018). Eight cross-market reforms: (1) bolder enforcement against harmful practices; (2) legislative change and CMA power to impose substantial fines; (3) publish the size of the loyalty penalty by market and supplier; (4) empower intermediaries; (5) press ahead with Smart Data, especially in telecoms; (6) share evidence on 'nudge' remedies; (7) targeted pricing interventions or caps where there is clear harm; (8) match price data to large surveys. Mobile (to Ofcom): providers should not keep charging the same rate once the handset is effectively paid off, and bundled customers should be moved to a fairer tariff at the end of the minimum period; raise SIM-only awareness. Broadband (to Ofcom): consider pricing interventions, including tackling legacy pricing and targeted safeguard caps for vulnerable consumers, plus smart data and collective switching.

GOVERNMENT RESPONSE: 'Competition and Markets Authority loyalty penalty investigation report: government response' (BEIS, 18 June 2019), a letter from Greg Clark to Andrea Coscelli. It accepted the roughly GBP 4bn estimate. It committed to legislate so the CMA can decide consumer-law breaches and impose fines directly, and to consider tackling subscription traps. On telecoms it agreed that charging the same price after a handset is paid off 'is not right' and backed a telecoms smart-data initiative.

CMA FOLLOW-UP (gov.uk case page): Loyalty Penalty Working Group terms of reference, 12 March 2019. 6-month update 'Loyalty penalty update: getting better and fairer deals', 19 June 2019. 12-month update 'January 2020: Loyalty Penalty Update', 21 January 2020, with news story 'CMA publishes loyalty penalty update'. 'July 2020: Loyalty Penalty Update', 13 July 2020 (progress affected by COVID-19). 'Loyalty penalty update - progress two years on from the CMA's super-complaint investigation', 1 December 2020, published with E.CA economic research on loyalty price discrimination. The case is 'Closed' and was last updated 1 December 2020.

CMA JANUARY 2020 UPDATE, TELECOMS. Mobile (citing Ofcom July 2019): of 2 million out-of-contract bundled customers, about 1.4 million would save an average GBP 11 a month on a cheaper SIM-only deal, while about 600,000 would pay about GBP 6 a month more. Voluntary commitments from all major providers except Three take effect from February 2020: Virgin Mobile, Tesco Mobile and O2 (direct customers) move to the equivalent 30-day or best airtime deal; EE gives 10% off and Vodafone GBP 5 off after 3 months out of contract. Broadband (citing Ofcom September 2019): about 8.8 million out-of-contract customers (41%), of whom 1.5 million are potentially vulnerable.

CMA DECEMBER 2020 (TWO YEARS ON) UPDATE: Ofcom and the FCA together estimated that more than 28 million customers were paying a loyalty penalty of GBP 3.4bn (with possible double counting). Broadband: out-of-contract customers (about 40%) paid just under GBP 500m a year more than their provider's average price for the same service. Commitments could benefit out-of-contract customers by over GBP 270m a year, and about 1 million vulnerable customers by about GBP 70 each. Mobile: Ofcom estimated the commitments cover 80% of the harm; the CMA remained 'significantly concerned' that Three had not engaged. The CMA welcomed the ECN rules in force from February 2020 and the proposed Open Communications (smart data) scheme.

OFCOM END-OF-CONTRACT NOTIFICATIONS: consultation 14 December 2018 (closed 1 February 2019), then the statement 'Helping consumers get better deals: Statement on end-of-contract notifications and annual best tariff information' (15 May 2019), in effect 15 February 2020 after a nine-month implementation period. Broadband, mobile, home phone and pay-TV providers must notify residential and business customers before the minimum contract period ends; residential customers receive a standalone notice 10-40 days before. The notice gives the end date, current and post-contract prices, notice period, and the provider's best tariffs, including at least one SIM-only deal for bundled handset customers and new-customer prices. Out-of-contract customers receive best tariff information at least annually.

OFCOM NEWS 14 FEBRUARY 2020 ('Companies must tell customers about their best deals'): about 20 million customers were out of contract, including 8.8 million broadband customers, with about 25,000 broadband customers reaching contract end each day. Out-of-contract broadband customers could save about GBP 100 a year (up to about GBP 150). About 1.4 million mobile customers could save by moving to SIM-only, about GBP 75 a year on average.

CURRENT LAW (verified 28 September 2026): Ofcom's 'General Conditions of Entitlement: Unofficial Consolidated Version' (with effect from 8 April 2026) contains the ECN rules at C1.21-C1.29: C1.23 duty to send; C1.24(m) consumer notice must include the provider's best tariffs; C1.27 timing; C1.28 durable medium and separate communication; C1.29 12-month record-keeping. It contains the ABTN rules at C1.30-C1.36 (C1.33(i) best tariffs; C1.34 at least once every 12 months). Ofcom's January 2025 C1 guidance (para 1.169) expects consumer ECNs to be sent 10-40 days before the Commitment Period ends. The version history records the 15 May 2019 changes as effective 15 February 2020, and an ABTN scope change on 27 October 2020 (EECC implementation).

OFCOM MOBILE HANDSETS REVIEW: 'Helping consumers to get better deals in communications markets: mobile handsets' (statement and consultation, 22 July 2019). About 2 million bundled customers were out of contract (11% of bundled customers, under 5% of pay-monthly). About 1.4 million were overpaying by just under GBP 11 a month, about GBP 182m a year in total, below Ofcom's initial GBP 330m estimate. About 600,000 would pay GBP 39m a year more if forced onto SIM-only. Three refused to apply any discount. Ofcom's November 2021 review found the aggregate overpayment had fallen from GBP 182m a year (2018) to GBP 83m a year (2020).

OFCOM FIXED BROADBAND PRICING REVIEW: 'Initial conclusions' (25 September 2019) found about 8.8 million out-of-contract customers (41%), 3.3 million of them out of contract for 2 or more years and 1.5 million potentially vulnerable. Out-of-contract customers could save GBP 800m-900m a year by re-contracting. Ofcom said it was not helpful to call the price difference a 'loyalty penalty'. The 'Update' (28 July 2020) found about 40% (8.7 million) out of contract, paying about GBP 4.70 a month above their provider's average price (GBP 3.90 for vulnerable customers, who stay out of contract longer: 44% for 2+ years vs 37%). The total impact was just under GBP 500m a year (just under GBP 80m for vulnerable customers). Provider commitments (BT, EE, Plusnet, Sky, TalkTalk, Virgin Media) were valued at over GBP 270m a year.

IMPACT EVIDENCE. Ofcom (30 November 2021): out-of-contract broadband customers fell from 40% (8.7 million, September 2019) to 35% (7.4 million, September 2020); the out-of-contract differential was about GBP 5.10 a month; the vulnerable-customer differential fell from GBP 4.40 to GBP 2.30; mobile out-of-contract share fell from 27% to 25%. Ofcom (6 May 2022) broadband ECN evaluation: re-contracting rose up to 13 percentage points (Plusnet) and 10 points at BT, EE and Virgin Media, with average savings over GBP 110 a year for some. Ofcom (10 May 2024) mobile evaluation: ABTNs had a small positive effect on re-contracting (1-2 percentage points at O2 and Tesco, largest at Three); ECN effects on switching were mixed, about 2 points where significant.

CURRENT MARKET CONTEXT: Ofcom's 'Pricing and consumer engagement' report (published 26 February 2026) found 28% of fixed-broadband customers of the largest operators out of contract for at least one service at end of June 2025, unchanged year on year. In Q2 2025, out-of-contract customers' average spend was 11%-25% above in-contract customers for most bundle types. The reverse held for bundles including mobile, because in-contract mobile customers are more often paying for a handset. The loyalty-penalty problem has therefore narrowed but not disappeared, which is relevant context for churn and retention modelling.

DATA (USE AND ACCESS) ACT 2025 AND OTHER LATER LAW: the DUA Act 2025 does not amend Enterprise Act 2002 s.11 or Ofcom's General Conditions. Its Part 1 (access to customer data and business data, i.e. Smart Data schemes) came into force on 20 August 2025 (SI 2025/904), giving a legal route for the CMA's 2018 Smart Data recommendation and the 'Open Communications' idea; the DBT 'Smart Data 2035' strategy followed on 26 March 2026. DMCC Act 2024 Part 3 (CMA direct consumer enforcement, including the power to impose fines) has been in force since 6 April 2025 (SI 2025/272), implementing recommendation 2. DMCC Part 4 Chapter 2 (subscription contracts) is not yet in force; government has announced January 2027. Sch. 22 para 5 (prospective) will exclude contracts bound by Ofcom general conditions, so telecoms contracts would stay under Ofcom's C1 regime.
legal.quotable: The CMA estimated the loyalty penalty at around GBP 4bn a year, 'nearly £1 billion in broadband and £0.3 billion in mobile' (CMA, 2018b, p. 50).
legal.uncertainties: (1) Date: Citizens Advice's page is dated 27 September 2018, but the CMA records receipt, and titles its response, as 28 September 2018. Cite 28 September 2018. The CMA case page links to an old Citizens Advice URL that now returns 404; the live page is at /policy/publications/..., and the PDF is hosted on a Contentful CDN, not gov.uk. (2) The CMA case page shows 'Closed' with no explicit closure date (last updated 1 December 2020). No later CMA loyalty-penalty update was found on gov.uk, but absence cannot be proven. The CMA's 2024 'loyalty pricing' groceries review is a separate topic. (3) CMA Table 4.1 prints the Citizens Advice broadband total as 'GBP 1,1280 million', apparently a typo; the Citizens Advice document gives GBP 1,277m. The CMA text cites mobile averages of 'GBP 264 and GBP 220', while the table shows GBP 222 for the Ofcom estimate. (4) Telecoms 'loyalty penalty' figures differ by source and definition. Mobile: Citizens Advice GBP 473m; Ofcom/CMA GBP 330m (2018); Ofcom GBP 182m (July 2019) falling to GBP 83m (2020). Broadband: Citizens Advice GBP 1,277m; CMA GBP 990m; Ofcom just under GBP 500m (July 2020 price differential). Ofcom explicitly avoids the term 'loyalty penalty', so do not present Ofcom figures as Ofcom's own 'loyalty penalty' estimates. (5) The ECN/ABTN condition numbers in the 2019 statement differ from the current numbering (C1.21-C1.36 in the 8 April 2026 consolidated version). The intermediate renumbering statements (EECC implementation, October/December 2020) were only seen through the GC version history. The consolidated GCs are Ofcom's 'unofficial' version; the legally operative texts are Ofcom's statements and notifications. (6) Most PDFs could not be parsed by the fetch tool. Their text was extracted locally (pdftotext/PyMuPDF) from the files downloaded from the cited URLs, and figures are reproduced as found. (7) The January 2027 date for the DMCC subscription regime comes from a No 10 press release (9 August 2026). No commencement SI was identified, so the date could still change. (8) No telecoms-specific Smart Data scheme regulations under DUA Act 2025 Part 1 were identified. The Smart Data 2035 strategy's telecoms content was not reviewed in detail. (9) Related Ofcom fairness measures outside the loyalty-penalty programme were not re-verified here: the ban on inflation-linked mid-contract price rises (from 17 January 2025), One Touch Switch, and the ban on locked handsets.

(1) DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Chapter 1 (unfair commercial practices, ss.224-252) has been in force since 6 April 2025 (SI 2025/272 reg 2), except the consumer private rights-of-redress sections ss.232, 234 and 235, which remain 'Prospective'; the CPUTR 2008 were revoked the same day with savings. (2) DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Chapter 2 (subscription contracts, ss.253-281: reminder notices s.258-259, easy cancellation s.260, cooling-off ss.264-266) is NOT in force as of today: every substantive section is still marked 'Prospective' on legislation.gov.uk; only regulation-making powers (ss.255, 256, 258, 267, 277) took effect at Royal Assent for the purpose of making regulations. Three commencement SIs exist (2024/1226, 2025/272, 2026/284, plus amending SI 2026/1040) and none commences Chapter 2; no 'subscription contracts' SI (made or draft) exists on legislation.gov.uk. Government timeline: DBT consultation response (2 April 2026) said 'spring 2027'; a Prime Minister's Office press release (published 9 August 2026) then said 'New rules will now come into force in January 2027'. Critically for a telecoms report, Schedule 22 para 5 excludes from Chapter 2 any contract supplied by a person bound by an Ofcom general condition (i.e. broadband, landline and mobile contracts), so the DMCC subscription regime will not govern telecoms subscriptions even once commenced; Ofcom's General Conditions (C1 end-of-contract notifications, one-month notice after auto-prolongation; C7 switching) are the applicable regime. (3) Ofcom's One Touch Switch went live on 12 September 2024 for residential broadband and landline switching under General Condition C7 (C7.18-C7.27 in the consolidated GCs effective 8 April 2026); it remains fully operational (over 1.6 million switches in the first year per Ofcom, 12 September 2025). No amendment to any of these provisions by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 was found.

key_points: DMCC Act 2024 (c. 13; Royal Assent 24 May 2024). Under s.339(1) most of the Act commences by regulations; s.339(2)(c) brought regulation-making powers into force at Royal Assent.

Part 4 Chapter 1 (ss.224-252, prohibition of unfair commercial practices: misleading actions/omissions, aggressive practices, Sch. 20 banned practices) came into force on 6 April 2025 via SI 2025/272 reg 2(1)(3), replacing the CPUTR 2008 (SI 2008/1277 revoked 6 April 2025 by s.251(1), with transitional savings for CPUTR Part 4A private redress until regulations are made under s.233 - see ss.235, 243, 252).

Not yet in force in Chapter 1: ss.232, 234 and 235 (consumer private rights of redress) were expressly excluded from SI 2025/272 and remain marked 'Prospective' on legislation.gov.uk as of 28 September 2026. Public enforcement (s.231; CMA direct enforcement with fines up to the higher of GBP 300,000 or 10% of global turnover) is in force.

CMA guidance CMA207 (updated 18 November 2025) applies to practices from 6 April 2025 and treats retention/cancellation friction as potentially unfair: an aggressive practice can include requiring 'onerous or disproportionate action' to exercise rights (example given: a termination process requiring multiple clicks), and omitting that a contract runs for a minimum period can be a misleading omission. The CMA reported (17 April 2026) 14 investigations opened, GBP 4.7m fines and GBP 760k refunds in year one, including an investigation into Adobe's early cancellation fees.

Part 4 Chapter 2 (ss.253-281, subscription contracts) is NOT in force as of 28 September 2026. legislation.gov.uk (page dated 'up to date... on or before 28 September 2026') marks the substantive sections 'Prospective' ('not in force at Royal Assent, see s.339(1)'); ss.255, 256, 258, 267 and 277 are in force 'for specified purposes' only (making regulations).

Chapter 2 core duties once commenced: s.258-259 reminder notices before each renewal payment (at least six-monthly, with content/timing rules); s.260 arrangements for ending the contract must be 'straightforward' and not require 'any steps which are not reasonably necessary', with online exit where the contract was entered online; s.261 duties on cancellation; ss.264-266 14-day initial and renewal cooling-off periods; s.273 terms of no effect; ss.268-271 offences.

Commencement instruments to date: SI 2024/1226 (No. 1), SI 2025/272 (No. 2, 6 April 2025: Part 3 and Part 4 Ch. 1), SI 2026/284 (No. 3, made 11 March 2026: Part 4 Ch. 4 ADR and Schs 25-27 from 6 April 2026), SI 2026/1040 (made 16 September 2026: extends ADR transitional dates from 5 October 2026 to 7 January 2027). None commences Chapter 2. A legislation.gov.uk title search for 'subscription contracts' returns zero made or draft instruments.

Government timeline for Chapter 2: DBT's consultation response (2 April 2026) stated 'we anticipate that the regime will commence in spring 2027' and 'We will legislate when parliamentary time allows'; it confirmed reminder notices must be in writing on a durable medium with their purpose immediately apparent, that 'if a consumer can sign up online, they must be able to exit online', proportionate refunds on renewal-period cancellation, exclusion of charitable memberships, and forthcoming business guidance. A Prime Minister's Office press release (published 9 August 2026) then stated: 'New rules will now come into force in January 2027, in time for when customers often start new subscriptions for the year ahead', citing 155 million active UK subscriptions and c. GBP 1.6bn a year spent on unwanted ones.

Telecoms carve-out (essential for this report): Schedule 22 para 5 excludes from Chapter 2 'A contract for the supply of goods, services or digital content by a person who is bound, in relation to that supply, by a general condition set by OFCOM under section 45 of the Communications Act 2003'. Broadband, landline and mobile contracts supplied by Ofcom-regulated providers will therefore sit outside the DMCC subscription regime; the sector-specific equivalents are Ofcom GC C1.21-C1.29 (End-of-Contract Notification before the commitment period ends; one-month termination notice after automatic prolongation with no costs beyond the notice-period fee) and C1.30-C1.36 (Annual Best Tariff Notification). Chapter 1 (unfair practices) still applies to telecoms operators.

Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18): legislation.gov.uk records 0 changes to the DMCC Act made by that Act. The only related effect is SI 2026/386 (made 26 March 2026, not yet applied; commences when DUAA s.119 is fully in force), which substitutes 'the Information Commission' for 'the Information Commissioner' in DMCC ss.11(5)(b), 107(3) and 151(1)(k) - Parts 1 and 3 only, nothing in Part 4. A separate outstanding change (s.151(1)(ha) inserted by the Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026, c. 18, Sch. 14 para 32(2)) concerns Part 3 enforcer lists and does not touch Part 4.

Ofcom One Touch Switch (OTS): decided in Ofcom's statement 'Quick, easy and reliable switching' (September 2021) amending General Condition C7 with effect from 3 April 2023; industry missed that deadline (Ofcom enforcement programme, update 12 March 2024) and OTS went live on 12 September 2024 for residential broadband and landline customers. Customers contact only the gaining provider, which manages the switch; the losing provider cannot require contact, consent or other steps (C7.19); the process is free (C7.20); providers may not charge for notice periods running beyond the switch date; loss of service must not exceed one working day; compensation is payable for failed switches/loss of service (C7.47-C7.48).

OTS current status: Ofcom's 11 October 2024 letter confirmed decommissioning of the interim NoT+ process on 24 October 2024 and that OTS is 'the only switching process for residential customers switching fixed services which is compliant with Ofcom's General Conditions'. Ofcom reported (12 September 2025) over 1.6 million switches via OTS in its first year and more than 300 providers signed up. The current consolidated General Conditions (effective 8 April 2026) retain OTS at C7.18-C7.27 unchanged in substance. Mobile switching remains under the separate Auto-Switch/PAC process (C7.30-C7.46).
legal.uncertainties: 1) The January 2027 commencement date for DMCC Part 4 Chapter 2 rests on a Prime Minister's Office press release (gov.uk metadata: published 2026-08-09T22:30 BST; law-firm commentary dates the announcement 10 August 2026). As of 28 September 2026 no commencement regulations or implementing 'subscription contracts' regulations have been made or laid in draft on legislation.gov.uk, so the date is an announced intention, not a legal fact; it also conflicts with the DBT response's 'spring 2027' estimate of 2 April 2026, and a report should cite both and flag that commencement regulations were still awaited on the access date. 2) The 13 April 2026 written ministerial statement (Commons HCWS1498 / Lords HLWS1503, 'Subscription Contracts Regime: Response to Implementation Consultation') was located via search but parliament.uk returned HTTP 403 / a JavaScript challenge on every retrieval attempt, so its text was not read directly; the gov.uk consultation response of 2 April 2026 is used as the primary source instead. 3) SI 2026/284's explanatory table of earlier commencements was summarised by the fetch tool as implying ss.232/234/235 commenced in 2025; this was rejected in favour of the operative text of SI 2025/272 reg 2 (which excludes them) and legislation.gov.uk's 'Prospective' markers on those sections as at 28 September 2026. 4) The Ofcom 'Statement: Quick, easy and reliable switching' page shows a February 2021 consultation date and a September 2021 final decision; the reference is given as 2021. 5) Section-level annotations were read via an automated fetch of legislation.gov.uk; the 'Changes to legislation' banners confirm the pages were current to 27-28 September 2026, but the reader should re-check legislation.gov.uk immediately before submission because a Chapter 2 commencement SI could be made at any time. 6) Schedule 22 para 5 was verified verbatim; whether specific bundled or non-communications add-on services sold by a telecoms operator fall outside the Ofcom general conditions (and hence inside Chapter 2) is a fact-specific question not resolved here. 7) Ofcom's One Touch Switch enforcement programme: the 12 March 2024 update page does not state a formal closure date; Ofcom's 11 October 2024 letter says the programme continues to monitor compliance.
legal.quotable: DMCC Act 2024 s.260(1): 'A trader must make arrangements to enable a consumer to exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end - (a) in a way which is straightforward, and (b) without having to take any steps which are not reasonably necessary for bringing the contract to an end.' (Prospective as at 28 September 2026.) Sch. 22 para 5 excludes 'A contract for the supply of goods, services or digital content by a person who is bound, in relation to that supply, by a general condition set by OFCOM under section 45 of the Communications Act 2003.' Prime Minister's Office (9 August 2026): 'New rules will now come into force in January 2027, in time for when customers often start new subscriptions for the year ahead.' Ofcom (11 October 2024): 'Since 3 April 2023, OTS is the only switching process for residential customers switching fixed services which is compliant with Ofcom's General Conditions.'

legal.status_summary: Verified on legislation.gov.uk on 2026-09-28. Sections 4 (protected characteristics), 13 (direct discrimination), 19 (indirect discrimination) and 29 (provision of services) of the Equality Act 2010 (c. 15) are all in force in England, Wales and Scotland and legislation.gov.uk states each is 'up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 28 September 2026'. Sections 4 and 19 are textually unamended since commencement. Section 13 was amended from 1 January 2024 by the Equality Act 2010 (Amendment) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1425): s.13(6)(b) now refers to 'pregnancy, childbirth or maternity' and s.13(7) was omitted, extending breast-feeding protection to the work context; the same Regulations inserted s.19A (indirect discrimination: same disadvantage) from 1 January 2024. Sections 4-27 (Part 2) and Part 3 (ss.28-31) commenced 1 October 2010 (SI 2010/2317, art. 2) except in relation to age; Part 3 was extended to age (adults only) on 1 October 2012 (SI 2012/1569), with age exceptions inserted into Schedule 3 Part 7 by SI 2012/2466 (paras 30A-30D, including para 30A on age-based concessions). None of ss.4, 13, 19 or 29 has been amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18). The only DUAA-related effect on the Equality Act 2010 is a consequential change to Schedule 19 Part 1 (list of public authorities: 'The Information Commissioner' replaced by 'The Information Commission') made by SI 2026/386 Sch. 2 para 16, which comes into force when DUAA s.119 is fully commenced; SI 2026/1015 reg. 2(c) appoints 30 September 2026 for s.119, so as at 2026-09-28 the Sch. 19 text still reads 'The Information Commissioner'. Outstanding prospective amendments by the Employment Rights Act 2025 (c. 36) affect ss.40, 40B, 78, 153, 154 and 208 only, not the sections in question. Two 2025-2026 developments affect how the sections are read: For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers [2025] UKSC 16 (16 April 2025) unanimously held that 'man', 'woman' and 'sex' in the Act refer to biological sex; and the EHRC's revised Code of Practice for services, public functions and associations (issued under s.14(2) Equality Act 2006) came into force on 5 August 2026, revoking the 2011 Code.
legal.in_force: Yes. As at 2026-09-28: s.4 in force from 1 October 2010 (unamended); s.13 in force from 1 October 2010, as amended from 1 January 2024 by SI 2023/1425; s.19 in force from 1 October 2010 (unamended), with s.19A inserted from 1 January 2024; s.29 (and ss.28, 31 and Schedule 3) in force from 1 October 2010 for all characteristics other than age, and from 1 October 2012 for age (persons aged 18 and over only, per s.28(1)(a)). Extent: England, Wales and Scotland (Parts 2 and 3 do not extend to Northern Ireland). No amendment to any of these four sections by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Consequential DUAA change to Sch. 19 Pt 1 takes effect 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015).

key_points: Section 4 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation. In force since 1 October 2010 (SI 2010/2317 art. 2); unamended; extent E+W+S. Section 5 defines age by reference to 'age group' (a particular age or a range of ages) and section 11 defines sex by reference to 'a man or to a woman'.

Section 13(1) (direct discrimination): A discriminates against B if, because of a protected characteristic, A treats B less favourably than A treats or would treat others. Section 13(2) provides that for AGE only, direct discrimination is not unlawful if A shows the treatment is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim; there is no such justification defence for direct SEX discrimination. Amended from 1 January 2024 by SI 2023/1425 (s.13(6)(b) extended to 'maternity'; s.13(7) omitted) - these amendments do not affect the age or sex analysis for service pricing.

Section 19 (indirect discrimination): applying a provision, criterion or practice (PCP) that puts persons sharing a characteristic at a particular disadvantage, and puts B at that disadvantage, is discrimination unless A shows the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim (s.19(2)(d)). Relevant characteristics under s.19(3) include age and sex (pregnancy and maternity is not listed). Unamended since 2010. Section 19A (inserted 1 January 2024) extends indirect discrimination to a person who does not share the characteristic but suffers 'substantially the same disadvantage' - relevant where an AI model's proxy variables disadvantage people who correlate with, but do not have, a protected characteristic.

Section 29 (Part 3, services): a 'service-provider' concerned with the provision of a service to the public or a section of the public (for payment or not) must not discriminate by not providing the service (s.29(1)), or, in providing it, 'as to the terms on which A provides the service to B', by terminating the service, or by subjecting B to any other detriment (s.29(2)); parallel victimisation prohibitions in s.29(4)-(5); a reasonable-adjustments duty in s.29(7). A UK telecoms operator supplying consumer contracts is squarely a service-provider; differential pricing or retention offers are 'terms on which A provides the service'. Section 31(2) confirms 'service' includes goods and facilities.

Commencement of Part 3 for age was deferred: SI 2010/2317 art. 2 commenced Part 3 on 1 October 2010 'except so far as they apply to the protected characteristic of age'; SI 2012/1569 commenced ss.28-31 and Sch. 3 for age from 1 October 2012. Section 28(1)(a) excludes age in relation to persons under 18, and s.28(1)(b) excludes marriage and civil partnership from Part 3 entirely.

Age exceptions for services: Sch. 3 Pt 7 paras 30A-30D (inserted by SI 2012/2466, in force 1 October 2012). Para 30A permits age-based 'concessions' (a benefit, right or privilege making the service MORE favourable to an age group, e.g. student or senior discounts); it does not authorise LESS favourable pricing for an age group. Less favourable age-based pricing or withholding retention offers by age therefore falls to be justified, if at all, under s.13(2) (direct) or s.19(2)(d) (indirect). Sch. 3 Pt 5 financial-services age exceptions (risk-based pricing) apply to financial services, not telecoms.

Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18): does NOT amend ss.4, 13, 19, 19A or 29. The only DUAA-driven change to the Equality Act 2010 is consequential: SI 2026/386 Sch. 2 para 16 substitutes 'The Information Commission' for 'The Information Commissioner' in Sch. 19 Pt 1 (public sector equality duty list), taking effect when DUAA s.119 is fully in force - appointed for 30 September 2026 by SI 2026/1015 reg. 2(c) (made 10 September 2026). As at 2026-09-28 Sch. 19 Pt 1 on legislation.gov.uk still reads 'The Information Commissioner'.

Other outstanding changes: legislation.gov.uk flags prospective amendments by the Employment Rights Act 2025 (c. 36) to ss.40, 40B, 78, 153, 154 and 208 (employment and equality-duty provisions) - none touches ss.4, 13, 19 or 29 or Part 3.

Meaning of 'sex': For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers [2025] UKSC 16 (16 April 2025, unanimous) held that 'man', 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex; a Gender Recognition Certificate does not change a person's sex for the purposes of the Act, while gender reassignment remains a separately protected characteristic (s.7). This bears on how a churn model's 'sex'/'gender' feature maps onto the statutory characteristic.

Statutory guidance: the EHRC's revised Code of Practice for services, public functions and associations (issued under s.14(2) Equality Act 2006) was published on GOV.UK on 21 May 2026 and 'came into force on 5th August 2026', revoking the 2011 Code on the same date. Courts and tribunals must take a statutory code into account where relevant (s.15(4) Equality Act 2006). Cite the 2026 Code, not the 2011 Code.

Regulatory context for AI churn models: ICO Guidance on AI and data protection (last updated 15 March 2023; flagged 'under review' because of the Data (Use and Access) Act) states that the Equality Act 2010 sits alongside data protection law and protects individuals from direct and indirect discrimination 'whether generated by a human or an automated decision-making system'. Ofcom's General Conditions of Entitlement (consolidated version in force from 8 April 2026), Condition C1, separately require end-of-contract and annual best-tariff notifications and fair treatment of end-users; these are telecoms-regulatory duties distinct from the Equality Act.
legal.quotable: Equality Act 2010, s. 29(2) (Crown copyright, Open Government Licence): 'A service-provider (A) must not, in providing the service, discriminate against a person (B)- (a) as to the terms on which A provides the service to B; (b) by terminating the provision of the service to B; (c) by subjecting B to any other detriment.' Supreme Court press summary, [2025] UKSC 16: the Court 'holds that the terms "man", "woman" and "sex" in the EA 2010 refer to biological sex.'
legal.uncertainties: 1) legislation.gov.uk 'up to date' banners on individual section pages carried dates between 25 and 28 September 2026 (server-side caching); no substantive difference between versions. 2) The legislation.gov.uk 'changes affecting' table marks SI 2026/386 Sch. 2 para 16 (Sch. 19 Pt 1) as applied, but the Sch. 19 Pt 1 text still shows 'The Information Commissioner' and DUAA s.119 is shown as prospective until 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015); treat the substitution as effective from 30 September 2026 and re-check after that date. 3) Whether an AI-driven differential retention offer constitutes 'less favourable treatment because of' a characteristic (s.13) or a PCP causing 'particular disadvantage' (s.19) is fact-specific; no reported UK judgment applying ss.13/19/29 to algorithmic pricing was located on official sources, so the report should present this as a legal-risk analysis rather than settled law. Note that s.13(2) offers a justification defence only for age, not sex. 4) The EHRC website (equalityhumanrights.com) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so the Code's in-force date (5 August 2026) was verified from the GOV.UK publication page rather than the EHRC page. 5) The Supreme Court holding was verified from the official press summary PDF; the National Archives Find Case Law page excerpt was truncated before the concluding paragraphs. 6) ICO AI guidance is explicitly 'under review' following the DUAA and may be revised; DUAA changes to automated decision-making (UK GDPR Arts 22A-22D) are outside this item and should be verified separately. 7) Extent: ss.4-31 extend to England, Wales and Scotland only; Northern Ireland has separate equality legislation. 8) Ofcom General Conditions are a separate regime; their 'consolidated version' is described by Ofcom as unofficial.

key_points: Ofcom's unofficial consolidation of the General Conditions of Entitlement that bind UK providers of public electronic communications services. It incorporates every modification since September 2017. The cover reads 'Version with effect from: 8 April 2026' (latest change: the Annex to C4, on ADR), and Ofcom's General Conditions page (last updated 8 April 2026) still lists it as current on 31 October 2026. Condition C1 (contract requirements for consumers and small businesses): C1.8 requires providers to ensure that conditions or procedures for contract termination do not act as disincentives against changing provider. C1.10 bars renewal for a further commitment period without express consent. C1.11 caps commitment periods at 24 months. C1.22 gives a right to end an automatically prolonged contract on one month's notice, with no costs beyond the notice-period service fee. C1.23-C1.29 require end-of-contract notifications that include best tariffs. Supports the Part 5 claim that obstructive cancellation would breach GC C1.8.
legal.uncertainties: Whether a given cancellation procedure is a disincentive to switching is fact-dependent, so the report says obstructive cancellation 'could' breach C1.8. Unofficial consolidation: the notifications take precedence.
legal.quotable: Ofcom (2026a, C1.8): termination conditions or procedures must not act as disincentives to changing provider.

legal.status_summary: Verified against primary sources on 2026-09-28. Ofcom's flagship pricing/engagement report has been RETITLED: the December 2024 edition is 'Pricing trends for communications services in the UK' (published 12 December 2024); the latest edition is 'Pricing and consumer engagement: Trends in the UK communications sector' (published 26 February 2026, data to Q2/September 2025). Ofcom's ban on inflation-linked / percentage-based mid-contract price rises (modifications to General Condition C1.3, C1.5, Annex Table A and new definition 'Core Subscription Price Change Information') was made by notification under s.48(1) Communications Act 2003 on 19 July 2024 and entered into force on 17 January 2025 for new contracts; it remains in force in the unofficial consolidated General Conditions with effect from 8 April 2026 (C1.3(a)(ii) and the definition are present verbatim). The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 does not amend the Communications Act 2003 ss.45-48 or the General Conditions (its telecoms-adjacent content is Part 5 Chapter 2 amending PECR). Latest quarterly Telecommunications Market Data Update is Q1 2026 (published 23 July 2026); Q2 2026 is scheduled for 14 October 2026. Communications Market Report 2026 published 30 June 2026. Switching statistics: Ofcom Switching Tracker 2025 (biennial; fieldwork Aug-Sep 2025) - broadband 18%, mobile 16%, pay TV 13%, fixed voice 11%, any service 26%. Out-of-contract: 28% of fixed-broadband customers out of contract for at least one bundled service at end-June 2025 (unchanged YoY); 41% of pay-monthly mobile users out of contract in Q2 2025 (up from 37%). Government (DSIT) Telecoms Consumer Charter (11 February 2026, updated 19 June 2026) adds voluntary commitments that April 2026 is the last inflation-linked rise on legacy contracts.
legal.in_force: The mid-contract price-rise rules (amended GC C1.3, C1.4-C1.5, Annex to C1 Table A para 3 'Price', definitions of 'Contract Summary' and 'Core Subscription Price Change Information') entered into force on 17 January 2025 and apply to contracts entered into from that date; customers on pre-17 January 2025 contracts may still see inflation-linked rises (Ofcom, 2026, p.24 ff.). Confirmed still in force in Ofcom's unofficial consolidated General Conditions of Entitlement 'Version with effect from: 8 April 2026' (the 8 April 2026 change concerned C4 Annex / ADR, not C1). The accompanying 'Ofcom's guidance under General Condition C1 - contract requirements (January 2025)' applies from 17 January 2025. No amendment by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (which amends PECR via Part 5 Ch.2, ss.109-116, not the Communications Act 2003 general-conditions regime). Ofcom market reports and statistics are publications, not legal instruments; the latest editions as at 2026-09-28 are those listed in primary_sources. Pending: Q2 2026 Telecommunications Market Data Update due 14 October 2026; Ofcom says a full assessment of the pounds-and-pence rules will be published in 2027; next pricing report shown on the 2026 statistical release calendar as postponed to February 2027.

MID-CONTRACT PRICE RISES (Ofcom 2024b, statement 19 July 2024): Ofcom modified GC C1 (preamble; title before C1.3; C1.3; C1.5; Annex Table A para 3 'Price'; definition of 'Contract Summary'; new definition 'Core Subscription Price Change Information') under ss.45 and 48(1) Communications Act 2003; modifications 'shall enter into force on 17 January 2025' (Annex A2.10) and apply to new contracts from that date. Providers may no longer include inflation-linked or percentage-based rises to the Core Subscription Price; any in-contract rise must be stated in pounds and pence with the date it takes effect, prominently at point of sale and in the Contract Summary.

STILL IN FORCE: the consolidated General Conditions 'Version with effect from: 8 April 2026' contains C1.3(a)(ii) ('any Core Subscription Price Change Information') and the definition ('the changed Core Subscription Price(s), expressed in pounds and pence ... and the date from which any changed Core Subscription Price(s) ... shall have effect'). The 8 April 2026 amendment concerned C4 (ADR), not C1.

Scale of exposure before the ban: Ofcom estimated 'around six in ten broadband and mobile customers' were on contracts with inflation-linked price-rise terms in April 2024 (Ofcom 2024b para 1.x; repeated in Ofcom 2024a p.8); consumer research: 55% of broadband customers did not know what CPI/RPI measure and only 16% of fixed broadband / 12% of mobile customers were both aware of the rise and could identify it as inflation-linked plus a percentage (Ofcom 2026b).

Transition: Ofcom (2026b) reports 2026 in-contract rises announced at GBP 1.80-2.50/month for mobile and GBP 2-4/month for broadband; customers on pre-17 Jan 2025 contracts may still face inflation-linked rises in March/April 2026, but by March/April 2027 no in-contract customers will be subject to inflation-linked rises. Ofcom says it lacks sufficient evidence yet on impact and will publish a full assessment in 2027.

Government Telecoms Consumer Charter (DSIT, published 11 February 2026, updated 19 June 2026; signatories incl. BT Group, VMO2, Vodafone Three, Sky, TalkTalk, KCOM, Community Fibre, WightFibre, Hyperoptic): voluntary commitments that 'April 2026 will be the final increase expressed in [inflation-linked] terms for the core subscription' on legacy contracts, that the core subscription price signed up to is the price paid (barring unforeseen external events), and on social-tariff signposting, ECN/ABTN clarity and One Touch Switch / Text-to-Switch. Voluntary, not Ofcom rules.

Ofcom statement on O2 price rises (30 October 2025): Ofcom said O2's decision to raise in-contract prices above what customers signed up to 'goes against the spirit of our rules'; Ofcom wrote to major mobile providers reminding them of fairness obligations; customers may exit penalty-free where the rise exceeds contract terms. Relevant as a churn-trigger event.

SWITCHING RATES (Ofcom Switching Tracker 2025, biennial; fieldwork Aug-Sep 2025, n=2,767; reported in Ofcom 2026b pp.14-15): 26% of UK households switched provider for at least one communications service in the past year; by service: fixed broadband 18% (up from 14% in 2023; 23% standalone vs 13% bundled), mobile 16% (stable; standalone and bundled similar), pay TV 13% (up from 7% in 2020), fixed voice 11% (17% standalone vs 9% bundled), dual-play bundle 11%, triple-play bundle 10%. Switching lower among over-64s (19% any service) vs 25-44s (29%), and DE households (21%) vs AB (27%). 35% of households re-negotiated or changed services with their existing provider.

One Touch Switch (fixed broadband/landline) launched 12 September 2024: 'over 2 million' residential switches by end-2025 (Ofcom 2026b); 1.6 million in first year with 300+ providers signed up (Ofcom 2025a, 12 Sept 2025); 'around 3.5 million' switches in two years, 3,431,195 OTS processes initiated as at 3 September 2026 (Ofcom 2026h, 12 Sept 2026).

OUT-OF-CONTRACT SHARE (operator data, Ofcom 2026b): 28% of customers with a fixed broadband service were out of contract for at least one service in their bundle at end-June 2025, unchanged year on year; dual-play (broadband+landline) out-of-contract share rose 3pp to 39% in year to June 2025; 41% of pay-monthly mobile users were out of contract in Q2 2025 (up from 37%), partly because <30-day SIM-only plans are classed as always out of contract; 43% of SIM-only subscriptions with MCP >30 days out of contract; 78% of handset+airtime customers in contract. Earlier data (Ofcom 2024a, end-June 2024): 36% of dual-play and 32% of triple-play customers out of contract, paying 18% and 16% more than in-contract customers; 51% of pay-monthly SIM-only mobile customers out of contract.

PRICE PENALTY FOR NOT ENGAGING (Ofcom 2026b): in-contract customers save GBP 7-9/month vs out-of-contract for standalone broadband, dual-play and triple-play; promoted-vs-list price gap for dual-play GBP 4 (standard) to GBP 8 (ultrafast); triple-play out-of-contract customers pay GBP 78/month vs GBP 69 in-contract and could save 'over GBP 100 a year by switching' (Ofcom 2026h).

PRICE TRENDS (Ofcom 2026b): most telecoms prices flat or falling in real terms; average-use mobile basket 6% cheaper in real terms in 2025 vs 2024 and 20% cheaper than 2020 despite data use more than doubling; superfast/ultrafast dual-play prices fell faster than standard; SIM-only = half of pay-monthly subscriptions (June 2025); 70% of dual-play households made no outgoing landline call in Q2 2025; 78% of premises have full-fibre access; UK ranked third of six countries for communications prices in 2025.

AFFORDABILITY/ARREARS (Ofcom 2026b): 7% of fixed broadband households and 5% of mobile users found their service difficult to afford (Oct 2025); 0.6-0.7% of fixed and 1.0-1.1% of mobile contracts missed two or more payments (Jul 2024-Jun 2025); disconnections for non-payment ~1.0% fixed (~250,000) and 1.1% mobile (~510,000) in H1 2025; 532,000 social-tariff customers (June 2025), 70% of eligible households unaware, take-up <9%. Ofcom 2026h adds: 4% missed a payment in the last quarter; 12% changed services due to cost; 7% cancelled a service.

MARKET SIZE (Telecommunications Market Data Update Q1 2026, published 23 July 2026): 29.4m fixed broadband lines (+282k, +1.0% YoY); 90.6m active mobile subscriptions excl. M2M (+881k, +1.0%); mobile retail revenues GBP 3.57bn in the quarter (+1.6% YoY); average monthly retail revenue per mobile subscriber GBP 13.10 (post-pay GBP 15.54, pre-pay GBP 5.40); fixed voice revenues GBP 891.9m (-17.9% YoY); fixed lines 20.7m; mobile data 3,042 PB (+13.1%); SMS/MMS -21.3%. Q4 2025 (published 16 April 2026): 29.3m broadband lines; 91.1m mobile subs; ARPU GBP 13.24.

MARKET SIZE (Communications Market Report 2026, published 30 June 2026): UK telecoms revenue GBP 34.7bn in 2025 (-0.8%); retail fixed GBP 14.9bn and retail mobile GBP 14.5bn; 29.3m fixed broadband connections at end-2025, 42% full fibre (12.3m lines, +38%); FTTC down to 9.9m; ADSL 1.3m; 123m total mobile subscriptions (incl. M2M), 82% post-pay (101m post-pay, 22m pre-pay); 11.8 GB/month average mobile data per user; fixed voice connections 21.4m (-12%).

REGULATORY CONTEXT FOR RETENTION: GC C1.21-1.29 (end-of-contract notifications) and C1.30-1.36 (annual best tariff notifications) have applied since 15 February 2020 and remain in the 8 April 2026 consolidated GCs; the Telecoms Consumer Charter commits providers to keep ECNs/ABTNs clear and timely. Ofcom notes a 'notable proportion of customers do not re-contract or switch' at contract end (Ofcom 2026b p.~52).

PENDING/NEXT: Q2 2026 Telecommunications Market Data Update scheduled 14 October 2026; Ofcom impact assessment of pounds-and-pence rules in 2027; next pricing report shown as postponed to February 2027 on the release calendar; Switching Tracker is biennial (next expected 2027).

legal.status_summary: As at 28 September 2026, regulations 21 (unsolicited marketing calls) and 22 (marketing by electronic mail, which includes SMS) of the Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2426) are in force. They remain the rules that govern a UK telecoms operator sending churn-triggered retention offers to its own customers. Under reg 22(2), direct-marketing e-mail or SMS to individual subscribers needs prior consent unless the commercial soft opt-in in reg 22(3) applies. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA) did not change the wording of reg 22(3): the details must be obtained in the course of a sale or negotiations for a sale, the marketing must cover the sender's similar products and services only, and a simple, free opt-out must be offered at collection and in every message. DUAA s.114 added a separate charity soft opt-in (reg 22(3A) and (5)) from 5 February 2026. It does not apply to a commercial operator. The text of reg 21 was last amended on 9 January 2019: callers must show a number, must not call TPS/CTPS-registered numbers or anyone who has objected, and the 28-day grace period and the consent override in reg 21(4)-(5) still apply. Reg 21 must now be read with the DUAA-amended definition of 'call' in reg 2(1), which includes an attempt to connect, and new reg 2(1A), under which 'recipient' means the intended recipient. Both have been in force since 5 February 2026. All of the DUAA's PECR provisions (Part 5 Chapter 2, ss.109-116, and Sch 13) have commenced. Commencement No. 1 (SI 2025/904) brought in s.109, s.110 except (2)(a), (2)(b) and (3) (this inserted the statutory definition of 'direct marketing'), s.111 (72-hour breach notification) and s.113 on 20 August 2025. Commencement No. 6 (SI 2026/82, reg 2(v), (w), (x), (y), (z), (z14)) brought in the rest of s.110, s.112, s.114, s.115, s.116 and Sch 13 on 5 February 2026. Since then, breaching regs 5-8, 14, 19-24 or 32B(4)-(5) can lead to a penalty of up to the 'higher maximum amount' in DPA 2018 s.157(5), which is GBP 17.5m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. The previous PECR maximum was GBP 500,000. Under SI 2026/82 reg 11, the new penalty regime only applies to acts or omissions on or after 5 February 2026. One change is still pending, and it is institutional only. On 30 September 2026, two days after the access date, DUAA ss.118-119 come into force (SI 2026/1015). They abolish the office of Information Commissioner and transfer its functions, including PECR enforcement, to the Information Commission. SI 2026/386 then replaces 'Commissioner' with 'Commission' throughout PECR. legislation.gov.uk still lists these changes as not yet applied. ICO guidance: the detailed 'Guidance on direct marketing using electronic mail' is final and was updated on 28 April 2026 for the DUAA. The Guide to PECR landing, e-mail marketing and telephone marketing pages still say they are 'under review' because of the DUAA. The ICO says separate PECR fining guidance is still being developed.
legal.in_force: Yes. PECR regs 21 and 22 are in force. Reg 22 is as amended by DUAA 2025 s.114 with effect from 5 February 2026, which added the charity soft opt-in only; the commercial soft opt-in in reg 22(3) is unamended. Reg 21 has not been amended since 9 January 2019, but it operates through the DUAA-amended reg 2 definitions. The DUAA definition of 'direct marketing' has applied since 20 August 2025, and the wider 'call' definition and reg 2(1A) since 5 February 2026. All DUAA PECR provisions (ss.109-116, Sch 13) have commenced: partly on 20 August 2025 (SI 2025/904) and the rest on 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82). UK GDPR-level PECR fines (up to GBP 17.5m or 4% of turnover) apply to contraventions on or after 5 February 2026. Pending: on 30 September 2026 the Information Commission takes over from the Information Commissioner (SI 2026/1015), and 'Commissioner' becomes 'Commission' in PECR (SI 2026/386). Also still awaited: ICO PECR fining guidance and rewritten Guide to PECR pages.

key_points: Reg 22(2) PECR (current revised text, legislation.gov.uk, no outstanding effects): except where reg 22(3) or (3A) applies, a person must not transmit, or instigate the transmission of, unsolicited direct-marketing communications by electronic mail to individual subscribers unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent. 'Electronic mail' (reg 2(1)) expressly includes messages sent by short message service, so both e-mail and SMS retention offers are caught. Reg 22 applies only to individual subscribers (reg 22(1)); corporate subscribers are outside it.

The commercial soft opt-in in reg 22(3) is UNCHANGED by the DUAA 2025 (DUAA s.114 amends only reg 22(2) and adds reg 22(3A) and (5)). A sender may use e-mail or SMS marketing without consent where: (a) it obtained the recipient's contact details in the course of the sale, or negotiations for the sale, of a product or service to that recipient; (b) the marketing is about its 'similar products and services only'; and (c) the recipient was given a simple, free means of refusing (apart from the cost of sending the refusal), both when the details were collected and in each later communication.

ICO interpretation (Guidance on direct marketing using electronic mail, final, updated 28 April 2026): the 'similar products and services' test turns on whether people would reasonably expect marketing about that product or service, given their previous interactions. The details must be collected while selling or negotiating to sell, and browsing alone is not enough. The opt-out must be clear and prominent, both when details are collected and in every message; burying it in a privacy policy does not count. For SMS, 'reply STOP' is an acceptable mechanism.

Application to AI-driven retention offers by a telecoms operator: the customer's e-mail address or mobile number was captured when they contracted for the service. If an opt-out was offered then and is repeated in each message, and the customer has not opted out, e-mail/SMS retention offers for the operator's own similar services (discounted renewals, tariff changes, add-ons) can rely on reg 22(3). Otherwise PECR-standard prior consent is needed. Reg 23 also applies: the sender's identity must not be disguised or concealed, and a valid address must be given for opt-out requests.

Retention messages will usually be 'direct marketing'. Since 20 August 2025, reg 2(1) defines direct marketing as 'the communication (by whatever means) of advertising or marketing material which is directed to particular individuals' (DUAA s.110; SI 2025/904 reg 2(o)). The ICO's 'Identify direct marketing' guidance (updated 20 August 2025) treats as a service message only a message that advises customers factually of their end-of-contract options without encouraging or promoting one option over another. A message that encourages take-up of a special offer is direct marketing. A churn-model-triggered 'stay with us' offer is therefore within regs 21/22.

Reg 21 PECR (live unsolicited marketing calls; textually unchanged since 9 January 2019, no outstanding effects). Callers must not withhold calling line identification and must present a number on which they can be contacted (reg 21(A1)). They must not make unsolicited direct-marketing calls to a subscriber who has told the caller not to call, or to a number on the TPS/CTPS register kept under reg 26 (reg 21(1)). There is a 28-day grace period after a number is registered (reg 21(3)). A TPS-registered subscriber may tell a particular caller that they do not object to its calls, and may withdraw that at any time (reg 21(4)-(5)). Reg 24 requires the caller's name and, on request, an address or freephone number. The ICO Guide to PECR telephone page says being an existing customer does not by itself override TPS registration: the customer must have told the caller they do not object.

The DUAA widened 'call' and added reg 2(1A), both in force 5 February 2026 (DUAA s.110(2)(a) and (3); SI 2026/82 reg 2(v)). A reference to making a call now includes attempting to establish a connection. Where an e-mail or SMS is sent but not received, or a call attempt is unsuccessful, 'recipient' is read as the intended recipient. Unanswered retention calls and undelivered retention messages therefore still engage regs 21/22.

DUAA s.114 (in force 5 February 2026, SI 2026/82 reg 2(x)) inserts reg 22(3A) and (5): a soft opt-in for registered charities (England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). It covers marketing whose sole purpose is to further the charity's charitable purposes, where the details were obtained when the person expressed an interest in, or offered or gave support to, those purposes, with the same opt-out conditions. It is irrelevant to a commercial telecoms operator. No DUAA provision widens the commercial soft opt-in.

Enforcement and fines: DUAA s.115 and Sch 13 (in force 5 February 2026; SI 2026/82 reg 2(y) and (z14)) substitute PECR reg 31 and Sch 1. Parts 5-7 of the DPA 2018 now apply to PECR with modifications, and regs 5B, 31A and 31B are omitted. Under PECR Sch 1 para 18 (DUAA Sch 13 para 18, as amended by s.116(4)), DPA 2018 s.157(2)(a) applies the 'higher maximum amount' to failures to comply with regs 5, 6, 7, 8, 14, 19, 20, 21, 21A, 21B, 22, 23, 24 or 32B(4)-(5). Under s.157(5), that amount is GBP 17,500,000 or 4% of total annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. The higher maximum also applies to breaches of s.142(8B). Other PECR contraventions attract the 'standard maximum amount' of GBP 8,700,000 or 2% (s.157(6)). The ICO confirmed PECR fines of up to GBP 17.5m or 4% of global turnover in its 5 February 2026 statement and 23 June 2026 blog.

Before the DUAA, PECR Sch 1 applied DPA 1998 s.55A monetary penalties (version at 4 February 2026). The maximum was GBP 500,000 (SI 2010/31 reg 2). Transitional rules in SI 2026/82 regs 8-11: the new investigatory powers can be used from 5 February 2026 even for earlier conduct (reg 8); powers exercised and audits begun before that date are completed under the old rules (regs 9-10); enforcement and monetary penalties for acts or omissions before 5 February 2026 stay under the pre-DUAA PECR, and conduct on or after that date is under the new regime (reg 11).

Other DUAA PECR changes relevant to a telecoms operator: s.111 (in force 20 August 2025, SI 2025/904 reg 2(p)) requires a public electronic communications service provider to notify a personal data breach to the Commissioner without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, as under UK GDPR. s.112 and Sch 12 (in force 5 February 2026) restructure the reg 6 cookies/storage rule and add new exceptions. s.116 (in force 5 February 2026, SI 2026/82 reg 2(z)) inserts regs 32A-32C on PECR codes of conduct.

Commencement audit: DUAA Part 5 Chapter 2 is ss.109-116. It was commenced by SI 2025/904 (Commencement No. 1: ss.109, 110 except (2)(a), (2)(b) and (3), 111 and 113, from 20 August 2025) and SI 2026/82 (Commencement No. 6: rest of s.110, ss.112, 114, 115, 116 and Schs 12-13, from 5 February 2026). Commencement Nos 2, 3 and 4 (SI 2025/982, 2025/996, 2025/1213) contain no PECR provisions. legislation.gov.uk shows no outstanding DUAA effects on regs 21, 22, 23 or 24.

Pending, institutional only: on 30 September 2026 DUAA s.117(4)(a), s.118 (abolition of the office of Information Commissioner) and s.119 (transfer of functions to the Information Commission) come into force (SI 2026/1015 reg 2, made 10 September 2026). SI 2026/386 (made 26 March 2026) comes into force when s.119 is fully in force. Its Sch 3 para 6 changes PECR references from 'Commissioner' to 'Commission' (reg 2(1) definitions, regs 5A, 5C, 6A, 25, 26, 29A, 31, 32, 32A, 32B, 33 and Sch 1). legislation.gov.uk still lists these as outstanding effects on regs 2 and 31 and Sch 1. Substantive regs 21 and 22 are unaffected.

Currency of ICO guidance: the Guide to PECR landing, e-mail marketing and telephone marketing pages still say 'this guidance is under review and may be subject to change' because of the DUAA. The ICO lists an update to its PECR advice for small organisations as being drafted, due Summer 2026. The ICO says separate PECR fining guidance is still being developed (23 June 2026 blog), and no published version was found at 28 September 2026.
legal.quotable: Under PECR reg 22(3)(b), an operator may send unsolicited marketing e-mails or texts to an existing customer without consent only where the marketing concerns its "similar products and services only" (SI 2003/2426, reg 22(3)(b), unamended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; accessed 2026-09-28). Since 5 February 2026, a breach of regs 21-24 can lead to a penalty of up to GBP 17.5 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover (PECR Sch 1 para 18 as substituted by DUAA 2025 Sch 13, applying DPA 2018 s.157(2)(a) and (5)).
legal.uncertainties: (1) legislation.gov.uk and ICO pages were read through an automated fetch and summariser, not by reading the printed SIs. Verbatim wording was requested and returned for regs 21, 22, 23 and 24, the reg 2 'call' definition and reg 2(1A), DUAA Sch 13 para 18 and DPA 2018 s.157(2), (5) and (6). The paragraph letters of SI 2026/82 reg 2 ((v), (w), (x), (y), (z), (z14)) and the list of PECR provisions in SI 2026/386 Sch 3 para 6 come from summaries and should be spot-checked against the SI PDFs before quoting. One summary of PECR Sch 1 para 18 wrongly said regs 19-24 attract the standard maximum. Cross-checking DUAA Sch 13 para 18 against the unmodified structure of DPA 2018 s.157(2) confirms they attract the higher maximum (GBP 17.5m/4%). (2) The commercial soft opt-in text is unchanged, but it is a matter of ICO and Tribunal interpretation, not statute, whether a particular retention offer is a 'similar' product and whether a contract-end message is neutral service information or marketing. The ICO Guide to PECR pages are still formally 'under review', so ICO views may be refined. (3) The Information Commission takes over on 30 September 2026, two days after the access date. After that date, PECR references to 'the Commissioner' should be read as 'the Commission', and the revised legislation.gov.uk text should be re-checked. (4) Separate ICO PECR fining guidance had not been found as published at the access date. How the new GBP 17.5m/4% maximum will be calibrated in practice is therefore uncertain, and the first penalties under the new regime can only concern conduct on or after 5 February 2026. (5) Out of scope but relevant in parallel: the UK GDPR lawful basis for the churn-scoring profiling itself; the absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling, under Art 21(2)-(3); Art 22 automated decision-making as amended by the DUAA; and Ofcom General Conditions and CMA consumer law on retention and cancellation practices. These are covered in other items. (6) The ICO e-mail guidance sub-page 'How do we comply...' shows no page-level date; its 2026 date is taken from the parent guidance's 28 April 2026 update.

legal.status_summary: Verified against legislation.gov.uk 'latest available (revised)' text on 2026-09-28. UK GDPR Articles 13, 14 and 21 (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as retained and amended) are in force. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18) ('DUAA') HAS changed the transparency wording on automated decision-making: Article 13(2)(f) and Article 14(2)(g) now require controllers to give 'the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, which is subject to the requirement to provide safeguards under Article 22C and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject' (DUAA Sch. 6 paras 3 and 4; in force 5 February 2026 via S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2). The previous cross-reference to 'Article 22(1) and (4)' has gone because DUAA s.80 replaced Article 22 with new Articles 22A-22D (in force 5 February 2026). DUAA s.103 / Sch. 10 inserted Art 13(2)(ca) and Art 14(2)(da) (right to make a complaint to the controller under new DPA 2018 s.164A) from 19 June 2026, and DUAA s.77 inserted new paragraphs 5-7 into Arts 13 and 14 (research/archiving 'disproportionate effort' exemption) from 5 February 2026. Article 21(2) (right to object at any time to processing for direct marketing, 'which includes profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing') and Article 21(3) ('the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes') are UNAMENDED and carry no DUAA annotation; the ICO continues to describe this as an absolute right with no exemptions. Article 21(1) was amended by DUAA s.70(5) to add the new 'recognised legitimate interests' basis (Art 6(1)(ea)) to the grounds that can be objected to, and Art 21(6) was amended by DUAA s.87(1)(d), both from 5 February 2026. New Art 6(11) (DUAA s.70(4), in force 5 February 2026) expressly lists direct marketing as an example of processing that may be necessary for a legitimate interest, which reinforces the practical importance of Art 21(2)-(3) for churn-driven retention marketing. Only pending change touching these Articles: substitution of 'Commissioner' with 'Commission' in Art 13(2)(d) and Art 14(2)(e) (S.I. 2026/386, Sch. 3), tied to DUAA s.119, which S.I. 2026/1015 brings into force on 30 September 2026; Article 21 is not amended by that instrument.
legal.in_force: Yes. As of 2026-09-28 Articles 13, 14 and 21 UK GDPR are in force in their DUAA-amended form. Art 13(2)(f) / Art 14(2)(g) (Article 22C reference), Arts 13(5)-(7) / 14(5)-(7), Art 21(1) '(ea)' and Art 21(6): in force since 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2). Art 13(2)(ca) / Art 14(2)(da) (complaint to controller): in force since 19 June 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 3). Art 21(2)-(4): unamended since the retained-EU-law adaptation on 31 December 2020 (S.I. 2019/419). Pending: 'Commissioner' to 'Commission' substitution in Art 13(2)(d) and Art 14(2)(e) expected from 30 September 2026 (S.I. 2026/386 read with S.I. 2026/1015); legislation.gov.uk lists this as a change 'yet to be applied'.
