key_points: Current text (2026-09-28): Art 13(2)(f) and Art 14(2)(g) UK GDPR require controllers to inform data subjects of 'the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, which is subject to the requirement to provide safeguards under Article 22C and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject'. The words 'referred to in Article 22(1) and (4)' were replaced by DUAA 2025 Sch. 6 paras 3-4 (Art 15(1)(h) was amended identically by para 5).

Reason for the change: DUAA 2025 s.80 replaced UK GDPR Article 22 with Articles 22A-22D. Art 22A defines a 'significant decision' (legal or similarly significant effect) and 'based solely on automated processing' (no meaningful human involvement, taking into account the extent of profiling); Art 22B restricts solely automated significant decisions using special category data; Art 22C requires safeguards (information about the decision, right to make representations, human intervention, right to contest); Art 22D lets the Secretary of State make regulations on 'meaningful human involvement' and 'similarly significant effect'. In force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2(z8) with reg. 5 transitional provision: does not apply to decisions taken before 5 February 2026).

Practical effect for a churn model: the specific ADM disclosure in Art 13(2)(f)/14(2)(g) is triggered only where the processing is a 'significant decision' 'based solely on automated processing' within Art 22A (i.e. one that attracts Art 22C safeguards). Purely analytical churn scoring that feeds a human-led retention campaign will usually not be a 'significant decision', but the general transparency duties in Arts 13-14 (purposes, lawful basis, legitimate interests pursued under Art 13(1)(d)/14(2)(b), right to object under Art 13(2)(b)/14(2)(c)) still apply, and the controller must document its 'meaningful human involvement' analysis.

DUAA s.103 and Sch. 10 paras 3-4 inserted Art 13(2)(ca) ('the right to make a complaint to the controller under section 164A of the 2018 Act') and Art 14(2)(da), in force 19 June 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 3); new DPA 2018 s.164A obliges controllers to facilitate complaints (e.g. electronic form), acknowledge within 30 days and respond without undue delay - privacy notices for the churn programme must now mention this route alongside the ICO complaint route in Art 13(2)(d)/14(2)(e).

DUAA s.77 inserted new Arts 13(5)-(7) and 14(5)-(7) (in force 5 February 2026): an exemption from providing privacy information where processing is for scientific/historical research, archiving in the public interest or statistical purposes and provision is impossible or a disproportionate effort (factors: number of data subjects, age of the data, safeguards), with a duty to protect rights e.g. by publishing the information. Commercial churn prediction will not normally fall within this research exemption.

Article 21(2) UK GDPR is unamended: 'Where personal data are processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject shall have the right to object at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her for such marketing, which includes profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing.' Article 21(3) is unamended: 'Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes.' legislation.gov.uk shows no F-note against either paragraph; the only annotations on Art 21 are F1 (para 1, DUAA s.70(5), 5 February 2026), F2-F3 (S.I. 2019/419, 31 December 2020) and F4 (para 6, DUAA s.87(1)(d), 5 February 2026).

Article 21(4) (unamended) requires the right to object under paras 1 and 2 to be 'explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject' at the latest at the first communication and 'presented clearly and separately from any other information' - relevant to how retention/marketing contacts generated by the churn model are worded.

The ICO's right-to-object guidance (carrying a DUAA 'under review' banner) continues to state that the objection to direct marketing is 'an absolute right and there are no exemptions or grounds for you to refuse'; suppression (rather than erasure) is the recommended way to honour it.

DUAA s.70 (in force 5 February 2026) added Art 6(1)(ea) 'processing is necessary for the purposes of a recognised legitimate interest' (Annex 1 list) and new Art 6(11) which names 'processing that is necessary for the purposes of direct marketing' as an example of processing that may be a legitimate interest under Art 6(1)(f). Art 21(1) was amended in consequence so that the general (non-absolute) right to object now covers processing under Art 6(1)(e), (ea) or (f), 'including profiling based on those provisions'. Direct marketing is NOT a recognised legitimate interest under Annex 1, so the Art 6(1)(f) balancing test still applies to churn-driven marketing.

Commencement chronology (primary sources): Royal Assent 19 June 2025; S.I. 2025/904 commenced first provisions 20 August 2025; S.I. 2026/82 (made 29 January 2026) commenced the bulk of Part 5 including ss. 70, 71, 77, 80 and Schs 4-9 on 5 February 2026 and s.103/Sch. 10 on 19 June 2026; S.I. 2026/1015 (made 10 September 2026) commences ss. 118-119 (abolition of the Information Commissioner; functions transfer to the Information Commission) on 30 September 2026. The ICO hub page states all provisions affecting data protection law and PECR are now in force.

Pending wording change only: S.I. 2026/386 Sch. 3 Part 4 substitutes 'Commission' for 'Commissioner' in Art 13(2)(d) and Art 14(2)(e) (and inserts Art 4(A2A) 'the Commission'); it does not amend Article 21. legislation.gov.uk still lists these as 'changes yet to be applied' as at 2026-09-28; they should take effect with s.119 on 30 September 2026. Substantive obligations are unchanged by this.

ICO guidance status: the ICO's 'Rights related to automated decision making including profiling' page and the 2023 'Guidance on AI and data protection' still refer to the old Article 22 and carry 'under review' banners. The ICO consulted on updated ADM/profiling guidance (31 March - 29 May 2026); the final version 'including amendments in the Data (Use and Access) Act' is scheduled for 'Winter 2026' on the ICO guidance pipeline, and the ICO has announced work on a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. For the report, cite the legislation for the current law and flag ICO guidance as transitional.
legal.uncertainties: 1) Legislative text was extracted from legislation.gov.uk by automated fetch; the quoted wording of Arts 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 21(1)-(4) matched across two independent fetches, but the report author should eyeball the pages before final submission. 2) The 'Commissioner' to 'Commission' substitution in Arts 13(2)(d)/14(2)(e) (S.I. 2026/386) had not been applied on legislation.gov.uk as at 2026-09-28; its commencement is tied to DUAA s.119, which S.I. 2026/1015 commences on 30 September 2026, so any report finalised after that date should refer to the 'Information Commission' for post-30-September material and to the 'Information Commissioner's Office' for earlier publications. 3) The Art 21(6) amendment (F4, DUAA s.87(1)(d)) was noted from the annotation only and not independently traced; it concerns research/statistical processing and does not affect paras 2-3. 4) The GOV.UK commencement page (last updated 5 February 2026) gives stages rather than section-by-section dates; individual dates above were taken from S.I. 2026/82, S.I. 2026/1015 and the I-notes on legislation.gov.uk. 5) No regulations under Art 22D (defining 'meaningful human involvement' or 'similarly significant effect') were located as at 2026-09-28, but this was not exhaustively searched. 6) Whether a given churn-prediction workflow amounts to a 'significant decision' 'based solely on automated processing' under Art 22A is fact-specific; the DUAA did not change Arts 21(2)-(3), so the absolute right to object to profiling for direct marketing applies regardless of that classification. 7) The ICO's updated ADM/profiling guidance was still unpublished ('Winter 2026'); any reliance on ICO ADM guidance in the report should note it predates Arts 22A-22D.
legal.quotable: Art 13(2)(f) / Art 14(2)(g) UK GDPR (as amended by DUAA 2025 Sch. 6, in force 5 February 2026): 'the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, which is subject to the requirement to provide safeguards under Article 22C and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject'. Art 21(2) UK GDPR (unamended): 'Where personal data are processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject shall have the right to object at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her for such marketing, which includes profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing.' Art 21(3): 'Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes.'

legal.status_summary: VERIFIED AS AT 2026-09-28. Section 80 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18) repealed UK GDPR Article 22 and substituted a new Chapter III Section 4A comprising Articles 22A-22D. The substitution is fully in force: the regulation-making elements (Article 22D powers) commenced on Royal Assent, 19 June 2025, under s.142(2)(h), and the remainder commenced on 5 February 2026 under regulation 2(j) of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82, C. 10), with Schedule 6 consequentials commenced by reg. 2(z8) and a saving in reg. 5 for decisions taken before 5 February 2026. legislation.gov.uk shows Articles 22A-22D as the current text, 'up to date as of 27 September 2026', with the only outstanding change to the UK GDPR being unrelated (Art. 4(A2A) via SI 2026/386, which itself commences only when s.119 is in force). Under the new regime a solely automated 'significant decision' (legal or similarly significant effect, taken with no meaningful human involvement) that is NOT based on special category data is no longer prohibited by default: it may be taken on any Article 6 lawful basis except recognised legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(ea)), provided the controller has Article 22C safeguards in place (information about the decision; ability to make representations; ability to obtain human intervention; ability to contest). Where special category data is involved, Article 22B(1)-(3) restricts such decisions to explicit consent, or contract/legal authorisation combined with the substantial-public-interest condition in Art 9(2)(g). No regulations have been made under Article 22D as at today. The ICO published draft updated guidance on automated decision-making including profiling on 31 March 2026 (consultation closed 29 May 2026); final guidance is listed by the ICO as due 'Winter 2026', so it remains draft today. The ICO's legacy 'Rights related to automated decision making including profiling' page still describes the pre-DUAA Article 22 regime without a DUAA banner, while the ICO's AI-and-data-protection page on Article 22 carries an 'under review' banner. Note also that the office of Information Commissioner is abolished and replaced by the Information Commission on 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015), two days after the access date.
legal.in_force: YES - fully in force. UK GDPR Articles 22A-22D (inserted by DUAA 2025 s.80(1)) have applied since 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, reg. 2(j)); Schedule 6 consequential amendments (including omission of DPA 2018 s.14 and amendment of Art 15(1)(h) to refer to Art 22C) also in force from 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, reg. 2(z8)). The Article 22D regulation-making powers have been in force since Royal Assent on 19 June 2025 (DUAA s.142(2)(h)). Saving provision: SI 2026/82 reg. 5 - the s.80/Sch 6 amendments do not apply to any decision taken before 5 February 2026 to which old Art 22(3) or DPA 2018 s.14/s.50(2) applied. No regulations under Article 22D have been made as at 2026-09-28. Pending but unrelated to substance: the Information Commission replaces the Information Commissioner on 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015, reg. 2), and SI 2026/386 will then substitute 'Commission' for 'Commissioner' throughout the UK GDPR.

key_points: Structure of the reform: DUAA 2025 s.80(1) repeals UK GDPR Article 22 and substitutes a new Chapter III 'Section 4A - Automated individual decision-making' made up of Articles 22A (definitions), 22B (restrictions), 22C (safeguards) and 22D (regulation-making powers). legislation.gov.uk annotates Article 22 as 'Ch. 3 Section 4A substituted for Art. 22' (Explanatory Notes para 634).

Commencement - precise: s.142(1) makes commencement by regulations the default; s.142(2)(h) brought into force on Royal Assent (19 June 2025) 'any other provision of this Act ... so far as it confers power to make regulations', i.e. the Article 22D powers. SI 2026/82 reg. 2 then provided that s.80 ('(j) section 80 (automated decision-making)') and Sch 6 ('(z8) Schedule 6 (automated decision-making: minor and consequential amendments)') come into force on 5 February 2026 'so far as not already in force'. The regulations were made on 29 January 2026 by Ian Murray MP, Minister of State, DSIT.

Transitional/saving: SI 2026/82 reg. 5 - 'The amendments made by section 80 of, and Schedule 6 to, the 2025 Act do not apply in relation to any decision taken before 5th February 2026 to which Article 22(3) of the UK GDPR ... or section 14 or 50(2) of the 2018 Act ... applied.' Decisions taken on or after 5 February 2026 are governed by Articles 22A-22D.

Article 22A(1)(a): a decision is 'based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision'. Article 22A(1)(b): a decision is a 'significant decision' if '(i) it produces a legal effect for the data subject, or (ii) it has a similarly significant effect for the data subject'. Article 22A(2): when assessing meaningful human involvement 'a person must consider, among other things, the extent to which the decision is reached by means of profiling'. Note: the enacted text contains no 'adverse' qualifier; an earlier Bill draft used 'adverse legal effect', so secondary sources quoting 'adverse' are citing superseded Bill wording.

Solely automated significant decisions NOT based on special category data (the churn-prediction scenario): there is no longer a general prohibition. Article 22B only restricts (a) decisions 'based entirely or partly on processing described in Article 9(1)' (special category data) and (b) decisions where the processing 'is carried out entirely or partly in reliance on Article 6(1)(ea)' (recognised legitimate interests, Annex 1). Otherwise the decision may proceed on any Article 6(1) lawful basis - the ICO draft guidance lists consent, contract, public task and ordinary legitimate interests (three-part test) - subject to the Article 22C safeguards. The ICO summarises this as opening up 'the full range of reasons, or lawful bases' for significant automated decisions, 'so long as you continue to apply appropriate safeguards', while it 'keeps the restriction on the use of special category personal information'.

Special category data (Article 22B(1)-(3)): a significant decision based entirely or partly on Art 9(1) data 'may not be taken based solely on automated processing' unless (first condition, 22B(2)) 'the decision is based entirely on processing of personal data to which the data subject has given explicit consent', or (second condition, 22B(3)) the decision is '(i) necessary for entering into, or performing, a contract between the data subject and a controller, or (ii) required or authorised by law, and (b) point (g) of Article 9(2) applies' (substantial public interest). The ICO draft guidance adds that inferred information counts as special category data where the controller intends to infer, or treats someone differently on the basis of, a special-category characteristic - relevant to churn features that could proxy for health, ethnicity, etc.

Safeguards (Article 22C): where a significant decision is 'based entirely or partly on personal data' and 'based solely on automated processing', the controller 'must ensure that safeguards for the data subject's rights, freedoms and legitimate interests are in place' which 'must consist of or include measures which - (a) provide the data subject with information about decisions ... taken in relation to the data subject; (b) enable the data subject to make representations about such decisions; (c) enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions; (d) enable the data subject to contest such decisions.' The ICO draft guidance expects information to be given at the point the decision is delivered, responses to requests 'without undue delay and at the latest within one month' (extendable by two months for complex requests), and human reviewers who can actually alter the outcome, are suitably trained, and consider any additional evidence; periodic spot-checks do not satisfy the individual's right to intervention.

Article 22D: the Secretary of State may by regulations (affirmative procedure) provide that there is or is not 'meaningful human involvement' in described cases (22D(1)), that a description of decision is or is not to be taken to have a 'similarly significant effect' (22D(2)), and may add to or supplement the Article 22C safeguards (22D(3)), but 'may not amend Article 22C' (22D(4)). As at 2026-09-28 the Article 22D page on legislation.gov.uk lists no regulations made under it, so 'meaningful human involvement' and 'similarly significant effect' currently rest on the statutory words and ICO (draft) guidance.

Consequential amendments (Sch 6, in force 5 February 2026): DPA 2018 s.14 (safeguards for ADM authorised by law) is omitted (Sch 6 para 11); UK GDPR Art 15(1)(h) now refers to 'automated decision-making, including profiling, which is subject to the requirement to provide safeguards under Article 22C and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved' (Sch 6 para 5). Transparency duties under Arts 13-15 therefore continue to attach to solely automated significant decisions.

ICO guidance position as at 2026-09-28: the ICO published DRAFT updated guidance 'Automated decision-making, including profiling' on 31 March 2026, restructured around Articles 22A-22D (sections: What is ADM?; What does the UK GDPR say about ADM?; How do we carry out ADM lawfully?; When can we use special category data in our ADM?; What are the ADM safeguards?; What rights do people have?; What else do we need to consider?). The consultation ran 31 March - 29 May 2026 and is closed. The ICO's guidance-plans page lists the final version as 'Drafting' with publication due 'Winter 2026'. Until then the draft is the ICO's most current statement but has no final status.

ICO draft guidance on 'similarly significant effect': defined as an effect with 'an equivalent impact on someone's circumstances, behaviour, opportunities, or choices'; assessed by reference to financial circumstances, employment opportunities, health, access to education, access to housing, 'access to essential public and private services', reputation, behaviour and choices. Examples given include automatic refusal of an online credit application, an automated bank-account freeze, algorithmic pay-setting and e-recruiting; a video-on-demand recommendation engine is given as typically NOT significant. Profiling-driven engagement/incentive strategies (the online-game example) are treated as potentially significant because of their effect on behaviour and choices. For a telecoms churn model, whether outputs are 'significant' therefore turns on what the decision does: pure propensity scoring feeding human-led retention calls or marketing prioritisation is unlikely to be a solely automated significant decision, whereas automated denial or withdrawal of service, automated price or credit-term changes, or automated contract-termination decisions with no meaningful human involvement would engage Articles 22B-22C.

ICO draft guidance on meaningful human involvement: human involvement must be 'active and not just a token gesture'; the reviewer must engage before the decision is applied to the person, while they can still change the recommendation, and must have the authority and competence to alter the outcome; where profiling is complex the ICO warns it can be difficult for reviewers to explain or challenge the output, which cuts against treating rubber-stamp review as meaningful.

ICO draft guidance on accountability for ADM: a DPIA is mandatory 'if you carry out systematic and extensive ADM or other significant decisions based on profiling'; the controller cannot base such decisions 'entirely or partly on the recognised legitimate interest lawful basis'; the ICO expects sample-based manual review of automated decisions 'to identify any bias or discriminatory effects', 'appropriate mathematical or statistical procedures for profiling', correction of inaccuracies, and clear information to individuals about the processing and their rights.

Inconsistency in ICO web estate to flag in the report: the legacy page 'Rights related to automated decision making including profiling' still describes the old Article 22 prohibition with three exceptions and carries no DUAA banner, whereas the AI-and-data-protection page on Article 22 states 'Due to changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act, this guidance is under review and may be subject to change'. Cite the statute (Articles 22A-22D) and the 2026 draft guidance rather than the legacy page for the current rules.

Regulator identity: SI 2026/1015 (made 10 September 2026) brings DUAA ss.117(4)(a), 118 and 119 into force on 30 September 2026, abolishing the office of Information Commissioner and transferring functions to the Information Commission; SI 2026/386 then substitutes 'Commission' for 'Commissioner' throughout the UK GDPR/DPA 2018. Material accessed on 2026-09-28 is correctly attributed to the Information Commissioner's Office; anything published from 30 September 2026 should be attributed to the Information Commission, and the legislation.gov.uk 'outstanding changes' banner on Article 22 (Art 4(A2A) via SI 2026/386) relates to this and not to the substance of Articles 22A-22D.
legal.uncertainties: 1) The ICO's updated ADM guidance is still a DRAFT (consultation closed 29 May 2026; final due 'Winter 2026' per the ICO plans page) - wording on 'meaningful human involvement', response timings and examples may change in the final version, and the report should describe it as draft. 2) No regulations have been made under Article 22D as at 2026-09-28 based on the legislation.gov.uk Article 22D page and searches; absence of a listing is strong but not absolute proof, so re-check before submission. 3) The Information Commissioner is replaced by the Information Commission on 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015), two days after the access date; reference author names are correct for 2026-09-28 but URLs/branding may change afterwards. 4) The ICO's overview DUAA pages (summary of changes last updated 20 August 2025; 'what does it mean for organisations' updated 19 June 2026; GOV.UK guidance dated 27 June 2025) do not state the 5 February 2026 commencement date themselves - that date is taken from SI 2026/82 and the legislation.gov.uk annotations, which are the authoritative sources. 5) Article 22A does not define 'similarly significant effect'; whether a given churn-driven action (e.g. automated retention pricing or service restriction) is a 'significant decision' is a fact-specific judgement guided only by the ICO draft's factor list. 6) Page contents were read through an automated fetch-and-summarise step; verbatim statutory quotations were cross-checked across the DUAA s.80 page and the consolidated UK GDPR article pages, but any quotation used in the report should be re-read against the live legislation.gov.uk text. 7) The ICO consultation page and Citizen Space page differ on status wording ('closed' vs 'open' cached text); the ICO plans page and the closing date of 29 May 2026 confirm it is closed.
legal.quotable: UK GDPR Article 22C(2), as inserted by DUAA 2025 s.80 and in force from 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82 reg. 2(j)): 'The safeguards must consist of or include measures which - (a) provide the data subject with information about decisions described in paragraph 1 taken in relation to the data subject; (b) enable the data subject to make representations about such decisions; (c) enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions; (d) enable the data subject to contest such decisions.' Article 22A(1)(a): 'a decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision'.

legal.status_summary: UK GDPR Article 35 (data protection impact assessment) is in force and has NOT been substantively amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA). legislation.gov.uk (accessed 28 September 2026) shows Article 35 'up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 28 September 2026', with one outstanding change: S.I. 2026/386 Sch. 3 para. 41 substitutes 'Commission' for 'Commissioner' in Art 35(4)-(5). That change takes effect when DUAA s.119 (transfer of functions to the Information Commission) is fully in force, which S.I. 2026/1015 (Commencement No. 9, made 10 September 2026) sets for 30 September 2026 - two days after the access date. Does AI-driven churn profiling/targeting need a DPIA? Yes, in practice. Art 35(3)(a) makes a DPIA mandatory for systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions with legal or similarly significant effects are based. Independently, the ICO's Article 35(4) list (10 operations) captures churn modelling on several grounds: 'innovative technology' (including AI) combined with any WP248 criterion, 'large-scale profiling', 'data matching', behavioural 'tracking', and 'denial of service' (decisions about access to a product, service, opportunity or benefit based 'to any extent' on automated decision-making including profiling). The ICO's Guidance on AI and data protection states that in 'the vast majority of cases' AI use will trigger the legal requirement to do a DPIA, and that a decision not to do one must be documented. ICO Guidance on AI and data protection: current version is the update of 15 March 2023 (cite as ICO, 2023). It has not been re-issued since; every page carries the banner 'Due to changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act, this guidance is under review and may be subject to change', and it has no entry on the ICO 'Our plans for new and updated guidance - Technology' page. The ICO DPIA pages carry the same 'under review' banner, but their content is unchanged and no DPIA update is scheduled. 2025-2026 developments: ICO 'Preventing harm, promoting trust: our AI and biometrics strategy' (launched 5 June 2025) plus 'AI and biometrics strategy update - March 2026'; DUAA Part 5 changes (ss.70, 71, 80, including new Arts 22A-22D on automated decision-making) in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82); ICO draft 'Automated decision-making, including profiling' guidance (31 March 2026; consultation closed 29 May 2026; final due Winter 2026); S.I. 2026/425 (in force 12 May 2026) requires a statutory ICO code of practice on AI and ADM, not yet published; ICO agentic AI guidance consultation due September 2026 (final Spring 2027); ICO said on 29 May 2026 that a new AI strategy with its 2026/27 workplan will be published 'in the coming months'.
legal.in_force: YES - UK GDPR Article 35 is in force. Its text is unchanged in substance since the post-Brexit amendments that took effect on 31 December 2020 (EU supervisory-authority references replaced with 'the Commissioner'). DUAA 2025 makes no substantive amendment to Art 35. Pending: S.I. 2026/386 (made 26 March 2026) substitutes 'Commission' for 'Commissioner' in Art 35(4)-(5) with effect from 30 September 2026, when DUAA ss.117(4)(a), 118 and 119 come into force under S.I. 2026/1015 (made 10 September 2026) and the Information Commission replaces the Information Commissioner. Related DUAA provisions: ss.70 (recognised legitimate interests), 71 (purpose limitation) and 80 (Arts 22A-22D automated decision-making) in force 5 February 2026 under S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2, and the s.80 amendments do not apply to decisions taken before 5 February 2026; s.103 (complaints) in force 19 June 2026; s.92 (new DPA 2018 s.124A codes of practice power) in force 20 August 2025 under S.I. 2025/904. S.I. 2026/425 (statutory AI/ADM code requirement) in force 12 May 2026, but the code itself has not been published.

key_points: Article 35 status (legislation.gov.uk, accessed 2026-09-28): 'up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 28 September 2026'. The only outstanding effect is S.I. 2026/386 Sch. 3 para. 41 ('Commissioner' becomes 'Commission' in Art 35(4)-(5); new Art 4 definition of 'the Commission' as the Information Commission). It commences with DUAA s.119, which S.I. 2026/1015 brings into force on 30 September 2026. On the access date the text still refers to 'the Commissioner'.

Art 35(1): where processing, 'in particular using new technologies', is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must carry out a DPIA before the processing. Art 35(3)(a): a DPIA is required in particular for 'a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect the natural person'. Art 35(4): the Commissioner must publish a list of processing operations that require a DPIA. Art 35(7): minimum content of a DPIA (description, necessity and proportionality, risk assessment, mitigating measures).

ICO Article 35(4) list (source: 'When do we need to do a DPIA?', verbatim): (1) Innovative technology - 'processing involving the use of innovative technologies, or the novel application of existing technologies (including AI)', where combined with any WP248 criterion; (2) Denial of service - 'Decisions about an individual's access to a product, service, opportunity or benefit that is based to any extent on automated decision-making (including profiling) or involves the processing of special category data'; (3) Large-scale profiling - 'any profiling of individuals on a large scale'; (4) Biometrics (+criterion); (5) Genetic data (+criterion); (6) Data matching - 'combining, comparing or matching personal data obtained from multiple sources'; (7) Invisible processing (+criterion); (8) Tracking - 'tracking an individual's geolocation or behaviour, including but not limited to the online environment' (+criterion); (9) Targeting of children or other vulnerable individuals for marketing, profiling or other automated decision-making; (10) Risk of physical harm. The ICO also lists the nine WP29/WP248 criteria (including 'Evaluation or scoring' and 'Matching or combining datasets'), notes that two criteria usually indicate a DPIA is needed, and says 'If in any doubt, we would always recommend that you do a DPIA'.

Application to AI churn prediction at a UK telecoms operator: a DPIA is required. At least these ICO list items apply: innovative technology (ML/AI) combined with WP248 'evaluation or scoring', large scale and dataset matching; large-scale profiling of the customer base; data matching across billing, usage, network and CRM data; and behavioural tracking. Where scores drive retention offers, pricing or eligibility, 'denial of service' also applies, because it covers decisions 'based to any extent' on automated decision-making or profiling. If the profiling feeds decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, Art 35(3)(a) makes a DPIA mandatory on its own. The ICO's indicative examples list 'AI applications' under large-scale profiling and 'direct marketing' under data matching.

ICO Guidance on AI and data protection, accountability chapter (verbatim): 'In the vast majority of cases, the use of AI will involve a type of processing likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, and will therefore trigger the legal requirement for you to undertake a DPIA.' Where an organisation concludes that its AI processing is not high risk, it must document how it reached that assessment.

Current version of the ICO Guidance on AI and data protection: the 'What's new?' page says 'This guidance was updated on 15 March 2023' and records no later update. Chapters: What's new?; About this guidance; accountability and governance implications of AI; transparency; lawfulness; accuracy and statistical accuracy; fairness; security and data minimisation; individual rights; Annex A: Fairness in the AI lifecycle; AI and data protection risk toolkit; Glossary. First published in July 2020. As of 28 September 2026 it carries the DUAA 'under review and may be subject to change' banner and is NOT listed on the ICO Technology guidance-plans page, so no revision is scheduled. Harvard citation year: 2023.

ICO guidance plans, Technology page (verbatim status on 2026-09-28): 'Automated Decision Making (ADM) and Profiling Guidance update' - Stage: Drafting; consultation closed; final due 'Winter 2026'. 'Agentic AI guidance' - Drafting; public consultation 'due to launch September 2026'; final 'Spring 2027'. 'Foundation Models' - Drafting; final 'Summer 2026', not yet published. Also listed: neurotechnology (consultation due October 2026), DLT, smart data, and anonymisation/pseudonymisation for research. The General data protection plans page lists many DUAA-driven updates but no DPIA or accountability guidance project.

ICO AI and biometrics strategy: 'Preventing harm, promoting trust: our AI and biometrics strategy', launched 5 June 2025 (ICO news release of 5 June 2025). Its focus areas are generative AI foundation models, ADM (recruitment and public services), police facial recognition, and a statutory code of practice, with agentic AI as an emerging risk. 'Our plan of action' commits to 'consult on an update to our ADM and profiling guidance by autumn 2025' (delivered late, on 31 March 2026) and to 'develop a statutory code of practice on AI and ADM' covering transparency and explainability, bias and discrimination, and rights and redress. 'AI and biometrics strategy update - March 2026' reports delivery so far, including the 'ICO tech futures: Agentic AI' report (January 2026), and says the government was developing the secondary legislation for the code. In its response to government of 29 May 2026, the ICO said that for 2026/27 it will develop the AI code of practice and dedicated agentic AI guidance, and publish more details 'in our new AI strategy in the coming months'.

Statutory AI/ADM code of practice: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/425) were made 16 April 2026, laid 21 April 2026 and came into force 12 May 2026, under DPA 2018 s.124A(1)-(2) and s.124B(11). Reg. 2 requires the Commissioner to prepare a code giving guidance on good practice in processing personal data in relation to (a) developing and using AI and (b) automated decision-making, including provision on children's data. No draft or final code had been published by 28 September 2026. After 30 September 2026 the Information Commission will prepare it.

ICO draft ADM guidance, 'Automated decision-making, including profiling': 'Latest updates - 31 March 2026 ... We have updated this draft guidance to reflect changes to the UK GDPR following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA)', including the scope of Art 22A. The consultation ran from 31 March to 29 May 2026 and is closed; the final version is due Winter 2026. The previous version remains available as a PDF until the new guidance is finalised. The draft chapter 'What else do we need to consider?' repeats that a DPIA is mandatory under Art 35(3)(a) and recommends a DPIA for ADM because it is likely to be high risk.

DUAA commencement relevant to profiling and churn models: Royal Assent 19 June 2025. On 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82) the following came into force: s.70 (Art 6(1)(ea) recognised legitimate interests), s.71 (purpose limitation, new Art 8A) and s.80 (Art 22 replaced by Arts 22A-22D). Under Art 22A, a decision is solely automated if there is 'no meaningful human involvement', and profiling is relevant to that test. Significant solely automated decisions are now allowed on any lawful basis except recognised legitimate interests (special category data remains restricted), subject to the Art 22C safeguards. DSIT's 'plans for commencement' page (last updated 5 February 2026) confirms that most of Part 5 commenced on 5 February 2026. The DPIA duty under Art 35 applies whether or not Arts 22A-22D are engaged.

legal.status_summary: UK GDPR Article 5 (principles) and Article 6(1)(f) (legitimate interests) remain the governing provisions for churn-prediction profiling of existing customers, and both are in force as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA, c. 18, Royal Assent 19 June 2025). legislation.gov.uk shows Articles 5 and 6 as up to date with all changes in force on or before 27 September 2026. DUAA s.70 inserted a new lawful basis, Article 6(1)(ea) 'recognised legitimate interests', together with Article 6(5) (the condition must be one listed in new Annex 1, inserted by DUAA Schedule 4) and Article 6(6)-(12); Article 6(11) now lists direct marketing, intra-group administrative transfers and network/information security as examples of processing that 'may be' necessary for a legitimate interest under 6(1)(f). Article 6(1)(f) itself is textually unchanged; only the closing sub-paragraph of 6(1) was amended so that neither (ea) nor (f) is available to public authorities performing their tasks. DUAA s.71 amended Article 5(1)(b) (purpose limitation now framed by reference to the purposes for which the controller collected the data), inserted Article 5(3) (compatibility with the original purpose does not by itself make processing lawful) and omitted Article 6(4). These amendments commenced on 19 June 2025 for specified purposes (regulation-making powers, s.142(2)(h)) and in full on 5 February 2026 under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82, reg. 2(c), 2(d) and 2(z6)). Annex 1 contains only five public-interest purposes (disclosures for public tasks, national security/public security/defence, emergencies, crime, safeguarding vulnerable individuals), so commercial churn profiling cannot use Article 6(1)(ea); a telecoms operator must rely on ordinary Article 6(1)(f) with a documented three-part legitimate interests assessment (LIA). The ICO's detailed legitimate-interests guidance and its new 'Recognised legitimate interest' guidance were both updated/published on 23 March 2026 to reflect DUAA, and the ICO direct marketing guidance was updated on 28 April 2026; the ICO confirms the balancing test is dispensed with only for Annex 1 purposes, that direct marketing (including profiling for it) is subject to an absolute right to object under Article 21(2)-(3), and that legitimate interests cannot be used where PECR requires consent for the marketing channel.
legal.in_force: Yes. As at 2026-09-28: (1) UK GDPR Article 5 and Article 6 (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as retained) are in force in their DUAA-amended form; legislation.gov.uk states both articles are up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 27 September 2026. (2) DUAA 2025 s.70 (lawfulness of processing: Art 6(1)(ea), Art 6(5)-(12)), s.71 (purpose limitation: Art 5(1)(b), new Art 5(3), omission of Art 6(4)) and Schedule 4 (new Annex 1) came into force on 19 June 2025 for specified purposes (regulation-making powers, s.142(1),(2)(h)) and otherwise on 5 February 2026 by SI 2026/82 reg. 2(c) (s.70), reg. 2(d) (s.71) and reg. 2(z6) (Sch. 4); SI 2026/82 was made on 29 January 2026 under ss.142(1) and 143(1). (3) The wording of Article 6(1)(f) has not been amended since IP completion day (31 December 2020). (4) No pending or prospective amendment to Article 5 or Article 6 is recorded in the legislation.gov.uk changes table; the only outstanding prospective change flagged on the UK GDPR relates to Article 4 (see uncertainties). (5) gov.uk (DSIT, updated 5 February 2026) confirms SI 2026/82 brought the majority of Part 5 data-protection provisions into force on 5 February 2026, and the ICO states (page updated 19 June 2026) that all DUAA provisions affecting data protection law and PECR are now in force.

key_points: Article 5 UK GDPR still sets the seven principles (lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, accountability). DUAA s.71(2) amended Art 5(1)(b) so that purpose limitation is assessed against the purposes for which the controller collected the data (whether from the data subject or otherwise), and DUAA s.71(3) inserted Art 5(3): further processing that is compatible with the original purpose is not, for that reason alone, lawful - a lawful basis under Art 6 is still needed. Art 5(1)(e) was also amended by s.87(1)(a) to cross-refer to new Article 84B. All in force since 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82 reg. 2(d)); 19 June 2025 for regulation-making purposes only.

Article 6(1)(f) (legitimate interests) is textually unchanged: processing must be necessary for the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, except where overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject, with particular weight where the data subject is a child. The closing sub-paragraph of Art 6(1) was amended (DUAA s.70(2)(c)) so that points (ea) and (f) are both unavailable to public authorities performing their tasks - irrelevant to a private telecoms operator.

DUAA s.70(2)(b) inserted Article 6(1)(ea), a new lawful basis for processing necessary for the purposes of a 'recognised legitimate interest'. Under new Art 6(5) this applies only where a condition in new Annex 1 (inserted by DUAA Sch. 4) is met. Annex 1 contains five public-interest conditions: disclosures to public bodies for their public tasks, national security/public security/defence, emergencies (Civil Contingencies Act 2004 sense), crime, and safeguarding vulnerable individuals. None covers commercial marketing, customer retention or profiling, so a telecoms churn-prediction system cannot rely on Art 6(1)(ea). In force 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82 reg. 2(c) for s.70; reg. 2(z6) for Sch. 4).

New Article 6(6)-(10) give the Secretary of State an affirmative-procedure power to amend Annex 1, so the recognised-interest list may change in future; as at 2026-09-28 no such regulations affecting Annex 1 are recorded on legislation.gov.uk.

New Article 6(11) (DUAA s.70(4)) writes recital 47-49 examples into the operative text: direct marketing, intra-group transmission for internal administrative purposes, and network and information security are named as examples of processing that 'may be' necessary for a legitimate interest under 6(1)(f). Article 6(12) defines the latter two terms. This strengthens the purpose limb of an LIA for retention marketing driven by churn scores, but it does not remove the necessity and balancing tests - the ICO's guidance treats it as an example only.

Article 6(4) (the compatibility test for further processing) was omitted by DUAA s.71(4); the compatibility assessment now lives in new Article 8A (with Annex 2, DUAA Sch. 5, listing processing deemed compatible). Re-using billing, usage and service data collected for contract performance to build churn models is 'further processing' that must satisfy both the Art 8A compatibility rules and a lawful basis (Art 5(3)).

ICO detailed guidance on legitimate interests (updated 23 March 2026 to reflect DUAA) retains the three-part test: purpose test (is the interest legitimate), necessity test (is the processing necessary and proportionate for it), and balancing test (do the individual's interests, rights and freedoms override it). The ICO says organisations must carry out the three-part test, should document the outcome and keep an audit trail (accountability, Art 5(2)), and provides a sample LIA template (.docx, live as at 2026-09-28).

The ICO describes an LIA as a lighter-touch risk assessment than a DPIA; where the LIA identifies potential high risk to individuals, a DPIA is likely to be required (Art 35). Large-scale profiling of customers to predict behaviour is the kind of processing the ICO flags for DPIA consideration, so the report should present the LIA and DPIA as complementary, not alternatives.

On reasonable expectations, the ICO applies an objective test (what a reasonable person would expect), taking account of the privacy notice, the nature of the relationship and whether the person is an existing customer; it cites recital 47 (legitimate interests more likely where there is a relevant and appropriate relationship, e.g. controller and client). An existing telecoms customer relationship supports, but does not settle, the balancing test for churn profiling.

ICO 'When can we rely on legitimate interests?' states that where PECR requires consent for a marketing channel (e.g. unsolicited electronic mail without the reg. 22 soft opt-in, calls to TPS-registered numbers), legitimate interests must not be used as the lawful basis for that marketing; legitimate interests is generally appropriate for postal marketing and, subject to PECR, for calls and electronic mail within the soft opt-in. The ICO also says legitimate interests should be avoided where people would not understand or reasonably expect the use, where there is a risk of significant harm, or where another basis more obviously applies.

ICO 'Recognised legitimate interest' guidance (published 23 March 2026) confirms that, for Annex 1 purposes only, the controller need not carry out the balancing test because the law has already done so, but must still satisfy itself that the processing is necessary for the specific condition; the guidance describes the basis as limited to the listed public-interest purposes and does not extend it to commercial marketing or profiling.

ICO Direct marketing guidance (updated 28 April 2026): profiling to target direct marketing must be fair and transparent (people must be told and the profiling explained), must have its own lawful basis, and organisations should address risks such as discrimination or stereotyping; profiling may engage special category data where inferences about health, race, etc. are drawn. Under 'Respect people's preferences', the Art 21(2)-(3) right to object to direct marketing expressly covers profiling for direct marketing and there are no grounds on which the objection can be refused - so churn-driven retention campaigns must honour objections and stop profiling the objector for that purpose.

Timeline for the report: DUAA Royal Assent 19 June 2025; regulation-making powers commenced that day (s.142(2)(h)); the substantive Art 5/6 amendments, Annex 1, purpose-limitation and automated-decision-making reforms commenced 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, made 29 January 2026); DSIT (updated 5 February 2026) confirms this brought the majority of Part 5 into force, with s.103 (complaints) scheduled for a later stage; the ICO (updated 19 June 2026) states that all DUAA provisions affecting data protection law and PECR are now in force.

Recommended framing for the report: churn-prediction profiling of existing customers by a UK telecoms operator should be grounded in Article 6(1)(f) supported by a documented LIA (purpose, necessity, balancing), with Article 6(11)(a) cited as statutory recognition that direct marketing may be a legitimate interest; Article 6(1)(ea)/Annex 1 should be cited only to explain why it does NOT apply; PECR and the absolute right to object under Article 21(2)-(3) constrain how churn scores may be acted upon; and Articles 5(1)(a)-(b), 5(2), 5(3) and new Article 8A govern fairness, transparency, purpose compatibility and accountability.
